en: The Stage of the Hearers (Śrāvakabhūmi).
I. The Stage of the Spiritual Lineage (Gotrabhūmi).
The non-deficiency of the sense faculties, clarity regarding the sense bases, and the state of having unerring conduct.
In that context, what is human status?
It is when a certain individual here is reborn into the commonality of human beings and is endowed with the male faculty as a man.

This is called "human status. What is birth in a noble land (*āryāyatana*)? It is when someone is born in the central regions (*madhyama janapada*), as previously described, up to where there is access for virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*); this is called birth in a noble land.
What is the non-deficiency of the sense faculties?
It is, for example, as when someone here is not born without [physical] defects, and so forth.

Being complete in major and minor limbs— that is, being endowed with the integrity of major and minor limbs such as the absence of deafness and so forth, which makes one capable of accomplishing the side of wholesome qualities— this is called the non-deficiency of the faculties (*indriyāvaikalya*). What is the clarity regarding the sense bases (*āyatanagata-prasāda*)?

For example, suppose someone here has acquired faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, and there is clarity of mind. This is called "clarity directed toward the sphere," for that sphere— the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata— is the basis for the arising of all mundane and supramundane wholesome qualities (*śukladharma*).
Furthermore, the faith that exists therein,
through its sovereignty as preceded by that [faith], is the clarity directed toward the sense bases (*āyatana*).

It is the removal of the turbidity of the stains of all afflictions and the state of having one's karmic activities not reversed, by which [one abandons] the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).

For example, when one has not committed or performed in this very life any of the immediate (*ānantarya*) karmas— such as matricide, patricide, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or giving rise to a malicious thought of malice toward a Tathāgata—
this is called "the state of having an unturned course of action" (*aparivṛttakarmāntatā*).

Thus, these five actions of immediate retribution, when committed and accumulated, are transformed in this very life; one becomes incapable of attaining parinirvāṇa and the arising of the noble path. Therefore, these are called "the transformation of karmic ends. By means of these five factors, he himself brings about that very personal existence.
Therefore, it is called "perfection of oneself. What is the perfection of others?
Namely: the arising of the Buddhas;
the persistence of the teachings once they have been taught; the continued practice of those teachings while they persist;
and the compassionate concern shown by others.
In that regard, what is the arising of the Buddhas?

It is as follows: here, a certain person, having generated a resolute intention for the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings whatsoever, and through many thousands of difficult feats and a great accumulation of merit and knowledge, upon obtaining a physical body, sits at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Having abandoned the five hindrances,
with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
and having cultivated the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, one fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is called the arising of the Buddhas.

In the past, future, and present time periods, it is exactly thus that the afflictions have come forth; and in this very way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having arisen in the world and out of compassion for the world of their disciples, have set forth this Dharma by taking up the Four Noble Truths, beginning with suffering.
This arising of the Buddhas is taught, praised, and proclaimed by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
What is the persistence of the teachings that have been taught?
When the true Dharma has been taught,
when the Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion, and as long as the Buddha, the Blessed One [remains].
Whether the Buddha, the Blessed One, is living and remaining present, or has entered final nirvana;
For as long as practice does not decline and the true Dharma does not disappear, this is called the duration of the true Dharma; such is to be understood as its [the Dharma's] endurance.
What is the continuous application of the established teachings?

It is when those who have realized the true Dharma, knowing and perceiving that [others] possess the capacity and ability to realize the true Dharma, continue to provide conformable instruction and admonition exactly as they themselves have realized it; this is called the continuous application of the established [teachings].
The continuous turning of the wheel of phenomena.
What is compassion from others?

Those spoken of as "others" are donors and masters of giving; they show compassion toward one through those means of sustaining life that are conducive [to one's practice], namely, by means of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This is called compassion from others.
What is wholesome desire for the Dharma? It is when someone here, having heard the Dharma from a Tathāgata or from a disciple of a Tathāgata, attains faith.
Having attained that, he trains himself thus:
"Dwelling at home is a confinement, an abode of dust;
having gone forth into the open air, I shall indeed [strive]."
I shall renounce my entire circle of kinsmen, as well as wealth, grain, and gold, and go forth from the home into the homeless state in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
having gone forth, (Śbh_Sh: 9)
And [thinking], "May I accomplish [the goal] through the practice of going forth"—
this desire that has thus arisen toward wholesome qualities is called wholesome desire for the dharma (*kuśala-dharmacchanda*).

What is going forth (*pravrajyā*)? It is the undertaking of the training in the eighty virtuous precepts through the formal act of speech consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-vākkarman*), having made that very desire for the wholesome Dharma the predominant influence.
This is called going forth.
What is the restraint of ethical discipline?
Having thus gone forth, he dwells possessed of ethical discipline, restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa.
He is perfect in conduct and resort;
seeing danger even in the slightest faults,
he trains himself by undertaking the precepts of training.
This is called the restraint of ethical discipline.
What is restraint of the sense faculties?
Relying on that very restraint of ethical discipline, he becomes one whose mindfulness is guarded,
one of constant mindfulness,
whose mind is protected by mindfulness, and who dwells in a state of equanimity.
Having seen forms with the eye,
he does not seize upon their general signs (*nimitta*) nor seize upon their secondary details (*anuvyañjana*), from which basis evil states might arise in him.
He practices for the restraint of those unwholesome states that might flow into the mind;
with the ear he [guards against] sounds,
and with the nose he [guards against] odors.
Having cognized tastes with the tongue,
tangible objects with the body,
and mental phenomena with the mind, one does not grasp at their signs (*nimitta*) nor grasp at their secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), from which basis evil states might arise for him.
When unwholesome states might flow into the mind, one practices for their restraint; one guards the faculty of the mind and attains restraint through the faculty of the mind.
This is called restraint of the faculties (*indriyasamvara*).
What is moderation in eating? It is that,
having thus restrained the sense faculties, he takes food with wise reflection, not for the sake of intoxication, nor for sport, nor for adornment, nor for beautification.
Not for the sake of intoxication,
not for the sake of beautification,
and not for the sake of adornment.
"Only for the maintenance of this body, for its sustenance, and for the support of the holy life."
"I shall abandon old feelings and shall not give rise to new ones;
thus there will be for me sustenance."
Strength, happiness, blamelessness,
and a state of dwelling in comfort— this is called moderation in eating.
What is the application to wakefulness? By means of walking and sitting during the day, one thoroughly purifies the mind of obstructive states.
Having purified his mind during the day from obstructive states through walking and sitting,
he then departed from the monastery, washed his feet outside the monastery, and...
He lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, perceiving light,
mindful, and clearly comprehending.

Keeping the perception of rising in mind, he wakes up very quickly during the last watch of the night and, through walking and sitting, purifies his mind from obstructive states; this is called being devoted to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
What is dwelling with clear comprehension?
Thus devoted to wakefulness,
he dwells with clear comprehension in going forth and returning, in looking ahead and looking aside, and in bending and stretching his limbs.
In the wearing of the saṃghāṭī robe, the outer robe, and the bowl; in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; and in the dispelling of drowsiness and fatigue.
When walking, standing, or sitting,
Whether lying down, waking, or speaking,
He dwells with clear comprehension in silence;
this is called dwelling with clear comprehension.
What is seclusion (*prāvivekya*)? Having purified the ground for practice through these factors, he dwells in secluded lodgings, such as forest retreats or at the roots of trees.
Empty dwellings, mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces, cemeteries, forest retreats, and remote lodgings— this is called seclusion (*prāvivekya*).
What is the purification of the hindrances?
It is when he has gone to the forest, or...
Whether gone to the foot of a tree or gone to an empty dwelling, he purifies his mind of the five hindrances.
From sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt;

having purified the mind of these hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), he establishes it in the state of being free from hindrances and fit for concentration (*samādhi*). This is called the purification of the hindrances.
What is the basis of meditative concentration? It is when one,
having abandoned the five hindrances— which are mental defilements that cause affliction— [attains it].

Secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.

Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He who dwells in happiness, being equanimous and mindful. Having attained and dwelled in the third dhyāna, through the abandoning of pleasure and the previous disappearance of both mental gladness and dejection, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
This is called the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhisanniśraya*).

By means of this sequence, he brings about a series of ever-increasing, more distinguished, and most distinguished, fresh attainments—beginning with the excellence of self and culminating in the basis for meditative concentration.
Thus, when the mind is completely pure, cleansed, free from blemish, devoid of secondary afflictions, upright, pliable, and stable...

If, having attained imperturbability, he receives from another the voice of instruction and the teaching of exhortation concerning the four noble truths— beginning with them for the sake of their full comprehension, abandonment, realization, and cultivation—
then he becomes capable and competent to generate the mental attention that has yoga as its object.
And by means of that right view preceded by it, one realizes the four noble truths, fulfills liberation,
and attains final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
In this regard, that which is the fulfillment of liberation based upon right view,
as well as parinirvāṇa without remainder, should be understood as the realization of the lineage (*gotra*). Therein,
from the attainment of self-perfection up to the reliance upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this is [the process].
The inferior condition for realization should be understood as follows:
therein, it consists of the voice from another, which has the instruction on the teaching of the Four Truths as its dominant influence,
and wise attention.
This should be understood as the primary condition for the full realization [of awakening];
this is called the establishment of the lineage (gotra).
What are the marks of a person who abides in the lineage?
It is said:
they are the same as the marks of one whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa.
[He] said:
"The signs of one who does not possess the nature of parinirvāṇa—
by the reversal of those, the signs of a person established in the lineage (gotrastha) are to be understood."

What, then, are the marks of one whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa, endowed with which one is to be known as "one whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa"? There are many such marks of one whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa.
(Only a brief indication: I shall provide only a brief indication.
Here, for a person whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa, from the very beginning there is craving that is entirely and in every way [unrelinquished].

It is established within the basis of all Buddhas; it is of a nature that cannot be abandoned, is unproduced, has come from afar, and is firmly established—this is the first mark of a person abiding in the lineage (*gotra*).

Furthermore, a person who does not abide in the lineage, having heard in many ways the various and abundant qualities of cyclic existence, and having heard in many ways the various and abundant qualities of nirvāṇa,
[yet] possesses only a slight perception of the faults and disadvantages of the proliferation of cyclic existence.

He has not produced even a mere sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) with respect to the past; he will not produce it with respect to the future; and he does not produce it with respect to the present. For only a limited and inferior duration of time has passed since the destruction of craving and the fading away of passion.

Regarding cessation, one who aspires to see its qualities possesses merely a clarity of vision; with respect to the past, future, and present time periods, such a person has not produced, will not produce, and does not produce [this aspiration].
This is the second mark of a person who abides in the absence of lineage (*agotra*).
Furthermore, a person who abides in the non-lineage (*agotra*) is endowed with a lack of shame (*ahrīkya*) and a lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) through many modes of expression;
by means of which he, with a heart devoid of compassion, with a heart that does not shrink back, and with a joyful heart, transgresses against everyone,
and never at any time [feels remorse].
One feels regret regarding a gift,
and not otherwise.
This is the third mark of one who does not abide in a spiritual lineage.
Furthermore, one who abides in the supreme lineage possesses a mind that is complete in all aspects,
yet endowed with faults.
Whether beginning with suffering, or with its origin, or with its cessation, in this village...

Or, while the True Dharma is being taught, one does not attain even a mere turning of the mind toward the path, nor a mere liberation— namely, with respect to the past time, with respect to the future time, and with respect to the present time.

This is the fourth mark of one who does not abide in the lineage (*agotra*). Furthermore, if a person who does not abide in the lineage should at any time or on any occasion go forth into homelessness within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya;
That king was either convicted, or accused as a thief, or afflicted by debt.
Either out of fear for the lack of a livelihood, or out of fear of Māra, one who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa—
One who is not a practitioner of celibacy yet claims to be a practitioner of celibacy—
just so should the going forth of a person who does not abide in the lineage be understood throughout the past, future, and present time periods. Furthermore,
for a person who desires the training, there is no going forth, no full ordination, and no status as a monk.

Thus, by this method and with this underlying intention, from the point of view of the actual meaning—that is, in terms of leading to liberation—a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage (agotra) comes to be reckoned as one who has gone forth.
This is the fifth sign of a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage.
Furthermore, whatever wholesome action a person who stands outside the lineage performs—
whether by body, speech,
or mind— all of it is motivated by a desire for existence.
Desiring a distinguished future rebirth, he has the intention for enjoyments;
this is the sixth mark of a person who does not abide in a spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
Furthermore, many other marks of this kind exist in him, endowed with which—
One who does not possess the nature of final nirvāṇa is reckoned as "one whose nature is not to attain final nirvāṇa."
In that regard, who are the persons established in the lineage?
It is said:
there is a person established in the lineage.
One who remains merely within the lineage (*gotra*), neither having entered nor having emerged; or one who has entered but not yet emerged; or one who has both entered and emerged.
one of dull faculties, one of medium faculties, and one of sharp faculties.
One whose temperament is dominated by passion, one whose temperament is dominated by hatred, and one whose temperament is dominated by delusion.
One born in an unfavorable state,
one who is not heedful, and one who has entered upon a wrong path.
one who has entered upon the wrong path,
one who is obstructed, one who is unobstructed, one who is far away, and one who is near.
It is both mature and immature,
and both pure and impure.
In that regard, who is the person established in the lineage?
It is said:
it is like a certain person here who has come from the seed of supramundane dharmas through delusion.
Furthermore, even now, he does not obtain the service of virtuous persons or the hearing of the true Dharma,
nor does he take up faith and ethical discipline within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
He does not grasp what he has heard;
he does not increase his renunciation;
he does not make his view straight.
This is called the person who abides precisely in the spiritual lineage.
By the opposite of this, through the white side (*śuklapakṣa*), one should be understood as being established in the lineage (*gotrastha*) and having entered [the path] (*avatīrṇa*).
However, this is the distinction: he has not yet become an attainer of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
And [it is the cause] of its fruit, which is the dissociation from the afflictions.
Who is the one who abides in the lineage, has entered, and has emerged?
Having said this very thing, there is this distinction:
he becomes an attainer of the Noble Path and its fruit.
In that regard, who is the person of dull faculties?
One whose faculties proceed either excessively slowly or sluggishly toward an object of knowledge that serves as a focal point, whether by means of what consists of hearing, or...
They are associated with attention consisting of reflection or attention consisting of cultivation;
that is to say, faith.
Energy, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom.
They are neither capable nor competent for the penetration of the Dharma or the penetration of its meaning;
such a person is called one of dull faculties.

Who is the person of medium faculties? It is one whose faculties proceed neither too slowly nor too quickly with respect to the object of knowledge as their focal point. Everything should be stated in detail as before; this is called the person of medium faculties.
What is a person of sharp faculties?
It is that person whose faculties proceed without sluggishness and proceed without dullness regarding the object of knowledge, the focal point.
They are associated with mental attention consisting of that which is derived from hearing, or that which is derived from reflection, or that which is derived from cultivation.
Namely: faith, vigor,
and mindfulness.
Whether it be concentration or wisdom,
they become capable of penetrating the Dharma or its meaning, and of penetrating them swiftly.
Or rather, this is called a person of sharp faculties.
What is a person whose temperament is dominated by passion?
One who possesses both intense passion and long-standing passion toward an object that is provocative of desire is called a person of passionate temperament (rāgacarita).
What is a person of hateful temperament?
One who, toward an object that is a basis for aversion, possesses intense hatred and enduring hatred; this is called a person of hateful temperament.
What is a person of deluded temperament?
One who possesses intense delusion and prolonged delusion regarding an object of knowledge is called a person of deluded temperament.
Who are the persons born in unfavorable conditions, those who are heedless, and those who have entered upon a wrong path?
It should be understood that those born in unfavorable conditions, those who are heedless, and those who have entered upon a wrong path are [respectively] unobstructed.
What is a person who is distant?
There is a person who is distant from *nirvāṇa* due to the distance of time;
there is [one] who is distant due to the distance of application.
In that regard, what is distant by way of distance in time? It is that which, after many hundreds of births, many hundreds of thousands of births,
or many hundreds of thousands of births, subsequently becomes capable of obtaining the favorable conditions for swift realization.
For the sake of final nirvāṇa,
in that regard,
due to the distance from application, a person remains situated in the lineage alone.
He has not yet entered [the stream];
he is capable of obtaining the conditions for swift progress toward final nirvana.
Because he is distant from the undertaking of the application for the sake of nirvāṇa, and because he is distant in terms of the time of application, this person is said to be "distant."
The person is near.
(Śbh_Sh: 23) (Śbh_Sh: 24)
II. The Stage of Entry: ...
by means of these six, one who is capable is endowed with weak roots of virtue and endowed with middling roots of virtue.
Endowed with superior roots of virtue,
he is one who has reached the culmination of the preparatory stage and one who has attained the final goal.
In this regard, who is the person who is indeed capable? It is one who abides in the lineage (*gotrastha*)...
[and] does not [abandon it].
The meditator first attains faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,
and he straightens his view.
In this regard, who is one endowed with weak roots of virtue?
It is one who, while abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), has first attained faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,
up to the point where their view has been made straight.
This is called one endowed with weak roots of virtue.
A person established in the lineage who is endowed with middling roots of virtue, having first obtained faith in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, [proceeds as follows].
To the extent that, having made his vision straight, he brings about the production of one,
two, or many births for the sake of excellence.
He who passes away and does not obtain a final physical existence, remaining where he is until he attains parinirvāṇa— this is called [the one who attains nirvāṇa in the intermediate state].
A person endowed with superior roots of goodness. In this context, who is the person engaged in the application for finality?
It is that person who, having obtained their final physical existence, [seeks] correct instruction and admonition for the destruction of the outflows.
Or, having obtained the hearing of the true Dharma, one applies oneself correctly;
yet one does not become puffed up,
and one practices in every way and in all respects.

He attains the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), yet he does not reach the ultimate goal; such a person is called one who has reached the stage of application for the ultimate goal (*niṣṭhāprayogika*). In that regard, what is a person who has reached the ultimate goal (*niṣṭhāgata*)?
He who has been correctly informed and correctly instructed practices accordingly for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (āsrava),
so that he attains the destruction of all outflows in every respect and in every way.
He has accomplished what was to be done and has attained supreme coolness;
he is called a person who has reached the ultimate goal.
In that regard, a person of a capable nature, relying upon and established in the lineage (*gotra*), acquires weak roots of virtue and becomes one who has entered [the path].
Having thus entered, relying upon and established in the weak roots of goodness,
he attains the middling roots of goodness and matures himself by means of them.

As he is thus being matured, by relying upon and establishing himself in the middling roots of goodness, he attains the superior roots of goodness and becomes fully matured. Then, through the acquisition of a physical existence brought about by the cause of those superior roots of goodness, he accumulates the necessary provisions.
He touches one-pointedness of mind and enters the certainty of rightness;
or [he attains] the fruit of stream-entry.
He realizes either the fruit of once-returning or the fruit of non-returning, but he does not realize the supreme fruit, arhatship.
Then he is said to be one who has reached the culmination of the preparatory stage;
but when he realizes arhatship, which is the abandonment of all afflictions, [he is an arhat].
Then one has reached the ultimate goal.
This very practice of all the śrāvakas, which has a beginning, a middle, and an end, is demonstrated through the six established stages of persons (*pudgala*).
Among these, the beginning of the śrāvaka’s practice is demonstrated by means of the lineage (*gotra*),
and the culmination (*niṣṭhā*)—
The conclusion has been shown; by means of that other [verse], the middle has been demonstrated.
Regarding those individuals who have entered therein, is the time for their parinirvāṇa fixed and equal for all, or is it unfixed and not measured?
The time for all of them is unfixed and not determined as equal.
It is not for the sake of their final nirvāṇa; rather, neither is there a fixed time limit for them, nor is it the same for all of them regarding their final nirvāṇa.
Instead, their final nirvāṇa should be understood as occurring according to what is appropriate and according to the attainment of conditions—some after a long time, [others sooner].

For some, parinirvāṇa occurs after a very long time, while for others it occurs very quickly; nevertheless, whichever person (pudgala) abides in the spiritual lineage (gotrastha), even if they attain parinirvāṇa most rapidly,
they necessarily undergo three births.
In one [state] one descends; in one [state] one is liberated; in one [state]...
He becomes mature in that very birth and attains parinirvāṇa right there;
if he does not attain parinirvāṇa, [he proceeds further].

Thus, he necessarily undergoes the period of training (*śaikṣa*) and brings about no more than seven further existences; this is called the "establishment of entry. What are the marks of a person who has entered?
In this case, a person established in the lineage, at the very moment of entering [the path], experiences a lapse of mindfulness even through the transition of another birth.

Even though there exists a Teacher and a well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, or even when there is a poorly expounded Dharma and Vinaya, upon hearing the praise of that poorly expounded Dharma and Vinaya in many ways, they do not enter [the path].
He does not go forth;
even if he has gone forth, having entered [the path],
he very quickly turns back.
By his very nature, a distaste for that [teaching] persists within him;
just as a creature born in honey feels revulsion when cast into a conch shell, or as one who indulges in sensual pleasures feels revulsion when cast into mud or a stream,
so too, by the power of the causal force established previously, he does not perceive even the slightest praise, laudation, or commendation of the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
He either hears or experiences an itch;
having heard even a slight or minor thing,
or even without having heard anything, he very quickly descends [into the world] or goes forth into homelessness.
Likewise, having gone forth and entered [the path], he does not turn back;
by his very nature, his inclination remains fixed there,
just as a honey-bee's inclination remains fixed on honey.

Or, for one who enjoys sensual pleasures, it is through excellent conduct regarding desires; this is due to the influence of causal power established in the past. This is the first mark of a person who has newly entered [the path].
Furthermore, a person who has entered [the path] is not yet dissociated from those afflictions that lead to rebirth in the unfortunate states,
yet he is no longer reborn in those unfortunate states.
And with reference to a person who has entered [the path], the Blessed One said:
"He who possesses even a superior degree of mundane right view does not go to an evil rebirth, even for thousands of births."
When he becomes established in superior roots of virtue that are to be brought to maturity through gradual progression, he is thus not reborn in the inopportune states (*akṣaṇa*),
but not in others.
This is the second mark of a person who has entered [the path].
Furthermore, a person who has entered [the path], having heard the qualities of the Buddha, or the Dharma, or the Saṅgha,
Or, by recollecting it,
one attains a noble clarity of mind that is wholesome.
Connected with renunciation,
through that same object again and again,
by virtue of a mind melting with serene faith, one obtains [signs such as] horripilation from the falling of tears; this is the third mark of a person who has entered [the path].

Furthermore, a person who has entered [the path] is by their very nature endowed with intense moral shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*). That is to say, they possess a sense of shame regarding all instances of faulty conduct; this is the fourth sign of a person who has entered [the path].
Furthermore, a person who has entered [the path] becomes desirous; he possesses intense desire for the formal instruction.
In private recitation, in inquiry,
and in yoga.
In his mental attention,
he becomes one who seeks what is wholesome.
This is the fifth sign of a person who has entered [the path].

Furthermore, a person who has entered [the path] is firm in undertaking, steady in undertaking, and resolute in undertaking all blameless occupations and applications toward the side of wholesome qualities for the sake of attaining [the goal]. This is the sixth mark of a person who has entered [the path].
Furthermore, the person who has entered [the path] is of a nature with little passion;
they give rise to very mild outbursts of the afflictions.

Furthermore, he does not establish a continuous stream [of faults], and he becomes free from deceit, free from guile, having destroyed intoxication, pride, and egoism, being intent upon virtues and a hater of defects.
This is the seventh mark of a person who has entered [the path].

Furthermore, a person who has entered [the path] possesses a mind that is not cowed regarding the noble states to be realized; they do not disparage themselves, nor do they fall into a sense of incapacity;
they abound in resolute conviction.
This is the eighth mark of a person who has entered [the path].
These and other similar signs of many individuals who have entered [the path] are to be understood.
Of which this has been declared as merely a small portion.
Furthermore, these signs are weak in one who abides in weak roots of virtue and has entered [the path];
they are characterized by gaps, are not continuous, and are impure.
In one who abides in middling roots of virtue, they are middling;
For one who abides in superior roots of goodness, these— being supreme friends, constant,
and pure— are called the marks of a person who has entered [the path].

Endowed with which marks one comes to be reckoned as "one who has entered"? Furthermore, these should be understood as the inferential marks of persons established in the lineage and those who have entered.
However, only the Blessed Buddhas and the Śrāvakas who have attained the supreme perfection [and are] saviors [know them directly].
In that regard, those who perceive directly experience it through their perfectly purified knowledge and vision; namely,
the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the entry (*avatāra*).
Which persons have entered?
There is a person who has entered;
he is indeed one who has entered.
It is not ripening, not fully ripened,
and not emerged.
There is one who is matured but has not gone forth;
there is one who has gone forth but is not matured. The distinction between these should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, those other individuals of dull faculties and so forth who have been described in the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi)—
their classification should also be understood here according to their respective application.
In this regard, there is the intrinsic nature of this entry,
its systematic arrangement,
and these signs of those who have entered.
And all these individuals who have entered [the path], taken together, are called the "stage of entry."
// Summary Verse //
In brief, all of this— the intrinsic nature, its establishment, the signs, and the person itself— is to be understood as the stages of entry.
The Stage of Entry in the *Śrāvakabhūmi* is completed.
(Śbh_Sh: 33) (Śbh_Sh: 34) (Śbh_Sh: 35)
The Stage of Renunciation.
What is the stage of renunciation?
It is said:
And that which is the attainment of detachment by means of the mundane path,
and that which is the attainment of detachment by means of the supramundane path, and...
The equipment for these two, condensed into their unity, is called the stage of renunciation (*naiṣkramyabhūmi*).
What is the attainment of detachment by means of the mundane path?
It is when someone here perceives the realm of desire as coarse.
From the very beginning, he perceives peace in the joy and bliss born of seclusion within the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and rebirths (*upapatti*).
Seeing thus and dwelling frequently in that state, he attains detachment from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*) and enters the first *dhyāna*.
Thus, above all dhyānas, he views all lower stages as coarse,
and he views all higher stages as peaceful; viewing them in such a way and dwelling frequently therein, he attains detachment up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana).
And one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is no further attainment of detachment by means of the mundane path beyond this; there is nothing more than this.
What is the attainment of detachment by means of the supramundane path?
It is when, for instance, a certain person here sees true persons, is skilled in the noble dharmas, and understands suffering as suffering according to reality,
or the origin as the origin.
He is endowed with the knowledge and vision of a trainee regarding cessation as cessation, or regarding the path as the path.

Then, cultivating the higher path, he dissociates and liberates himself from the phenomena of the three realms that are to be abandoned through vision and cultivation; in this way, he transcends the three realms.
This is called the attainment of detachment by means of the supramundane path.
In that regard, what is the equipment?
It is as follows: the excellence of oneself, the excellence of others, and skill in [the path].
Desire for the Dharma,
restraint through ethical discipline,
and moderation in eating.
Application to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night,
dwelling with clear comprehension,
and association with spiritual friends.
Hearing the true Dharma, reflection,
the absence of obstacles, renunciation, and the ornaments of a śramaṇa— these factors are called the equipment for attaining mundane and supramundane detachment.
In that regard, the excellence of oneself, the excellence of others, and the desire for wholesome qualities—
their analysis should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding what was said concerning the inferior causal condition for the full realization of the seed:
therein, what is the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*)?
It is as follows: here, a certain person dwells possessed of ethical discipline, up to and including taking up and training in the precepts of training (*śikṣāpada*).
And how does one dwell possessed of ethical discipline? That is, by undertaking and training oneself in the precepts of training.
How does one dwell possessed of ethical discipline?
Just as, regarding the training rules he has undertaken, his bodily actions are unimpaired;
indeed, his bodily actions are unimpaired. He is one whose conduct is unbroken, undiminished...
In this way, one who wanders in the forest is possessed of ethical discipline.
How does one become restrained by the Prātimokṣa vow?
The morality that leads to liberation in seven ways is called the Prātimokṣa vow;
these vows become numerous according to the divisions of the schools.
Regarding this matter,
with reference to the restraint of a monk, it is said: "How does one become perfected in conduct while being restrained by the Prātimokṣa restraint?"
Just as he does so by conforming to the world and not overstepping the world, based upon his deportment, his duties, or his application to the side of wholesome qualities.
He becomes endowed with conduct that conforms to the discipline and does not transgress the discipline;
therein, conduct is based upon the modes of deportment.
How is it that he has neither transcended the world nor transcended discipline?
It is as follows: wherever one ought to walk.
And as for how one should walk: therein, one walks in such a way that one does not become censured by the world.
Not of the virtuous, of those who are rightly intent, of true persons.
He becomes one who cannot be harmed by those who follow the same Dharma, by those who uphold the Vinaya, and by those trained in the Vinaya.
[a] That which is not a ground for censure:
as it is with walking, so it is with standing and sitting.
The manner of lying down should be understood;
therein lies the conduct regarding what is to be done. How does one not transgress worldly norms?
It is said that one must not act in transgression of the Vinaya;
[this includes] the wearing of robes and the disposal of excrement and urine.
The use of water and the tooth-stick; entering the village; and the preparation and consumption of alms-food.
The washing of the bowl, its setting aside,
and the washing of the feet.
The preparation of beds and seats,
as well as their subsequent dismantling, the work concerning the alms-bowl, and the work concerning the robes—
whatever else belongs to this category is called "that which is to be done" (itikaraṇīya).
And he applies that [mental application] appropriately to where it is to be applied, and in whatever manner it is to be applied, he applies it accordingly;
by means of which he does not [obstruct] worldly...
He becomes one who is appropriate and beyond reproach;
he is blameless and beyond censure in the eyes of those who uphold the Vinaya and those trained in the Vinaya.
For his fellow practitioners of right conduct, his behavior—grounded in such duties to be performed—is not transgressive of worldly norms.
And he does not transgress the Vinaya.
In this regard, conduct is the basis for the application of the side of wholesome qualities.
How is it that it does not transcend the world, and how is it that it does not transcend the discipline?
The side of wholesome qualities is said to be as follows: namely, the practice of proper conduct toward one's teachers, attending upon them,
likewise attending to the sick, and the application of giving with zeal while maintaining a mind of mutual compassion.
Inquiry,
being skillful and untiring in hearing the Dharma, and performing services with one's body for wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.

The instigation of others toward the side of wholesome qualities, the teaching of the Dharma, and sitting cross-legged upon entering into seclusion— whatever other such qualities there may be, this is called [the perfection of concentration].
The application to the side of the wholesome.
He thus applies himself to the side of the wholesome, as is appropriate and as has been described.
He imagines in whatever way it should be imagined there,
so that he does not become subject to questioning or reproach by worldly people or those who uphold the Vinaya.
Of those trained in the Vinaya,
who are perfectly devoted,
and who are true persons.
This is called the conduct of those who share the same dharma, which is based on the application of the side of wholesome qualities and does not transcend the world.
And he does not transgress the discipline.
When one is endowed with these modes, this conduct is called the perfection of conduct;
and thus one becomes perfected in conduct.
And how does one become perfected in terms of range?
There are five improper ranges for a monk.
What are the five?
Namely:
a marketplace, a brothel, a tavern, and the royal court.
And the fifth is the "caṇḍāla-like" [place].

When one avoids these objects of conduct prohibited by the Tathāgata and instead conducts oneself in another object of conduct that is blameless, then, in that regard, one is thus endowed with a proper sphere of activity at the proper time.
How does one perceive danger in even the slightest faults?
A "slightest fault" is defined as follows: [text continues]
The minor and minute training rules are those in which both transgression and recovery are recognized;
the transgression of these constitutes a fault that is merely atomic.
Furthermore, it is because one emerges from that transgression with little difficulty that it is called "minute.
In that regard, how does one come to see danger? He himself says:
Or, due to the transgression of these sheep, one might become incapable of attaining what has not been attained,
of comprehending what has not been comprehended, or of realizing what has not been realized.
Or we might go to a state of misery, or be headed for a state of misery; or my own self might reproach me, or the Teacher.
Or deities, or wise ones, or fellow practitioners of the holy life might censure him for unrighteousness.

And if a wicked reputation, fame, renown, or verse about me were to arise in the cardinal and intermediate directions, he perceives fear in those superior qualities— both pertaining to the present life and the future life— which are caused by that [reputation],
and by which those minor and trivial [qualities] [are surpassed].
He does not violate even the minor rules of training for the sake of his life, nor does he transgress out of attachment.
Should he ever, at any time,
fall into an offense through a lapse of mindfulness, he very quickly remedies it according to the Dharma and emerges from it.
In this way, he perceives danger even in the slightest faults.
How does he undertake and train in the precepts?
He said:

Previously, while being ordained by means of this formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*jñapticaturtha-karman*) for the undertaking of the Prātimokṣa restraint, he heard the substance of a few training rules (*śikṣāpada*);
and on the following day, he accepted with his own vow more than a hundred other training rules recited in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, thinking, "I shall obtain [them] in their entirety."
Having heard it from his preceptors and teachers— those with whom he is conversant, familiar, and well-acquainted— from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra,
he then acquires the Prātimokṣa restraint through the undertaking of all the training rules; thereafter, he becomes proficient in those training rules.
He does not transgress those precepts; and if he has transgressed them, he remedies it in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, he becomes skilled in those training rules in which he is proficient.
One whose intellect is untrained previously undertook those [vows] by formally accepting a commitment; now, however, one undertakes them through skill in training.
From those aforementioned points, as before, from either a teacher (*ācārya*) or a preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
Furthermore, through proficiency in training and having undertaken the precepts, he trains exactly as instructed, neither omitting nor adding anything;
and regarding those training rules designated by those in the position of a teacher, he grasps both the meaning and the phrasing without error.
Having thus undertaken them, he trains in the precepts; this, then, is the detailed analysis of the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*) presented at length.
In that regard, what is the summarized meaning?
Thus, this summarized meaning consists precisely of three characteristics;
the aggregate of ethical discipline has been elucidated by the Blessed One.
Namely:
the characteristic of non-disappearance,
and the characteristic of intrinsic nature.
And [it consists of] the characteristics of its intrinsic nature and qualities.
As for how this is so: first, by the statement "he dwells possessed of ethical discipline," the characteristic of non-dissipation of the restraint of ethical discipline is explained.
Furthermore, as for what he says, "restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa," by this the characteristic of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa) is explained. Moreover, as for what he says:
"Endowed with proper conduct and range of activity":
by this, the characteristic quality of the Prātimokṣa restraint as it is undertaken in comparison with others is explained.
Nevertheless, others, upon perceiving that perfection of conduct and sphere of activity, become confident where they were previously lacking in confidence,
and for those already confident, their confidence increases further; and being confident, they perform acts of service toward those who possess such confidence.
Nor do they corrupt their minds or utter dispraise;
otherwise, this would not be the quality or benefit consisting in the influence of others for one who is endowed with ethical discipline and endowed with proper conduct and sphere of activity.
Or else, this would be the opposite; or rather, there would indeed be a fault in this case.
Furthermore, as for what he said:
Seeing fear even in the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains in the precepts of training;
by this, the characteristic of the benefits of qualities based on internal sovereignty is explained.
For what reason? Because he would thereby obtain this excellence of qualities, which has others as its sovereign influence and is perfected through right conduct and sphere of activity.
Moreover,
having violated the precepts, with that as the cause and that as the condition, one is reborn in the states of woe.
Or, for one who has not yet attained it, there is the state of incapacity regarding its prior attainment; furthermore,
he perceives danger even in the slightest faults.

How much more so, then, regarding those who have taken up the training rules in their entirety; they train in the precepts without transgression. Therefore, with that as the cause and that as the condition, after the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a happy destination.

Or, they become capable of attaining what has not yet been attained, as previously described. For this reason, this is called the quality and benefit of the restraint of ethical discipline governed by internal mastery.
Furthermore, there is another formulation:
in brief, the Blessed One has elucidated both the morality of undertaking vows and the morality that leads to liberation.
And there is the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla-bhāvanā*). In that regard,
by the statement "he dwells possessed of ethical discipline," the state of having undertaken ethical discipline (*samādatta-śīlatā*) is explained.
Furthermore, as for what he says:
by the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa," the nature of morality that leads to liberation (*nairyāṇika-śīlatā*) is expressed;
for indeed, the morality comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint is called the training in higher morality (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
Relying upon the training in higher ethics,
and cultivating the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom, he thus brings about the exhaustion of all suffering.

He becomes one who has set out; that is to say, by relying upon and making the higher training in ethics (adhiśīla) the precursor, the restraint of the Prātimokṣa is therefore called "ethics leading to liberation" (nairyāṇika-śīla). Furthermore, as it says:

"Endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains himself in the precepts"—by this, the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla-bhāvanā*) is explained.
Through these aspects, that morality of the Prātimokṣa restraint is to be cultivated;
and when cultivated in this way, it becomes well-cultivated. Thus, this single restraint of ethical discipline should be understood as being presented through six modes of instruction.
Furthermore, this restraint of ethical discipline should be understood as being deficient in ten ways;
conversely, it is perfected by those same ten causes.
By what ten causes does it become ruined?
From the very beginning, it is wrongly grasped; it is overly indolent; it is not relinquished; and it is possessed by negligence and laziness.
He becomes one whose resolve is false;
he is possessed by a failure of conduct; he is possessed by a failure of livelihood; and he has fallen into the two extremes.
It leads to a lack of deliverance,
and one becomes fallen away from what has been undertaken.
In that regard, how is ethical discipline wrongly grasped from the outset?
It is when, for example, a certain person has been condemned by a king, or having gone forth into homelessness, has been condemned by thieves.
Or one who is afflicted by debt,
or afflicted by fear, or terrified by the fear of not making a living.
or not for the state of a śramaṇa, nor for the state of a brāhmaṇa,
nor for the pacification of the self;
It is wrongly grasped if it is not for the sake of self-taming, nor for the sake of one's own parinirvāṇa from the very beginning.

How does one become overly indolent? It is when someone here is shameless, possesses little remorse, is lax, and acts with slackness regarding the training as it has been taught; this is how one becomes overly indolent.

How does one become excessively remorseful? It is when someone here grasps what has been wrongly grasped and feels remorse for what is not a ground for remorse; that is, feeling remorse regarding matters that ought to cause remorse.

When one generates a mind of contempt toward others in an improper place, or speaks of it, or makes it known, it is thus called "transgressed. How does it become "governed by negligence and indolence"?
For example, here a certain person has fallen into an offense based on the past time, and because of a lapse of mindfulness, he has not rectified it according to the Dharma;
just as he has fallen into an offense based on the past time, so too has he fallen into an offense based on the future or the present time.

And because of this lapse of mindfulness, she does not act in accordance with the Dharma in some instances; nor does she, prior to committing an offense, apply intense effort toward ensuring that she does not commit one in the future,
thinking, "What if I were to conduct myself in such a way?"
In whatever way he conducts himself and dwells so as not to commit an offense, in that very way he conducts himself and dwells.
He commits an offense according to its nature;
by means of this,
he is associated with the past and associated with the future.

Possessed of negligence that is accompanied by the middle and the end, that must be attended to beforehand, and that follows along with [one's companions], he indulges in the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of reclining.
He indulges in the pleasure of lying on his side;
he becomes unskilled, lazy, and lacking in the vigor of exertion.
One does not perform personal service with one’s own body for learned fellow-celibates;
thus, it becomes characterized by negligence and indolence.
How is it wrongly directed?
For example, here a certain person practices the holy life having made a vow:
"By means of this morality, or..."
Whether by religious observance, or by austerity, or by living the life of a celibate student.
Whether he be a god or one among the gods,
he becomes desirous of gain and honor.
One seeks gain and honor from others and craves gain and honor;
in this way, one's aspiration becomes false.
How is one possessed by a failure of conduct?

It is when someone here, whether with respect to deportment, or in regard to duties, or in the application of the side of wholesome qualities, transgresses both worldly norms and the discipline (*vinaya*), as previously described; thus one is possessed by a failure of conduct.
How is it that one is possessed by a failure in livelihood?
It is when, for example, a certain person here possesses great desire and lacks contentment.
He is difficult to deceive and difficult to restrain;
furthermore, he seeks robes through unrighteous means.
He does not seek alms-food, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick, either by righteous means or by unrighteous means.
Not by means of the Dharma.

And for the sake of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he adopts an extraordinary and composed deportment for the purpose of making himself appear virtuous; he displays to others a state of unagitated faculties, unflustered faculties, and tranquil faculties.
By this means, others develop an appreciation for his virtues and think that they must give and do for him—
namely, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick—
and he becomes like a crow, talkative and loquacious.
Bold,
playful,
and one whose name and lineage are proclaimed.
He is one who has heard much,
a bearer of the Dharma,
and he speaks the Dharma to others solely for the sake of gain.
Or he speaks what has been spoken by the disciples,
or his own virtues;
or further, having superimposed something real upon it, he himself becomes the speaker.
Or he causes others to speak [on his behalf], or he acts as a guide with unsurpassed [eloquence],
or he is desirous of robes,
or desirous of any one or another of the requisites of a recluse.
Whether it be abundant or superior,
even while not being deprived of it, he makes use of ordinary robes.
When faithful brahmins and householders, perceiving that he might suffer a lack of robes, will think to provide and give him abundant and excellent robes;
and just as with robes, so too with any other requisite for the ascetic life, failing to obtain it from faithful brahmins and householders according to his wish—
Or, when wealth does not exist and is unavailable, he begs with such importunity;
and having squeezed her dry again and again, he speaks harshly to her. Or, even after obtaining a meager amount while wealth is indeed present, he treats that gain as if it were flesh.
He disparages and discourages the donor and the master of the gift, speaking thus:
"O, noble son!"
There are certain sons of good family and daughters of good family who are even lower-born and more impoverished than you, yet they give such excellent and pleasing gifts in this way and that;
why then, being equal or even higher-born than them, do you give only what is agreeable, yet not excellent or abundant?
Whoever, by relying on these modes— whether through hypocrisy, or flattery, or hinting— ...
Or, through extortion, seeking from others robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, desiring to secure gain by means of gain.
That which is by means of what is not Dharma—
furthermore, that which is by means of what is not Dharma constitutes his wrong livelihood.
In this way, that ethical discipline is encompassed by a failure in livelihood.
How does it fall into the two extremes? It is when someone here is devoted to the pursuit of sensual pleasure, being another who is intent upon it.
Whether by lawful or unlawful means, one enjoys robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
seeing only the danger and not knowing the way of escape—this is called one extreme.
Furthermore, in this world, some person is devoted to self-mortification and torments himself in many ways.
He causes himself torment and undertakes difficult ascetic observances;
for example, he may resort to sitting upon thorns.
He is one who carries ashes, one who relies on a pestle,
or one who relies on a wooden plank;
he stands in a squatting posture, devoted to the practice of the yoga of the squatting posture.
He becomes an attendant of the fire;
he serves the fire as many as three times,
and he carries water as many as three times.
"Standing on one foot, one revolves wherever the sun is"—
whatever is of this kind, a devotion to self-mortification, this is called the second extreme. Thus, it falls into the two extremes.
How does it become non-leading to liberation? It is when someone here grasps at a certain morality or vow with a [wrong] view, thinking:
"By this very morality or vow, purity will come about."
"Liberation and deliverance will come about"— thus [he thinks].
And all the well-guarded ethical discipline of those outside [this path] is inferior to this.

Even that which is perfectly pure is said to be "not leading to liberation" (anairyāṇika) by virtue of its purity being merely comparable to that [previous state]. In this way, it becomes non-leading to liberation.
How does it become fallen away from its formal undertaking?
For example, there is here a certain person who is entirely and completely shameless and indifferent; he is one who has failed in the life of a recluse,
being immoral, of evil character, internally rotten, leaking [impurity], and like a water-born weed.
One whose conduct is like the sound of a conch shell,
who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and who does not live the holy life yet claims to live the holy life— in this way, one becomes fallen from the undertaking [of the vows].
By these ten causes, one is ruined.
The Blessed One has spoken of "virtue" and "the failure of virtue";
furthermore, the Blessed One has also spoken of the "cultivation of virtue.
And this [distinction] is to be understood from these reasons through two causes.
That which is the state of not leading to liberation,
the failure to maintain what has been undertaken, and other such causes should be understood as the failure of ethical discipline (*śīlavipatti*).

Conversely, by reversing these very causes that belong to the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the fulfillment of ethical discipline (*śīlasampatti*) should be understood through the causes belonging to the bright side (*śuklapakṣa*).
And there is the purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*).
Furthermore, in some instances, the Blessed One has described ethical discipline by way of its root, as it was said:
"One should have well-established roots and delight in the tranquility of the mind."
"Bound and unbound, visible and invisible, noble and sinful"—thus says the verse.
In some places it is expressed by the word "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*);
as it is said: "A monk or a nun endowed with the ornament of ethical discipline (*śīlālaṃkāra*) abandons the unwholesome and cultivates the wholesome.
In other places it is expressed by the word "ointment" (*anulepana*).
As it is said: "A monk or a nun who is perfected in the ointment of ethical discipline," as stated previously;
in some places, this is expressed by the word "fragrance."
There is that kind of gift which is a type of fragrance whose scent wafts with the wind, and whose scent also wafts against the wind and with the wind;
in some places, this is expressed by the term "well-conducted conduct" (*sucarita*).
As it is said:
"The desirable ripening of good conduct of body is experienced both in the present life and in future lives; likewise for good conduct of speech."
In some places it is expressed by the word *saṃvara*;
as where it says: "The donor, the master of giving, is one who possesses ethical discipline (*śīlavat*)."
Abiding in restraint, possessing the view of the scriptures, and seeing the fruit;
moreover, it is said:
"He dwells possessed of ethical discipline."
"Restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa," and so forth.
For what reason did the Blessed One describe ethical discipline (*śīla*) using the word "root"? Because the meaning of "root" is the sense of being a foundation and the sense of being a support.

And this very ethical discipline is the foundation for the arising and attainment of all mundane and supramundane, pure, blameless, foremost, excellent, and bliss-bestowing [virtues]; therefore, it is called by the word "root."

Just as the earth serves as a foundation and a support for the growth of grasses, shrubs, herbs, and forest trees, even so should ethical discipline (*śīla*) be explained in detail, as previously stated.
For what reason is ethical discipline designated by the term "ornament"?
He replied:
As for those other ornaments, such as necklaces,
earrings, or armlets;
Or a seal-ring, or a garland of gold and silver—these [are worn] as long as he is young, a child with black hair. (Śbh_Sh: 54)
When endowed with fresh youth, his ornaments, when put on, produce mere beauty;
but it is not so for one who is aged or elderly.
Of one who is aged, whether eighty or ninety years old,
or of one with teeth like those of a bull.
With gray hair,
he appears as if mocked by those ornaments he wears,
or else by his misfortune of ill health.
When misfortune regarding wealth or misfortune regarding kinsmen has arisen, [wealth] does not shine;
however, ethical discipline (śīla), on the other hand, is a source of splendor for everyone at all times.
Therefore, it is designated by the term "ornament" (alaṃkāra).
For what reason is ethical discipline (*śīla*) spoken of by the term "ointment"?

In this regard, the undertaking of ethical discipline—which consists of many wholesome and blameless qualities—removes the burning of the body and the burning of the mind caused by the undertaking of all forms of immorality.

Just as sandalwood ointment or camphor ointment is used when one is tormented by heat at a time when the supreme summer heat has arrived, for this reason ethical discipline is spoken of by the term "ointment."
For what reason is ethical discipline called a "type of fragrance"?
Indeed, from a virtuous person, a fine report of their reputation and fame issues forth in all directions and intermediate directions.
Or, when various kinds of root-fragrances,
heartwood-fragrances,
or flower-fragrances are stirred by the wind, a pleasing scent issues forth in all directions and intermediate directions.
For this reason, ethical discipline is called by the term "a variety of fragrances."
For what reason is ethical discipline (*śīla*) called "good conduct" (*sucarita*)?
Because this practice leads to happiness, leads to heaven, and leads to a happy rebirth;
such is this practice.
Therefore, it is called "well-practiced."
For what reason is ethical discipline (*śīla*) expressed by the term "restraint" (*saṃvara*)?
This dharma has the nature of cessation; it is characterized by cessation and has the nature of abstention.
Therefore, it is expressed by the term "restraint."
Indeed, for this restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*), there are three kinds of reflection for the sake of complete purity.
What are the three? Namely, reflection upon bodily action (*kāyakarma*).
Examination of verbal action and examination of mental action;
furthermore, by examining these actions therein, one purifies the restraint of ethical discipline.
Whatever action has been intended by the body to be performed, he examines that very thing:
"Is this deed of mine harmful to myself, an obstacle for others, unwholesome, resulting in suffering, and having suffering as its maturation; or is this bodily action of mine harmless to myself?"

If, while reflecting thus, he understands that this bodily action of his, though it may be for the welfare, the arising of happiness, and the ripening of happiness for others, is nevertheless harmful to himself or to another,
or gives rise to unwholesome states such as passion;
It is the ripening of passion;
if, while reflecting in this way, he does not engage [in it],
he does not perform that karma.
He does not perform it.
However, if he knows, "This bodily action of mine is non-afflictive and wholesome," as previously described, he performs that bodily action. (Śbh_Sh: 56)
He does not withdraw it,
but bestows it;
furthermore, whatever bodily action has been performed by him with reference to the past time, [he likewise bestows].
He examines that as well repeatedly, thinking:
"But this is harmful to me," as before.
If, while examining in this way, he comes to know among his wise fellow-celibates: "This action of mine is harmful to me," as before;
In the presence of his conscious fellow practitioners,
he withdraws and relinquishes whatever bodily action he has performed in the past.
He also repeatedly examines that:
"Is this [action] of mine harmful? as before.
If, while examining thus, he knows in the presence of his conscious fellow-practitioners: "This action of mine is harmful," as before.
He confesses it in the presence of his wise fellow-celibates and makes amends according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, if, while reflecting in this way, he knows: "This bodily action of mine is harmless," as described before;

With that very same joy and gladness, he dwells extensively practicing day and night; thus his bodily action becomes well-examined and thoroughly purified with respect to the past, future, and present time periods.
Just as it is with bodily action, so should verbal action be understood.
The mind arises in dependence on past formations;
the mind arises in dependence on future and present formations.
He repeatedly examines that mind:
"Is this mind of mine harmful? and so on, as before, until he does not give rise to it.
He withdraws it and does not bestow it;
that is mental action.
By means of the bright fortnight, one produces it again,
does not withdraw it,
and bestows it; this is mental action.
In this way, that mental action has been examined and thoroughly purified by him with respect to the past, future, and present time periods.
For what reason? Because in the past, in the future, and even in the present, whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be,
their bodily action—
Having examined and purified vocal action and mental action, having purified them again and again.
They spoke extensively;
having all of them thus reflected and purified [themselves].
As it was said by the Blessed One concerning the Venerable Rāhula:
"O Rāhula, constantly examine your bodily action, your verbal action, and your mental action, remembering the instruction of the Buddhas."
This is the work of a śramaṇa; train in this, Rāhula.
For you who are training in this, there will be only what is beneficial, not what is evil.
In that regard, when one investigates in this way— whether my bodily action, vocal action, or mental action is harmful— and so forth in detail, (Śbh_Sh: 58)
As before, this is "examination":
that one withdraws certain things, confesses certain things, and grants certain things;
by means of that very joy and gladness, one dwells frequently practicing the training day and night—this is called "purification."
In this regard, ten benefits of such completely purified restraint of ethical discipline should be understood.
What are the ten?
Here, a person endowed with ethical discipline dwells, possessing purity of ethical discipline for himself.
Contemplating thus, one attains freedom from regret; for one who is without regret, joy arises; for one whose mind is joyful, gladness is born;
and for one whose mind is glad, the body becomes tranquil.
One whose body is pliant experiences happiness;
the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated;
and one whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
One sees things as they truly are.
Knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes weary [of saṃsāra]. Being weary, one becomes dispassionate.
One who is dispassionate is liberated;
for one who is liberated, there arises the knowledge and vision of liberation, which is mindfulness.

Until one attains final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder— when a virtuous person, established in the purity of ethical discipline, obtains freedom from remorse and proceeds by stages toward the attainment of nirvana— this is the first benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, when the time of death has arrived for a virtuous person, they reflect:
"This well-spoken [teaching] has been practiced by me; this good conduct has been performed."
"By body, speech, or mind, this misconduct was not committed by me," as previously described regarding bodily conduct;

"Whatever destination belongs to those who have performed merit, who have performed wholesome deeds, and who have acted out of fear for the fearful—having died, I shall go to that destination. Thus he attains the second state of being free from remorse.
For the sake of proceeding to a happy destination,
for a person who is free from remorse, death is auspicious;
their passing away is auspicious, and their future state is auspicious.
This is the second benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, from a virtuous person, a beautiful reputation, fame, glory, renown, and praise issue forth.
This is the third benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a virtuous person sleeps in ease and awakens in ease;
with body and mind free from feverish distress—this is the fourth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, one who is virtuous...
Even when a person is asleep, they are protected by the gods;
this is the fifth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a virtuous person does not feel apprehensive regarding evil from others,
nor is their mind terrified by fear.
This is the sixth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a person endowed with ethical discipline is protected even when encountered by executioners, adversaries, or enemies, even if they have found a vulnerability;
for they always perceive this person as such and treat them with friendliness.
Or abiding in the middle way;
this is the seventh benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, even when a lapse occurs, one is protected from non-human beings who dwell as yakṣas and have previously placed great trust in him;
that is to say, by making that very same ethical discipline the dominant influence.
This is the eighth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, a virtuous person obtains gains from others with ease and according to the Dharma—
namely, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick—
precisely because of their excellence in ethical discipline.
And for the sake of battle,
he is honored and held in high esteem by kings, royal ministers, citizens and country folk, wealthy men, guild-leaders, and caravan leaders.
This is the ninth benefit of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, as before, all his vows are fulfilled. If he so desires, [he may be born] in the desire realm into great kṣatriya families or great brahmin families.
Or among families of great householders like the Sāla trees, or among the gods of the Four Great Kings, or among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
of the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, and the Nirmāṇarati gods;
May I be reborn in the fellowship of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods;
and because of the purity of my moral conduct and observances, having thoroughly attained the meditative absorptions, may I dwell in happiness in this very life,
and may I be reborn in the fellowship of the gods of the Form Realm.
This is the fame [of one who dwells thus]; and this aspiration of the virtuous one who is free from passion is fulfilled.
If he so desires:
"May I attain the liberations... or may I dwell having fully attained them."
Or he may be reborn among the classes of gods who have attained the formless realm, as previously described.
If he desires, "May I attain ultimate, final nirvana," he attains it.
Because of the purity of his conduct regarding that [state],
and because he is free from passion in all respects— this should be understood as the tenth benefit of ethical discipline.
The aggregate of ethical discipline has been explained in detail;
misfortune and prosperity have been explained;
and the synonymous names have been explained.
The examination of purification has been explained,
and the benefit has been explained.

This very restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*), complete in all its aspects and embraced by the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*), has been declared, explained, disclosed, and revealed; herein noble sons who desire their own welfare, and those who desire the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*) or a brahmin (*brāhmaṇya*), ought to train.
// Summary Verse //
The analysis (*vibhaṅga*) should be known as threefold; the perfection (*sampad*) is tenfold;
the synonyms (*paryāya*) are of six aspects; and purity (*viśuddhi*) is considered to be threefold.
The benefit (*anuśaṃsa*)...
This restraint of ethical discipline is of ten kinds.
What is restraint of the sense faculties?
It is, for example, when a certain person here dwells with the doors of the senses guarded, with mindfulness protected, with constant mindfulness; and so forth in detail.

In that regard, how does one dwell with the doors of the sense-faculties guarded, with mindfulness protected, and with constant mindfulness? [This is explained] in detail up until: he guards the faculty of the mind by means of the faculty of the mind.
He enters into meditative attainment in this manner.
In this way, he dwells with the doors of his sense faculties guarded. In that regard, how does he become one whose mindfulness is protected?
It is when someone here, having made the very guarding of the doors of the sense faculties their primary focus, has mastered what they have heard.
Or again, it has been reflected upon or cultivated.
By means of that, he has acquired mindfulness dominated by hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

For the sake of not losing, for the sake of realization, and for the sake of non-destruction of that very mindfulness which has been acquired, he from time to time applies himself to and practices that very same teaching.
He practices yoga, that is, cultivation, regarding reflection;

he does not become one who has merely performed the preliminary application. In this way, he effects the protection from time to time of that mindfulness which has been fully acquired through hearing and fully acquired through reflection, by means of the practice of yoga consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
In this way, one becomes one whose mindfulness is guarded.
How does one become one whose mindfulness is steadfast?
One becomes one who practices constantly within that very mindfulness.
And one becomes a practitioner who effects deliverance.
In this context, that which is constant practice is called uninterrupted practice;
therein, that which is practice effecting deliverance is called respectful practice.
Thus, one who acts with constancy and acts with reverence is called "one of prudent mindfulness. Such a person maintains mindfulness in that manner and does not allow that mindfulness to be lost.
He becomes thus possessed of steady mindfulness;
thus, while that very mindfulness remains unlost, he attains the acquisition of strength.
By means of which one becomes capable and competent for the overcoming of forms, sounds, odors,
and tastes.
For the sake of overcoming tangible objects and mental phenomena,
how does one become one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness?
Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
immediately after eye-consciousness, [mental consciousness] arises.
The conceptualizing mental consciousness is that by which, through conceptualization, one becomes attached to forms of a pleasant nature and feels aversion toward forms of an unpleasant nature.
Taking that very [consciousness] as the dominant influence, he protects himself from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction.
Just as defilement does not arise [in that way],

so too, depending upon the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and depending upon mental objects (*dharma*), mental consciousness arises. And that mental consciousness, accompanied by improper conceptualization (*ayoniśovikalpa*), is the originator of defilement.
By means of which he becomes attached to phenomena that have a pleasant form and becomes hostile toward phenomena that have an unpleasant form—
he protects his mind from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction; thus, affliction does not arise for him.
In this way, one becomes one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness.
How does one become one who dwells in an even state?
An "even state" is now explained.
Equanimity is either wholesome or neutral.
Having protected his mind from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction, he directs it toward either wholesome or neutral equanimity.
Therefore, it is called "one who dwells in an even state.
In this way, one becomes one who dwells in an even state.
But how, moreover, does one protect the mind from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction?
He does not seize upon signs regarding those forms and sounds.
in odors, tastes, and tangibles,
He does not seize upon the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) of phenomena, on account of which evil and unwholesome states might flow into his mind.

However, if— due to a lapse of mindfulness or an abundance of afflictions— an apprehension of signs (*nimittagraha*) or an apprehension of secondary characteristics should nevertheless arise even in one who is avoiding them;
It is wrongly grasped as something evil and unwholesome;
for which phenomena [would] simply follow along?
Their mind proceeds toward restraint;
