by these two modes, their mental faculty is protected from that improper conceptualization which gives rise to affliction.
Furthermore, how does that mind, having been guarded by those two aspects, apply itself to wholesome equanimity or to neutral equanimity?
It does so by means of those very same two aspects.
Which two?
As it is said: "He guards the eye-faculty; he attains restraint with the eye-faculty.
Just as he attains restraint with the eye-faculty, so too [does he] with the ear, nose, tongue, and body."
He guards the mind-faculty and attains restraint through the mind-faculty;
by these two modes, he directs that very mind toward either wholesome or neutral equanimity.
How does one not grasp at signs (*nimitta*) regarding forms cognizable by the eye? Grasping at signs is defined as follows:
Whatever form is the objective range of visual consciousness, one becomes a grasper of that objective range by means of visual consciousness;
in this way, one becomes a grasper of signs.
That is to say, among forms cognizable by the eye, and among forms cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, there is another kind of birth as a sign.
If, however, one avoids that objective sphere,
then for the visual consciousness, it is thus not [produced].

He does not seize upon the signs (*nimitta*) among forms cognizable by the eye-consciousness, nor likewise among phenomena (*dharma*) cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness.
How is it that he does not seize upon the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*)?
Regarding forms cognizable by the eye:

the grasping of secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana-grāha*) refers to that which is the objective range (*gocara*) for the conceptual mental consciousness— which arises either immediately following or simultaneously with the visual consciousness— with respect to those very same forms cognizable by the eye, and which leads toward passion.
Whether for the sake of aversion or for the sake of delusion, he avoids that object-field and does not give rise to it as a mental focal point.
Thus, that mental consciousness does not grasp at secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) with respect to forms cognizable by the eye;

likewise, it does not grasp at secondary characteristics with respect to phenomena (*dharma*) cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is another class of grasping at signs (*nimitta*) and grasping at secondary characteristics.

In that regard, "grasping at signs" (*nimittagrāha*) is when one, having brought to presence the mental attention (*manaskāra*) arising from them, sees forms (*rūpa*) that have come into the range of vision. In that regard, "grasping at secondary characteristics" (*anuvyañjanagrāha*) is when one,
having brought to presence the mental attention arising from them, sees those very same forms that have come into the range of vision.
Furthermore, having previously heard from another, one hears:

"There are such-and-such forms, such-and-such forms, cognizable by the eye. Taking as his dominant influence those names, phrases, and syllables that correspond to them, and relying upon and establishing himself in them, this person discriminates the forms cognizable by the eye exactly as they were heard; this is called [discrimination].
Grasping at secondary characteristics:
as it is with regard to forms cognizable by the eye, so it should be understood regarding phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Furthermore, there is this grasping at signs (*nimittagrāha*) and grasping at secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjanagrāha*), on account of which, with which as basis, and with which as predominant condition, evil and unwholesome states flow into his mind; and there is that very cause, that basis, and that predominant condition by which evil and unwholesome states flow into the mind.

In this regard, this grasping at signs, this grasping at secondary characteristics, and this improper grasping (*ayoniśogrāha*)—on account of which, with which as basis, and with which as predominant condition, evil and unwholesome states flow into his mind—is what constitutes those conditions.
He avoids grasping at the signs and grasping at the secondary characteristics of that form.
What are the evil, unwholesome states? They are: lust, and the misconduct of body originated by lust.
Misconduct of speech,
misconduct of mind,
hatred, and delusion.
And bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct arising from delusion— these are called evil, unwholesome states.
How do these [defilements] flow along with the mind?
When mental consciousness arises with an object as its focal point, [the defilements flow along with it].
They go forth, they pursue;

with that mind, thought, and consciousness as their objective support, those greed, hatred, and delusion which are associated with it and which give rise to misconduct of body, speech, and mind arise, go forth, and pursue.
Therefore, they are said to follow after the mind.

In this way, first of all, that affliction which arises through the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) and the grasping of secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) regarding forms cognizable by the eye, up to mental objects cognizable by the mind, does not arise for him as he avoids the grasping of signs and the grasping of secondary characteristics. However, if, moreover, through a lapse of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃpramoṣāt*), it should arise...

Either due to an abundance of afflictions, or even when dwelling alone, taking as a dominant condition forms cognizable by the eye that were previously seen, or taking as a dominant condition phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind that were previously experienced, evil and unwholesome states arise; he tolerates those that have arisen.
He abandons, purifies, and brings to an end.
Therefore, it is said that he practices for their restraint:
regarding those forms toward which the eye should be directed,
and regarding those phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind toward which the mind should be directed.
He impels them in such a way that they do not become afflicted;
thus, by this means, the mind-faculty is protected from that affliction.
Therefore, it is said that one guards the faculty of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding those forms cognizable by the eye for which the eye-faculty should not be incited,
and regarding those phenomena cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind for which the mind-faculty should not be incited— one guards them.
In regard to these, he does not incite [the mind] in any way whatsoever;
therefore it is said that "he practices restraint with the faculty of the eye," and so on,
up to "he practices restraint with the faculty of the mind."
This, then, is the detailed analysis of the restraint of the faculties that should be understood;
as for the summary meaning: that by which one restrains, and...
That from which one restrains, the manner in which one restrains,
and that which is the restraint itself.
All of that, condensed into a single unity, is called "restraint of the sense faculties. In this regard, by what does one restrain?
One restrains by means of that mindfulness which is guarded.
What does it restrain?
It restrains the eye faculty;
it restrains the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
This conceals.
From what does it conceal?
It conceals from forms, sounds, and so forth up to mental phenomena that are either pleasant or unpleasant; therefore, it conceals.
How does he restrain himself?
He does not seize upon signs (*nimitta*) nor seize upon secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*),
from which basis evil and unwholesome states (*pāpakā akuśalā dharmāḥ*) flow into the mind.
He practices for their restraint;
he guards the faculty with the faculty;
he attains restraint.
In this way, he restrains [the mind].
What, then, is this restraint?
It is that by which the mind becomes guarded by mindfulness.
It is that which operates within a state of equilibrium;
this is called conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
Furthermore, there is another summary meaning.
That which is the means of restraint,
that which is the object to be restrained, and that which is the restraint itself.
Summarizing that unity, it is called "restraint of the faculties.
In that regard, what is the means of restraint (*saṃvaropāya*)? It is as he said: one becomes one whose mindfulness is guarded.

"Being possessed of steadfast mindfulness" means that having seen forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs (*nimitta*) nor grasp at their secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); likewise,
up to having cognized mental phenomena with the mind, one does not grasp at their signs.
He does not grasp at secondary characteristics;
rather, he practices for the sake of restraint regarding those conditions through which evil and unwholesome states flow into the mind.
One who guards the faculty by means of the faculty attains restraint;
this is called the means of restraint.
What is the object to be restrained?
The eye and visible forms, and so on up to the mind and mental phenomena—this is called the object to be restrained.
In that regard, what is restraint? It is as follows:

He becomes one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness and who dwells in a state of equanimity; this is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). Indeed, this restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) is, in brief, of two kinds.
It is comprised of the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyānabala*) and the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*).
Among these, that which is comprised of the power of discernment is by means of which one perceives the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) in sense objects,
yet does not eliminate that disadvantage.
He abandons them.
In that regard, that which is comprised by the power of cultivation is that by which one perceives the disadvantage in sense objects,
and furthermore, one removes that disadvantage.
He abandons them;

therein, by means of restraint of the faculties comprised within the power of analytical discernment, he does not give rise to, nor bring face-to-face, the obsession of the afflictions regarding objective referents.
Nor does one abandon or eradicate the latent tendency (anuśaya) as it resides within its support.

Therein, by means of the restraint of the sense faculties comprised within the power of cultivation, one does not give rise to, nor manifest, the obsession of the afflictions regarding objects of perception;
and at all times and for all durations, one abandons the latent tendencies (anuśaya) residing in the basis.
He eradicates it;
this is the distinction,
this is the intended meaning.

This non-commissioning refers to the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) comprised by the power of analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyānabala) and the power of cultivation (bhāvanābala).
Among these, that restraint of the sense faculties comprised by the power of analytical discernment is included within the path of equipment (saṃbhāramārga);
whereas that restraint of the sense faculties comprised by the power of cultivation—
He should be known as one who has fallen into the stage of dispassion.
What is moderation in eating?
It is when a certain person here partakes of food with discernment, not for the sake of intoxication, nor for sport, nor for luxury, nor for adornment.
"Not for the sake of adornment, not for the sake of beautification," and so on in detail as before.
How does he consume food with discernment?
Discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is that wisdom by which one perceives the disadvantage of edible food; having become disgusted through the perception of its disadvantages, one consumes it.
Furthermore, what is that perception of disadvantage? It is as follows:
namely, whatever pertains to the sequence of consumption or the sequence of transformation of that very same physical nutriment.
Or [it is] the danger following from the pursuit [of food]. What is the danger following from its consumption?
It is as follows: here, at whatever time a certain person takes food, even when it is endowed with excellent color, [and so forth].
It is endowed with fragrance, endowed with flavor, and most excellent.
As soon as that food by mouthful has been cast into the mouth and ground by the mechanism of the teeth,
it becomes moistened by the flow of saliva and enveloped by saliva.
At that time, it becomes stuck in his throat;
it is that same former,
ancient, and unpleasant state [of the food].
He abandons it entirely in every respect and undergoes a further transformation;
and in that transformation—
The present [food] is known to be like a morsel of food that has been crumbled;

and if this consumer, the person (puruṣapudgala), were to attend to it and recollect it in its actual state— even when the excellent food has not yet undergone any transformation— his desire for enjoyment would not persist at all.

What need is there to speak further of its state at that time? For when one makes the consumption of food the primary focus through these various kinds of methods and this sequence, that beautiful appearance of color which was there vanishes,
and a disadvantage arises, comprised of impurity.
This is called the danger arising from enjoyment,
namely, with regard to food.
In that regard, what is the disadvantage of food resulting from its transformation?
When one has consumed that food, it undergoes transformation during the middle watch of the night or the final watch of the night.
Then he increases and produces within this body many various kinds of impure substances, such as blood, flesh, sinews, bones, skin, and so forth.
And in terms of its actual nature,
it becomes excessively matured and moves toward the lower part of the body,
such that it must be cleared away by him every day.
And by that [wind], whatever is touched—
whether the hand, the feet,
or any other part whatsoever.
Every limb and member must be guarded externally for oneself and for others.
And on account of that,
many bodily afflictions arise in his body,
such as, for example, a boil.
scabies, ringworm, and eczema.
Itching, leprosy, and skin eruptions.
Leucoderma,
fever, cough, swelling, consumption,
and epilepsy.
Dysentery, jaundice, hemorrhage,
and fistula-in-ano— these and other such diseases of this kind are terrifying.
Physical ailments arise in his body;
or what he has eaten becomes indigestible,
whereby choleraic cramps settle within his body.
This is called the disadvantage resulting from transformation (*vipariṇāma*), namely, with respect to food. In that regard, what is the disadvantage resulting from seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*)?
The disadvantage regarding food is manifold, following from the pursuit [of it]: that which is caused by the accumulation [of wealth],
and that which is caused by the guarding [of what has been acquired].
It is caused by the loss of unctuousness,
caused by lack of contentment,
caused by lack of autonomy, and caused by misconduct.

In that regard, what is the disadvantage of food? It is the toil of its acquisition; for instance, here some person, for the sake of food and on account of food, is struck by the cold in the cold season.
Being struck by heat with heat,
he exerts himself and strives.
He exerts himself through agriculture, or cattle-rearing, or trade.
By means of the calculation of scripts, the obsession with counting, numerical seals, and various kinds of crafts and occupations, for the sake of obtaining food not yet obtained,
or for its increase—
just as in the case of food.
Of one who thus exerts himself, strives, and endeavors for the sake of the cause of food; [of him] so striving,
exerting, and endeavoring.
If those undertakings of his fail,
he grieves and becomes exhausted on account of that cause.
He laments,
beats his breast,
cries out, or falls into a state of attachment.
"Alas, my own exertion is indeed in vain and yields no fruit"—
this is the disadvantage associated with the act of gathering, namely, in regard to food.
If he succeeds in acquiring them, he falls into intense anxiety for the sake of guarding them, thinking:
"Might my enjoyments not be seized by the king or by thieves?
Might they not be consumed by fire or swept away by water?"
Or perhaps well-hidden treasures might perish;
or ill-conducted enterprises might collapse; or unpleasant heirs might come into possession [of one's wealth].

Or a "burner of the family" might be born into the clan—one who brings those enjoyments to ruin through improper means. This is the danger associated with the protection [of food], namely, regarding food:
what is the danger caused by the loss of affection?
For example, on account of food, with food as the cause and food as the basis, a mother speaks dispraise of her son; likewise, a son [speaks dispraise] of his mother,
a father of his son, and a son of his father.
A brother [is the relative] of a father; a sister [is the relative] of a brother;
a companion is [the relative] of a companion.
[It is so] for a companion,
let alone for one person toward another.
They...
Furthermore, they become mutually embroiled in conflict;

having fallen into dispute, even such noble brahmins, kṣatriyas, householders, and great landowners, for the very sake of food, being thus embroiled and having fallen into dispute, strike one another with their hands, and even with clods of earth.
They strike even with a staff and even with a weapon; this is called the disadvantage caused by the destruction of affection.
In that regard, what is it?
The disadvantage caused by lack of contentment is as follows:
for instance, there are kings who are Kṣatriyas consecrated by coronation.
Dissatisfied while dwelling within their own villages, towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals, they marched out against both sides’ attacking armies and battle arrays,
with conchs being blown and banners being waved.
As various arrows were being discharged there, they encountered him along with his galloping horse.
They encounter a confused elephant, a chariot, and infantry.
With their limbs mangled by arrows or spears,
they either meet death or experience suffering that is tantamount to death. This is called the state consisting of suffering.
The danger caused by lack of contentment, or whatever else is of a similar nature.
In this regard, what is the disadvantage caused by lack of independence? It is,
for example, when a king's men assault fortified cities.
They are drenched with heated oil,
with heated fat, and so forth.
With a heated ball of cow dung,
with molten copper,
and with molten iron.
With their limbs mangled by arrows and spears,
they either meet death or experience suffering equal to that of death.
This is called the disadvantage caused by lack of independence, or whatever else is of a similar nature.
In that regard, what is the disadvantage caused by misconduct? It is when, for the sake of food, a certain person has committed and accumulated much bodily misconduct.
As it is with the body, so it is with speech and the mind; and that body becomes afflicted with disease.
He was suffering and severely ill;
for him, that previous misconduct of body, speech, and mind [was the cause].
Or, at the time of evening, whatever shadow hangs over the mountains or the mountain peaks;
He hangs down,
he hangs down far;
it occurs to him thus:
"Alas, evil has been done by me; alas, merit has not been performed by me, whether by body, speech, or mind."
Thinking, "I shall go after death to that same destination which belongs to those who have committed evil," he dies with remorse;
and having died at an untimely moment, he is reborn in the states of woe.
Namely, in the hells, among animals, and among hungry ghosts;
this is called the disadvantage caused by misconduct.
It occurs to him:
"Thus, this food is fraught with danger even while being sought."
Even while being consumed, it is accompanied by disadvantages;
even when consumed, its transformation is a disadvantage.
Nevertheless, this nutriment does possess some benefit.
Furthermore, what is that measure?
This body is sustained by nutriment; it persists depending upon nutriment.
This is merely a small portion of its benefit:
that this body, sustained by such food, may remain for a very long time, or indeed endure for a hundred years.
Furthermore, when it is properly avoided for some time or even more,
there is for him an interruption [of the flow] before that point;
therein, those who...
Those who have set out merely for the maintenance of the body are not well-set-out; they are not satisfied by the mere maintenance of the body, yet they are not dissatisfied.
Furthermore, they do not experience the full, blameless, and beneficial benefit resulting from food;
rather, those who [subsist] by means of nothing more than the mere maintenance of the body...
Those who are content with merely maintaining the body and have set out [in practice] are not well-practiced; rather, they are merely intent upon that maintenance of the body itself.
Having resolved upon and relied upon it, they have set out for the full realization of the holy life.
Having practiced well,
they in turn experience the full, faultless benefit.
It would be appropriate for me to dwell content with even a very inferior amount of the benefit of food.

"It would not be fitting for me to fall into the company of fools or to share the nature of fools; thus, having understood in every way the full extent of the danger in food, he, having reflected upon this, seeking both the danger and the escape, takes food as a dharma-means solely for the purpose of escaping from food."
It occurs to him:
"In this way, these givers and masters of generosity have acquired wealth with great difficulty,
experiencing the vast disadvantage consisting of the toil of seeking it."
Having repeatedly pressed, having repeatedly pressed, the skin and flesh.
They offer their own blood to us—

those who, out of compassion, seek a distinguished fruit. For us, this would be a fitting and appropriate use of the alms-food thus obtained, were it such that I [should regard myself as] thus humbled.
Having set it aside, one should enjoy it,
so that the services rendered to them may become exceedingly fruitful, of great benefit,
and of great splendor.
"O you of great expansiveness,
may I, like the moon, approach families with body withdrawn and mind withdrawn."
Possessing a sense of shame, he is not arrogant; he does not exalt himself nor disparage others,
and his mind is well-composed with whatever gains he has received.
May I be well-disposed;
likewise, may my mind be well-disposed and joyful at the gain of another as well.
Furthermore, with such a state of mind, I should enter among families. For how could it be appropriate for one who has gone forth to expect from other families that others should show me honor—
honoring me and not treating me with disrespect?
Abundant, not meager; excellent, not coarse;
swift, not slow.
Thus practicing as I go from family to family, if others should not give to me, I would not become defiled toward them through a mind of malice or a mind of resentment.
Furthermore, on that account, after the dissolution of the body, I would not meet with ruin by being reborn in a state of misery—
namely, that very state of malice.
Taking a mind of resentment as the dominant influence, if it is done without respect and not with respect;
if it is meager and not abundant; if it is coarse and not refined.
If they should not quickly give the bound person,
thinking, "By that, I would be defiled by a mind of malice and a mind of resentment," [he should reflect] in detail as previously described.

And depending upon this edible food, I shall practice in such a way and realize such a measure that there may be no cessation of my life-faculty, nor shall I become exhausted by the search for alms-food.
"May there be support for my celibate life, and may this consumption of alms-food, while I am established in the state of a śramaṇa and the state of one who has gone forth,
be pure and blameless"— in these ways, having reflected, he partakes of food.
Furthermore, what is nutriment?
There are four nutriments: edible food, [contact, mental volition, and consciousness].
In this context, however, contact, mental volition, and consciousness are intended as "edible food."
Furthermore, what is that? It is as follows: either parched grain or cakes, or boiled rice and gruel, or ghee, oil, and molasses.
Meat, fish, and dried meat.
Salt, milk,
and curd.
Fresh butter and other such articles of consumption which are taken after being made into mouthfuls—
therefore, they are called "edible morsels" (*kavaḍaṃkāra*).
"He takes" means he eats;
he partakes of, consumes, chews, and swallows.
"Eats," "tastes," "drinks," and "sucks" are synonyms.
"Not for the sake of pleasure" means those who indulge in sensual desires.
They say: "We, having our limbs refreshed and our bodies satisfied by food, at the time when evening has arrived and the night has passed,"
He was playing with women who wore their hair tied in topknots, whose arms were hairy like those of a gourd, and whose breasts were like balls.
"Delighting ourselves and providing entertainment, we shall manifest levity and frivolity"— this,
Noble One, is frivolity in the Dharma and Vinaya, namely that which is associated with sensual passion.
Evil, unwholesome states associated with sexual intercourse,
and discursive thoughts,
by which he is being devoured.
Being oppressed, his faculties become either excited or unexcited,
and his mind becomes restless.
With a mind that is agitated, unsettled, and unpacified, they consume food excessively; this is called consuming food for the sake of indulgence.
But the learned noble disciple, possessing the power of discernment, seeing the danger and understanding the escape,
partakes [of food],
not in the manner that those who indulge in sensual pleasures partake.
Therefore he said: "not for the sake of sport, not for the sake of intoxication, not for the sake of beautification, nor for the sake of adornment.
This means that those very same enjoyers of sensual pleasures consume food for the sake of [mere] sustenance.
Today we have taken food— namely, abundant and satisfying, according to our capacity and strength;
it is both nourishing and invigorating.
It is nourishing, endowed with excellent color, and endowed with excellent fragrance.
When it has become fuel-like and the night has passed, we shall be capable [of action], being endowed with vigor.
Capable, performing physical exercises,
namely,
by means of stretching or by means of striking.
Whether by means of physical exercise, or by jumping up and down, or by digging into the earth;
Whether by the exertion of the arms,
or by the pressing of the feet, or by leaping; (a)
Or by means of leaping.
In that regard, through physical exercise,
and furthermore by relying on repeated exercise, we shall become strong.
(a) Our limbs will be well-proportioned, we shall be long-lived and free from disease, and our youth will endure for a long time.
But they do not think, "The aging that causes deformity will soon overcome the body," nor do they think, "We shall live for a very long time."
And we shall be capable of consuming large quantities,
and what has been eaten will be properly digested.
"The humors will be diminished," thinking thus for the sake of pride in one's health.
They enjoy them for the sake of the pride of youth and for the sake of the pride of life;
furthermore, it occurs to them as follows:
"Having finished our exercise, we shall prepare for bathing;
that is to say, we shall wash our limbs with pure water. And having washed our limbs, [we shall wash] our hair."
We shall adorn ourselves;
having anointed our bodies with various ointments,
we shall decorate our bodies with various garments, various garlands, and various ornaments.

In this context, that which consists of bathing, grooming, and anointing is called their "adornment. Likewise, for those who have engaged in such adornment, the wearing of clothes, garlands, and ornaments is what is called [the act of adorning].
Regarding "ornamentation":
they enjoy [these things] for the sake of beautifying and adorning themselves; thus, being intoxicated with pride, their bodies are adorned with various kinds of ornaments.
At the time of midday,
or at the time of evening,
during the mealtime, they were thirsty and hungry.
With supreme joy, with supreme delight, and with supreme gladness.
Seeing the danger but not knowing the way of escape, they take food as it is provided,
merely for the sake of repeated refreshment.
For the sake of adornment and for the sake of embellishment; however,
the learned noble disciple [does not do so].
One who possesses the power of discernment, seeing the danger and knowing the escape, partakes [of food];
but not in the manner that those who indulge in sensual pleasures partake.
He does so thinking: "It is only by consuming this food—which is not for the sake of physical attachment—that I shall abandon what is to be abandoned."
"Only for the maintenance of this body"—having eaten, and not without having eaten—is what is called the maintenance of the body for the sake of life.
Thinking, "Having taken this food, I shall live; I shall not die," one partakes of food.
Therefore, he says: "I take food only for the maintenance of this body and for its sustenance. (Śbh_Sh: 89)

There are two kinds of sustenance: that which is with difficulty and that which is without difficulty. What is sustenance with difficulty? It is that form of nutriment by which hunger or weakness arises.
Or he is suffering or severely ill;
or he seeks almsfood through unrighteous means, not through righteous means.
He consumes with attachment, clinging, and greed.
He is bound,
infatuated, attached, and has fallen into attachment;
moreover, his body becomes heavy and unwieldy.
It is incapable of being abandoned,
by which his mind enters into concentration slowly, or by which inhalation and exhalation proceed with difficulty.
When the mind is overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, it is said that one's livelihood is achieved with difficulty.
What is livelihood without difficulty?
Just as when one consumes such food that neither hunger nor weakness occurs, nor does it become excessive, nor does one become suffering or severely ill.
He seeks almsfood in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to the Dharma;
or, being well-attached, he consumes it, or being unattached, he consumes it.
He is not greedy, not bound, not intent, and has not fallen into a state of obsession;
furthermore, his body does not become heavy.
He becomes workable and capable of abandonment,
whereby his mind is quickly concentrated.
Inhalation and exhalation proceed with little difficulty,
and the mind is not overwhelmed by sloth and torpor.
The third is said to be sustenance with little difficulty. In that regard, by means of that sustenance which involves difficulty, the maintenance of life occurs;
however, for the body, it is faulty and afflicted.
In that regard, that maintenance of life which occurs with little difficulty for the body is,
moreover, irreproachable.
It is unafflicted. In this regard, the learned noble disciple avoids a way of life that is blameworthy and afflicted.
He leads and practices a livelihood that is blameless and unafflicted;
therefore, it is said: "for the sake of maintenance."
Furthermore, how does he maintain that blameless and unafflicted livelihood which was previously described?
He says:
If this [eating] is for the sake of ending hunger,
for the support of the holy life,
so that I may abandon old feelings and not produce new ones;
And for me there will be a journey,
as well as strength, happiness, blamelessness, and a state of dwelling in comfort.
Practicing in this way, he maintains a livelihood that is blameless and unafflicted.
Furthermore, how does he take food for the sake of allaying hunger? When the time for a meal has arrived, [he takes it].
When hunger has arisen,
he eats in order to remove that very obsession of hunger and the weakness of hunger, and he eats in such a measure that,
having eaten, the weakness of hunger does not again afflict him at an improper time.
at the time of evening, or when the night has passed, or on the following day,
When the time for food has arrived,
he eats in this way for the sake of removing hunger;
how does he eat for the sake of supporting the holy life?
He consumes that measure and takes such food that,
for him who is engaged in the side of wholesome qualities, immediately after eating or on that very day, his body becomes free from heaviness and becomes serviceable.
And it is capable of abandonment, by which his mind is very quickly concentrated;
inhalations and exhalations proceed with little difficulty.
He does not become overwhelmed by sloth and torpor,
whereby he becomes capable and competent.
For the sake of quickly attaining what has not yet been attained,
for the sake of realizing what has not yet been realized, and for the sake of manifesting what has not yet been manifested.
In this way, he takes [food] for the sake of supporting the holy life.

"How shall I abandon past sensations?"— thinking thus, one consumes food; yet even so, it may have been consumed in immoderate measure, or it may have been unwholesome (*apathyam*) with respect to the past time.
or if it is undigested, by which a various bodily affliction arises for him;
such as, for example, itching.
Leprosy, ringworm, and vitiligo— in detail as previously described—
and for him, bodily sensations that are painful, intense, and rooted in disease arise.
Harsh, pungent,
and unpleasant.

Seeing what is beneficial, wholesome, agreeable, and conducive for the pacification of that affliction and for the pacification of those painful sensations caused by it, he partakes of medicine according to the method prescribed by the physician;
and he consumes suitable food.
He takes food with the thought: "By this means, there shall be the abandonment of this arisen affliction and of the painful feelings caused by it; thus I shall abandon old feelings.
Relying on the present time, he is happy and free from disease.
He consumes [food] either with strength or in moderation;
it is neither unwholesome nor undigested,
and it does not cause him harm in the present or in the future.
Either tomorrow or the day after,
cholera might take hold in his body,
or some other kind of physical ailment might arise in his body.
Namely: itch, leprosy, and scabies.
"Leucoderma," and so on in detail as before;
whatever bodily sensations might arise due to that cause, as before.
And thus, thinking "I shall not give rise to new feeling," he takes food [with the thought]:
"How will my sustenance be maintained?"
He brings about complexion, happiness, blamelessness,
and a state of easeful abiding;
insofar as one lives having eaten, such is sustenance.
Furthermore, that which removes hunger and weakness—
this is its color;
furthermore, that which abandons old feelings— this is its function.
And he does not give rise to new [afflictions]; thus he experiences happiness.
Furthermore, having sought almsfood in accordance with the Dharma, he remains unattached.
"Unattached," and so forth in detail, as previously explained, constitutes faultlessness. Furthermore, for one who has eaten, the body does not become heavy,
but becomes serviceable.
Being capable of abandonment in detail as previously described, such is his state of dwelling in ease (*sparśavihāratā*).
Therefore, it is said: "He takes food with discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāya*);
not for the sake of sport."
"Not for the sake of intoxication,
nor for the sake of adornment"— this,
as explained in detail previously, is the extensive analysis of moderation in eating.
Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning? It is said:
that which one consumes, and...
And how he consumes it— namely, solid food, such as barley meal or other edibles.
Whether it be cakes,
or boiled rice with gruel, as described in detail previously;
how does he consume it?
He consumes it with discernment,
not for the sake of sport, not for the sake of intoxication, and not for the sake of adornment— thus in detail as previously described.
Furthermore, the summary meaning is this:
he consumes [food] while it is embraced by its antidote.
It avoids the extreme of devotion to sensual pleasure and avoids the extreme of self-mortification, for the sake of supporting the holy life.
As it is said:
"Having reflected wisely, one partakes of food;
how does one avoid the extreme of devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires?"
As it is said:
"Not for the sake of intoxication, nor for the sake of exhilaration."
"Not for the sake of adornment, nor for the sake of beautification.
How is it free from the extreme of self-mortification?
As it is said: "For the sake of allaying hunger,
and so that I may abandon former sensations..."
I shall not give rise to new [defilements],
and I shall have sustenance,
strength, and happiness.
How does he consume [food] for the sake of supporting the holy life?
As it is said:
"for the sake of supporting the holy life."
"And there will be for me blamelessness and a state of dwelling in comfort"—
this is another summary of the meaning.
There are these two: eating and non-eating.
Among them, non-eating is when one does not consume anything at all, in any way, and in every respect.
And one dies from not eating.
In that regard, food is of two kinds: balanced food, and...
And there is irregular eating.
In that regard, balanced eating is that which is neither too little nor too much.
It is not unwholesome, nor is it defiled by being undigested;
therein lies irregular eating.
If it is too little or too much,
or if it is undigested, or if it is unwholesome;
Or he consumes [food] that is defiled.
In that case, when eating moderately and not eating too little, he does not produce, nor does he allow to arise, the weakness of hunger.
One abandons what has arisen;
therein, by not eating too much,
one avoids uneven eating.
The body becomes heavy and unwieldy, incapable of exertion for abandonment, as described in detail previously.
In that regard, by means of digested food and balanced eating, one abandons old sensations.
And he will not produce new [defilements]; thus his maintenance,
strength, and happiness proceed through food that is undefiled.
Through moderate eating, there is both blamelessness and a state of well-being. In this regard, "extremely little food" is that by which one merely survives.
Excessive eating, by which his body becomes overwhelmed by a heavy burden and he does not eat at the proper time.
It transforms [in the stomach].
There, by means of food that has not been properly digested, cholera (viṣūcikā) remains in the body,
or some other kind of physical ailment arises in the body.
It arises just as it does from food that has not been properly digested; likewise, it arises from unwholesome food.
In this regard, the distinction concerning unwholesome food is as follows:
The humors increase,
or he encounters a harsh affliction.
In that regard, by means of defiled food— having sought alms through unrighteous means— he consumes it with attachment.
"Attached, greedy, and fettered," and so on in detail as before;
thus, he who partakes of moderate food.
He also avoids irregular eating;
therefore, he is said to be one who practices moderation in food.
This practice of moderation in food has been explained by these characteristics.
It has been laid open, disclosed, and fully revealed.
That is to say, he takes food with discernment:
not for the sake of amusement, nor for the sake of intoxication.
"Not for the sake of adornment, not for the sake of beautification," and so on in detail as before.
(Śbh_Sh: 96)
In that regard, as for what he said:
"One consumes food with discernment,
not for the sake of amusement,"
Not for the sake of intoxication,
not for the sake of beautification, nor for the sake of ornamentation.
...only for the maintenance of this body, for its sustenance; by this much, it is not [the case that] he abstains from food.
He rejects [that view].
Furthermore, as for what he says: "for the sake of the cessation of hunger,"
"For the sake of supporting the holy life," and so on at length, "up to for the sake of dwelling in comfort"—by this, he rejects irregular eating.
And how, moreover, is there irregular eating? (It is) excessive eating.
He rejects it.
First, by saying "for the sake of supporting the holy life," he rejects excessive eating;
this is what he says.
By the thought, "I shall abandon old feelings and shall not give rise to new ones," he rejects both eating undigested food and eating unwholesome food.
As it is said:
"By this [moderation], there will be for me sustenance and strength; thus, [it prevents] excessive scantiness of food."
And he demonstrates (or rejects) the state of food being composed of primary elements;
for when he says, "I shall have happiness," by this he demonstrates the state of food being transformed.
When he says, "I shall have happiness," he demonstrates the practice of eating wholesome food;
as it is said:
"By the statement, 'I shall possess blamelessness and a state of dwelling in comfort,' he demonstrates the quality of eating without affliction.
This refers to one who, having sought almsfood through improper means, is [thereby] impassioned."
He partakes [of it],
being attached— as described in detail previously—
and he partakes while being afflicted.
And there is faultfulness for him regarding that very seclusion and yoga of one who is devoted to the side of the wholesome.
In attention, in recitation, and in reflection on the meaning, those very same evil and unwholesome thoughts flow along with his mind, which are constant for him.
They cause the continuum of consciousness to proceed as being inclined toward that, tending toward that, and leaning toward that.
By means of which he does not have a pleasant abiding (*sparśavihāra*).

And this state of having a pleasant abiding is twofold: through the avoidance of excessive food, by which his body does not become heavy, unwieldy, or incapable of exertion for abandonment—as described in detail previously.
By not making it delicious through subsequent [flavoring], he does not experience a state of non-comfort caused by the agitation of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*).
This being so, the practice of moderation regarding food is explained by all these phrases.
This is called moderation in eating.
In detail and in brief.
What is the practice of being devoted to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?
In that regard, what is the first watch of the night? What is [the last watch of the night]?
The latter part of the night.
What is the application to wakefulness?
What is the state of being devoted to the application to wakefulness?
In that regard, this is the evening and the midnight.
The first part of the night, beginning from sunset at the end of the afternoon, is "more than one watch" (*sātireka-prahara*).
In that regard, this is the practice of wakefulness (*jāgarikā-yoga*).
As it is said:
"By means of walking and sitting during the day, he purifies his mind of obstructive states;
having purified it,"
Having washed his feet outside the monastery and entered the monastery, he prepares his bed on his right side,
placing one foot upon the other, perceiving light, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Keeping the perception of rising in mind, he wakes up very quickly during the last watch of the night and purifies his mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting meditation.
In this regard, this is the application to the practice of vigilance:
namely, when one is a listener to the Blessed Buddha’s teaching on the yoga of vigilance for his disciples,
and therein desires to train.

Regarding this state as it truly is, whatever desire, vigor (*vīrya*), exertion, and striving there is, [arising from] the thought, "I shall accomplish the application to wakefulness that has been authorized by the Buddhas," beginning with the practice of wakefulness— this is [the basis for non-laxity].
The undertaking of the basis for valor consists of enthusiasm,
fortitude, and the non-retrogression of the mind;
it is the gathering [of resources], which may be with fault.
In that regard, how does one purify the mind from obstructive states through walking and sitting?
"Day" is said to be the period beginning from the time of sunrise until the time of sunset.
The walking meditation path (*caṅkrama*) is described as follows:
on a level stretch of ground that has been prepared over a vast area, it consists of the practice of going back and forth.
The sitting posture for the practice of the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) is described as follows:
namely, when a certain person here sits upon a couch or a stool.
He sits upon a grass mat,
having folded his legs crosswise,
set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
The obscurations are said to be the five hindrances (*pañca nivaraṇāni*).
What, then, are the obscuring factors—those factors conducive to the hindrances that lead to further hindrances? They are as follows:
Sensual desire, ill will, sloth, torpor, and restlessness.
remorse, doubt,
and impurity;
The sign of resistance is darkness;
the recollection of kinsmen, one's native land, and immortality; discursive thoughts concerning past laughter, play, and enjoyment; and the three times.
And improper reflection on phenomena pertaining to the three times—
from these, how does one purify the mind through walking meditation?
And from how many [factors] does one purify it?
He purifies [the mind] from the hindrance of sloth and torpor, as well as from that which nourishes sloth and torpor; by means of this,
he thoroughly and properly cultivates the sign of light.
It is well-grasped,
well-attended to, and well-relished.
It is well-penetrated;
with a mind accompanied by light and accompanied by great radiance, whether in a sheltered place, or...
Or, while walking back and forth in an open space on a walking path, he directs his mind toward one or another inspiring object of focus.
He inspires and gladdens them, namely, by means of the recollection of the Buddha.
Or by means of the recollection of the Dharma, the Saṅgha, ethical discipline, renunciation, and the deities;
or else, he has heard, taken up, and retained teachings concerning the disadvantages of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*) with respect to the body,
such as those found in the Sūtras and so forth.

In that exposition— which consists of prose discourses, verses, inspired utterances, introductory narratives, legends, historical accounts, birth stories, extensive teachings, marvelous events, and instructions—
in which sloth and torpor have been censured in many ways,
The abandonment of sloth and torpor, moreover, is censured; yet its abandonment is praised, extolled, and commended.
He recites them aloud to them in detail,
or explains them to others, or reflects upon their meaning.
He weighs and examines them,
or he gazes toward the directions;
or he fixes his gaze upon the four lunar mansions, planets, and stars, or moistens his face with water.

In this way, that obsession of sloth and torpor which has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen passes away; thus, by this means, his mind is purified from those obstructive states.
In that regard, by means of sitting, from which obstructive states does he purify the mind?
[He strives] against sensual desire, ill-will, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt, as well as against those factors that nourish them;
and he does so for the purpose of dispelling sensual desire when it has arisen, or for the purpose of keeping it at a distance when it has not yet arisen.
Having sat down,
having folded his legs crosswise, and having set his body erect,
Having established mindfulness directed toward the front, [he contemplates] the livid corpse, or...
Or as putrefied, or as festering, or as bloated,
Or a gnawed corpse, or a blood-stained corpse, or a skeleton.
Or he attends to a skeleton, or to any other suitable object of concentration (samādhinimitta),
or to those teachings which, concerning the very abandonment of sensual desire, have been undertaken for the sake of abandoning sensual desire.
They were retained, mastered through speech, examined by the mind,
and thoroughly penetrated by insight.
Namely: the discourses (sūtra), the songs (geya), the prophecies (vyākaraṇa), and so forth, in detail as previously described.
Those who, by way of many methods, [have abandoned] sensual desire,
sensual longing, attachment to sensual pleasures, and fixation on sensual pleasures;
They censure, disparage, and loathe attachment to sensual desires.
They praise, extol, and laud the abandonment of sensual desire in many ways.

Seated thus, he attends to those phenomena in an improper manner; in this way, the obsession of sensual desire that has not yet arisen does not arise in him, and the obsession of sensual desire that has already arisen passes away.
In that regard, this is the distinction concerning ill-will (*vyāpāda*).

Seated thus, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— free from enmity, free from ill will, free from affliction, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated— he, having resolved upon one direction, dwells pervading it with mindfulness.
Having attained it, he dwells therein;
likewise the second,
likewise the third.
Likewise, having brought to mind the fourth [state]— the entire infinite world above, below, and across—
and having attained it, he dwells therein; the rest is as before.
In that regard, there is a distinction concerning restlessness and remorse:
namely, while seated, he settles the mind within itself and settles it thoroughly.
He thoroughly purifies it,
makes it one-pointed,
and brings it into meditative equipoise.
The rest is as before;
however, there is a distinction regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*).
He sat down in that manner.
He does not attend to the past time in an improper manner;
he does not attend to the future or the present time in an improper manner. He does not think: "Did I indeed exist in the past? Who was I in the past?"
Or rather, does he think: "Was I not in the past? Who indeed was I?
How indeed was I in the past?
Who indeed shall I be?"
In the future time,
how shall I be in the future time?
Being what, what shall we become?
From where has this being come?

What is that which has the self as its dominant influence?

By means of that which causes affliction of the mind, which causes weakness of wisdom, and which belongs to the side of harm— in this way, having made himself the master, he purifies his mind from those factors that are obstructive.

The deities as well,

herein, when an hindrance has arisen,

Thus he thinks: "If I were to give rise to an unarisen hindrance,

Making the world itself his authority,
he does not give rise to an unarisen hindrance,

Thus, making the world his authority, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. Furthermore,

for the sake of protecting his bedding and seating and in order to conform to worldly conduct, he purifies his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting during the first watch of the night.
Having purified his mind of obstructive states, he washes his feet outside the monastery;
having washed them and entered the monastery,
he prepares his bed.
It is solely for the sake of the accumulation of the primary elements that constitute one's own growth;
once this body has been accumulated, it will become more serviceable.
And why does one lie on one’s side when practicing the application of the wholesome side continuously and with single-minded devotion? It is for the sake of similarity with the creature, the lion.
What, then, is the point of similarity here?
A lion is the most powerful among all living beings belonging to the animal realm.
Zealous and firm in his prowess,
the monk also dwells devoted to wakefulness and has initiated heroic effort.
Being valiant, energetic,
and of firm prowess,
a lion-like posture is therefore appropriate for him as a bed.
but not the bed of a hungry ghost, nor the bed of a god, nor the bed of sensual enjoyment.
For indeed, they are all entirely indolent,
lacking in vigor, and deficient in strength and prowess.
Moreover, it is the very nature of things that when one arranges a lion-like posture for sleep on the right side, there is no such displacement of the limbs;
nor does there occur a loss of mindfulness while lying down,
nor does one fall into a deep sleep.
And he does not see evil dreams;
however, for one who prepares his bed otherwise, all faults should be understood to arise by way of the opposite.
Therefore, it is said that he prepares his bed on his right side.
By this, the sign of light has been well-grasped,
well-attended to,
well-cultivated, and well-penetrated.
Whatever he brings to mind, with a mind accompanied by that radiance, he prepares his bed;
and even while asleep, because of this, there is no state of mental darkness for him— thus, perceiving light, he prepares his bed.
How does he, being mindful, prepare his bed?
It is by means of those dharmas which have been heard, reflected upon, or cultivated by him.
His mindfulness— consisting of wholesome states connected with the goal and following in their wake— continues even during the time of sleep;
such that even while he is asleep, those very same phenomena speak to him as if he were awake, and his mind repeatedly dwells upon those very phenomena.
Thus, according to his mindfulness and as he has remembered it,
he prepares his bed with either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
Thus, being mindful, he prepares his bed. How does he prepare his bed with clear comprehension?
When, while he is thus asleep or even while he is awake, his mind becomes afflicted by any one of the secondary afflictions,
he correctly understands that very affliction as it arises and does not tolerate it.
He abandons, he penetrates,
and he turns back his mind.
Therefore, it is said that he lies down with full awareness.
How does he lie down while attending to the perception of rising?
Having firmly grasped his mind with vigor, he prepares his bed with a state of full alertness and a joyful heart,
just like a wild deer in the forest.
But he does not make his mind entirely pierced through, inclined toward entry,
or flowing toward that,
nor even fully absorbed in it.
And this thought occurs to him: "O, would that I might accomplish in every way and in all respects the state of wakefulness authorized by the Buddhas!"
And for the sake of accomplishing that, one should act with aspiration, with aesthetic flavor (rasa),
and with practical application.
He dwells with zeal and is devoted;
moreover, it occurs to him:
"Just as I am today... (Śbh_Sh: 108)
I dwelt having initiated vigor for the sake of wakefulness,
for the cultivation of wholesome qualities,
being skillful and untiring.
Endowed with diligence,
at dawn tomorrow,
when the night has passed, he set out.
"I shall dwell with even greater intensity of exerted vigor and be endowed with alertness.
In that regard, by means of one notion of alertness, he sleeps soundly;
whereby I—
He is able to rise very quickly indeed at the time for rising;

By means of the second perception of rising, he arranges the lion’s posture authorized by the Buddha—neither deficient nor excessive.
By means of the third perception, that of exertion, he does not let his zeal slacken;
even when there is a lapse of mindfulness,
he applies himself to further and further undertaking.
Thus, attending to the perception of rising itself, he prepares his bed.
In the last watch of the night, he awakens very quickly and purifies his mind from obstructive states;
this is called the last watch.
The latter part of the night lasts for more than one watch; and during that time,
he remains mindful and clearly comprehending, perceiving light.
Keeping the perception of rising in mind,
having allowed sleep to descend for slightly more than a watch during the middle watch, at which time—
He emerges at the proper time;
he emerges at that very moment.
The body becomes fit for action;
having risen, he is not overcome by an excessive obsession of sloth and torpor,
by which there might be sluggishness or dullness in him as he rises.
Or laziness and indolence; or, even in the absence of that sluggishness,
[the lack of application].
In the state of sluggishness,

laziness, and indolence, there is an extremely swift arousal [of energy] by mere attention; or else, having engaged in combat against the obstructive factors (*āvaraṇīya-dharma*), purification is to be understood as before.
This, then, is the detailed analysis of the application to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night. What, however, are the summarized points?
Here, for a person who is devoted to the practice of wakefulness, there are four things that must be correctly performed.
Which four?
As long as one is awake, one does not abandon the side of wholesome qualities.
He practices the cultivation of wholesome qualities belonging to one side with continuity, and he goes to sleep at the proper time,
not at an improper time;
and while asleep, he enters into sleep with an unafflicted mind.
His mind is not afflicted;
he awakens at the proper time and does not let the time for rising pass by.
Thus, with reference to these four things that ought to be correctly practiced, the Blessed One taught the practice of wakefulness to his disciples.
And how was it taught? First, he said:
During the day, he purifies his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting;
likewise during the first watch of the night— by this, the first thing that ought to be correctly performed has been explained.
That is to say, as long as they remain awake, they do not abandon the side of wholesome qualities;
they practice the cultivation of wholesome dharmas belonging to a single side with continuity.
Furthermore, it says: having washed his feet outside the monastery and entered the monastery, ...
He prepares his bed on the right side,
placing one foot upon the other; by this, the second thing to be correctly practiced is declared,
namely, that he prepares his bed at the proper time.
Not at an improper time;
furthermore, as it says:
"possessing the perception of light, mindful."
By the statement, "being fully aware and keeping in mind the perception of rising, he prepares his bed," the third thing to be correctly practiced is explained.
That is to say, he enters into sleep with an unafflicted mind,

not with an afflicted mind. Furthermore, when it says that in the final watch of the night he wakes up very quickly and purifies his mind from obstructive states, by this the fourth right practice is explained.
That is to say, he awakens at the proper time; he does not let the time for rising pass by.
In this regard, it was said: "Possessing the perception of light and being mindful."
Being fully aware and keeping the perception of rising in mind, he lies down;
thus, by these two causes, he enters into sleep with an undefiled mind.
Namely, through mindfulness and clear comprehension;
furthermore, by two causes, he awakens at the proper time.
But he does not let the time pass,
namely, by means of the perception of light and the perception of rising.
Furthermore, how does one sleep after having grasped a wholesome object of focus?
By means of clear comprehension;
therefore—
He very quickly and correctly understands the mind as it falls away from a wholesome object and as it becomes defiled;
thus, by these two causes, his sleep occurs with an undefiled mind.
Therein, by means of the perception of light and the perception of rising,
one does not sleep deeply.
That obsession of sleep does not persist for him for long;
thus, by these two causes, he awakens at the proper time and does not let the time for rising pass by.
This is the summary of the meaning of the application to wakefulness:
both that which was the previous detailed analysis and this present summary of the meaning.
This is called being devoted to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.

Whether emaciated, or afflicted with leprosy, or one whose limbs are pained and ruined,
whose body is decayed, and whose sense faculties are impaired;
Or dead, having passed away; or dead for one day, or dead for two days.
Or [a corpse] dead for seven days,
being devoured by crows, ospreys, and vultures;
Being devoured or dragged away by dogs, jackals, or various other creatures belonging to the animal realm,
he is placed upon a bier with a canopy spread over it; furthermore—
And behind him was a great multitude of people weeping and wailing. (Śbh_Sh: 124) From that... [he departed].
With disheveled hair and loose locks,
he was likewise overcome by grief and filled with suffering.

One should see forms such as those born of lamentation, born of mental distress, and born of despair— thinking "this is what must be seen by me"— as well as other forms of a similar kind that should be seen.
Those which conduce to the support of the holy life and to the manifestation of wholesome thoughts.
One should not approach shaking the body, nor shaking the arms, nor shaking the head.
Not by holding [the bowl] too high, nor by grasping it with the hand,
nor by lifting it up,
nor without having been permitted.
One should not sit down on a seat without first inspecting it, nor should one sit with the entire body pressed against it.
He should not place one foot upon the other, nor cross one thigh over the other, nor draw his feet together.
Not with feet crossed, not with the head covered by a cloth, nor with [the body] raised high.
Not with the robe tucked up, not with the robe hanging down, nor with the robe draped over one shoulder, but having put on the robe evenly all around.
Neither too high, nor too low, nor crooked.
One should not wear a garment made of elephant-ear cloth, nor one made of palm-leaf, nor one made of *nāgaphalaka* wood,
nor one made of a lump of fermented beans.
The bowl should not be held out for hard food before it has been brought forward,
nor should one cause [the bowl] to be placed over hard or soft food. Nor [should one do so] on a patch of ground that is not strewn [with grass], or on a precipice.
The bowl should be placed down, and the alms-food should be taken in order.
It should be used;
a bathing cloth must not be covered with boiled rice.
Not by means of curry,
nor by means of rice, nor by being devoted to the practice of sour gruel.
It should be eaten;
it should not be too large nor too small; one should form mouthfuls that are round in shape (one should form each mouthful).
One should not lick the hands; one should not lick the bowl;
one should not snap the fingers.
One should not rinse the bowl;
one should not cut up morsels of almsfood.
It should be consumed.
Even when I have gone to the monastery and returned from those families, I [should remain mindful].
Having gone forth, whether by day or by night.
One should practice walking meditation on a walkway designated for individuals,
not one that is out of sight,
nor one that is untrustworthy, nor one where one has not been invited.
without having been assigned [a task],
with body exhausted, with body fatigued.

When the mind is neither excited nor suppressed, being applied to the side of the wholesome, accompanied by non-mental engagement, with the sense faculties turned inward and the mind not directed outward,
he should practice neither too hurriedly nor too restlessly.
Not exclusively engaged in going and returning,
but going from time to time and staying from time to time.
Likewise, in his own monastery,
in his own group of cells, or in his own small hut.
In a [house] designated for a specific person,
intended for an individual, not belonging to another faction, not being untrustworthy, and where one has not been invited;
Likewise, on a couch, or on a chair, or on a bed of grass.
or in the forest, or at the foot of a tree,
or in an empty dwelling,
One should sit down,
having folded the legs crosswise and set the body erect.
Having established mindfulness directed toward the front,
one should sleep during the middle watch of the night.
And the first watch of the day should be spent in the cultivation of wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, one should sleep in this manner:
perceiving light, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Keeping the perception of rising in mind,
awakening very quickly in the final watch of the night, whether for the sake of recitation or...
Or one should apply oneself to the practice of recitation,
or to abandonment, or to seclusion, or to reflection on the Dharma.
And one should avoid those Lokāyata mantras which consist of variegated syllables and variegated words and phonemes,
which are connected with what is meaningless, and which do not lead to super-knowledge.
They do not lead to full enlightenment, nor to nirvana;
yet there are those dharmas spoken by the Tathagata which [do so].
Profound,
appearing profound,
and associated with emptiness.
This conditionality,
which conforms to dependent origination, should be grasped with reverence,
firmly and steadfastly.
They should be well-grasped and not allowed to be lost,
for the sake of accomplishing them through practice.
Not for the sake of gain or honor;
furthermore, those teachings should be thoroughly mastered through speech,
and one should not spend time in social company.
Not by delighting in work,
nor by delighting in talk,
but by means of mindfulness established from time to time, having understood [the situation].
They should be addressed and conversed with by those practicing the holy life (brahmacārins).
They should be encouraged to attain full awakening;
one should be inclined toward inquiry and seek after what is wholesome.
With a mind of non-apprehension,
speaking measuredly, and speaking appropriately.
And with speech that is perfectly tranquil.

Having delivered a discourse on the Dharma to others, one should not indulge in sinful and unwholesome thoughts through silence when one does not wish to speak, nor should one engage in improper reflection on unrighteous matters.
In this way, many such qualities have been grasped by him—
retained and mastered through speech.
They have been examined by the mind and thoroughly penetrated by vision;
in this way, one becomes one of great learning.
How does one become an attainer?
One becomes a possessor of the perception of impermanence.
the perception of suffering in the impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering,
and the perception of repulsiveness in food;
the perception of the livid, the perception of the scattered, and the perception of the skeletal;
He becomes a possessor of the perception of the contemplation of emptiness regarding the first dhyāna.
Of the second,
the third, the fourth— the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
of loving-kindness,
compassion,
and equanimity.
of sympathetic joy,
of the fruit of stream-entry, and of the fruits of once-returning and non-returning;
Of the two objects,
of the recollection of past lives,
and of the divine ear.
He becomes capable of [knowing] death and rebirth, the diversity of minds, arhatship, and the meditative cultivation of the eight liberations.
And he is capable of instructing others by means of the three miracles:
the miracle of supernatural power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.
Through the miracle of instruction,
one becomes thus an attainer;
how does one become compassionate?
He is compassionate toward others; he is endowed with sympathy and desires their welfare.
Desirous of welfare, desirous of happiness, desirous of comfort, and desirous of security.
In this way, he is compassionate;
how is it that he becomes one whose mind is untiring?
He is one who demonstrates the excellence of the practice.
He is one who encourages,
inspires, and gladdens;
he understands the four assemblies.
He is skillful and untiring in teaching the Dharma, endowed with diligence,
and has initiated heroic effort.
One who is of a nature that has initiated vigor thus becomes one whose mind is free from weariness. How does one become patient?
When reviled, he does not revile in return; when provoked to anger, he does not respond with anger;
when struck, he does not strike back.
Though adorned, he does not adorn others;
by this, his taking and giving are equal even when subjected to severe bonds.
in confinements, in beatings, in threats, and in mutilations.
Regarding gifts, he recognizes his own fault and turns instead toward the ripening of karma;
he does not become angry with others.
Nor does he harbor any latent resentment;
thus, even when insulted or reviled, [he remains unperturbed].
Even when reviled,
he does not become corrupted; rather,
he intends only for the sake of the goal and remains patient.
of cold and heat, of hunger and thirst,
[Places] infested with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and crawling reptiles,
and [subjected] to the harsh words of others that are ill-spoken and offensive.
of falling,
of bodily sensations,
and of sufferings.
intense, harsh, and bitter.
He is patient toward unpleasant things and life-threatening [conditions], being by nature one who endures them;
thus he is one who possesses patience.
How does one become confident?
With an undaunted mind,
one teaches the Dharma in the assembly.
He possessed a voice free from stammering, with unfailing memory and eloquence;
and for him, there was no cause for timidity.
Or he experiences fear, or is overcome by it, on account of timidity.
Nor is sweat released through trembling, nor from diseases or exhaustion;
thus he becomes confident.
How is one endowed with the faculty of speech?
One is possessed of noble speech.
With speech that was beautiful,
clear, intelligible, and worthy of being heard;
It is non-contradictory,
independent, and inexhaustible.
Thus, he is endowed with eloquence;
he is one who speaks well.
Being possessed of these eight qualities, he becomes an exhorter.
One who reminds, one who advises, one who instructs, and one who teaches the Dharma.
And how does one become an exhorter?
Namely, by means of a failure in morality regarding higher morality,
and by means of a failure in conduct regarding higher conduct.
One reproaches based on what has been seen, what has been heard, or through suspicion.
It is true, not false;
it is timely, not untimely; it is connected with benefit, not connected with harm.
With gentleness, not with harshness,
and with friendliness.
Not out of malice.
Thus is one an exhorter.
How is one a reminder?
Or he causes [the other] to remember an offense,
or the Dharma, or the meaning.
How does he cause [the other] to remember an offense?
For example, when one commits an offense and remembers it,
he reminds him:
"Venerable sir, in such and such a place..."
In this matter, in that [matter].
At the proper time, he causes [the monk] to remember the offense by saying, "It was of such a nature, and at such a time you fell into it.
How does he cause him to remember the Dharma?
Just as when one, being alone, recollects the teachings (dharma) that have been heard and mastered,
and desires to recollect them—
such as a discourse (sūtra)— ...
He does not remember, as before in detail, the *geya*, the *vyākaraṇa*, and so forth;
he causes him to remember it.
Or he provides him with a reminder,
or an inquiry and a further questioning;
in this way, he causes him to remember the teachings.
How does one cause [the other] to remember the Dharma (or its meaning)? Just as one does not cause [them] to forget the teachings (or their meanings).
He causes him to remember this; he makes it fresh once again; he clarifies it.
He teaches and fully elucidates that which is wholesome, conducive to the goal,
and conducive to the holy life.
He causes one to remember even what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago;
in this way, he is a reminder.
How does one become an instructor regarding seclusion,
solitary retreat,
and yoga?
While attending to [the object], he from time to time imparts appropriate instruction regarding calm abiding and insight,
and from time to time engages in discourse connected therewith.
Namely: a discourse on ethical discipline, or a discourse on wisdom, or a discourse on liberation, which leads to the removal of mental hindrances and is conducive to well-being.
Or discourse on having few desires, or discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation, or discourse on contentment.
a discourse on abandonment,
a discourse on dispassion, and a discourse on cessation;
discourse on diminution, discourse on non-association, and discourse on specific conditionality; (Śbh_Sh: 133)
He delivers a discourse that accords with dependent origination;
in this way, he becomes an instructor.
How does one become an instructor? One becomes either a teacher within the instruction of the Instructor, according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya.
Whether it be a preceptor, a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, or a teacher.
Or, one who occupies the position of a teacher,
having recognized that another person has transgressed or exceeded the bounds regarding any particular matter.
From time to time he reproves him and inflicts disciplinary measures upon him.
He causes him to bow down, and furthermore, he accepts his lawful, timely offer of hospitality, proper conduct, and apology;
and he becomes one who heals [the offense].

Regarding what should be done and what should not be done, he teaches and instructs concerning proper conduct and improper conduct, both that which has been practiced and that which has not been practiced; thus he is an instructor.
And how does one become a teacher of the Dharma? From time to time, one delivers discourse on matters to be practiced beforehand; that is to say, discourse on generosity, and so forth.
a discourse on ethical conduct, a discourse on heaven, and the peril of sensual pleasures along with the means of escape from them.
He extensively elucidates the dharmas belonging to the side of purification;
from time to time, he delivers discourses connected with the four noble truths,
beginning with suffering.
or the origin, or the cessation,
or the fruit;
Either for the sake of the maturation [of beings], or for the sake of the affliction of beings, or for the sake of the purification of beings.
Or for the sake of the long endurance of the true Dharma,
[he teaches] with words and syllables that are logical, coherent, conformable, appropriate, and skillful means.
With appropriate and skillful accumulations of limbs for one who is wise, he further delivers that discourse at the proper time, with respect,
and in a coherent sequence.
Gladdening, pleasing, encouraging,
and not discouraging,
[he spoke] that which was appropriate and consistent.
Unmixed,
in accordance with the Dharma,
and with a mind of loving-kindness toward the assembly.
Possessing a mind of benefit and a mind of compassion,
he does not exalt himself by relying on gain, honor, or praise.
He does not disparage others;
thus he becomes a teacher of the Dharma.
And whoever [is endowed] with these eight—
He is endowed with [these] qualities;
thus, from time to time, he becomes one who exhorts and one who reminds.
Because he provides instruction and guidance, he is therefore called a "virtuous friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This, then, is the detailed analysis of the nature of a virtuous friend.
What, however, is the summary meaning?
If he is compassionate toward friends and companions, desiring their welfare from the very beginning and desiring their happiness,
and furthermore understands that welfare and happiness as they truly are;
He is undeluded and possesses non-perverted views;
he is capable and skillful in means.
That is to say, for the sake of the attainment and gathering together of this very welfare and happiness, he is dexterous and free from laziness.
He is endowed with exertion and is of a nature characterized by the arousal of vigor;
that is to say, with regard to that very same bringing about of benefit and happiness.
By these four causes,
one should understand that, in brief, a spiritual friend is complete in every respect.
Furthermore, this is the summary meaning of the nature of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
That which was the previous detailed analysis and this present summary of the meaning— this is called the state of having a virtuous friend.
What is the hearing and reflection upon the true Dharma?
The true Dharma is that which has been proclaimed, taught, made plain, and revealed by the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, the virtuous ones, those who have gone rightly, and the true persons.
It has been fully elucidated.
Furthermore, what is it? Namely:
the Sūtra, and so forth.
Geya,
vyākaraṇa, and so forth in detail as previously described;
that which is contained within these twelve branches of speech is called the True Dharma (saddharma).
In this context, what is the Sūtra?
It is that which was spoken by the Blessed One here and there concerning various [topics].
And with reference to the conduct of those to be trained, a discourse was delivered concerning the aggregates, or a discourse concerning the elements,
or one concerning the collection of elements.
Or those connected with the sense bases, or connected with dependent origination, or connected with food, the truths, and the foundations.
Or those associated with the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas;
or those associated with the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the limbs of the path.
A discourse connected with the foul, mindfulness of breathing, the trainings, and the clear faiths was delivered;
and that discourse, having been compiled by the redactors for the long endurance of the Teaching,
was arranged in successive order according to its proper application.
Arranged in successive order,
consisting of appropriate sets of names, phrases, and syllables for the purpose of indicating various meanings—
namely, those meanings that are wholesome, connected with the goal, and connected with the conduct of a Buddha— this is called a *sūtra*.
What is *geya*? It is that at the end or conclusion of which verses (*gāthā*) are chanted, and whatever sutra is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*); this is called *geya*.
What is the prophecy? It is that which concerns a disciple who has passed away from this world.
It is prophesied regarding rebirth;
and that sūtra which is of explicit meaning (nītārtha) is called a prophecy (vyākaraṇa).
What is a verse (gāthā)? It is that which is not spoken in prose, but rather composed in metrical feet, consisting of either two lines, or—
Whether consisting of three lines, four lines,
or five lines;
Or this verse is said to consist of six feet.
What is an *udāna*?
It is that which is spoken with reference to a person, without explicitly mentioning their name or clan, for the sake of the future endurance of the true Dharma.
And for the sake of the stability of the teaching;
this is called an *udāna*.
What is the introductory cause (*nidāna*)? It is that which is spoken by announcing and pointing to the name and lineage of an individual.
That which is connected with the Vinaya, together with its origin and its causal basis—the Prātimokṣa Sūtra—is called the Nidāna.
What is an Avadāna? It is that which is cited together with an illustrative example.
