That illustration by means of which the purification of a given subject matter occurs is called an *avadāna*.
What is a *vṛtta*?
Whatever is connected with former lives (*pūrvayoga*) is called a *vṛttaka*.

What is a *jātaka*? It is that which, based on the past time, describes in various instances the Blessed One’s conduct as a bodhisattva and his difficult practices during his deaths and rebirths; this is what is proclaimed.
This is called a Jātaka.
What is the Vaipulya? It is that wherein the path of the bodhisattvas is taught for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For the sake of the attainment of the ten powers and unobstructed knowledge— this is called the Vaipulya.
What are the marvelous qualities (*adbhutadharmāḥ*)? They are those [qualities] which belong to the Buddhas...
And of the Buddha’s disciples—
the monks and the nuns—
of those in training, of female renunciants, and of laywomen,

These specific qualities—which are both common and uncommon, and which are distinguished from others and regarded as marvelous and wonderful—are declared and called "marvelous phenomena" (adbhutadharmas).
What are the *upadeśas*?
All the *mātṛkās*, the *Abhidharma*, and the extraction of the essential meaning from the *sūtras*;
the explanation of the *sūtras* is called *upadeśa*.
And this twelvefold collection of the word of the Buddha exists: there is the Sūtra, there is the Vinaya, and there is the Abhidharma.
Regarding that, first of all, as for what he says:
The Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Avadāna, Vṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, and Adbhutadharma— this, first of all, is the Sūtra. Furthermore, as for what he said:
This is called the *nidāna*; it is the Vinaya.
Furthermore, as for what he said:
These are called "instructions";
this is what is termed Abhidharma.
And this twelvefold scriptural tradition, comprised within the three baskets (piṭaka) and taught by the virtuous who have attained the right path,
is called the "True Dharma" (saddharma).
Hearing that is hearing the true Dharma.
Furthermore, what is that?
For instance, there is here someone who is either a bearer of the Sūtras or a bearer of the Vinaya.
Or one who upholds the Mātṛkā, or one who upholds the Sūtra and Vinaya,
or one who upholds the Sūtra and Abhidharma.
Or one who upholds the *vinayamātṛkā*.
This is called hearing the true Dharma (*saddharmaśravaṇa*).
Furthermore, that [hearing] is as follows:
Listening is of two kinds: listening to the phrasing and listening to the meaning.
What is reflection?
It is when someone here, having gone alone into seclusion, reflects upon those very teachings exactly as they were heard—
namely, the six inconceivable points, as follows:
reflection on the self, reflection on sentient beings, reflection on the world, and reflection on reality.
Apart from the reflection on the maturation of karma for those who reflect,
the domain of meditation for those who meditate, and the domain of the Buddhas for the Buddhas— considering them according to their own specific characteristics.

And he contemplates by way of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, that contemplation is twofold: it has the aspect of counting, by means of the method of counting, and it has the aspect of weighing (*tulanākāra*).

It also has the aspect of examining virtues and faults through reasoning. If he contemplates a teaching associated with the aggregates, or if he contemplates any one of the various previously established teachings, he contemplates by means of these two.
Furthermore, how is it described as being of three kinds?

It is said that there are ten material bases (*rūpīṇy āyatanāni*), and that form included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is also the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). These are the three.
Feeling is the aggregate of feeling; the six groups of perception are the aggregate of perception;
the six groups of volition are the aggregate of volition.

One contemplates the enumeration of the aggregates (*skandha-gaṇanā*) in the form of numerical calculation, such as "the aggregate of consciousness consists of the six groups of consciousness," by means of successive subdivisions; or alternatively, one should understand that there is an immeasurable method of entry into this contemplation in the form of numerical calculation. How does one contemplate the teaching on the aggregates through contemplation in the form of investigation by reasoning?
One examines by means of four reasonings. By which four? Namely, by the reasoning of dependence, and by the reasoning of cause and effect.
By means of the reasoning of logical proof and by means of the reasoning of the nature of phenomena.
What is the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*)?
Dependence is twofold: dependence for arising (*utpatty-apekṣā*) and dependence for designation (*prajñapti-apekṣā*).
Among these, dependence for arising refers to those causes and conditions by which the manifestation of the aggregates (*skandha*) occurs.
In the arising of those aggregates, those causes and those conditions are required,
by means of which— the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes— the designation of the aggregates occurs.
In that designation of the aggregates, those sets of names, phrases, and phonemes are required;
this is called dependence on arising with respect to the aggregates and dependence on designation.
That which is dependence for arising and that which is dependence for designation— this is the reasoning, the yoga, and the skillful means for the arising of the aggregates.
Therefore, the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*) is stated for the sake of the designation of the aggregates (*skandha-prajñapti*).

The reasoning of cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-yukti*) is the application of the aggregates that have arisen through their own causes and their own conditions toward their respective individual effects; for example:
"Forms are to be seen by means of the eye."
Sounds are to be heard with the ear;
likewise, phenomena are to be cognized by the mind.
Form should remain within the range of the eye.
By means of sound for the ear,
and likewise by means of mental objects for the mind;
or whatever else is of this same category.
In each case, the mutual relationship of cause and effect among phenomena— this application, this conjunction, this method— is called the principle of causal efficiency (*kāryakāraṇayukti*).
What is the principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*)?
The aggregates are impermanent,
dependently originated,
and suffering.
One examines them as empty and selfless by means of three types of valid cognition, namely: authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), [direct perception, and inference].

By means of these three instruments of knowledge— direct perception, inference, and [scriptural authority]— which are endowed with logical justification and are persuasive to the hearts of the wise, the establishment and proof [of the object] is carried out.
Namely: the impermanence of the aggregates, their dependent origination, or their nature of suffering.
This is called the reasoning that establishes through proof regarding emptiness.
What is the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-yukti)?

For what reason are these aggregates such as they are? For what reason is the arrangement of the world such as it is? For what reason does earth have the characteristic of solidity, and water the characteristic of fluidity?
Fire has the characteristic of heat;
wind has the characteristic of motion;
the aggregates are impermanent.
For what reason is nirvāṇa called "peaceful"?
Likewise, form has the characteristic of being formed;
feeling has the characteristic of experiencing.
Perception has the characteristic of perceiving;
volitional formations have the characteristic of conditioning;
consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.
This is the nature of these phenomena; this is their intrinsic essence, being such as it is.
This is indeed their *dharmatā*, and that very *dharmatā* is here the logic, the yoga, and the skillful means.
Whether it be thus,
or otherwise, or not at all— in every case, the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the very nature of things as they recede, is the logical justification.
For the purpose of contemplating the mind and for the purpose of bringing the mind to realization, this is called the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*).
Thus, the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*) is examined by means of these four reasonings.

"Whatever other teaching there may be"—this refers to the correct contemplation (*samyagupanidhyāyanā*) of each respective teaching through these two modes: the mode of counting and enumerating, and the mode of investigating by means of reasoning. This is called "listening to and reflecting upon the true Dharma" (*saddharma-śravaṇa-cintanā*).
What is the absence of obstacles?
The absence of obstacles is twofold.
Based on the internal and the external.
In that regard, he will explain the obstacle based on the internal and the external;
[he will explain it] by way of its opposite.
An obstacle should be understood [in this way].
What is an obstacle based on the internal?
It is when, for example, a certain person here has previously performed meritorious deeds.
Due to his virtuous deeds,
he becomes a recipient of appropriate requisites for life from time to time.

That is to say, he has intense passion and prolonged passion for the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick; he has intense hatred and prolonged hatred [for them].
There is intense delusion and pervasive delusion;
or else, he has previously performed actions conducive to affliction,
by reason of which he becomes one who experiences much illness.
In this very life, he becomes one who engages in unwholesome conduct;
that by which his wind or bile is frequently provoked.
Phlegm or cholera remains in the body;
he becomes heavy from food.
He has many concerns, many duties,
and is frequently occupied with large assemblies;
or he delights in worldly activities.
Or one who delights in talk,
one who is fond of sleep, or one who delights in socializing.
One who is self-conceited, fickle,
heedless, or dwells in an unsuitable locality—
such factors as these should be understood as obstacles arising from within oneself.

What are the internal obstacles based on external factors? They are as follows: relying upon an unwholesome person, because of which one does not receive, from time to time, appropriate advice and instruction.
Or he dwells in an improper location,
where, while he is making his dwelling, there is either the glare of the sun during the day or a harsh glare from the sun.
Abundant, whether by night or by day;
loud sounds, great noises, the clamor of a great multitude of people;
and the contact of wind and heat that is intense and harsh.
One should understand that even fear originating from humans— being of this same nature— is an external obstacle based on the lower realms (*apāya*).
This, for now, is the detailed analysis.
Furthermore, what is the summarized meaning?
In brief, there are three kinds of obstacles:
the obstacle to application, [the obstacle to attainment, and the obstacle to enjoyment].
There is the obstacle to seclusion (*prāvivekya*) and the obstacle to withdrawal (*pratisaṃlayana*).

Among these, the obstacle to application (*prayogāntarāya*) is that obstacle which, when present and manifest, renders one incapable and powerless to apply oneself to the side of the wholesome in every respect.
Furthermore, what is that?
It is when one becomes afflicted,
severely ill.
His wind, bile, or phlegm frequently becomes aggravated.
Or cholera may remain in his body;
or else a scorpion or a centipede may bite him.

Either a human or a non-human being harasses him, and he does not obtain the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick; this kind of obstacle should be understood as an obstacle to application (*prayogāntarāya*).
What is the obstacle to seclusion (*prāvivekyāntarāya*)?
When one becomes heavy with food,
having many concerns, and many duties;
Having much to do,
he takes delight in the pleasure of being occupied with work.
With his mind distracted by various such duties,
he becomes one who delights in talk,
even though he is capable and competent.
In seclusion, in abandonment, in solitary retreat, and in cultivation, [he is satisfied] with mere instruction and recitation.
Being contented, he becomes one who delights in sleep;
overcome by sloth and torpor,
he is of a lazy nature and finds pleasure in sleep.
He indulges in the pleasure of reclining on one's side and the pleasure of lying down;
he delights in socializing with householders and renunciants alike.
He engages in talk about kings, or talk about thieves,
or talk about food.
Or talk about drinks, or talk about household matters, or talk about courtesans.
He passes the time with talk of such a kind as stories about streets, stories about provincial ministers, or stories about the ocean— talk that is connected with what is unprofitable.
And there he takes delight, frequently being one who is full of gatherings with the community.
In various matters, his mind becomes distracted; his mind becomes agitated;
he finds delight in social association.
He undergoes separation from householders and renunciants who are not concentrated; he finds delight in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
takes pleasure in conceptual proliferation, and is a leader among those things that lead to downward entry.
Having laid down the burden regarding states of seclusion—
one should understand that such factors as these constitute an obstacle to seclusion.
When these are assembled and present, it is not easy to dwell in remote lodgings in forest groves, wilderness tracts, or remote areas—
whether in the forest, at the foot of trees, or in empty dwellings.
What is the obstacle to seclusion?
It is as follows: seclusion is said to be calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Among these, there is an obstacle to calm abiding.
There is an obstacle to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Among these, the obstacles to tranquility (*śamatha*) are: [living in] a dissolute place and living in an unsuitable location;
such that, for one who is thus negligent, sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*) envelop the mind.
Or he relishes mere calm abiding;
or he inclines the mind toward laxity;
or there arises a state of mental darkness.
And by dwelling in an improper location,
there may arise an external disturbance caused by others,
by which his mind is distracted outwardly.
This is an obstacle to serenity (śamatha);
it should be understood as an obstacle to withdrawal (pratisaṃlayana).
What is an obstacle to insight (vipaśyanā)?
Namely, self-conceit and restlessness.
Therein, self-conceit is as follows: for instance, thinking, "I have gone forth from a high-born family;
I am not inferior."
Furthermore, thinking "others are not like that," he exalts himself,
gathers [followers],
and disparages others.
Thus he has gone forth from a wealthy family; he is undaunted,
and thus handsome and pleasing to behold.
He is pleasing,
thus very learned, and possesses a store of knowledge.
"In this way, I am one whose speech is virtuous and endowed with the faculty of eloquence,
whereas other monks are not so"— in this manner,
he exalts himself.
He exalts himself and disparages others;
thus he exalts himself, and these [faults] come to be.
O monks, you are elders,
knowers of delight,
and those who have fully entered the holy life.
He does not inquire of them from time to time,
nor does he question them;
and they, in turn, do not from time to time reveal to him those points that have not yet been revealed.

They reveal those points that have been left open, and they thoroughly illuminate the profound words of meaning— having penetrated them well and perfectly with wisdom— for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision.
In this way, his grasping at a self becomes an obstacle,
namely, to insight (vipaśyanā).
Furthermore, he becomes an obtainer of merely a small amount, merely an inferior amount— merely a knowledge and vision, merely a state of easeful dwelling.
On account of that mere knowledge and mere vision, he exalts himself.
He exerts himself;
yet, while exerting himself, he becomes satisfied with that much alone and does not strive further.
In this way, an obstacle is created for him.
Through self-exaltation— that is, [the pursuit] of insight (vipaśyanā)—
one becomes either fickle, with unpeaceful faculties, or with excited faculties.
With exalted faculties,
he becomes one whose mind is purified and who speaks well-spoken words.
One who performs evil deeds does not contemplate the teachings with stability,
nor does one contemplate them with firmness.
Because of this restlessness, he neither fulfills nor purifies insight; thus,
it becomes an obstacle for him,
namely, to insight.
There are two factors that obstruct calm abiding (śamatha):
namely, negligence and dwelling in an unsuitable location.

There are two factors that are obstacles to insight (vipaśyanā), namely self-exaltation and restlessness. Thus, there is that which is an obstacle to tranquility (śamatha) and that which is an obstacle to insight.
This is called the obstacle to withdrawal (*pratisaṃlayanāntarāya*).
Furthermore, this is the summarized meaning of the obstacle.
This summary meaning and the previous detailed analysis,
when condensed into a single unity, are called an "obstacle."

And the absence of obstacles should be understood as the opposite of this obstacle. That which is the non-existence, the departure, the lack of association, and the non-occurrence of these obstacles is called "absence of obstacles" (anantarāya).
What is renunciation? It is that blameless giving which is for the sake of adorning the mind and for the sake of equipping the mind.
One gives for the sake of the equipment for yoga, for the attainment of the supreme goal.
In that regard, who gives? To whom does one give? Where does one give? And by what means does one give?
How does one give? For what reason does one give? By means of which [does one give]? (Śbh_Sh: 151)
The gift becomes blameless.
He said:
"The giver, the master of giving, bestows;
this is called the giver."
That which is one's own is given;
and it is given by one who desires to give, not by one who does not desire to give.
This is called a donor.
In that regard, where does he give? He says:
One gives to four [recipients]: to one who is suffering, to one who does what is beneficial, to one who is dear, and to one who is distinguished.
In that regard, "to those who are suffering" refers to those who are miserable, or travelers on a road,
or beggars.
whether they were blind, or deaf,
or without a protector;
Or those who are without refuge,
or lacking in basic necessities;
or whatever others there may be who belong to this same category.
Who are those who have been helpful? Namely: mother and father, those who have nourished and sustained one, and those who have raised one.
Or again, those who deliver others from the wilderness of forests,
or from famine, or from the fear of foreign armies;
Whether from bondage or from affliction, they become his instructors in what is beneficial and instructors in what is conducive to happiness.
They bring about welfare and happiness;
they are companions in whatever matters arise;
and they rejoice together.
Those who do not abandon one even in calamities, sharing in one's sorrows— whosoever else there may be of this same kind, these are benefactors.
Who are the beloved ones?
Those who are well-spoken of,
and toward whom one feels either affection or reverence.
They are speakers of devotion, those with whom one has conversed, those with whom one is well-acquainted, and those who are dear to one.
Or again, others of this same category are also called "desired."
Who are those distinguished ones? They are the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are recognized as being of virtuous character.
They are unassailable, delighting in being unassailable;
they are free from passion,
and have set out for the subduing of passion.
Free from hatred, they have set out for the subduing of hatred;
free from delusion,
they have set out for the subduing of delusion.
Furthermore, whatever others there may be who belong to this same category, these are called "distinguished."
Regarding that, he says what it gives:
in brief, that which is reckoned as a sentient being and that which is reckoned as non-sentient.
One gives material things (*vastu*). Among those, what is a thing comprised within sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*)?
It is as follows: the gift of a son; female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens; and women, men, boys, and girls.
Or again, whatever other thing is of a similar nature; or furthermore, taking from within himself, he gives away his hands, feet, head, flesh, blood, fat, and so forth.
This gift, too, is reckoned among those pertaining to persons wherein the awakenings of bodhisattvas are seen;
however, in this context, this [particular] gift is not intended.
Rather, it refers to those [gifts] in all of which one possesses sovereignty.
He possesses mastery and sovereign power,
and he is worthy to bestow those sentient beings upon others.
And by thus establishing himself as blameless,
others do not become malicious toward him because of that cause or on account of those conditions.
And those beings who have been entrusted to others and are killed by them— this is called a faultless being.
The gift of material objects.
What is a thing not reckoned as a sentient being (*asattvasaṃkhyātavastu*)?
It is as follows: the object of wealth (*dhanavastu*), the object of grain (*dhānyavastu*), and the object of land (*deśavastu*).
In that regard, the category of wealth consists of such things as gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, emeralds, sapphires, gold, silver, rubies, and right-spiraling conch shells;
or whatever else is of a similar nature, whether it be a jewel or otherwise.
Either gold, or silver,
or clothing.
or household utensils, or various kinds of perfumes, or various kinds of garlands;
This is called wealth.
What is grain? Whatever is edible, or—
Or a drink, such as barley or rice.
Or wheat, or jujube fruits, or horse gram.
Or sesame seeds, or beans, or sugarcane juice.
Whether it be grape juice or whatever else of this kind, this is called grain.
What is the object consisting of places?
It is as follows: the object of a field, the object of a house, the object of a shop, and the establishment of a hall for merit or a monastery.
Furthermore, whatever else is of this same category is called the "object of the place" (*deśavastu*);
therein, that object which is reckoned as a sentient being (*sattva*) is what one gives.
By what does one give?
It is the volition accompanied by non-greed,
which is the mental formation that constitutes the action of mind.
And whatever bodily action or vocal action is instigated by that [intention], for the purpose of relinquishing a place or an object,
or within one's own continuum.
By this he gives. In that regard, how does he give?
One gives with faith,
possessing the vision of the scriptures and seeing the fruit.
He gives with respect;
with a humble mind, he gives with his own hand (or with both hands);
and without casting it aside, he gives at the proper time.
When this [wealth] is useful to others, he gives it to them without harming others,
in accordance with righteousness, according to agreement, and without violence.
Having procured it, he gives what is pure;
he gives what is excellent and appropriate.
By which neither others nor oneself become blameworthy;
he gives repeatedly.
Having subdued the stain of self-interest and the stain of hoarding, he gives a gift;
even before giving, he is well-disposed, and while giving, he clarifies his mind.
Or, having given, he feels regret;
thus he gives.
Why does he give?
He said:
One gives out of compassion;
that is to say, one gives out of gratitude toward those who are suffering.
That is to say, one gives out of love, respect, and devotion toward those who have been beneficial.
That is to say, one gives out of a desire for specific worldly or supramundane excellence regarding what is desired;
that is, toward those who are distinguished.
Therefore:
It is said that he gives.
By these modes, for this reason, whether he be a householder or one who has gone forth, it is for the sake of adorning the mind.
For the purpose of purifying the mind,
for the purpose of gathering the equipment for yoga, and for the attainment of the supreme goal, that gift becomes irreproachable;
this is called relinquishment.
What is the adornment of a śramaṇa?
It is as follows: for instance, a certain person is endowed with faith.
He is free from deceit,
has little affliction, is by nature one who has initiated vigor, is wise, has few desires, and is contented.
Easy to support, easy to satisfy, endowed with the ascetic virtues (dhutaguṇa), pleasing,
moderate in eating, and endowed with the qualities of a true person (satpuruṣadharma).
Endowed with the qualities of a wise person;
endowed with the marks of a wise person; patient, [and] excellent...
He becomes devoted and refined.
How does one become faithful? One becomes abundant in serene confidence and abundant in the conceptualization of the meaning.
Abounding in liberation and desirous of wholesome qualities,
he has faith in the Teacher and does not waver.
He does not doubt;
he honors and respects the Teacher.
He honors, worships,
treats with respect, and treats with reverence.
Having honored, having worshiped,
and having relied [upon it], he dwells.
As toward the Teacher, so toward the Dharma, toward one's fellow practitioners of the holy life,
and toward the training, the instruction, and the admonition.
In hospitality and in heedfulness,
as well as in meditative concentration, he is thus faithful. How does he become free from deceit?
He becomes one who confesses his faults,
one of a nature to confess them; he reveals himself as he truly is in the presence of the Teacher.
And regarding consciousness, he is likewise free from deceit toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
How does he become one who has little affliction?
He is of a healthy constitution;
he possesses a digestive faculty that is balanced,
being neither too hot nor too cold.

By means of food that is neither too cold, nor harmful, but pleasant at all times, through which whatever he has eaten, drunk, chewed, or tasted undergoes proper digestion, he thus becomes one who has little affliction.
How is one of a nature that has initiated vigor? One dwells possessing stamina,
being vigorous, energetic, and firm in prowess.
Having laid aside the burden regarding wholesome qualities, he becomes skillful, untiring, and endowed with exertion;
he becomes a doer who personally performs services for his wise fellow-celibates; thus, he is one who has initiated vigor.
How does one become wise?
One becomes endowed with both mindfulness and intelligence in two ways: having unobstructed faculties, and...
one whose faculties are unconfused, who is not deaf,
and who is capable;
In order to understand the meaning of teachings that are well-spoken or ill-spoken,
he is endowed with both innate intelligence and acquired intelligence.
In this way, he becomes wise.
How does he become one of few desires?
He does not seek to have others know him for as many qualities as he possesses, beginning with his state of having few desires.
Thinking, "May others not know me," or "He is one of few desires," or "He is endowed with such qualities," he thus becomes one of few desires.
How does one become content?
With regard to robes and almsfood, whatever they may be.
He is content and well-satisfied with his bedding and seating; having obtained a robe, whether it be coarse or...
He does not long for what is excellent,
nor does he become distressed;
and having obtained it, he consumes it without attachment.
"He is unattached," and so on in detail as before.
Just as with robes, so too with almsfood; just as with lodgings, so he is content.
How is one easy to support?
One’s own self alone is to be supported by him,
and not others, such as children or others.
"Or humans," meaning those others, whoever they may be, for whose sake one undertakes this search.
And if others—namely, donors and masters of giving—were to perceive him as difficult to support, he does not do so;
thus, he becomes easy to support. How does he become easy to maintain?
He maintains himself even with coarse food;
he maintains himself even with meager food—in this way, he is easy to support.
How does he become endowed with the qualities of purification (dhutaguṇa)?
He is an alms-food eater; he is one who goes for alms in regular order; he is a one-session eater.
Indeed, he is one who eats after the meal,
one who possesses only three robes, and one who wears felt garments.
One who wears robes made of rags from a dust heap;
one who dwells in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in the open air.
The cemetery-dweller, the sitter,
and the one who uses whatever seat is available—
these constitute the twelve ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) beginning with alms-food, robes, and lodgings.
Or there are thirteen [dhūta qualities].
Among them, the practice of eating only alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*) is divided into two types: one who obtains alms-food (*prāptapiṇḍapātika*), and...
By means of the practice of a sequential alms-goer, having begged for alms from families in succession from house to house,
and having wandered about, he consumes the alms-food as it is obtained and as it has been properly offered.
But he does not approach families with his trunk raised high,
thinking, "From this I shall obtain exquisite food."
Regarding solid food, up to the point of satiety;
therein, starting from alms-gathering without distinction, there are twelve [practices].
Furthermore, regarding the classification, there are thirteen [practices].
Among them, what is "eating at a single sitting"?
It is sitting on a single seat for as long as one must consume the meal.
He partakes [of food] for that long;
and having risen from that seat, he does not partake again. This is called [the practice].
The practice of eating at a single sitting.
Now, what is the state of eating after the proper time? It is when one who is seated for the purpose of eating does not yet partake of the meal.
He accepts all food until he knows: "I will be able to sustain myself with this," and when he further knows: "Beyond this, there will be no need for more food for me."
Then, having set aside everything else, he begins to consume [the food]. In this way, indeed, one becomes a "post-meal eater" (*paścādbhaktika*).
How does one become a wearer of the three robes? One maintains oneself with only three robes: either the outer robe (saṃghāṭī),...
With the upper robe and the inner garment,
he does not possess more than three robes as an extra or surplus; thus, he is one who possesses the three robes.
How does one become a Nāmatika?
Whatever robe he wears—
whether it be the three robes or an extra robe— he wears them all made of wool.
But he does not wear anything else;
thus he wears [only] a hempen garment.
How [does he wear] a dusty one?
He becomes a wearer of robes that have been discarded by others, or left as refuse,
or cast away on the street.
Whether on a street, or at a crossroads,
or at a junction.
Whether on the path, or off the path,
or mixed with excrement;
Or if it is mixed with urine,
or defiled by feces, urine, pus, blood,
or phlegm; then, whatever therein is impure, that too should be removed.
having extracted the essence, having purified it, and having sewn it together;
Having dyed them so that they are discolored, he wears them; thus he becomes one who wears robes made of rags from dust heaps.
How does he become a forest-dweller?
He dwells in forest retreats, remote lodgings in the wilderness, which are far removed from villages and market towns; thus he becomes a forest-dweller.
How does one become a tree-root dweller? One makes one's dwelling at the foot of a tree,
relying upon the root of a tree.
Thus he is one who dwells at the foot of a tree.
How is he one who dwells in the open air?
He makes his dwelling in the open air.
In an open, unsheltered place;
in this way, one becomes one who dwells in the open air.
How does one become a cemetery-dweller?
He makes his dwelling in a cemetery where the bodies of the deceased are being carried out;
in this way, he becomes one who dwells in a cemetery.
How does one become a practitioner who remains in a sitting posture?
One passes the time by sitting on a couch, a stool, or a spread of grass.
But not on a couch, nor on a stool, nor against a wall.
The root of a tree,
or the root of a tree,
or a bed of grass.
Or, relying on a bed of leaves,
he gives his back or his side [to the ground]; in this way, one becomes a practitioner of the "sitting posture" (*naiṣadyika*).
How does one become a person who uses whatever seat is available?
It is when one prepares one's bed upon whatever grass mat or leaf mat is provided.
Whether it be a bed of grass or a bed of leaves, it is prepared with due care;
in that very manner, he prepares his bedding.
But he does not disturb it;
rather, he prepares it in such a way that he becomes one who uses whatever seat is provided.
Why are these called *dhutaguṇas*? It is because, just as wool or cotton, when shaken out, becomes free from impurities and is no longer entangled.
And at that time, it becomes supple, light, and workable.
That is to say, either in the production of a discourse or in the production of cotton.
In the same way, here some person’s mind becomes attached to almsfood through attachment to almsfood; it becomes thoroughly attached.
Through attachment to robes, and through attachment to lodgings, the mind becomes attached to lodgings; it becomes thoroughly attached.

By means of these ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), he purifies and straightens himself, making it supple, workable, upright, free from outflows, and obedient—namely, for the sake of dwelling in the holy life (brahmacarya); therefore they are called "ascetic qualities."
In that regard, one practices eating at a single sitting (*ekāsanika*) for the sake of abandoning attachment to food;

one practices eating from a bowl (*khalupaścādbhaktika*) for the sake of abandoning attachment to abundant food; and one practices wearing a set number of robes (*nāmatika*) for the sake of abandoning attachment to fine robes.
In order to abandon attachment to fine robes, he becomes one who possesses only the three robes;
in order to abandon attachment to the soft touch of robes, he becomes one who wears robes made of rags from a dust-heap.
Attachment to bedding and seating is fourfold; namely, attachment to physical contact and attachment to shelter.
There is attachment to the pleasure of lying on one's side and attachment to the pleasure of sleeping;
there is attachment to bedspreads, counter-spreads, and coverlets.
Among these, for the sake of abandoning attachment to social association, one becomes a forest-dweller.
For the sake of abandoning attachment to dwellings, he becomes one who dwells at the foot of trees, one who dwells in the open air,
and one who dwells in cemeteries.
Moreover, by dwelling in cemeteries, one abandons attachment to sleep;

by being a sitter, one abandons attachment to the pleasure of reclining on one's side and the pleasure of sitting; and by using whatever mat is available, one abandons attachment to bedding, coverlets, and rugs. In this way, one becomes endowed with the qualities of ascetic purification (*dhutaguṇa*).
How does one become pleasing?
One becomes endowed with pleasing deportment in advancing and retreating, and in looking ahead and looking aside, as well as in drawing back and extending the limbs.
By carrying his outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), inner robe, and alms bowl in such a manner, he becomes pleasing to behold.
How does he become one who knows the proper measure?
In this case, faithful brahmins and householders provide [offerings] that are not in vain.
That is to say, regarding robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he knows the proper measure in accepting them. In this way, he is one who knows the proper measure.
How does he become endowed with the qualities of a true person?
Whether he has gone forth from a high-born family or from a wealthy family,
he is handsome and pleasing to behold.
Being pleasing and endowed with the equipment of great learning,
or having obtained some particular degree of mere knowledge, mere vision, or a dwelling in contact with what is meaningful, he exalts himself on account of this.
He disparages others;
he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and thus he becomes endowed with the qualities of a true person. How does he become endowed with the marks of a wise man?
The fool is characterized by his actions; the wise person is characterized by his actions.
How so? The fool is one who thinks ill-thought thoughts.
One who speaks ill-spoken words and performs evil deeds is not a wise person;
rather, a wise person is one who reflects upon what is well-considered.
One who speaks well-spoken words and performs well-performed deeds is thus endowed with the marks of a wise person.
How is one patient?
When reviled, one does not revile in return;
when provoked to anger, one does not respond with anger.
When reviled, he does not revile in return; when insulted, he does not insult in return;
and that venerable one remains patient.
Of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles.
[Endurance] toward ill-spoken words from others, and toward offensive paths of speech.
of bodily sensations,
of sufferings,
of those that are intense,
He is patient toward things that are harsh, pungent, unpleasant, and life-threatening, being by nature one who endures them.
In this way, he is patient.
How is he well-disposed? It is because he is endowed with friendly bodily action.
With friendly verbal action, with friendly mental action,
in the presence of the Teacher and of the wise,
He shares common enjoyments with his fellow practitioners, yet he does not consume them;
he eats without being secretive about his food.
With gains that are righteous, obtained through the Dharma,
placed in the alms-bowl, and contained within the bowl, he also comes to share in the commonality of ethical discipline.
And having attained a commonality of view,
being endowed with these six qualities that inspire affection— qualities which cause endearment, respect, and esteem— he becomes pleasant to dwell with.
He is by nature non-violent,
and the wise fellow-celibates take delight in him.
He is single-mindedly resolute;
thus he becomes well-pleased.
How does he become gentle?
He is free from frowning, possesses a bright and open countenance, approaches others with a smile, speaks first, and utters pleasant words.
Possessing the virtue of gathering [disciples],
with a well-disciplined continuum,
he is thus gentle.
Endowed with these qualities, he becomes one who desires the Dharma and desires virtuous qualities,
rather than desiring gain, honor, fame, or renown.
He does not become possessed of a false view that superimposes [what is non-existent],
nor of one that denies [what exists]; he does not superimpose a phenomenon that is non-existent.
He does not disparage the peaceful Dharma. Whatever that may be— whether it is spoken or to be spoken, whether it is clothed or naked— [he does not disparage it].
That which is perishable, consisting of signs, words, and phonemes,
and associated with worldly materialism—
that is meaningless.
Having recognized this, one avoids it from afar;
one does not take pleasure in it, nor does one delight in it.
And with that, he wears robes given by himself or others,
together with householders.
They avoid association that increases the afflictions;
they cultivate association with the noble ones.
It purifies knowledge; furthermore,
one does not associate with or accept gifts from families of friends.

On that account, for him there will be, in many ways, distraction or busyness; or else, due to the transformation and alteration of those [objects], sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair will arise.
And he does not tolerate the afflictions and secondary afflictions as they arise one after another.
He abandons it, dispels it, and brings it to an end.
"Whether it be suffering pertaining to the present life or to future lives, that [fault] arises for me on this account;
and he does not cause the arising of faith to fall away."
Possessing unshakable virtue and unfallen in his vows,
he partakes of what has been given out of faith.
He does not reject what has been given out of faith,
nor does he renounce the training;
rather, he seeks out his own faults and internal lapses.
He conceals his own virtues and reveals his faults;
he pays no attention to the faults or lapses of others, and he does not commit an offense even for the sake of his life.
And having fallen [into a transgression], he remedies it very quickly according to the Dharma;
he is skillful and untiring in his duties,
acting for himself.
He does not seek the service of others for his body,
nor does he [seek] the inconceivable power of the Buddhas and the Buddha-disciples.
He has faith in the profound teaching and does not reject it, thinking:
"The Tathāgatas alone are the progenitors and the seers; I am not."
Having seen [this], he does not himself persist in dogmatic attachment to views, nor does he grasp what is improper, nor does he counsel on how to relinquish [faults] with difficulty;
he is endowed with these qualities.
Dwelling thus and training thus,
adorned with the ornament of a recluse, he shines.
For example, suppose there were a certain man who was young, of a passionate nature, and a seeker of sensual pleasures.
Having bathed and anointed himself,
clothed in the garments for instruction,
and adorned with various ornaments, he shines.
That is to say,
by means of necklaces, or armlets,
or finger-rings.
Just as one adorned with a necklace of gold and silver,
even so he, adorned with the various qualities that are the ornaments of a śramaṇa,
shines, glows, and radiates light.
Therefore, it is called the adornment of a śramaṇa;
this is what is called the adornment of a śramaṇa.
// Summary Verse //
There may be the desire for the perfection of oneself and others, as well as ethical discipline, the faculties,
moderation in food, wakefulness, and dwelling in clear comprehension.
Likewise, hearing and reflecting [upon the true Dharma], non-obstruction, and renunciation; the last is by way of adornment.

Faith, honesty, little affliction, vigor, wisdom, fewness of desires, contentment, ease of maintenance, being easy to support, the practice of the ascetic virtues (dhuta) and so forth, moderation, patience, amiability, and gentleness.
The First Yoga Station, contained within the *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
(Śbh_Sh: 167) (Śbh_Sh: 168) (Śbh_Sh: 169)
II. The Second Stage of Yoga: Worldly detachment as well as that which is supramundane;
the equipment for both of these is the stage designated as "Renunciation."
In this regard, how many types of persons (*pudgala*) are there who emerge from the stage of renunciation (*naiṣkramyabhūmi*) as it has been taught and proclaimed?
How is the classification of persons established?
And what is the objective support (*ālambana*)?
What is instruction? What is training?
What are the factors conducive to training?
What is the failure of yoga?
What are the yogas?
What is mental attention?
How many types of practitioners of yoga (yogācāra) are there? What is that which is to be done by the practitioner of yoga (yogakaraṇīya)?
What is the cultivation of yoga (yogabhāvanā)?
What is the fruit of cultivation?
How many synonyms for individuals are there?
How many Māras are there?
How many are the deeds of Māra?
How does an undertaking become fruitless?
In that regard, there are twenty-eight types of persons.
Which are the twenty-eight? They are as follows: those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties.
Intense passion,
intense hatred,
and intense delusion.
one whose pride is intoxicated,
one whose discursive thoughts are intoxicated,
and one who has attained equanimity;
One who belongs to the class with little dust,
one who has entered the path,
and one who abides in the fruit.
The follower by faith,
the follower by dharma,
and the one resolved upon the Buddha.
One who has attained vision,
a body-witness,
and one for whom there is only one more birth.
One who goes from family to family,
one who has only one interval remaining,
and one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
One who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion,
and one who flows upwards.
One who is liberated by occasion,
one whose nature is unshakable,
and one liberated through wisdom.
And one who is liberated both ways.
In that regard, what is a person of dull faculties?
It is a person whose faculties are dull.
"Moving slowly" and "moving sluggishly" refer to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu*), as explained previously.
Furthermore, that [person] should be understood as being of two kinds:
one who from the very beginning belongs to the lineage of dull faculties, and one who has not been fully cultivated.
And [the one with] dull faculties.
Who is the person with sharp faculties?
It is that person whose faculties proceed without sluggishness.
"Flowing unimpededly" refers to the objects of knowledge, as explained previously;
furthermore, that [concentration] should be understood as being of two kinds.
From the very beginning, he belongs to the lineage of sharp faculties,
and his faculties have been fully cultivated.
What is a person intoxicated by passion?
It is a person by whom passion was practiced and cultivated in previous births.
Because he has cultivated that [tendency] through those causes and conditions, he now possesses both intense passion and long-lasting passion toward an object that is provocative of lust.
This person is called one intoxicated by passion.
What is a person intoxicated by hatred?
It is a person by whom hatred was practiced in previous births.
Having been cultivated and frequently practiced,
by that cause and by that condition, one now experiences both intense hatred and prolonged hatred toward an object that provokes aversion.
This is called a person intoxicated by hatred.
What is a person intoxicated by delusion?
By whatever person delusion was practiced, cultivated, and repeatedly performed in previous births.

And by that cause and by that condition, one now possesses intense delusion and prolonged delusion regarding an object that provokes delusion; such a person is called a person intoxicated by delusion (*mohonmada*).
What is a person intoxicated by pride (*mānonmada*)?
By whatever person pride was practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in previous births, for that reason and by that condition [it arises].
Now, regarding an object worthy of respect, he possesses both intense pride and enduring pride.
This is called a person intoxicated by pride.
What is a person intoxicated by discursive thought?
It is a person by whom discursive thought was practiced in former births.

Having cultivated and frequently practiced it, by that cause and by that condition, one now experiences intense discursive thought and prolonged discursive thought regarding objects conducive to discursive thought;
this person is called "one intoxicated by discursive thought."
What is the person who has attained equanimity?
It is that person by whom, in previous births, passion, hatred, and... [were previously abandoned].
Delusion, conceit,
and discursive thought, when not cultivated, [do not lead to the destruction of suffering].
cultivated and frequently practiced,
yet these phenomena [are not fully realized].
They have been seen as a danger,
reviled, and thoroughly examined;
for that reason, he—
And by that condition, toward an object that is to be attracted to, or an object that is to be felt aversion toward,
or an object that is to be esteemed (or honored).
Regarding an object that is to be reflected upon, he does not have intense passion,
nor does he have pervasive passion;
and passion does not manifest within him.
That is to say, by means of that object;
as it is with attachment, so it is with hatred and delusion.
Pride and discursive thought—
this is called the person who has attained equanimity.
What is the person with little passion?
By whichever person, in previous births, passion was not practiced or cultivated,
and by whom the danger [of passion] was frequently perceived;
Having been corrupted and stirred up by that cause and that condition, he now, when an object of passion is encountered and has become present before him, [acts accordingly].
When it is intense, abundant, and excessive, one produces passion and attachment.
In the case of a moderate or slight [affliction], one does not produce [the thought of enlightenment] at all;
as it is with attachment, so it is with hatred and delusion.
Pride and discursive thoughts are to be understood [in this way].
This is called the person with little dust.
Who is the person who has entered upon the path?
It is said: there are four persons who have entered upon the path.
Namely: one who has entered the path to the fruit of stream-entry; one who has entered the path to the fruit of once-returning;
and one who has entered the path to the fruit of non-returning.
One who is practicing for the fruit of arhatship— this is called a person who is a candidate [for a fruit].
Who is the person established in the fruit?
It is said:
the stream-enterer.
The once-returner,
the non-returner, and the arhat—
this is called the person established in the fruit.
Who is the person who follows through faith?
It is that person who [learns] from another...
He seeks the instruction on debate and practices by its power,
namely, for the sake of attaining the fruit.
but not toward those dharmas that have been taken up, mastered, and reflected upon.
When those phenomena have been weighed and scrutinized, he himself becomes capable and competent to pursue them by way of cultivation.
He does not practice by means of any wisdom other than that which follows after a person;
therefore, he is called a "follower by faith."
What is a person who follows the Dharma? It is that person who, regarding the teachings as they have been heard, [proceeds accordingly].
When they have been mastered, reflected upon,
weighed, and thoroughly examined, he becomes capable of doing so by himself.
He is capable of following those dharmas by way of cultivation.
However, he does not seek instruction and admonition from another;
that is to say, for the sake of attaining the fruit—this is called a person who follows the Dharma.
What is a person resolved through faith?
That person who follows through faith,
at whatever time they attain the state of a śramaṇa, they touch it [realize it].
At that time, one who witnesses the path of instruction and admonition from another is called "resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
Who is the person who has attained through vision? It is said:
it is that very person who follows the Dharma at the time when they realize the fruit of asceticism.

At that time, having touched [the truth], realized it for oneself, and attained it through the instruction and admonition of another regarding the path, one is said to be "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
What is the person who is a bodily witness? It is that person who enters upon the eight liberations in both direct and reverse order.
And he emerges from that state,
and having realized it with his body, he dwells in it frequently;
yet he does not attain the complete destruction of all outflows— this is called the person who is a bodily witness (kāyasākṣī).
Who is the person who has seven births at most?

It is that person who, through the abandonment of the three fetters— namely, the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and [doubt]— [attains this state].
One who has overcome doubt becomes a stream-enterer;
one whose nature is not subject to falling into lower realms,
being destined for and headed toward perfect enlightenment.
One who is limited to seven more existences:
seven times at most among gods and humans.
Having pressed through and having transmigrated, he makes an end of suffering.
Both of these should be understood as persons who have entered the stream (*srotāpanna*).
Among them, what is the person who is "with one interval" (*ekavīcika*)?

When a person who is a once-returner and has entered the path toward the fruit of a non-returner has abandoned the superior, middling, and lower grades of the afflictions belonging to the desire realm,
and only the mild grade remains as the single [remaining] portion,
he will, after manifesting existence only once more in the desire realm, attain final nirvana right there.
Furthermore, he returns to this world once more; he is called an "ekavīcika" (one who has only one interval).
What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?
It is said: there are three types of persons who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
The person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin):

immediately upon passing away, at the very moment the intermediate state is being produced, he brings that intermediate state into existence; and as soon as it has been produced, he attains parinirvāṇa simultaneously.
It is just like a small spark of fire which, as soon as it arises—
He attains parinirvāṇa.
Second is the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; he brings forth the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), and having brought it forth... [he attains parinirvāṇa].
He may pass away at another time while remaining right there;
however, he does not cease to exist in the very same birth-existence by which he was reborn.

Just as, for example, from impure iron vessels or iron cauldrons that have been heated by a blazing fire, an iron spark flies up while they are being struck with iron hammers, even so does he attain parinirvāṇa.

The third type of person is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*); having brought forth the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), he approaches that place of rebirth (*upapattibhava*),
and once approached, he attains parinirvāṇa without even being reborn there.
It is, for example,
like a spark of iron that, having flown up,
is extinguished before it has even fallen to the ground.

These three types of persons who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, when condensed into one, are called "the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth?
It is one who attains parinirvāṇa immediately upon being reborn.
What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion?

It is one who, having been born there, attains parinirvāṇa after bringing the path into manifestation without exertion, without effort, and without weariness; this is called the person who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion?

One who, having brought the path of exhaustion into manifestation through exertion and effort, attains parinirvāṇa after being born there—this is called the person who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
What is the person who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*)?
It is a person who is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who,
having been reborn in the first dhyāna, does not attain final nirvana while remaining in that very state.
Rather, having passed away from there, by successively taking rebirth, he goes to the Akaniṣṭha gods or even beyond;
it is not a state of perception at all.
Nor from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is called the person who flows upwards (ūrdhvasrotas). What is the person who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta)?
The person who belongs to a lineage of weak faculties and falls away from the worldly dwellings in happiness in the present life,
or intends to die;
Or he guards his liberation, being endowed with an extreme fear of negligence;
that is to say, making this very decline his primary concern, his side of wholesome qualities becomes merely of such a measure,
and not [sufficient] throughout those various nights and days, moments, instants, and hours.
Through the path of insight, he proceeds toward extreme distinction until he exerts intense application;
this person is called one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta).
Who is the person of immovable nature?
The person of immovable nature should be understood as being the opposite of this.
What is a person liberated by wisdom? It is a person who attains the complete destruction of all outflows in every respect,
but does not dwell having personally realized and attained the eight liberations with the body.
This is called the person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
What is the person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)?
It is the person who attains the destruction of all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) in every respect.

Having attained the eight liberations with the body, he dwells therein; his mind is liberated from the obscuration of afflictions and from the obscuration to liberation. This person is called one who is liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
What is the classification of persons (*pudgalavyavasthāna*)?
It should be understood that the classification of persons is established through eleven distinctions.

By which eleven? Namely: by the distinction of faculties, the distinction of classes, the distinction of temperaments, [the distinction of vows, the distinction of paths of practice, the distinction of fruits of the path], and the distinction of applications.
By way of the distinction of meditative attainments, the distinction of rebirths, the distinction of retrogression, and the distinction of hindrances.
First, by way of the classification of faculties:
there is the establishment of persons with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties.
The establishment of seven types of persons according to the division of the schools consists of:
the bhikṣu, the bhikṣuṇī, the śikṣamāṇā, the śrāmaṇera, the śrāmaṇerī, the upāsaka, and the upāsikā.
In that regard, the classification of seven types of persons is established by way of the distinctions in their conduct:
the person who is intoxicated by passion is one whose conduct is dominated by passion;
the one who is intoxicated by hatred is one whose conduct is dominated by hatred.
One who is intoxicated by delusion is one whose temperament is dominated by delusion;
one who is intoxicated by pride is one whose temperament is dominated by pride; one who is intoxicated by discursive thought is one whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought.
One who has attained equanimity is one whose conduct is balanced; one whose defilements are slight is to be understood as one whose conduct is mild.
In that regard, what are the characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by passion (*rāgacarita*)?
Here, a person of passionate temperament produces a dense and excessive outburst of passion even toward a trifling, utterly inferior, and provocative object.
How much more so, then, for that which is middling or excellent?
Furthermore, that obsession with passion causes it to persist in the continuum for a long time;
it remains bound to one for a prolonged period.
By means of that obsession,
one is overwhelmed by objects that provoke passion,
but one is not able to overcome those very objects that provoke passion.
And his faculties become supple, not harsh;
they are not coarse and are unobstructed.
He is not by nature excessively inclined to harm others, namely through body or speech; moreover, he is difficult to alienate and difficult to cause to feel spiritual urgency.
He possesses inferior inclinations,
yet his professional activities are firm and his professional activities are stable.
He is firm in his vows,
steadfast in his vows,
and most abundant in provisions and requisites; yet he is by nature covetous and attached to them.
One who abounds in mental joy, is full of gladness, is free from frowning, has a bright facial complexion,
and is preceded by a smile— such characteristics as these should be understood as the marks of a person whose temperament is dominated by passion (*rāga*).
What are the marks of a person whose temperament is dominated by hatred (*dveṣa*)?

In this case, a person whose temperament is dominated by hatred produces a dense and abundant outburst of hostility toward an object that provokes hatred, even when the cause for that hostility is slight.
How much more so for one who is middling or superior [in intensity]?
Furthermore, he establishes a continuity of that obsession with aversion for a long time;
it remains bound to him for a long duration.
Through the obsession of repugnance,
he is overcome by hateful phenomena,
yet he is not able [to overcome] the hateful phenomena themselves.
Thus,
in order to overcome [them],
one becomes coarse in the faculties.
He possesses harsh faculties, rough faculties, and coarse faculties; he is excessively prone by nature to harming others,
namely through body and speech.
And he becomes easy to inspire with faith and easy to inspire with a sense of spiritual urgency.
He becomes like a crow: talkative, impudent, lacking in resolute faith,
and not firm in his undertakings.
He is one whose undertakings are unstable; he is not firm in his vows,
nor steadfast in his vows.
He becomes full of dejection and full of despair; he is impatient and lacking in magnanimity;
he is by nature contrary.
He is one who grasps things in a contrary manner, being difficult to lead back to the right path by nature, full of malice, cruel in his intentions, and fierce;
he is prone to seizing [faults] and speaks with direct harshness. Even when addressed with only a slight measure of reproach, he becomes resentful and grows angry.
He becomes malicious;
he sinks into despondency; he gives rise to anger.

He has a distorted frown and a lackluster facial complexion; he hates the prosperity of others and is full of envy— one should recognize such traits as the marks of a person whose temperament is dominated by hatred.
In that regard, what are the signs of a person of deluded temperament?
Here, a person of deluded temperament, with respect to an object conducive to delusion, whether it be slight or dense, [is characterized by...]
He gives rise to an abundant obsession of delusion,
let alone one that is middling or intense;
and he establishes a firm continuity of that obsession of delusion for a long duration.
And he becomes bound by that;
he is overcome by phenomena that cause delusion,
but he is not able to overcome those phenomena that cause delusion.
His faculties become sluggish,
and his faculties become dull.
With his faculties intoxicated,
with his bodily actions lax, he dwells on ill-considered thoughts.
One who speaks ill-spoken words, one who performs evil deeds,
one who is lazy and lacking in initiative.
One of meager fortune, dull-witted,
and of lost mindfulness.
Dwelling without clear comprehension,
grasping perversely, difficult to separate from [unwholesome states], and difficult to cause to feel spiritual urgency.
One who has inferior inclinations;
one born dumb and deaf, communicating only by gestures;
and one who lacks capability.

One who is unable to understand the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken words, and who is prone to abandoning [the truth], being led astray by others and guided by others— such characteristics as these should be known as the marks of a person whose conduct is dominated by delusion.
In that regard, what are the signs of a person whose temperament is dominated by pride?
Here, a person of proud temperament produces a dense outburst of pride even toward a minor object conducive to pride;
how much more so toward one that is moderate or great?
And he establishes a continuity of that obsession with pride for a long time; he remains bound by it. What are the signs of a person whose temperament is dominated by pride?

In this case, a person whose temperament is dominated by pride (*mānacarita*) gives rise to a dense outburst of pride (*mānaparyavasthāna*) even toward a minor object that serves as a basis for pride; how much more so, then, toward one that is middling or great!
He establishes a continuous stream of that outburst of pride for a long time, and being bound by it, he is overwhelmed by those phenomena that serve as bases for pride.
Yet he is unable to overcome those factors conducive to pride;
his faculties are agitated and his faculties are haughty. He is devoted to the adornment of the body and speaks words that are excessively arrogant rather than humble.
He does not, from time to time, perform the appropriate forms of service toward his preceptors and those who occupy the position of preceptors;
he is arrogant, with an unbowed body, and is not habituated to saluting, prostrating, rising to greet, or joining his palms in respectful homage.
He becomes one who grasps at a self, one who exalts himself and disparages others;
he desires gain, he desires honor, and he desires fame, renown, and praise; and he becomes one who is frivolous, a buffoon, and a seeker of notoriety.
He is difficult to inspire with a sense of spiritual urgency, possesses grandiose aspirations, and has weak compassion; furthermore,
he is excessively thick with many views regarding a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, and an individual.
And being resentful—these and similar traits should be understood as the characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by pride.

In that regard, what are the signs of a person whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*)? Here, a person of discursive temperament produces a dense obsession (*ghanaparyavasthāna*) even toward a trivial object conducive to discursive thought, and they maintain that obsession for a long time.
He becomes bound by that,
and he is overcome by those factors conducive to discursive thought,
yet he does not [overcome] the factors conducive to discursive thought.
He is unable to overcome [them];
his faculties are unstable, and his faculties are restless.
With unsteady faculties; with agitated faculties.
One whose bodily conduct is unstable,
whose verbal conduct is corrupt, who is difficult to separate from evil, and difficult to inspire with a sense of spiritual urgency.
Delighting in conceptual proliferation, devoted to conceptual proliferation,
full of doubt, and full of uncertainty.
He becomes impetuous, unstable in his vows, uncertain in his vows, and unstable in his undertakings.
One whose actions are undetermined,
who is full of doubt,
and whose mindfulness is lost.
He takes no delight in discernment,
is full of distraction,
and pursues desire and passion for the wonders of the world.
One should understand that such qualities as being skillful and not indolent are the characteristics of a person whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought.
This should be understood as the classification of persons by way of the distinctions in their conduct.
In that regard, the classification of individuals is established by way of the distinction of their vows:
there is an individual who has made a vow for the Śrāvaka vehicle;
there is one for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
There is [a category] in the Mahāyāna. In that regard, there is a person who has made a vow in the Śrāvakayāna and may possess the lineage of a true Śrāvaka or the lineage of a Pratyekabuddha.
One might belong to the Mahāyāna lineage.
In that regard, a person who has made a vow for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha might also belong to the pratyekabuddha lineage,
or they might belong to the śrāvaka lineage.
One might belong to the Mahāyāna lineage.
In that regard, a person who has made a vow for the Mahāyāna might also belong to the śrāvaka lineage,
or belong to the pratyekabuddha lineage.
There may be one belonging to the Mahāyāna lineage.
In that regard, there is this person of the śrāvaka lineage who has made a vow for either the awakening of a pratyekabuddha or for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Because he belongs to the lineage of the śrāvakas, at the very end he must necessarily turn back that former aspiration and remain fixed solely in the aspiration for the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
In the same way, those belonging to the lineage of the pratyekabuddha-vehicle and the lineage of the mahāyāna should be understood.
In that regard, for these individuals, there is an accumulation of aspiration and a deviation from aspiration,
but not an accumulation of the lineage (gotra) nor a deviation from the lineage.
In this context, however, these persons should be understood as those who have made the aspiration for the Śrāvaka Vehicle and belong to the Śrāvaka lineage.
Thus, the classification of individuals occurs according to the distinctions of their aspirations.
How is the classification of persons established by way of the distinctions in their practice?
For these persons as they have been enumerated and described, there is deliverance by means of four practices.
What are these four?
There is a practice that is painful with slow direct knowledge; there is a practice that is painful with quick direct knowledge;
there is a practice that is pleasant with slow direct knowledge; and there is a practice that is pleasant with quick direct knowledge.
The practice of that person with dull faculties who has attained the fundamental dhyānas is called "painful progress with slow superknowledge.
Therein, the practice of a person with sharp faculties who has attained the fundamental dhyānas is called "painful progress with quick superknowledge.
Therein, the practice of a person with dull faculties who has attained the fundamental dhyānas is called "pleasant progress with slow superknowledge."
In that regard, for a person of sharp faculties who has attained the fundamental dhyānas, this practice is called "easy with swift direct knowledge.
Thus, the classification of persons should be understood by way of the distinctions among practices.
In this regard, how should the classification of persons according to the distinctions of the path and its fruits be understood?
It is as follows:
Of the four candidates: the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning,
and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship.
Of the four who abide in the fruits— namely, the stream-enterer,
the once-returner,
the non-returner, and the arhat— those who abide in the paths of application are included.

Those who are practitioners are established by way of the path of practice; those who are established in the fruit of arhatship or the fruit of asceticism (śrāmaṇya) are established by way of the fruit of the path. Thus, there is an establishment of persons according to the distinctions of the paths and fruits.
How is the classification of persons established by way of the distinction of their application?
For example, there are those who follow through faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow through the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
A person who applies themselves by following through faith is one who follows through faith.

He is a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*) who is engaged in accordance with the discipline based on reliance upon others regarding the teachings; he is a follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārī*). Thus, the classification of persons (*pudgala*) occurs according to the distinction of their application.
In that regard, how is the classification of persons established by way of the distinctions of meditative attainments?
For example, there is the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), who dwells having personally realized and attained the eight liberations with the body.
Yet he has not attained the complete destruction of all outflows (āsrava-kṣaya) in every respect.
Possessing form, he sees forms;
having the perception of being formless internally, he sees forms externally.
Having personally realized the beautiful liberation with the body and having attained it, he dwells therein;
[likewise] the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
the sphere of nothingness,
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the cessation of perception and feeling, in both forward and reverse order.
He enters into meditative attainment and emerges from it;
thus, the classification of individuals is established according to the distinctions of their attainments.
How is the classification of persons established by way of the distinction of rebirth? For example, there is the one for whom seven existences are the maximum (*saptakṛdbhavaparama*).
[The distinction] of one who goes from family to family, of one with only one interval, of one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, of one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
and of one who flows upwards.
Thus is the classification of persons by way of the distinctions of rebirth.
How is the classification of persons by way of the distinctions of non-retrogression?
For example, in the case of an Arhat who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) and is susceptible to falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra),
there is a further classification based on the distinction of non-falling away.
Regarding the Arhat of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), who is incapable of falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*):
in this way, the classification of persons (*pudgalavyavasthāna*) occurs according to the distinction of non-falling away.
In that regard, how does the classification of persons occur according to the distinction of obscurations (*āvaraṇaprabheda*)?
For example, as in the case of an Arhat who is liberated through wisdom and liberated in both ways. Among them, an Arhat liberated through wisdom is liberated from the obscuration of afflictions,
but not from the obscuration of meditative attainments.
But one who is liberated in both ways is an Arhat, liberated from both the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance of the knowable.
And because of liberation from the hindrance to meditative attainment (*samāpatti-āvaraṇa*), he is therefore called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

Thus, the classification of persons (*pudgala-vyavasthāna*) occurs by way of the distinctions among hindrances; it should be understood that the classification of the persons as they were enumerated is established respectively according to these three aforementioned distinctions.
In this regard, what is the object (*ālambana*)?
He said: There are four noble objects of focus (*āryālambanavastu*).
What are the four?
The pervasive object,
the object for purifying conduct, the object for skillfulness, and the object for purifying afflictions.
In that regard, what is the pervasive object of focus?
It is said: that too is of four kinds.
Namely: conceptual reflection, non-conceptual reflection,
and the limitedness of objects.
and the accomplishment of the task.
In that regard, what is the conceptualized image?
It is when, for instance, a certain person, relying upon hearing the true Dharma or upon instruction and admonition, [engages in mental application].
Based on what has been seen, heard,
or conceptually constructed, one contemplates with the modes of insight belonging to the stage of meditative concentration a conceptual image that resembles the object of knowledge.
He investigates,
thoroughly investigates,
and examines.
One engages in thorough investigation;
therein is the object to be known,
such as, for example, the foul.
Either loving-kindness,
or dependent origination through specific conditionality, or the analysis of the elements.
Or mindfulness of breathing;
or skill in the aggregates,
skill in the elements, and skill in the sense bases.
Skill in dependent origination,
skill in what is possible and impossible,
and the coarseness of the lower stages.
The continuity of the higher stages,
the truth of origination,
and the truth of cessation.
This is called the truth of the path;
it is the object of knowledge.
Having relied upon the instruction and admonition regarding this very object of knowledge, [one proceeds].
Or, having heard the true Dharma, and having brought into presence a mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration based upon that,
one resolves upon those very same dharmas.
Thus, one is resolved upon the object of knowledge (*jñeyavastu*);
at that time, there proceeds a resolve (*adhimokṣa*) characterized by direct experiential realization regarding that object of knowledge.
And it is said: "upon the object of knowledge."
That object to be known becomes directly perceived; it is brought together and made manifest before one.
It is not, however, another substance of that same kind, but rather an experience of resolute conviction;
it is such an experience of mental attention belonging to the level of meditative concentration.
That by which there arises an appearance corresponding to that object of knowledge is what is called [the representation].
The reflection that has the nature (or the likeness) of the object to be known—
this is what [he]...
While investigating yoga with respect to that subject matter at hand, one examines the object of knowledge and determines its qualities and defects;
this is called the conceptualized image (*savikalpa-pratibimba*).
What is the non-conceptual image?
Here, this practitioner, having grasped the sign from the image, does not further investigate it.
He investigates,
he reflects thoroughly,
and he applies himself to thorough examination.
Rather, that very same object, being unattached, pacifies its causal signs by means of the form of the object;
furthermore, through the ninefold mental abiding, he settles the mind internally and establishes it thoroughly.
He settles it, establishes it, tames it,
and pacifies it.
He calms it,
makes it one-pointed,
and concentrates it.
At that time, for him, that non-conceptual reflection becomes the object of focus (*ālambana*),
wherein he establishes one-pointed mindfulness in its entirety;
that is the object of focus.
But he does not investigate, does not reflect upon,
and does not thoroughly examine it.
And that reflection is called "reflection.
Thus, these should be understood as the synonymous names for that reflection which shares the same nature as the object of knowledge (*jñeyavastu*).
What is the "reality of the object" (*vastupapannatā*) [or "the limit of the object" (*vastuparyantatā*)]?
Regarding the objective support (*ālambana*), there is its "extent of existence" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and its "mode of existence" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*). Among these, what is the "extent of existence"?
Because beyond that there is neither the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), nor the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), nor the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).
Or the aggregate of formations, or the aggregate of consciousness, or the aggregate of consciousness.
