The inclusion of all conditioned entities is by means of the five aggregates; the inclusion of all phenomena is by means of the elements and the sense-bases; and the inclusion of all objects of knowledge is by means of the noble truths. This is called "the extent of existence" (yāvadbhāvikatā).
In that regard, what is the state of being as-it-is?
It is the reality of the object of focus,
which is suchness, established by means of the four principles of reasoning.
Endowment with reasoning;
that is to say, by means of the reasoning of dependence and the reasoning of cause and effect.
By means of the reasoning that establishes through proof and by means of the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*),
there is the "extent of existence" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) of the object of focus.
That which is the state of being as-it-is (yathāvadbhāvikatā) and that which is the state of the limit of things (vastuparyantatā), when condensed into a single unity, is called the "limit of things.
In this context, what is the "accomplishment of the task" (kāryapariniṣpatti)?

It is the mental attention directed toward a reflected image (*pratibimba*) as its object, which arises for this practitioner through the sequence of cultivation, the sequence of meditative development, and the sequence of frequent practice of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
That is fulfilled; through its fulfillment, the mental attention that takes a reflected image as its object is fulfilled.
That is fulfilled.
Through the fulfillment of that,
the basis undergoes transformation,
and all forms of functional rigidity are calmed.

And through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), having transcended the mental image, there arises a non-conceptual, direct perception and vision of knowledge regarding that very object of knowledge.
This occurs for one who has attained the first dhyāna,
who has gained the first dhyāna, within the sphere of the first dhyāna.
For one who has attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
for one who has obtained the fourth dhyāna;
within the sphere of the fourth dhyāna.

For one who has attained the meditative absorptions of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
[the mastery] within their respective domains is called the "accomplishment of the task."
These are as follows:
there are four objects of focus that are universal,
which follow along with all objects of focus, and were taught by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present.
Therefore, this is called an external object of focus (*bāhyālambana*).
Furthermore, this object of focus belongs to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
It consists of all things,
real things, and things consisting of cause and fruit.
Therefore, it is said that this pervades that. As for what he stated:
"the conceptualized reflection."
This refers here to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*);
as for what was further stated,
namely "the limit of things" (*vastuparyantatā*).
This is what is meant here by "the state of having all things" and "the state of having real things," as it was said:
"the accomplishment of the task."
This is the connection between cause and fruit in this context,
as spoken by the Blessed One concerning the Venerable Revata.
Thus it is heard:
the venerable Revata asked the Blessed One a question:
"To what extent, Bhadanta, [is one considered a monk]?"
A monk who is a practitioner of yoga, a yogācāra, has bound his mind to an object of focus; to what object does he bind his mind?
Furthermore, how is the mind well-bound when bound to an object?
Excellent, excellent!
Revata, it is indeed excellent that you, Revata,
ask about this matter.
Therefore, listen well, attend closely, and I shall speak.
In this regard, Revata, a monk who is a practitioner of yoga, a follower of the way of yoga, may desire to purify his conduct,
or desire to achieve skillfulness,
or desire to liberate his mind from the outflows.
He binds the mind to a suitable object, and to one that is appropriate; he binds it correctly and remains a meditator therein without withdrawing.
How does he bind the mind to a suitable object?
Revata, if a monk who is a practitioner, a yogācāra...
One whose temperament is dominated by passion does not fix the mind upon a pure object; rather,
he fixes the mind upon an object that is concordant with it.

Furthermore, one whose temperament is characterized by hatred [should apply it] to loving-kindness; one whose temperament is characterized by delusion, to dependent origination as the conditionality of this;
and one whose temperament is characterized by pride, to the analysis of the elements.
If, Revata,
that monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought, fixes his mind upon mindfulness of breathing,
he thus fixes his mind upon a suitable object of focus.
If, Revata,
that monk is deluded regarding the specific characteristic of conditioned phenomena,
yet fixes his mind upon skillfulness;
One who is confused about causes [is deluded] regarding skill in the elements (*dhātu*); one who is confused about conditions [is deluded] regarding skill in the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Or, one may desire to effect detachment from the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Whether desiring to cultivate dispassion toward sensual pleasures due to their coarseness, or toward material forms due to their tranquility, or toward material forms themselves.
He fixes his mind upon the coarseness of forms and the tranquility of the formless realm; or, desiring to become disenchanted with the view of a self-existent body (satkāya) in all respects,
he desires to be liberated from it.
In the truths of suffering,
the truth of origin, and the truth of cessation,
He fixes his mind upon the truth of the path.
For it is thus, Revata,
that a monk is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga.
He binds the mind to a suitable object.
Here, Revata, whatever knowable thing a monk may wish to understand or discern, [he fixes his mind upon it].
Desiring to reflect upon it and desiring to investigate it thoroughly,
he has already seen that very thing previously.
Whether heard, or thought, or cognized.
Taking that very thing— whether seen, heard, or thought— as the dominant influence, he...
Having made that which was previously cognized the dominant factor, he attends to it with a mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration;
he conceptualizes it and resolves upon it.
He does not see that very object of knowledge as it is concentrated and present before him; rather, there arises for him a counterpart of it,
or its reflection,
or mere cognition.
Whether it be merely seen or merely recollected, whatever the object may be, this monk— a practitioner of yoga, a yogācāra— properly binds his mind to that very object.
If, Revata, he...
A monk who is a yogin, a practitioner of yoga, fixes his mind upon an object of focus until that which is to be known has been known.
And that mind which is thus according to reality and non-erroneous—
indeed, Revata, it is in this way that a monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, [is so called].
He binds the mind correctly to the object of focus.
And how, Revata, does a monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, become one who does not abandon meditative absorption?
If, Revata, that monk, thus correctly applying himself to the object of focus, becomes one who practices with continuity and one who practices with reverence, [he will attain success].
From time to time, he cultivates the sign of calm abiding (*śamatha*),

the sign of exertion (*pragraha*), and the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Through the sequence of practice, the sequence of cultivation, and the sequence of frequent application, by the subsiding of all functional rigidity (*dausthulya*), he attains the purification of the basis (*āśrayapariśuddhi*) and touches it.
He realizes it;
and through the discernment of the objects of knowledge, he attains purity of the focal object,
and through the fading away of passion, purity of mind, and through the fading away of ignorance...
He attains the purification of knowledge;
he touches it,
he realizes it directly.
In this way, Revata, that monk who is a yogi, a practitioner of yoga, becomes one who does not abandon meditation.
And because of this, Revata,
The monk fixes his mind upon this object; and by fixing his mind upon the object in such a manner, his mind becomes well-fixed upon that object.
In this regard, there is a verse:
The yogin who moves among signs, who understands the meaning of all beings,
and who constantly meditates on the image, attains complete purification.
In that regard, as for what was first stated:
Practicing with respect to the signs, by this it is explained that the practitioner’s constant application is directed toward the sign of serenity, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity.
Furthermore, as for what he said— that [the Buddha] is the knower of the meaning of all beings—
by this, the ultimate limit of things (*vastuparyantatā*) is explained.
Furthermore, as for what was said:
"One who constantly meditates on the image"—
by this, both the conceptual and non-conceptual reflected images are explained.
Furthermore, as for what he said—
that "one departs from complete purity"— by this, the accomplishment of the task is explained.
And it was further said by the Blessed One:
Skilled in the sign of the mind, he experiences the flavor of seclusion.
The meditator, prudent and mindful, enjoys a spiritual joy and happiness that is free from worldly attachment.
Regarding this, as for what was said:
By the phrase "skilled in the sign of the mind" (*cittanimittasya kovida*), both the conceptual and non-conceptual reflections are designated by the word "sign" (*nimitta*);
by the word "skilled" (*kovida*), the "limit of things" (*vastuparyantatā*) is indicated.
Furthermore, as he says:
By the phrase "and they find the flavor of seclusion," it is explained that for one who is correctly applied to this object of focus, there is delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation.
Furthermore, by the phrase "the meditator, prudent and mindful," the continuity of the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) is explained.
Furthermore, as for what he said—
“he enjoys spiritual joy and happiness free from worldly taint”— by this, the perfection of the body is explained.
Thus, this being so, it should be understood that this pervasive object of focus is purified by authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
And that which falls within logical reasoning—
this is called the pervasive object of focus (vyāpyālambana).
In that regard, what is the object of focus for purifying conduct?
Namely: the meditation on impurity,
loving-kindness,
and dependent origination through specific conditionality.
The analysis of the elements and mindfulness of breathing.
Among these, what is the meditation on the foul?
He said: There are six kinds of impurity;
namely, the impurity of the corpse.
The impurity of suffering,
the impurity of inferiority,
and the impurity of relativity.
The impurity of the afflictions and the impurity of perishability.
In that regard, what is the impurity of the secondary?
It is said:
the impurity of the secondary is based upon the internal.
And it should be understood as being based on the external.
Therein, with reference to the internal,
they are as follows: hair of the head, body hairs, and so forth.
Nails, teeth, and dust.
Filth,
skin, flesh, bone, and sinew.
the blood vessels, the kidneys, the heart, the spleen, and the lungs;
The intestines,
the mesentery, the stomach, and the large intestine.
urine, feces, tears, sweat, and phlegm;
nasal mucus, fat, and lymph.
marrow and fat, bile, and phlegm.
pus, blood, brain matter, and brain-marrow, and urine.
In that regard, what is the impurity (impurity) based on the external? It is as follows: a bloated corpse, or one festering with pus, or...
Or whether it be of a bloated nature, or of a fissured nature, or of a devoured nature.
Or a bloated corpse,
or a mangled corpse, or a skeleton.
Or a chain; or that which is made of excrement,
or that which is made of urine.
Or made of saliva, or made of snot,
or stained with blood.
Or pus mixed with filth,
or a lump of excrement,
or a stream of discharge.
In this way, the various forms of internal and external impurity based on the unattractive should be understood. This includes both that which is based internally and that which is based externally.
And that which is impurity based on external things is called the impurity of the secondary.
In that regard, what is the impurity of suffering?
It is that which arises in dependence upon contact to be experienced as suffering;
it is the unpleasant experience, whether physical or mental, that has come under the category of feeling—this is called [the impurity of suffering].
The impurity of suffering.
In that regard, what is the inferior impurity?
It is whatever object is most base.
The most inferior realm is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because there exists no other realm that is more inferior, more base, or more contemptible than it.
This is called inferior impurity.
What is relative impurity?
It is as follows: a certain object, though pure, appears as impure when compared with something else that is more pure.
For example:
in relation to the formless realm, the realm of form appears as impure;
and in relation to nirvāṇa, which is the cessation of the view of a self-identity, everything up to the peak of existence appears as impure.
It comes to be reckoned as such.
This is the relative impurity of this kind;
it pertains to those belonging to the three realms.
All fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, and secondary afflictions are called impurity.
In that regard, what is the impurity of perishability?
It is the impermanence of the five aggregates of clinging, their lack of stability, and their lack of reliability.
The nature of change—this is the foulness for the purification of one whose temperament is dominated by passion.
In that regard, passion is the object, namely:
internally, toward sensual pleasures.

Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), passion for sensual pleasures (*kāmarāga*), the desire for sexual intercourse regarding external objects of desire (*bahirdhā kāmeṣu maithunacchanda*), and passion for sexual intercourse (*maithunarāga*).
Desire for sense objects;
attachment to sense objects; desire for form.
Attachment to form, desire for the view of a self-identity, and attachment to the view of a self-identity—
this is the fivefold attachment.
For the sake of abandoning, dispelling, and the non-occurrence of those five kinds of attachment.

The sixfold foulness is the object of focus. Therein, by means of the internal, one purifies the mind from sensual desire and sensual passion regarding internal sense-pleasures through the object of the foulness of the individual body.

By means of the external object of meditation on the foulness of the external, one purifies the mind from those four kinds of passion associated with passion for the external— namely, passion for color, passion for shape, passion for touch, and passion for secondary qualities. In that regard, when [one contemplates] a livid corpse, or...
Or as festering,
or as putrid,
or as bloated.
Or when he brings to mind the devoured corpse,
he purifies the mind from attachment to color;
and when he further brings to mind the bloody corpse, [he purifies the mind from attachment to shape].
Then, one purifies the mind from attachment to shape;
furthermore, when one brings to mind a bone or a skeleton,
one purifies the mind from attachment to touch.
When one brings to mind a scattered corpse, one purifies the mind from attachment to the objects of sensory enjoyment.
For this very reason, the Blessed One established the various forms of external foulness within the four stages of the charnel ground (*śivapathikā*);
whichever charnel ground he has seen, [he applies it accordingly].
Whether dead for one day or dead for seven days,
being devoured by crows and ospreys;
By vultures, dogs, and jackals;
here and there, this very [body]...
He compares his own body [to that]: "This body of mine, too, will become like this;
it has become like this."
"In this way, it does not transcend the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
By this, first, everything from the "dissected" (*viniḷaka*) up to the "gnawed" (*vikhādita*) has been explained.
Furthermore, as for what he said:
That cemetery path which has been seen by him— whether it be devoid of skin, flesh,
and blood, or bound together with sinews— is called the *vilohitaka* (the bloody).
Furthermore, as for what was said:
those very places on the path of the cemetery, such as the backbone, the jaw,
and the skull;
A necklace of teeth, a human skull, and likewise fragments— whole or broken— from [human remains] one year old, two years old,
up to seven years old.
What are those that are white, resembling conch shells; and those that are the color of pigeons, like dust?
By the statement "they are seen as variegated in color," the *vikṣiptaka* (the scattered) is explained.
Thus, by means of the meditation on the foulness of the corpse as an external object, one purifies the mind from passion through loving-kindness (*maitra*).
Therein, by means of the object of the nature of suffering and the nature of impurity, and by means of the inferior object of impurity,
one purifies the mind from sensual desire associated with sense objects.
Therein, by means of the object of the impurity of expectation, one purifies the mind from desire for the realm of form.

Therein, by means of the object of the impurity of afflictions and the object of the impurity of perishability, he purifies the mind from all passion for the body, starting from the realm of desire up to the peak of existence.
This, first of all, is stated with reference to the purification of the conduct of one whose temperament is dominated by passion (*rāgacarita*), regarding the possibility of its having an object;
it includes every aspect of the object of impurity (*aśubhatā*).
However, in this context, specifically the impurity of the corpse (*pratyaśubhatā*) is intended.
That other form of impurity is the objective support for the purification of conduct other than that [specific one].
In that regard, what is loving-kindness?
It is that which [is directed] toward one's circle of friends or toward one's circle of enemies.
Or, toward those who are neutral,
having established an intention for their welfare, there is an adhimokṣa (resolute conviction) for the provision of mild, moderate, and intense happiness;
this belongs to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*).
In this regard, that which consists of the side of friends,
the side of enemies, and the side of neutral persons—
this is the objective support.
In this context, that which is the resolute intention for welfare and the resolve for the provision of happiness belonging to the level of meditative concentration— this is the subject (ālambaka),
as well as the object (ālambana).
That which takes [beings] as its object, having condensed them into a single unity, is called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*).

In this regard, when it says "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness," this refers to the three categories: the category of friends, the category of enemies, and [the category of neutral persons].
The disposition of wishing for the welfare of those who are neutral has been explained.
Furthermore,
by the statement "without enmity, without malice, and without ill-will," the threefold characteristic of that very same disposition of wishing for welfare has been explained.
In that regard, there is the resolute intention for welfare through non-hostility; furthermore, that non-hostility is described by two phrases:

"by way of incapacity" and "by way of non-affliction. Among these, "incapacity" has the sense of not abiding in a state of antagonism, and [non-affliction] has the sense of not being subject to the impulse to cause harm.
Non-affliction (*avyābādhyatā*). Furthermore, by the statement "with that which is vast, exalted, and immeasurable," the bestowal of pleasure that is weak, medium, and intense is explained.
Whether it belongs to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), or to the level of the first or second dhyāna,
or to the level of the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, as for what he said:
"Having become resolved upon these [attainments],
one dwells having fully attained them"— by this, the resolution that brings about happiness is indicated.
It is said to belong to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*). Furthermore, this bringing about of happiness is embraced by the resolute intention for welfare;
it is produced through resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*).
Accompanied by mental attention toward those who are neither suffering nor happy, whether they belong to the side of friends or the side of enemies.
It should be understood that this applies to one who is neutral and desires happiness;
however, as for one who is suffering, [it is not so].
Furthermore, whether it be the side of friends,
the side of enemies, or the side of neutral persons—
among these, whoever is suffering is the objective support for compassion.
He who is happy is the object of sympathetic joy (*muditā*); this is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
In that regard, a person whose conduct is dominated by ill-will (*vyāpāda*), while cultivating loving-kindness toward sentient beings, thins out whatever ill-will exists.
One purifies the mind from ill will.
In this regard, what is dependent origination through specific conditionality?
It is that which, throughout the three times, consists of mere formations and mere phenomena.
mere object, mere cause, and mere result;
It falls within the scope of reasoning,
namely, by means of the reasoning of dependence and the reasoning of cause and effect.
And by means of the reasoning that establishes through logical proof,
it is shown that phenomena alone are the bringers of phenomena,
and that they are devoid of an agent or an experiencer.
This is called the object of dependent origination through specific conditionality (*idampratyayatā-pratītyasamutpāda*).
When a person who is dominated by delusion and whose conduct is characterized by delusion attends to this object with the mind, they abandon delusion.
He attenuates it;
he purifies the mind from the conduct of delusion.
In that regard, what is the analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*)?
It is as follows: the six elements.
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
Among these, the earth element is twofold:
internal and external.
Therein, the internal is that which, within this body, is internal and personal, hard, more solid, and appropriated;
whereas the external is the earth element, which is external, hard, of a solid nature, not appropriated, and has come to be so.
Furthermore, what is the internal earth element? It is as follows:
head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth.
Nails, teeth, and dirt.
Filth,
skin, flesh, bone, and sinew.
The vessels, the kidneys, the heart, the spleen, the lungs, the small intestines,
and the large intestines.
The stomach,
the large intestine,
the liver, and what consists of excrement— this is called the internal earth element.
Furthermore, what is that external earth element? It is either pieces of wood or clods of earth.
Whether gravel, or clods of earth, or trees,
Or mountain peaks,
or whatever else is of this same category— this is called the external earth element.
What is the water element?
The water element is twofold:
internal and external.
Therein, what is the internal water element?
It is that which is internal, belonging to oneself, moisture or that which has become moisture;
water, or that which has approached the water element, and is appropriated.
Namely: tears, sweat, saliva,
nasal mucus,
fat, and lymph.
marrow, fat, and bile.
phlegm, pus, and blood;
The head,
the brain matter,
and the urine.
The internal water element is released.
What is the external water element? It is that which is external, water, or watery in nature.
Moisture is that which has entered into moisture, followed it,
and been appropriated; furthermore, it is either a pool, or...
Whether they be lakes, ponds,
rivers, or springs—
whatever else is of this same category is called the external water element.
What is the fire element?
The fire element is twofold: internal and external.
Therein, what is the internal fire element?
It is that which is internal, belonging to the individual, fire, consisting of fire, heat, consisting of heat, approached, and appropriated.
For example, it is the fire in this body by which this body is warmed.
It is heated and thoroughly heated;
and by means of this, what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes digestion with complete ease.
And because of its prominence, it receives the designation "consumed, consumed" (jārita).
What is the external fire element? It is that which is external, belonging to fire, characterized by heat, or possessing the nature of heat.
It is naturally unappropriated;
furthermore, it is that which humans seek from cow-dung powder kept with fire-drills,
and once produced, it burns even a village.
Even a village region,
or a city, or a city region, or a district;
or a district of the countryside,
or an island, or a thicket;
Whether it be a forest, or wood, or grass,
Or he goes toward burning cow dung;
or whoever else is of a similar nature.
In that regard, what is the wind element?
The wind element is twofold:
internal and external.
Therein, the internal wind element is that which is internal and individual,
consisting of wind or what has become wind.
Lightness and mobility have been acquired and taken up.
Furthermore, there are in this body winds that move upward and winds that move downward.
The winds that lie at the sides;
the winds that lie in the belly;
the winds that lie in the back.
The "wind-nodules" (vāyvaṣṭhīlā) are winds;
the "razor-like," "pepper-like," and "scalpel-like" winds are winds;
inhalation and exhalation are winds.
The winds that follow the limbs and sub-limbs.
What is the external wind element?
It is that which is external, wind or wind-like, characterized by lightness.
The state of agitation; it is not approached and not grasped. There are external winds in the east, and so forth.
The southern winds,
the northern winds, the western winds,
and the dusty winds.
The dustless winds, the limited winds, the vast winds, and all the winds.
There are the Vairambha winds, the winds of the wind-mandalas.
And there comes a time when a great mass of wind arises that fells even the tops of trees and fells even the tops of walls.
He causes even mountain peaks to fall;
having caused them to fall, he departs without any further grasping.
Those beings who seek him out by means of the corner of his robe—
Whether by means of a palm-leaf fan or a bellows—
such is wind, as well as anything else of this same category.
What is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*)?
It is that which is the eye, or its cavity.
Or the cavities of the ear,
or the cavities of the nose, or the cavities of the mouth;
Or it is the hollow of the throat;
that by which one swallows,
or that wherein one swallows.
That by which one swallows,
that which flows out through the lower part,
or whatever else is of a similar nature, such as excrement.
This is called the space element.
What is the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*)?
It is eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness;
furthermore, it is the mind (*citta*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This is called the consciousness element.

In this regard, a person of proud temperament, attending to this analysis of the elements, eliminates the perception of the body as a single mass and acquires the perception of its impurity; furthermore, he does not become conceited on account of it.
He diminishes pride and purifies the mind from that conduct;
this is called the analysis of the elements (dhātuprabheda).
The object for purifying the conduct of a person whose temperament is dominated by pride.
In this context, what is mindfulness of breathing? Mindfulness that takes inhalation and exhalation as its object is called mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
In that regard, there are two types of inhalation; which two?
Inhalation and intermediate inhalation.
What are the two exhalations?
They are the exhalation and the internal exhalation.
Among these, the exhalation is that wind which proceeds inward immediately after the [external] exhalation.
Up to the region of the navel:
therein, the "intermediate inhalation" is that which occurs when this inhalation has ceased but the exhalation has not yet arisen;
it is a wind that arises for a brief duration, accompanied by a state of rest in the interval, and is similar to that [preceding] inhalation.
This is called the intermediate inhalation.
Just as inhalation and the intermediate inhalation are to be understood, so too should exhalation and the internal exhalation be understood.
In this regard, there is this distinction:
the outward-moving wind proceeds externally,
starting from the region of the navel as far as the tip of the mouth or the tip of the nose, or even further beyond that.
There are two causes for inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
Karma that projects them, and—
And there is the cavity of the navel region;
furthermore, there is whatever cavity of the body has arisen from that.
What are the two bases for inhalation and exhalation?
There are two: body and mind.
For what reason?
Because of the accumulation of the body...
Inhalation and exhalation proceed based on the body and based on the mind;
and they do so according to their respective conditions. If they were to proceed based on the body alone, [the following would occur].

If they were to proceed only by depending upon the mind, then [the formations] would proceed for those who have attained the attainment of non-perception, for those who have attained the attainment of cessation, and for those beings born among the gods who are non-percipient beings.
Therefore, they would function for those beings who have attained or been born into the formless realms.
If they were to function based upon the body and based upon the mind,
then they would not, as is appropriate, [function] for those who have attained or been born into the fourth dhyāna by means of that [body].
If they were to function for beings who have reached the stage of *kalala*, the *arbuda*, or the *peśī*,
they do not so function.
Therefore, inhalation and exhalation proceed based upon the body and based upon the mind;
accordingly,
there are two modes of movement for inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
The downward movement of the inhalations and the upward movement of the exhalations.
There are two stages for inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
The coarse stage with cavities, and the subtle stage.
Hollowness:
therein, gross hollowness extends from the region of the navel up to the openings of the mouth and nose.
Starting from the openings of the mouth and nose up to the cavity of the navel region—
what is subtle porosity?
All the pores of the body.
There are four synonymous terms for inhalation and exhalation.
What are the four?
They are: winds, and inhalations and exhalations (ānāpāna).
"Inhalation and exhalation are bodily formations.
In this regard, there is one synonymous name shared with other winds.
Namely, "wind.
The other three are uncommon [to that state].
There are two disadvantages for one engaged in inhalation and exhalation.
Which two?
Non-laxity in application and application firmly grounded in the truths.
In that regard, for one who has fallen into laziness due to lax application, the mind is either enveloped by sloth and torpor or distracted outwardly;
likewise, for one who applies effort with excessive rigidity, a physical imbalance arises.
Or there is an imbalance of the mind.
How does an imbalance of the body arise?
By forcibly suppressing the inhalations and exhalations, uneven winds circulate within the body.
Those which first throb within those various major and minor limbs are called *sphārakāya* (or *sphuraka*).
Furthermore, those throbbing winds, as they increase, become painful;
they produce pain in these various limbs and members of the body.
This is called bodily disharmony.
How does mental imbalance arise? Or how is his mind distracted? Previously, he was not overcome by dejection or despair.
In this way, mental imbalance arises.
One should understand that there are five kinds of cultivation for this mindfulness of breathing:
namely, cultivation through counting, and so forth.
Familiarization with the entry into the aggregates; familiarization with the entry into dependent origination;
familiarization with the entry into the truths.
And there is the cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Among these, what is the cultivation of counting?
Briefly stated, the cultivation of counting is fourfold.
Namely: counting one by one,
counting two as one,
and counting in forward order.
And there is also counting in reverse order.
In that regard, what is counting one by one?
When the inhalation has entered,
one counts "one" with mindfulness fixed upon the inhalation and exhalation.
When, upon the cessation of the inhalation, the exhalation arises and goes out, one then counts the second; in this manner, one counts up to ten.
This counting by number is neither too brief nor too extensive; this is called "counting one by one."
What is the counting of pairs as one?
It is when the inhalation has entered and has ceased.
When the out-breath arises and has gone forth, he then counts it as "one.
By means of this method of counting, he counts up to ten.
This is called counting the pair as one.
By condensing this dyad—the inhalation and the exhalation—into a single unit, one counts them as "one"; therefore, it is called counting the pair as one.
What is counting in the forward order? It is by means of this very method of counting one by one,
or by counting two as one.
One counts in forward order up to ten;
this is called counting in forward order.
What is counting in reverse order?
Starting from ten in reverse order,
[one counts] nine, eight, and so on.
He counts seven, six, five, down to one.
This is called counting in reverse order;
when, relying on that single-unit counting or the two-unit-and-one counting, [one proceeds].
He becomes one who has practiced both counting in forward order and counting in reverse order,
and his mind does not become distracted in the interim.
And when he counts with an undistracted mind,
then his superior distinction in counting is designated. What is this distinction in counting?
Either by counting one by one,
or by counting two as one,
he counts having made two into one.
In that regard, by counting in groups of two, four inhalations and exhalations constitute one;
however, by counting each individually, one inhalation and exhalation constitute one, and he continues counting in this manner up to ten.
Thus, by increasing further and further, he even counts up to one hundred by making them into single units.
Then, by counting in groups of hundreds in successive order, he counts up to ten; thus,
for one engaged in counting, he counts by making ten into one,
until he completes the number ten.
By means of that counting up to ten, his mind is not distracted from the higher [object].
To this extent, he has achieved proficiency in counting.
If, while he is thus engaged in counting, his mind becomes distracted in the interim, then he returns once more to the beginning and begins to count again.
Whether in forward order or reverse order,
when his mind, through the power of cultivation, flows spontaneously by way of the natural flow of the path;
Having mounted [the practice], bound to the object of the inhalation and exhalation, proceeding uninterruptedly and continuously while inhaling...
It apprehends the occurrence [of inhalation];
when inhalation has ceased, it apprehends the state empty of exhalation;
and when exhalation has occurred, it apprehends its occurrence.
When it has ceased, however, there proceeds a grasping at cessation that is unshakable,
immovable, free from the mode of distraction,
and accompanied by delight.
To this extent, there is a transcending of the stage of counting;
at that point, one must count again,
except that the mind is no longer bound to the object of the inhalation and exhalation.
The inhalations and exhalations, along with the intervals between them and their states of occurrence and cessation, are to be followed and observed; this is called the cultivation of counting.
Indeed, this cultivation of counting is prescribed for those of dull faculties, as it serves as a point of focus to prevent their distraction.
For the sake of the stability of the mind and for the sake of delighting the mind;
otherwise, without counting, their mind might be overcome by sloth and torpor,
or the mind might be distracted outwardly.
However, this does not apply to those who are engaged in counting.
But for those with sharp faculties and keen intelligence, there arises a fondness for the application of counting;
having been instructed therein, they very quickly master the application of counting in this way.
And they do not take delight in that.
Furthermore, having bound their mindfulness to the object of inhalation and exhalation, they attend to where these [breaths] proceed and for as long as they proceed.
He investigates and discerns all of this— how they proceed and when they proceed— with established mindfulness.
Such is the nature of their preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Through the sequence of practicing that application, through the sequence of its cultivation, and through the sequence of its frequent repetition, physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) and mental pliancy (*citta-praśrabdhi*) arise.
He touches one-pointedness and emerges with delight in the focal object.
Having thus cultivated familiarity through the mental attention to the entities of the grasped and the grasper, he enters into the aggregates.
By attending to those inhalations and exhalations and to that body which is their basis, he enters into the aggregate of form.
That experience associated with the mindfulness that grasps those inhalations and exhalations enters into the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*);
that which is the act of perceiving enters into the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); and as for that mindfulness, that volition, and...
Therein, wisdom understands:
"This is a conditioned formation," and that which is mind and intellect.

One enters into the aggregate of consciousness as "consisting of consciousness. This state of frequently dwelling therein is called the cultivation of the entry into the aggregates for one who has thus entered into the aggregates.
And when he has seen that there are merely the aggregates,
thoroughly understood them as merely conditioned phenomena,
and as merely entities,
Then he enters into the dependent origination of these very formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
And how does he enter?
He investigates form in this way:
He investigates: "Upon what are these inhalations and exhalations based? What is their condition? To him, this thought occurs:
These inhalations and exhalations depend upon the body and have the body as their condition; they also depend upon the mind and have the mind as their condition.
Furthermore, what are the conditions for the body and the mind?
He enters into [the understanding] that this body and mind are conditioned by the life-faculty;
this is prior formative activity (*pūrva-saṃskāra*).
He enters into the understanding that the preceding formative predisposition has ignorance as its condition;
for thus, ignorance is the condition.
The prior formative force is the condition for the life-faculty;
the life-faculty is the condition for the body and consciousness.
Inhalation and exhalation have the body and mind as their conditions.
In this regard, through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations;
through the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of the life-faculty.
From the cessation of the life-faculty comes the cessation of body and mind;
from the cessation of body and mind comes the cessation of inhalation and exhalation.
In this way, he delights in the excellence of dependent origination.
One who dwells frequently therein and has cultivated familiarity with the aspects of dependent origination is said to have "cultivated familiarity with the entry into dependent origination.
This is called the cultivation of entry into dependent origination.
Having thus cultivated familiarity with dependent origination, he enters into the realization that these conditioned phenomena which have arisen dependently are impermanent;
and because they are impermanent, having not previously existed, they pass away.
Furthermore, these come into being after not having been, and having come into being, they pass away;
they are subject to birth.
Subject to aging, subject to illness, and subject to death.
Those things subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death are suffering;
those which are suffering are non-self and lack independence.
They are devoid of a master.
Thus, by way of the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, he has entered into the truth of suffering;
whatever is this production of these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
They have become suffering,
they have become disease,
they have become an abscess.
All this has craving as its condition.

Furthermore, the complete abandonment of this craving which gives rise to suffering—this is peace, this is sublime; and for me who knows thus and dwells frequently in this way, there will be the complete abandonment of craving.
In this way, one has entered into the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
When one who dwells frequently in that state realizes the truths,
this is called the cultivation of the entry into the truths. For one who has thus cultivated familiarity with the truths:
When the phenomena to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned, those to be abandoned by cultivation remain;
for their abandonment, one performs the cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
What, then, are the sixteen aspects?
Mindfully breathing in (*smṛta āśvāsa*), while breathing in...
Mindful, he trains himself: "I am breathing in"; mindful, while breathing out, he trains himself: "I am breathing out.
He breathes in long, he breathes out short, experiencing the whole body.
Breathing in, he trains himself: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in";
breathing out, experiencing the whole body.
He trains himself: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains himself: "Calming the bodily formations, I shall breathe in; calming the bodily formations, I shall breathe out.
Calming the bodily formations, he breathes out.
He trains himself: "Experiencing the bodily formations, I breathe out; calming the bodily formations, I breathe in.
He trains himself: "Experiencing rapture, experiencing pleasure;
experiencing the mental formations, calming the mental formations, I breathe in."
He trains himself: "Calming the mental formations, I shall breathe in";
breathing out while calming the mental formations, he trains himself: "Calming the mental formations, I shall breathe out."
Experiencing the mind,
gladdening the mind,
and concentrating the mind.
Breathing in while liberating the mind, he trains himself: "I shall breathe in liberating the mind.
Breathing out while liberating the mind, he trains himself: "I shall breathe out liberating the mind. Contemplating impermanence...

Contemplating relinquishment, contemplating dispassion, and contemplating cessation while breathing in, he trains himself: "I am breathing in. Contemplating cessation while breathing out, he trains himself: "I am breathing out."
What, then, is the distinction among these aspects?
That learner who has seen [the truth]...
When the rumor has been heard,
he undertakes a mental application that takes the four foundations of mindfulness and inhalation and exhalation as its object.
For the sake of abandoning the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*),
he is therefore called "mindful" (*smṛta*).
Breathing in, he trains himself: "I am breathing in mindfully.
When he takes either the inhalation or the exhalation as his object, he then trains himself: "I am breathing in long; I am breathing out long.
When [he attends] to the interval between inhalations or the interval between...

Or when one takes exhalation as the object of focus, one then trains oneself: "I am breathing in short, I am breathing out short. For in that case, the inhalations and exhalations proceed as long ones.
The intermediate inhalations and intermediate exhalations are likewise short; they proceed in that very manner,
and he observes them in that very manner.
He knows:
when he resolves upon and takes as his object the subtle inhalations and exhalations that have entered the head and are diffused throughout the body, even though they have entered into distraction.
When the out-breath has ceased and during the interval between out-breaths;
and when the in-breath has not yet arisen and during the interval between in-breaths.
He takes as his object of focus that white state which is empty of out-breath and in-breath, devoid of them, and separated from them.
At that time, calming the bodily formations while breathing in,
he trains himself: "Calming the bodily formations, I am breathing in."
Calming the bodily formations while breathing out, he trains himself: "Calming the bodily formations, I breathe out.
Furthermore, through the sequence of its cultivation, the sequence of its development, and the sequence of its frequent practice, [he attains this].
Those inhalations and exhalations which were previously coarse and unpleasant to the touch for one who has not yet practiced familiarity,
proceed as otherwise— becoming subtle and pleasant to the touch— for one who has practiced familiarity.
Therefore it is said:
"He trains himself, thinking, 'I shall breathe in while calming the bodily formations';
and he is thus engaged in the practice of mindfulness of breathing, and if he becomes an attainer [of this state]..."
Or at whatever time, while breathing in, he experiences joy during the first or the second dhyāna, experiencing joy...
He trains himself, thinking, "I shall breathe in experiencing rapture.
If, moreover, he becomes an attainer of the third dhyāna, which is devoid of rapture;
At that time, he experiences pleasure.
Above the third dhyāna, there is no association with mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti);
by this [association], everything up to the third dhyāna has been proclaimed and included.
While he is thus experiencing joy or experiencing happiness,
if at any time, anywhere—
From the loss of mindfulness regarding consciousness, [the thought] arises:
"I am," or "This is I," or "I shall be," or "I shall not be."
"I shall be possessed of form; I shall be formless; I shall be percipient; I shall be non-percipient;
I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient."
The thought "I shall become non-percipient" arises as a state of craving, accompanied by deluded perception and volition, stirred up, churned, elaborated, and conditioned.
As soon as it has arisen, he penetrates it very quickly with wisdom.
He does not tolerate it;
he abandons it;
he dispels it.
He brings them to an end.
Thus, experiencing the mental formations, he trains himself: "Experiencing the mental formations, I shall breathe in, calming the mental formations";
[breathing in,] he trains himself: "Calming the mental formations, I shall breathe in."
If, moreover, he is a possessor of the fundamental first, second, and third dhyānas, he is necessarily also a possessor of the *anāgamya*, the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna;
relying upon that, he examines his own mind as it has arisen.
Whether with passion or free from passion,
with hatred or free from hatred.
With delusion,
free from delusion, contracted;
sunk,
exerted, agitated, unagitated,
tranquilized, and untranquilized;
He understands, as it truly is, the concentrated mind and the unconcentrated mind, the well-developed mind and the unwell-developed mind, and the liberated mind and the unliberated mind.
He experiences it;
therefore, he is called "one who experiences the mind.
When his mind is dependent upon the hindrance of sloth and torpor, [he perceives it as such].
It occurs for one who is inwardly concentrating when they demonstrate and encourage [the mind] by means of any one of the various inspiring objects.
He inspires and kindles [them];
therefore, he says:
Gladdening the mind,
when he perceives it as hindered by the hindrance of restlessness or the hindrance of remorse,
he then uplifts it by means of some inspiring object of focus, causing it to settle within.
He pacifies it and composes it;
therefore, it is said that he "composes the mind" (*samādadhaṃścittaṃ*).
And when that mind, through the sequence of repeated practice and the sequence of cultivation...
Through the consequence of repeated practice, it becomes distant from the manifestation of the hindrances;
it is purified (or liberated) from the hindrances.
Therefore, he said:
Experiencing liberation of the mind while breathing in, he trains himself: "Experiencing liberation of the mind, I shall breathe in."

For one whose mind is liberated from the hindrances, yet for whom latent tendencies (anuśaya) remain as obstacles to the cultivation of the path, those must be abandoned. To abandon them, he brings the path into manifestation; that is to say, he thoroughly contemplates the very impermanence of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
And he examines it thoroughly and appropriately;
therefore, it is said:
Contemplating impermanence;

and by means of that, having previously relied upon the first, second, or third dhyāna, or else relying upon the threshold concentration (anāgamya), there is again the application of calm abiding (śamatha).
Now, he is one who contemplates impermanence with a straight mind.

He applies himself to yoga in insight (vipaśyanā). Thus, his mind, cultivated by both serenity (śamatha) and insight, is liberated from the elements (dhātu), that is to say, from the underlying tendencies (anuśaya). Which are these elements?
That which is the element of abandonment, that which is the element of dispassion, and that which is the element of cessation.
In this regard, the element of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*) arises from the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are to be abandoned by vision;
the element of detachment (*virāgadhātu*) arises from the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena that are to be abandoned by cultivation;
and the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*) arises from the cessation of all substrates (*upadhi*).
Thus, he attends to these three realms as peaceful, secure, and healthy.
He cultivates calm abiding and insight;
through the sequence of their repeated practice, cultivation, and frequent application, his mind is liberated from the remaining afflictions that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
Therefore, it is said:
Contemplating abandonment, contemplating dispassion,
and contemplating cessation, while breathing in, he trains himself: "I am contemplating cessation as I breathe in."
In this way, when the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation have been eliminated, one becomes an Arhat;
with outflows exhausted, there remains nothing further for him to do.
Or, it is the cultivation of what has been performed;
this is called its sixteenfold cultivation. Furthermore, this fivefold cultivation is also said to belong to it.
Mindfulness of breathing:
herein, a person whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought (vitarka-carita), when applying himself, practices with a sense of fondness and ease;
furthermore, this object of focus involves active mental engagement.

With a slight turning toward the interior, directed within and toward oneself, and becoming increasingly close, there arises no agitation of discursive thought for him as he applies himself therein; and his mind very swiftly becomes settled upon the object of focus.
He delights;
he is born.
This is the fivefold [type].
The object for purifying the conduct of a person whose conduct is dominated by discursive thought (*vitarkacarita*).
Among these, what is the object of skill (*kauśalyālambana*)? It is as follows:
skill in the aggregates, skill in the elements, skill in the sense-bases,
and skill in dependent origination;
Skill in the possible and the impossible.
In that regard, what are the aggregates, and what is [the aggregate of]...?
Skillfulness regarding the aggregates.
He said: "The five aggregates:
the aggregate of form and the aggregate of sensation."
The aggregate of formations and the aggregate of consciousness.

In that regard, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of whatever form there may be; all of it comprises the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and that which is derived from the four great elements (*upādāya*).
Furthermore, that which is past, future, or present; internal or external;
or coarse—
Whether subtle or coarse, inferior or sublime.
Whether far or near:
therein, what is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*)?
It is that which is to be experienced as pleasant (*sukha-vedanīya*).
Dependent upon contact,
there is that which is to be experienced as painful, or that which is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
The six groups of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact;
feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
In that regard, what is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
It is as follows: perception with signs (*sanimitta-saṃjñā*), perception without signs (*animitta-saṃjñā*), and so forth.
The perception of the limited, the perception of the vast, and the perception of the immeasurable.
The perception of the sphere of nothingness is the notion that "nothing exists.
These are the six bodies of perception.
Perception born of eye-contact.
Perception born of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact.

What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)? It consists of the six groups of volition: volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Excluding both volition and perception.
Those other mental factors which are distinct from those [three].
In that regard, what is the aggregate of consciousness?
It is that which is mind (*citta*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
furthermore, these are the six groups of consciousness.
Eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness; and this feeling, perception, mental formations, and this consciousness—
whether past, future, or present, and whether internal— [are to be viewed in this way].
"Whether internal or external," and so forth, in detail as before.
These are called the aggregates.
What is skill in the aggregates? It is knowing these aforementioned phenomena by way of their diverse natures and by way of their manifold natures.
Beyond that, one neither perceives nor conceptualizes;
this, in brief, is called skillfulness regarding the aggregates.

In that regard, what is the state of being diverse among the aggregates? The aggregate of form is one thing, the aggregate of feeling is another, and so on, up to the aggregate of consciousness being yet another; this is the state of being diverse.
In that regard, what is multiplicity? It is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) which is of many kinds and various types,
distinguished by the elements (*bhūta*), by the mundane and supramundane, and by the future, present, and so forth.
This is called "multitudinous nature" by way of the distinction of types.
Just as it is for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it should be understood accordingly for the remaining aggregates.
Furthermore, he perceives nothing beyond that, nor does he conceptualize it;
he perceives only the aggregates.
One perceives only a mere mass of phenomena, but does not perceive a self (ātman) distinct from the aggregates as something permanent,
stable, and of an unchanging nature.
Nor does one perceive anything here as "mine," nor does one conceptualize it beyond that. In this regard, what are the elements (dhātavaḥ)?
What is skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*)?
It is said: the eighteen elements.
The eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element and the sound element.
The element of ear-consciousness;
the element of the nose;
the element of odors.
The element of nose-consciousness;
the element of tongue and the element of taste;
the element of tongue-consciousness.
The body element,
the tangible element,
the body-consciousness element, the phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element— these are called the elements.

Furthermore, he knows, approves of, and reflects upon how these eighteen dharmas arise, are produced, and manifest from their respective elements, from their respective seeds, and from their respective lineages.
This is called skill in the elements.
When one knows the arising of the eighteen dharmas from their respective elements, that is skill in causes and conditions; this, namely, is skill in the elements (dhātu-kauśalya).
In that regard, what are the sense bases?
What is skill in the sense bases? It is said:
the twelve sense bases.
The sense-sphere of the eye,
the sense-sphere of visible forms;
the sense-sphere of the ear.
The sense base of sound,
the sense base of the nose,
and the sense base of odor.
The sense base of the tongue, the sense base of taste,
and the sense base of the body.
The sphere of the tangible,
the mental sphere, and the sphere of phenomena.
These are called the sense bases (*āyatana*).
What is skillfulness regarding the sense bases?
In this regard, the eye is the dominant condition and visible forms are the objective support for the arising of visual consciousness along with its associated mental factors.
The mind that has just ceased is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
therein, the ear is the dominant factor (*adhipati*) and sound is the objective support (*ālambana*).
The mind that has ceased immediately prior is the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the arising of auditory consciousness together with its associated mental factors.

Likewise, up to the point of the mind itself, the immediately preceding mind is the immediate antecedent condition, while the attention (*manasikāra*) produced from it is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), and phenomena (*dharma*) are the objective support (*ālambana*).
"For the arising of the association of mental consciousness" means by way of three conditions: the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The six groups of consciousness arise together with their associated mental factors;
such skill regarding the conditions for the internal and external sense bases is called "skill in the sense bases" (āyatana-kauśalya).
In that regard, what is dependent origination, and what is skillfulness regarding dependent origination?
He said: "Conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces;
conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness."
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises];
in detail, up until: "In this way there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering"—this is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, it is that phenomena themselves cause phenomena to flow forth.
It is phenomena alone that cause phenomena to move;

it is conditioned factors alone that bring about phenomena. Because they are produced from causes and because they are dependently originated, they come into being after having not existed, and having come into being, they pass away.
Therefore, these conditioned phenomena are impermanent; moreover, those which are impermanent are subject to birth, subject to aging, and subject to illness.
They are subject to death;
they are subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. This is because they possess the nature of aging, and so on, up to the nature of despair.
Those which are suffering, or moreover those which are suffering, being without autonomy and weak, are non-self.
When, through these aspects, there arises knowledge of impermanence and knowledge of suffering regarding dependently originated phenomena, [that is the application of mindfulness].
The knowledge of selflessness—
this is called skill in dependent origination.
Furthermore, skill in [discerning] what is possible and what is impossible should be understood as being precisely dependent origination itself.
In this regard, the distinction is as follows:
through skill in knowing what is possible and what is impossible, one understands that there is no discordant causality;
that is, there exists the ripening of the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Unwholesome states are undesirable.
This very knowledge is called skill in [discerning] what is possible and what is impossible.

And this skill in the five points, in brief, constitutes skill in specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kauśalya*) and skill in general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-kauśalya*). Among these, skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) is said to be skill in specific characteristics.
By means of the remaining [factors], this skill regarding general characteristics is called the objective support for skill.
In that regard, what is the object for the purification of afflictions? It is said:
it is the coarseness of the lower stages; namely, the coarseness of the first dhyāna relative to the desire realm, and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In this regard, what is coarseness?
Coarseness is twofold:
coarseness by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-audārikatā*)...

And there is grossness in terms of number. In that regard, grossness in terms of intrinsic nature is as follows: although the five aggregates exist even in the desire realm, those belonging to the desire realm in the first dhyāna are more fraught with disadvantages and more associated with painful abiding.
They are also more short-lived,
more inferior, and more contemptible;
this is their coarseness of intrinsic nature compared to the first dhyāna.
In that way, they are said by him to be more peaceful and more sublime.
In this regard, what is numerical coarseness?
The aggregate of form belonging to the desire realm is more extensive and thus more to be fully understood.
In this way, even up to the aggregate of consciousness, it is to be abandoned; this is called the coarseness of the aggregates.
In this way, in the higher stages, intrinsic nature,
coarseness, and numerical coarseness are to be understood as appropriate.
However, it should be understood that all the lower stages, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), are more gross than those in the higher stages;
they are characterized by a more painful dwelling and a shorter lifespan.
Furthermore, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is indeed peaceful, because there is no stage superior to it.
In brief, this refers to the meaning of disadvantage and the meaning of coarseness,
which [prevail] more abundantly in whichever respective stage (*bhūmi*).
It becomes a source of disadvantage;
that is, it is viewed as a disadvantage.
It is called "gross" because,
on that worldly level, there is relatively little disadvantage.
It is called "peaceful" because it is free from defects (*ādīnava*).

This is the object of focus for worldly beings using the mundane path to purify their afflictions; nevertheless, for one who perceives its lower stage as defective, as a disease, and as lacking security (*ayogakṣema*), [it is called peaceful].
And one views the higher stage as peaceful;
those afflictions belonging to the lower stages, from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness, are thereby abandoned.
However, they are not abandoned once and for all;
rather, those very same [afflictions] come to be linked again.
Furthermore, the object for the purification of afflictions by means of the supramundane path is fourfold, as follows:
the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin,
and the truth of cessation;
And the truth of the path.
In that regard, what is the truth of suffering?
It is as follows: birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness, death, association with the unpleasant, separation from the pleasant, and the frustration of one's desires are suffering.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Therein, the noble truth of the origin is craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there.
Therein, the noble truth of cessation is the complete abandonment of this very craving without remainder.
The truth of the path is the noble eightfold path.
Therein, based upon the dark side and the bright side, the establishment of the four truths is made through the determination of cause and fruit.
In that regard, the truth of suffering is the fruit;
the truth of origination is the cause;
and the truth of cessation is the fruit.
The truth of the path is the cause for attainment and for direct realization.
Among these, the truth of suffering is like a disease; it is that which must first be fully understood.
The truth of origination is like the cause of a disease; it must be completely abandoned. The truth of cessation is like the state of health.
And that [truth] is to be touched (to be felt), it is to be realized;
the truth of the path is like medicine.
And that should be practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed.
And this is real, thus, not unreal, not perverted, and not inverted:
suffering is [suffering] in the sense of suffering.
To the extent that the path exists in the sense of being a path, it is therefore called a truth;
its specific characteristic does not deceive,
and through the vision of it, non-erroneous cognitions arise.
Therefore, it is called "truth.
Why, then, are these truths of the noble ones (*āryas*) alone? Because the noble ones perceive these very things as they truly are; such is their truthfulness.
They know and see it as it truly is, whereas fools do not know it.
They do not see them as they truly are; therefore, they are called "Noble Truths.
By their very nature, these truths are not realized by the foolish.
For the noble ones, however, it is known in both ways; that is,
one knows [it] as suffering when, for one who is being born, painful feeling— both physical and mental— arises.
But birth itself is not suffering; rather,
it is the source of suffering,
and so on up to the frustration of desires being suffering.
Suffering, both physical and mental, would arise on account of the frustration of one's desires.
But it is not merely the frustration of one's desires that is suffering; rather, it is the source of suffering, as the formula continues.
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering—this is expressed through these synonyms such as birth and so forth.
The suffering of suffering itself has been fully elucidated;
therein, the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned formations remain.
Furthermore, that [remaining suffering] is elucidated by way of the suffering inherent in the five aggregates.
For it is thus: the five aggregates of clinging, being permeated by the three types of sensation, are the receptacles for that aforementioned suffering-as-suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā),
as well as for the unmentioned suffering-of-change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā) and the suffering-of-conditioned-existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
That [suffering] also should be understood as being included within these very [categories].
For what reason, then, did the Blessed One proclaim only the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) by its own specific term, while [the others],
such as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), [were not so designated]?
Furthermore, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is [to be understood] by way of an alternative explanation (*paryāyeṇa*).
For it is in this way that the cognition of suffering arises equally for both the noble ones and the foolish with respect to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

The nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) is extremely distressing for those who have not previously cultivated wisdom; yet, when it is taught in this way, there is an easy entry for those to be trained into the [Four] Truths.
In that regard, how is the threefold nature of suffering established?
Insofar as it is said that "birth is suffering" up to "the frustration of desires is suffering," by this, painful feeling together with its basis has been explained.

And that is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*). This is the formal establishment of the suffering of suffering; furthermore, those factors which are its opposites are likewise [established], such as youth in relation to old age.
Health from disease,
life from death, and union with the beloved from separation from the beloved.
The separation from the unpleasant is the inseparable concomitant of the separation from the pleasant; the fulfillment of desires is the inseparable concomitant of the frustration of desires;
and those afflictions, together with their bases, which operate within painful feeling.

The afflictions that arise with respect to those factors conducive to happiness—such as health and so forth—and with respect to the feeling produced from them, this is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
In that regard, pleasant feeling, together with its basis, undergoes transformation through impermanence;
because of the predominance of its excessive state, it produces suffering.
Furthermore, the afflictions, having arisen everywhere, constitute the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
In this way they become suffering;
and because that transformation pertains to the mind, it is therefore called the "suffering of change."
As it was said by the Blessed One: "Taking hold of a woman's hand with a mind that has entered into and undergone transformation," and so forth in detail.
And as it has been said: "One who is obsessed by sensual desire experiences, conditioned by that obsession with sensual desire and born of it, mental suffering and dejection."
In this way, one who is obsessed by ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret,
and doubt remains suspended even while afflicted by suffering due to the defilements— by means of this authoritative teaching, which is supremely authoritative.
It also has the sense of transformation;
therefore it is said that "the suffering of the transformation of the afflictions" is the formal definition of the suffering of transformation (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is pervasive throughout the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*). In brief, it consists of the noble suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*),
as well as that which is comprised of afflictions and characterized by the nature of change (*vipariṇāma-dharmatā*).
And setting aside pleasant feeling together with its basis,

those other aggregates which are accompanied by suffering, born from it, having it as a condition for their arising, and which serve as the vessel for the persistence of that which has arisen— this is called the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Those aggregates which are impermanent, subject to arising and passing away, accompanied by grasping, conjoined with the three types of sensation,
possessed of dysfunction, fallen into a state lacking security, and not yet liberated.
The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the lack of autonomy—
this is called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
This is the formal definition of the suffering of conditioned formations.
In this context, thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), longing (*prārthanā*), desire (*abhilāṣa*), and rejoicing (*abhinandana*) are synonyms. Furthermore, that longing proceeds by way of three aspects, namely:
longing for renewed existence (*punarbhava-prārthanā*), [longing for sensory pleasure, and longing for non-existence].
And there is the longing for sense objects.
In this context, that which is the longing for renewed existence is the craving for rebirth (*paunarbhavikī tṛṣṇā*);
furthermore, the longing for sense objects is of two kinds.
It is accompanied by the attachment to mental pleasure regarding objects already obtained,
and accompanied by the longing for union regarding objects not yet obtained.
Among these, that which is accompanied by the attachment to mental pleasure regarding objects already obtained is called "accompanied by delight and lust."
Furthermore, that which is accompanied by a longing for union with objects not yet attained and which delights in this or that is called "relishing.
Cessation is also twofold:
the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and...
And there is the cessation of the secondary afflictions.
The path is also twofold:
that of the learner (śaikṣa) and that of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
This object of focus for the purification of afflictions is to be understood by means of the supramundane path;
therefore, he spoke of the fourfold object of focus:
the pervasive object of focus, and so forth.
These are: the object for purifying conduct, the object for skillfulness, and the object for purifying afflictions.
In that regard, what is instruction?
Instruction is fourfold:
non-erroneous instruction; [and so forth].
Instruction on the gradual stages,
instruction on the scriptures,
and instruction on realization.
In that regard, what is non-erroneous instruction?
It is when one teaches and causes others to grasp the non-erroneous nature of phenomena and sentient beings.
That which issues forth from him is real,
for the sake of the complete destruction of suffering and for making an end to suffering.
This is called the non-perverted instruction.
What is the gradual instruction?
It is that which teaches the Dharma at the appropriate time.
First, he causes him to grasp and recite the most superficial topics;
thereafter, for the sake of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the first truth, he first instructs him on the profound topics.
Thereafter, one first instructs regarding the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as for the attainment of the first dhyāna.
Thereafter, this same kind of sequential instruction should be understood to apply to the other dhyāna attainments.
Therein, instruction based on scripture is that which has been received by him from his gurus,
those who stand in the place of gurus,
and those who possess knowledge of yoga.
Of the teachers or the preceptors,
or of the Tathāgata, or of a disciple of the Tathāgata.
In that very same way, having made [the teaching] neither deficient nor excessive, he instructs others;
this is called instruction based on scripture (*āgama-avavāda*).
Therein, [next is] instruction based on realization (*adhigama-avavāda*).
Just as by this those dharmas have been attained, touched, and realized.
Dwelling alone in seclusion,
for the sake of others' attainment, realization, and direct personal witness of that very same state.
He instructs; this is called instruction for realization.
Furthermore, there is instruction that is complete in all its aspects.
Furthermore, what is that?
It is that which he teaches by means of the three miraculous displays (*prātihārya*).
By the miracle of supernormal power,
by the miracle of mind-reading,
and by the miracle of instruction.
By means of the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*),
he displays various kinds of miraculous domains and generates great respect for himself among others, so that they become filled with such respect for him.
They become attentive and respectful toward the application of listening and mental engagement.
In that regard,

having examined their mental conduct through the miracle of teaching (*deśanā-prātihārya*), [the teacher] instructs them according to their faculties through the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsti-prātihārya*).
He teaches the Dharma according to their conduct and according to their entry,
and he instructs them in the antidote.
Therefore, this complete instruction is comprised within the three miracles.
In that regard, what is training?
It is said:
there are three trainings.
The training in higher ethics, and the training in higher mind and higher wisdom.
In that regard, what is the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)?
It is as follows: [the practice of] that ethical discipline, or one who possesses that ethical discipline.
"He dwells," and so forth, as detailed previously.

Therein, the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla*) is a mind secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*).
the joy and happiness born of seclusion,
and one-pointedness of mind.
Having attained and dwelling in the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna—
this is the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, it includes all formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and other meditative absorptions and attainments (*samādhi-samāpatti*).
It is called the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).

However, it is by relying on the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) that the initial entry into the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) occurs; it does not happen entirely without the meditative absorptions. Therefore, having established the meditative absorptions as primary, they are designated as the training in higher mind.
Therein, the training in higher wisdom is the knowledge of the four noble truths as they truly are.
For what reason are there exactly three trainings and no more than that?
He said:
For the purpose of establishing meditative concentration,
and for the purpose of providing a basis for knowledge.
And in the sense of performing what is to be done:
therein, for the purpose of establishing oneself in meditative concentration, there is the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
For it is by relying upon ethical discipline that one touches one-pointedness of mind.
concentration of mind.
In that context, the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) has the sense of being the basis for knowledge;
for when the mind is concentrated, there is one-pointedness,
and through mindfulness, the vision of knowledge as it truly is proceeds with respect to the object of knowledge.
In that regard, the training in higher wisdom (adhiprajñā-śikṣā) is so called in the sense of performing what is to be done;
for by means of perfectly pure knowledge and vision, one realizes the abandonment of the afflictions (kleśa-prahāṇa).
Indeed, this is one's own true interest, and this is the supreme task to be performed, namely, the abandonment of the afflictions.
Beyond that, there is nothing further to be done;
