therefore, there are only these three trainings.
What, then, is the sequence of these trainings? For one whose ethical discipline is pure, there is freedom from remorse.
For one who is without regret, there is gladness, joy, and pliancy.
There is happiness;
for one who is happy, there is concentration of mind.
One whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
One sees things as they truly are.
Knowing and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted;
being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate.
One who is dispassionate is liberated;
being liberated, one attains final nirvana without further clinging.
Thus, these precepts, when cultivated, lead to the highest state.
Namely, parinirvāṇa through non-clinging; this is the sequence of these trainings.
In that regard, for what reason is the training in higher ethics called "higher ethics"?
Likewise, [the training in] higher mind and higher wisdom are so called in the sense of being preeminent (*adhikārārthena*).

In this regard, how is it so? With respect to the sense of "governance" (*adhikāra*), the ethical discipline (*śīla*) that pertains to the higher mind (*adhicitta*) is the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*);
that which pertains to higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) is the concentration of the mind (*cittasamādhi*).
That which is knowledge and vision directed toward the abandonment of the afflictions is the training in higher wisdom.
The training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom—
these trainings are unique to this very teaching and not shared with those outside of it; such is the meaning of "superior" (adhika).
Furthermore, there is the training in higher mind which brings about the training in higher wisdom; there is also the training in higher wisdom which brings about the training in higher mind.
For example:
The noble disciple who is a learner (śaikṣa) and has not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas.

Having seen the stages, he subsequently applies himself to the abandonment of those afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
This is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
The training in higher mind is the bringer of [the training in] higher mind;
furthermore, it has already been stated that the training in higher mind is the bringer of the training in higher wisdom.
In that regard, there is training in higher ethical discipline,
but not training in higher mind, nor training in higher wisdom.
There is training in higher ethics and higher mind, but not in higher wisdom;
however, there is no training in higher wisdom that exists without higher ethics and higher mind.
Therefore, wherever there is training in higher wisdom, it should be understood that all three trainings are present there.
This, then, is the establishment of the trainings;
therein, a yogin engaged in yoga should train.
In that regard, three types of persons realize the truths.
Which three? Namely:
one who is not free from passion, one who is largely free from passion, and one who is completely free from passion.
In that regard, one who is entirely not free from passion, while realizing the truths, becomes a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) simultaneously with the clear realization of the truths.
One who is largely free from passion, moreover, becomes a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmī).
One who is free from passion becomes a non-returner simultaneously with the clear realization of the truths.
There are three faculties:
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
How is the establishment of these faculties [to be understood]?

For one who is engaged in the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths that have not yet been clearly realized, there is the establishment of the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*).

The establishment of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñendriya*) pertains to the learner (*śaikṣa*) who has attained clear realization; the establishment of the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) pertains to the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), the Arhat, who has accomplished what was to be done.

There are three gates of liberation; namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the signless (*animitta*). How is the establishment of these three gates of liberation to be understood? He said:
These two are the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Therein, the conditioned consists of the five aggregates associated with the three realms;
the unconditioned, moreover, is nirvana.
This is what is called both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Furthermore, as for that which is said:
"self" (ātman), or "sentient being" (sattva), or "living soul" (jīva);
Or, for a sentient being, this [conditioned world] is non-existent.
In that regard, because one perceives defects and perceives the peril in the conditioned, there arises a lack of aspiration.
And due to that lack of aspiration, the liberation door of wishlessness is established.
Furthermore, regarding that nirvāṇa, for one who possesses an aspiration,
there arises an aspiration characterized by the vision of peace and the vision of excellence.
And there is the vision of escape.

Furthermore, because of the vision of escape, the liberation door of the signless (ānimitta) is established. In that regard, since [the object] is non-existent and not found, no aspiration (praṇidhāna) arises at all.
"Just as it is non-existent, so it is non-existent"—
for one who knows and sees thus, the gate of liberation that is emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) is established.
In this way, the establishment of the three gates of liberation occurs.
In that regard, what are the factors conducive to training?
It is said: there are ten factors contrary to training;
as their antidotes, ten factors conducive to training should be understood.
In that regard, what are the factors contrary to the training? They are as follows: women; and children of noble appearance who are sexually attractive.
For a son of good family who is engaged in the training, there is an exceedingly great obstacle and hindrance:
namely, lack of restraint, indolence, and laziness regarding conditioned phenomena included within the view of a self-identity;
and, based on the view of a self-identity and the nutriment of physical food, a craving for flavors.
An inclination toward passion and attachment for various and manifold kinds of diverse stories concerning worldly affairs, as well as for [various] meters;
Reflection on the Dharma is a corruption of the mental application of yoga.
Furthermore, what is that? It is as follows: (Śbh_Sh 269)

Or, for one engaged in abandonment regarding the flavors, the truths, the aggregates, or the fruit of karma, there is the mental attention that acts as a defilement to serenity and insight when the body is characterized by heaviness and laxity.
It is either the overwhelming of the mind by sloth and torpor,
or the contraction of the mind,
or physical exhaustion in one who has exerted effort.
Mental distress is the failure to attain distinction and the exhaustion of the side of wholesome qualities by one whose vigor is excessively slackened,
whether due to greed or for the sake of fame.
Whether through praise,
or by means of any other mere fragment of pleasure, there arises delight, mental gladness, agitation, and lack of tranquility.
Agitation is the state of being tossed about;
it is the state of being paralyzed by fear toward the cessation of the view of a self-identity, which is nirvana.
Applying oneself without moderation; excessive talkativeness; and, even when speaking on a discourse concerning the Dharma, initiating a contentious debate and persisting in it.
The wandering of the mind and the distraction of the mind toward various objects previously seen, heard, or experienced— objects that are manifold and of many different kinds—
as well as the habituation to impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*): these should be understood as the defects of mental engagement through the application of reflection on those dharmas.
Relishing the pleasure of meditative absorption (*dhyānasamāpatti*);
for one desiring to enter the signless (*ānimitta*), following after the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāranimitta*);
and being touched by bodily sensations (*śārīrikā vedanā*).
The restraint of life by means of sufferings that are even life-threatening;
the lamentation and exhaustion of one who follows the hope for life and its associated expectations.
Regarding "lamentation":
these are the ten factors that run counter to the training.
What are the ten factors that run counter to the precepts of training? They are those which, as antidotes to the ten factors contrary to the training, become concordant with the training.
Namely: the perception of impurity;
the perception of suffering in what is impermanent;
and the perception of non-self in what is suffering.
The perception of repulsiveness in food; the perception of lack of delight in all worldly splendor;
and the perception of light.
The perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, and the perception of death.
Thus, these ten perceptions—
when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed— conduce to the abandonment of the ten kinds of obstacles to training and the ten factors contrary to training.
Among these, there is the illumination of the Dharma.
The light of meaning:
the light of calm abiding and the light of insight.
Taking these lights as the dominant influence, the perception of light is intended here;
it consists of mental attention through the application of reflection on the Dharma.
For the sake of abandoning obstacles.
In this regard, ten other factors conducive to training should be understood.
What are the ten? They are as follows: the prior cause.
Conformable instruction,
proper application,
constant and respectful practice, and intense aspiration.
The strengthening of the power of yoga,
the pacification of the dysfunctions of body and mind,
and constant analytical reflection.
absence of weariness, and absence of conceit.
Among these, what is the former cause?
That which is the prior maturation of the faculties (*indriya-paripāka*) and the full acquisition of the faculties (*indriya-samudāgama*).
In that regard, what is the concordant instruction (*anulomika-upadeśa*)? It is the instruction that is non-erroneous and conformable.
And regarding the previous [instruction],
therein is the proper application exactly as it was taught.
In that very way he applies himself;
applying himself in that manner, he gives rise to right view.
In that regard, there is the practice of constancy and reverence;
by means of a sixfold application,
one makes time fruitful and swiftly accomplishes the side of wholesome qualities through the side of wholesome qualities.
In that regard, intense zeal is as follows: one generates a longing for the higher liberation, thinking,
"When indeed shall I attain and dwell in that sphere?"
Regarding the statement, "The noble ones, having attained this sphere, dwell therein," it refers here to the application of the power of yoga.
One attains the application of the power of yoga through two causes.
And due to the sharpness of their faculties by nature, as well as through long-term habituation and cultivation,
therein [lies] the corruption of body and mind.
[Joy] and pliancy: just as there arises in one whose body is weary and whose body is exhausted a heaviness of body and a heaviness of mind.

One causes [the mind] to settle by conceiving another mode of deportment (*īryāpatha*). When bodily and mental rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) arises due to excessive discursive thought (*vitarka*) and excessive deliberation (*vicāra*), one then causes it to settle through application to tranquility (*śamatha*) of one's own mind.
Through the contraction of the mind and the sinking of the mind, the obsession of lethargy and torpor arises;
and there is the corruption of body and mind, which is to be overcome by the insight into phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*) through higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
And by means of a mental attention that inspires clarity, one brings about tranquility; or,
for one whose afflictions have already been abandoned, the corruption of body and mind belonging to the side of the afflictions—
which has not yet departed and is constantly adhering— becomes thoroughly stilled through the cultivation of the correct path.
In that regard, frequent reflection consists of frequently reflecting upon what has been ill-done and what has been well-done with respect to one's ethical discipline (*śīla*).
He reflects upon what has not been done and what has been done;
he desists from what is badly done and from what has not been done,
and he does not turn back from what has been well done.

Likewise, taking as his dominant influence the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*) regarding whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned, he repeatedly examines them.
Having there recognized their abandonment, he cultivates that very same path again and again.
In that regard, for one who is not yet satisfied,
it should be known and seen after some time has passed.
That which is to be attained,
for one who does not know it, does not see it, and does not realize it.
Exhaustion arises;
it is mental fatigue,
mental distress.
He does not tolerate that which has arisen; he abandons it. This is non-conceit regarding attainment and realization.
In the act of touching, he is free from conceit;
he grasps things without error,
and when something is attained, he perceives it as attained.
Perceiving what has been attained as attained—
these are the ten factors for a yogin who desires training.
Taking up the beginning, middle, and end, they conform to the training and do not oppose it;
therefore, they are called "those who conform to the training."
In that regard,
what is the loss of yoga?
It is said:
There are four failures in yoga.
What are the four?
There is a failure in yoga that is absolute.
There is that which is temporary;
there is that which results from decline;
and there is that which is produced by wrong practice.
In that regard, absolute failure in yoga is to be understood as pertaining to those persons who abide in non-yoga;
because they lack the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa, they are indeed utterly fallen away from yoga.
Among those, first is the temporary [attainment].
For example, those who abide in the lineage (*gotrastha*) and possess the nature for parinirvāṇa, yet lack the necessary conditions;
for they [remain] even for a long time...
Even after going further, they will inevitably obtain the conditions for realization;
and having brought yoga to presence and cultivated it, they will attain parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, their lapse is merely temporary.

In that regard, the failure of yoga through the loss of attainment is as follows: here, some individuals fall away from the state of knowledge, vision, and contact with the dwelling [of peace] that they have attained and realized. In that context, there is also the failure of yoga caused by wrong practice.
Just as, for example, some individuals here,
applying themselves in an improper manner, do not become successful in yoga, nor do they achieve success.
One should meditate upon the wholesome Dharma.
For instance, there is here a certain person who possesses many afflictions and is of a nature characterized by abundant passion.
And he possesses great consciousness,
great intelligence,
and great [power].
Endowed with intelligence,
he grasps what he has heard and masters what he has heard.
Whether it be little or much,
he dwells again in the forest for the sake of householders and renunciants who come to him one after another,
as well as for washermen.
He gratifies their minds by teaching the Dharma to those of such a disposition,
and by means of conduct associated with body and speech that is free from the practice of hypocrisy.
By that causal state and by that condition,
gain, honor, and fame arise for him.
He becomes well-known;
he becomes a recipient of great happiness,
[namely] the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.
And he is honored and revered by kings and royal ministers.
As long as there is the assembly of Arhats among the caravan leaders,
his disciples continue to exist.
Householders and renunciants;
even at the ends of the road, there are villages or market towns (api adhvānteṣu grāmo nigamo vā vartate).
Or [... for one who is thus restrained, it occurs:
"There are those disciples, both householders and renunciants,"
If those who have conceived confidence in me, for whom great respect has arisen, were to approach me and ask questions regarding yoga, mental attention, and calm abiding and insight;
And if, when questioned by them, I were to answer, "I do not know," then that reputation I have would be lost, and I would no longer be esteemed as an Arhat; therefore,
what if I were to reflect upon this myself?
Having weighed and examined it, I would establish the practice;
making this very purpose his primary concern, he— greedy for gain and honor— went alone into seclusion and reflected upon it himself, having weighed and examined it.
Having weighed and examined it, he establishes a practice;
yet that practice of his is not found in the Sūtras and does not appear in the Vinaya.
And he contradicts the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
saying: "These monks here are upholders of the Sūtras."
Those who uphold the Vinaya and those who uphold the Mātṛkā conceal that basis of their application from them.
He does not reveal [the Dharma] even to those who are his disciples,
whether they be householders or those who have gone forth.
He also commands them for the purpose of counteracting their yoga.
For what reason?
Lest those holders of the Sūtras should [suffer].
Those who uphold the Vinaya and those who uphold the Mātṛkā,
having heard this locus of yoga, should introduce it into the Sūtras.
And they would not introduce that into the two-fold Vinaya; yet, if they were to demonstrate it,
it is not seen there.
If one were to examine it by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
that would contradict the nature of phenomena; and on that account,
they would become dissatisfied and would reproach him with words of dissatisfaction.
And they might initiate legal disputes;
in this way, I would once again not be honored nor held in high esteem.

"May I not be deprived of gains from kings, royal ministers, and even from wealthy merchants, guild-leaders, and caravan-chiefs; and may I also be a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Making that very desire for gain and honor his primary motive, he perceives what is non-Dharma as Dharma.
Having set aside the perception of form, he illuminates and proclaims what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma;
therein, those who follow his view come to agree with it.
They perceive non-dharma as dharma;
because of their dullness and delusion, they perceive non-dharma as dharma even though they have been instructed accordingly.
Those who practice in such a manner should be known as having entered upon a wrong path.
This kind of failure in yoga caused by wrong practice is a counterfeit of the true Dharma, for it is a false Dharma that leads to the disappearance of the true Dharma.
Thus, these four failures in yoga must be fully understood and avoided by a meditating monk who is a practitioner of yoga.
In that regard, what is yoga?
It is said: yoga is fourfold.
Namely: faith, aspiration, vigor, and skillful means.
In that regard, faith has two bases: it has the aspect of conviction and the aspect of serene clarity.
It is based on the investigation of the reasoning of the Dharma and based on the conviction in the power of individuals.
Zeal is also fourfold;
for example, for the sake of attainment,
as when someone here generates a longing for higher liberations.
In detail, as before:
for the sake of inquiry.
Just as here someone generates a desire for inquiry, in detail, as before, for the sake of inquiry.
for the sake of going to the monastery, for the sake of hearing what has not been heard from wise fellow-practitioners who know the yoga,
and for the sake of purifying what has already been heard.
Zeal arises from the complete acquisition of the accumulations;

for instance, as when a certain person [exerts effort] for the sake of the complete purity of the restraint of ethical discipline and for the sake of the complete purity of the restraint of the sense faculties.
He generates an ever-increasing aspiration for moderation in eating, for application to wakefulness, and for dwelling in clear comprehension.
Zeal arises from application.

That which generates longing, aspiration, and the desire to act toward the cultivation of the path through continuous application and respectful application—this is the fourfold zeal. (Thus is the fourfold zeal.)
Namely: for the sake of attainment,
for the sake of inquiry,
and for the sake of the full accomplishment of the equipment.
And for the sake of application;
therein, diligence is also fourfold, namely: for the sake of hearing, and for the sake of reflection.
For the sake of cultivation and for the sake of the complete purification of hindrances.
In that regard, diligence for hearing is that which belongs to one who hears what has not been heard and brings it to complete purification.
It is mental enthusiasm and the state of not relaxing one's application toward the meaning of the teachings as they have been heard, while dwelling alone in seclusion.
The mental exertion of one who reflects, weighs, and examines;

of one who has thus entered into seclusion and cultivates tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) from time to time; and of one who is devoted day and night to purifying the mind of the hindrances through walking and sitting—this is that mental exertion.

Non-abandonment of application (*avinyastayogata*): Thus, while one who has gone alone into seclusion reflects on the meaning of the teachings exactly as they were heard, there is a long-term dwelling in that [reflection]. Furthermore, the skillful means (*upāya*) is fourfold; namely, having made the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*) and the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) the basis, there is the state of well-established mindfulness (*sūpasthitasmṛtitā*).
Likewise, non-negligence regarding established mindfulness is the protection of the mind;
it is the cultivation of wholesome qualities,
as well as the application of internal mental tranquility for one who is thus non-negligent.
And superior wisdom is the insight into phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*). This yoga is fourfold and consists of sixteen aspects.
In that regard, through faith, one attains the objective to be attained as the predominant factor;
because of one's conviction regarding attainment, one generates the desire to act toward wholesome qualities.
Desiring to act in this way,
he dwells devoted to the practice day and night,
full of enthusiasm.
He possesses firm prowess;
and having undertaken that vigor, he maintains it for the sake of attaining what has not been attained and for the sake of realizing what has not been realized.
It conduces to the realization of that which has not yet been realized;
therefore, these four factors are called "yoga."
In that regard, what is mental attention (*manasikāra*)? What are the four types of mental attention? What are the four?
And as he stabilizes [the mind] and investigates phenomena,
this continues until he attains mental attention (*manaskāra*).
At that time, his mental application is forceful;
having restrained that mind by force, he establishes it in one-pointedness.
Therefore, it is so called.
Regarding "forceful application":
what is attention that is applied with interruptions?
It is as follows: forceful application and [attention] applied with interruptions.
And it is effortless in its operation.
In that regard, what is attention that operates with effort?
It is, for example, that of a beginner who is establishing the mind precisely within.
And as he stabilizes [the mind] and investigates the phenomena,
this continues until he attains mental attention (*manaskāra*).
At that time, his mental application is forceful;
having constrained that mind by force, he establishes it in one-pointedness.
Therefore, it is called "forceful application."
What is the mental application that functions with interruptions?

It is the mental application that experiences the characteristics [of reality] for one who has already attained mental application while proceeding by means of either the mundane path or the supramundane path.
For in that state, concentration is established through reflection;
it does not proceed exclusively by way of the mode of cultivation.
In that regard, there is mental attention that operates without interruption.
From the mental application of discerning characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) upwards,
up to the mental application of the culmination of practice (*prayoganiṣṭha manaskāra*), there is the mental application that proceeds without effort (*anābhogavāhana*).
This is the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of practice (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala manaskāra*).
There are four other types of mental attention, namely: that which is conformable, that which is remedial, and that which is gladdening.
And there is that which is to be examined;
therein is the conformable mental attention,
by which one reviles the object of focus.
He undertakes correct application,
yet he does not abandon the afflictions.
In that context, the counteractive [sign] is that by which one abandons the afflictions;
therein, the gladdening [sign] is that by which one causes the sunken mind to be released through signs of upliftment and causes it to rejoice.
He takes it up.
In that regard, there is the attention consisting of investigation, which is as follows: [the attention of] examination.

Regarding mental attention (*manaskāra*): having made that the predominant influence, one examines whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not abandoned. In that regard, for one who is attending to the object of focus (*ālambana*), how many signs (*nimitta*) are there to be attended to?
He said: "There are four; namely:"
The sign of the object of focus; the sign to be discarded.
And there is the sign to be cultivated.
Among these, the sign of the object is the reflected image that corresponds to the thing to be known.
It is a manifestation.
In that regard, the causal sign (*nidānanimitta*) is as follows: the accumulation of the equipment for meditative concentration (*samādhisambhāra*),
concordant instruction (*anulomika upadeśaḥ*),
and that which is accompanied by cultivation (*bhāvanāsahagata*).
Intense aspiration,
a sense of spiritual urgency regarding things that inspire urgency,
and the thorough knowledge of distraction and non-distraction.
And attention from another;
or [an action] performed by a human being belonging to the Saṃgha— what [is it]?
Whether produced by humans,
produced by sounds, or produced by malice.
Likewise, preceded by insight (vipaśyanā),
there is an internal withdrawal of the mind;
this serves as the causal sign for more intense insight hereafter.
Likewise, insight preceded by calm abiding serves as the causal sign for a subsequently more refined calm abiding.
In that regard, there are four types of signs to be avoided.
Namely:
the sign of laxity and the sign of agitation.
The sign of attachment and the sign of distraction.
Among these, the sign of laxity is that sign of the object and sign of the cause by which the mind tends toward laxity.

In this context, *auddhatya* (restlessness) is that by which the mind arises through a sign of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*) and a sign of the cause (*nidāna-nimitta*). Therein, the sign of attachment is that sign of the object and sign of the cause by which the mind becomes attached to the object.
One becomes passionately attached;
one becomes afflicted.
In that regard, this is the cause of distraction.

By which objective sign (*ālambana-nimitta*) or causal sign (*nidāna-nimitta*) the mind is distracted outwardly—those signs are, moreover, as they are presented in the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitā bhūmi*); by means of these mental attentions (*manaskāra*), one resolves upon the object. How many types of resolve (*adhimokṣa*) are there?
He said:
There are nine types of resolve, namely:
the luminous and the non-luminous.
Dull, sharp, limited,
extensive,
and immeasurable.
It is either completely pure or not completely pure.
In that regard,
the luminous resolve is that which is accompanied by light when the sign of light has been well-apprehended.
Therein, the non-luminous resolve is as follows:
For example, when the sign of light has been well grasped, there is a dull resolve associated with darkness;
this is that which falls within the continuum of those with dull faculties.
In that regard, "sharp resolve" is that which occurs within the continuum of those with sharp faculties;
therein, "limited resolve" is that which belongs to those with limited faith.
It is the concentration with a limited object;
thus, through the limitation of mental attention and the limitation of the object, there is limited resolve.

In that context, "resolute belief directed toward the great" refers to that resolute belief which is accompanied by faith and aspiration toward what is great, or which resolves upon a great object of focus. This is what is meant by "resolute belief."
Because of the greatness of mental attention and the greatness of the object, there is a great resolve;
therein lies immeasurable resolve,
which is immeasurable faith.
Accompanied by joy,
one resolves upon an object that is either infinite or boundless;
this is what is called "resolute confidence" (adhimokṣa).
Due to the immeasurability of mental attention and the immeasurability of the object, there is immeasurable resolve (*adhimokṣa*).
Among these, pure resolve is that which is manifested, perfected, and has reached its culmination.
Furthermore, that which is impure is neither well-cultivated, nor perfected, nor brought to its final conclusion.
In this regard, how many are the duties to be performed by one engaged in yoga?
He said: "Four. Which four?"
Namely:
the cessation of the basis and the transformation of the basis.
Thorough knowledge of the object and delight in the object;
therein, the cessation of the basis for one devoted to the cultivation of application and mental attention is that basis which is accompanied by functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Thus it is gradually ceased;
and the basis, accompanied by pliancy, undergoes transformation.
This is the cessation of the basis; this is the transformation of the basis.
That which is to be accomplished through yoga consists therein of the thorough knowledge of the object and delight in the object.
There is both the thorough knowledge of the object and delight in the object.
Preceded by the transformation of the basis through the cessation of the basis:
when, having made the thorough knowledge of the object and delight in the object the predominant factor, the basis ceases and undergoes transformation.
There is the thorough knowledge of the object, delight in the object,
preceded by the purification of the basis,
and having the purification of the basis as its dominant influence.
Having established thoroughly purified knowledge of the objective support,
it proceeds at the time of the fulfillment of the task,
as well as with delight.
Therefore, it is said that there are four things to be done for yoga.
In that regard, how many types of practitioners of yoga (yogācāra) are there?
He replied: There are three, namely: the beginner (ādikarmika),...
One who has completed the practice and has transcended mental attention.
In that regard, the beginner practitioner of yoga (yogācāra) is one who is a beginner in mental attention (manaskāra),
and one who is a beginner in the purification of the afflictions (kleśa).
In that regard, there is the beginner in mental attention (*manaskāra*).
Among these, the first beginner does not attain mental attention regarding one-pointedness;
he does not touch upon one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
In that regard, the beginner in the purification of afflictions is as follows:

even when mental attention has been attained, for one who desires to liberate the mind from affliction, there is the undertaking and the sustained practice of the mental attention that experiences the characteristics [of the object].
This is the beginner in the purification of afflictions.
In that regard, what is "one who has practiced" (*kṛtaparicaya*)?

Setting aside the attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāraḥ*), one becomes one who has practiced with respect to the other six types of attention, up to and including those culminating in application (*prayoganiṣṭhāpanna*).
In this context, there are those who have transcended attention (*atikrāntamanaskāraḥ*).
It should be understood that in the mental application of the fruit of the culmination of practice,
one has transcended the mental application of the cultivation of practice.
He abides in the fruit of cultivation;
therefore, he is called "one who has transcended mental application."
Moreover, having based himself on a desire for wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-cchanda*),
while applying himself [to practice],
he does not yet produce the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
One is a beginner as long as one has not yet produced the aids to penetration,
such as the levels of heat.
The summits (mūrdhānaḥ),
the conformities to truth (satyānulomāḥ), and the patiences (kṣāntayaḥ).
When one has cultivated familiarity with the supreme mundane dharmas,
one then enters the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
He realizes the truths;
he becomes independent of others and not led by another;
at that time, he has transcended mental attention regarding the Teacher’s instruction.
Having transcended mental attention that relies on others, he abides in that which does not rely on others;
therefore, he is said to have "transcended mental attention.
In this regard, what is the cultivation of yoga?
He said: It is twofold:
the cultivation of perception and the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In that regard, what is the cultivation of perception? It is as follows: one engaged in the mundane path cultivates the perception of disadvantage regarding all the lower stages.
Or again, one who is engaged for the sake of abandonment—
in the element of abandonment, the element of dispassion, and the element of cessation—
One who perceives tranquility cultivates the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.
Furthermore,
one engaged in calm abiding cultivates the perception of upward and downward belonging to the side of calm abiding;
one engaged in insight cultivation likewise does so.
Afterwards, he again cultivates the perception belonging to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*);

being engaged in insight, he subsequently contemplates this very body, as it is situated and as it is disposed, from the soles of the feet upward to the hair of the head, as full of various kinds of impurity.
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth as before. Therein, subsequently,
he is again percipient of that very sign of contemplation through a certain portion [of it].
It is well grasped, thoroughly grasped, well attended to,
and well extracted.
It is well-penetrated;
for example, as one standing observes one sitting,
or one sitting observes one lying down.
Or, walking behind, he observes one who is walking ahead.
This indeed illustrates the observation through the mode of insight (vipaśyanā) regarding conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that have arisen dependently across the three times.
In this regard, as for what was said— that one standing observes one who is seated—
by means of this present mental attention (*manaskāra*), one observes the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) pertaining to the future.

Even the present state of mental attention is said to be "arisen" and "established. Furthermore, the future state of the object of knowledge is said to be "seated," because it has not yet arisen and is oriented toward arising.
Furthermore, as for what was said—
"or, while sitting, one reflects upon that which was lying down"— by this, the reflection upon a past object of knowledge by means of a present mental attention (*manaskāra*) is illuminated;
for the state of present mental attention is [the basis for such reflection].
It is said that when [the mind] is directed toward cessation, it is "seated";
furthermore, because it has already ceased, the past state of the knowable is said to be "lying down.
As for what was further stated:
"Or he observes one who is going ahead" refers to present mental attention (*manaskāra*).
By this, the observation of the mental attention that has just ceased is illuminated.
In that context, each successive mental attention that arises and ceases immediately thereafter is "one who goes ahead."
In that regard, it is "arisen immediately after":
the mental attention (manaskāra) arisen immediately after is the grasper of each preceding [moment] as it has just ceased. It is ever-new, grasping each moment that has just ceased.
He travels as one who follows behind;
there, cultivating both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), he cultivates the perception of light belonging to both sides.
This is the cultivation of perception (*saṃjñābhāvanā*).
In that regard, what is the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment?
It is that which pertains to the thirty-six (or thirty-seven) [factors].
The practice, cultivation, frequenting, and repeated application of the factors conducive to awakening— this is called the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening.
Namely, the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right endeavors.
Of the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties,
and the five powers.
[He generates desire] for the seven factors of enlightenment, for the noble eightfold path,
for the application of mindfulness to the body, and for the applications of mindfulness to feelings, mind, and phenomena;
he generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen states, that is, of evil and unwholesome states.
He exerts himself, arouses vigor,
and uplifts the mind.
He exerts himself for the sake of right abandonment:
for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.
For the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
for the stability, non-confusion, and fulfillment through cultivation of wholesome states that have already arisen.
He exerts desire, arouses vigor, and uplifts the mind for the sake of the increase, growth, and expansion of those states.

"He exerts" refers to the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting of the right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*) endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) and the concentration of desire (*chandasamādhi*),
as well as faith, vigor, mind, and investigation.
The basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of concentration and abandonment;
the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment through energy, mind, and investigation.

The faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom [are the causes] of the powers of faith, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, as well as of the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness,
right view, and right intention.
Of right speech, right action, and right livelihood; of right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In that regard, what is the body?
What is the contemplation of the body in the body? What is [the contemplation of feelings in feelings]...?
) What is mindfulness? Which are the foundations of mindfulness?
He said: The body is of thirty-five kinds;
namely, internal and external.
It is comprised of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and not comprised of the sense faculties;
it is reckoned as a sentient being (*sattva*).
And it is comprised within sentient beings;
it is accompanied by both coarseness and pliancy.
The body of primary elements and the body derived from primary elements;
the body of names and the body of form.
The hell-being, the animal,
the one belonging to the realm of the ancestors,
the human, and the divine.
The internal body with consciousness, or the internal body without consciousness, as well as the external body.
Transformed and untransformed.
The body of a woman, the body of a man, and the body of a eunuch; the body of a friend, and so forth.
the body of enemies,
the body of neutrals,
the inferior body, and the middling body.
And there is the excellent body, the youthful body, the young body, and the aged body.
This, first of all, is the body and its classification.
In that regard, there are three kinds of contemplation (*anupaśyanā*),
which, having made the body the primary object, consist of either wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) or wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
By means of that wisdom, one correctly examines the entire body in all its aspects; one investigates it,
penetrates it,
and thoroughly analyzes it.
Therein, with the body as the dominant influence, one establishes the foundation of mindfulness.
Those phenomena which have been taken up, the meaning of those very same phenomena which has been reflected upon,
and those which have been realized through cultivation;
In that regard, it is the non-confusion of the mind concerning the phrasing, the meaning, and the direct realization, such as: "Have these teachings been well-grasped by me, or not?"
Whether they are well-characterized here and there by wisdom or not;
whether they are well-touched here and there by liberation or not— this presence [of awareness] is the application of mindfulness.

Moreover, there is the application of mindfulness for the sake of protection by means of mindfulness, and for the sake of non-affliction regarding objects and for the sake of binding [the mind] to the focal object.
In that regard, protection by means of mindfulness is as previously stated: "one whose mindfulness is guarded" and "one whose mindfulness is constant."
In that regard, for the sake of non-affliction with respect to sense objects,
as it has been said: "One whose mind is protected by mindfulness acts while remaining in a state of equanimity."
He does not seize upon signs, nor does he seize upon secondary characteristics;
thus, in detail, he guards [the mind].
The mind-faculty attains restraint by means of the mind-faculty;
therein, for the purpose of binding it to the object,
one fixes mindfulness upon the fourfold object as previously described.
Namely: the pervasive object,
the object for purifying conduct, and the object for skillfulness.
Or, in the purification of the afflictions, that state of well-established mindfulness through these three modes is called the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
In that regard, what is feeling (*vedanā*)?
It is as follows: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Therein, there is also bodily pleasure,
bodily pain, and that which is neither painful nor pleasant; as with the bodily, so it is with the mental.
In the same way, mental [feeling]—
whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— is also accompanied by worldly attachment (sāmiṣā).
In this way, it is also free from worldly gain; in this way, it is not dependent on craving.
Feelings based on renunciation—
whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—
these constitute the twenty-one kinds of feeling.
Or it is of nine kinds.
In that context, what is the mind? It is as follows:
the mind with attachment, the mind with aversion, [and so forth].
free from hatred,
with delusion, and free from delusion;
Contracted, distracted, and sunken.
It is exerted;
it is agitated or unagitated;
it is tranquilized or untranquilized.
The concentrated and the unconcentrated, the well-cultivated and the uncultivated,
the well-liberated mind and the ill-liberated mind.
Summarizing this, there are twenty types of mind.
In that regard, what are the phenomena?
They are passion and the subduing of passion.
Hatred and the subduing of hatred; delusion and the subduing of delusion;
contraction and distraction.
Lay, exertion, agitation, non-agitation,
and tranquility.
Lack of tranquility,
lack of being well-concentrated, not being well-concentrated, and lack of having well-cultivated the path.
It is neither the state of having poorly cultivated the path,
nor the state of being poorly liberated, nor the state of having poorly cultivated liberation.
Thus, these twenty factors established in the dark and light sides should be understood as belonging to the categories of affliction and purification. Among them,
pleasant feeling is that which arises in dependence upon contact conducive to pleasant feeling.
It is pleasant, felt,
and belongs to the category of feeling;
it is that which is associated with the five consciousnesses.
That which is associated with body-consciousness is bodily; that which is associated with mind-consciousness is mental.
Just as it is with what is to be experienced as pleasure, so it is with the others.

Dependent upon a contact to be experienced as painful or a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises a feeling that is unpleasant, or neither-unpleasant-nor-pleasant; this feeling, which is free from passion,
is called the category of feeling, namely, painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness is bodily;
that which is associated with the mental consciousness is mental.
And that which is mental,
which is conducive to nirvāṇa,
is penetrative; it leads to ultimate finality and ultimate purity.
It leads to the ultimate consummation of the holy life;
that is the unworldly [offering].
Furthermore, that which falls within the realms and falls within existence is carnal;
whereas that which is associated with the form and formless realms is [otherwise].
Or, that which is conducive to dispassion is based on renunciation;
whereas that which is connected with the body [is otherwise].
And it is not conducive to dispassion;
that [craving] is based on greed.
In that regard, a mind with attachment is one that is obsessed by desire toward an object that is provocative of passion.
That which is free from passion is that which is devoid of the obsession of passion;
that which possesses hatred is that which is obsessed with hatred toward an object that provokes hatred.
That which is free from hatred is that which is devoid of the obsession of hatred;
therein, delusion is that which [occurs] regarding an object conducive to delusion.
These six states of mind should be understood as being associated with movement;
therein, three belong to the side of affliction,
and three are antidotes to affliction.
In that context, "contracted mind" is that which is bound inwardly by oneself through the mode of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
"Distracted mind" is that which has wandered outwardly among the five strands of sensual pleasure. In that context, "sunk mind" is...
That which is accompanied by sloth and torpor;
that which is over-exerted, being established upon an inspiring object;

the agitated mind, which is possessed by the obsession of agitation due to excessive exertion; and the persistently bound mind, which has attained equanimity at the time of exertion and at the time of withdrawal.
In that context, the "calmed mind" is that which is liberated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the "not yet calmed" is that which is not liberated.
Therein, the "concentrated mind" is that which, through liberation from the hindrances, has entered the fundamental dhyānas; the "not well-concentrated" is that which has not so entered.

In that regard, a well-cultivated mind is one that, through long-term familiarity with this very samādhi, becomes capable of attaining it at will, attaining it without difficulty, and entering it swiftly. (Śbh_Sh 298)
In this context, "not well-cultivated" mind should be understood as the opposite of that.
Therein, a "well-liberated" mind is one that is liberated from everything and absolutely;
[the opposite is] not well-liberated.
The mind that is neither liberated from everything nor liberated absolutely— these fourteen types of mind should be understood as pertaining to the [eight] dwellings.
In that regard, beginning from the stage purified of hindrances (*nivaraṇaviśuddhabhūmi*), eight states of mind belonging to the dwellings (*vihāra*) are to be understood:
the distracted, the contracted, and so on, up to the tranquilized and the non-tranquilized.

Furthermore, with regard to the purification of the afflictions, there are six states of mind pertaining to the dwellings, ranging from "the mind is well-liberated" to "the mind is not well-liberated.
Moreover, when an internal hindrance is present, one knows, "There is a hindrance in me";
when a hindrance is absent, one knows, "There is no hindrance in me."
He also understands how the arising of unarisen space occurs, and he likewise understands how the disappearance of arisen space occurs.
When there is the fetter of the eye, and so on up to the fetter of the mind, [he knows]: "I have [the fetter] of the eye," and so on up to the mind.
Regarding "fetter":
when there is no longer any fetter, he understands, "I have no mental fetter."
He also understands how the arising of the fetters, up to and including the mind-fetter, occurs for that which has not yet arisen,
as well as how their cessation occurs once they have arisen.
He also discerns this:
when the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is present within him, he discerns, "The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is present in me";
when it is absent, he discerns, "It is not present in me."
He also understands how the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness comes to arise,
and how the arisen factor remains stable.
He also understands non-forgetfulness, cultivation, fulfillment, further development, increase, and vastness.

When there is the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness within himself, he likewise understands the factors of enlightenment consisting of the Dharma, discipline, energy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

It should be understood that this thorough knowledge of afflicted phenomena by way of their intrinsic nature, disadvantages, and antidotes constitutes the body of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*),
just as the contemplation of the body within the body belongs to the side of the application of mindfulness.
The same should be understood, as appropriate, for feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena.
In that regard, how does one dwell contemplating the body within the body?
How [does one dwell] externally, and how internally-externally?
When one dwells contemplating the body in the body— internally, personally, within that which is reckoned as a sentient being.
In this way, he dwells contemplating the body within the body. How does he dwell [contemplating] the body externally? How does he dwell [contemplating] it both internally and externally?
When, with respect to the internal and individual self...

When one takes as an object external form not reckoned as a sentient being, in this way one dwells contemplating the body in the external body. When one takes as an object external form reckoned as a sentient being that is deceased, in this way one dwells contemplating the body in the internal-external body.
In that regard, based on internal form,
there is a subtle feeling that has arisen, which is reckoned as belonging to a sentient being.
Taking those phenomena as objects,
one [directs the mind] toward internal feeling.
He dwells contemplating phenomena in the mind and in phenomena,
based on external form that is reckoned as non-sentient.
Taking as an object those feelings, thoughts, and phenomena that have arisen.
He dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena externally.
Based on external, outward forms and beings,
whatever feeling and mind have arisen—
Taking those phenomena as his object, he dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena, both internally and externally.
Another formulation:
taking as an object form comprised within the sense-faculties, one dwells contemplating the body within the body.
Taking as his object that which is not comprised by the sense-faculties, which belongs to the category of form, and is non-appropriated, he dwells contemplating the body in the external body;
[taking] only that which is not comprised by the sense-faculties.
Taking as his object form that has entered within and is appropriated, he dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body;
taking as his object form that is not comprised by the sense faculties and is unappropriated, he dwells contemplating the body in the external body;
and taking as his object form that is not comprised by the sense faculties, yet has entered within and is appropriated, he dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body.
Thus, based on the threefold form previously mentioned,
whatever feeling and mind have arisen—
It should be understood that one dwells as a seer of suchness by taking those phenomena as objects according to their respective application.
There is another method:

when one takes as an object the form belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*) that is accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), in this way one dwells contemplating the body within the body internally.
When one takes as an object that very subtle internal form belonging to the stage of meditative concentration which is accompanied by functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*),
in this way one dwells contemplating the body in the external body.

When one takes as an object form that is accompanied by the functional rigidity of others and also accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) within the internal-external body, [one dwells contemplating the body in the internal-external body].
He dwells contemplating the body; likewise, he dwells contemplating feelings and the mind that have arisen based upon that [body].
The dharmas are to be understood according to their respective application.
There is another formulation:
taking internal derived form as an object, one dwells contemplating the body in the internal body.
Taking external derived matter as his object, he dwells contemplating the body in the external body;
that is, taking as his basis that derived matter which has arisen and is comprised within the sense faculties and their objects.
Taking form as an object, one dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body.
In the same way, whatever feelings, mind, and phenomena have arisen based upon that [body] should also be understood accordingly.
This is another method.
When one takes as an object the internal body together with its consciousness,
in this way one dwells contemplating the body within the body internally.

Taking as his object matter that is devoid of consciousness yet reckoned as a sentient being during states such as the bluish discoloration [of a corpse], he dwells contemplating the body in the external body. Furthermore,
regarding matter that was once endowed with consciousness, he contemplates its state of having been endowed with consciousness in the past.
And by taking as his object the future state of non-consciousness of form that is devoid of consciousness—
its commonality of nature and its equality of nature— he dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body, based upon that.
Those feelings, thoughts, and phenomena that have arisen should also be understood accordingly.
Another formulation:
taking as his object the internal body of oneself by way of its forms such as hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, he dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body.

Taking as an object the internal body of others through its forms such as hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in the external body; and taking as an object the internal mind and the external body in its transformed state through forms such as the livid (*vinīlaka*),
and likewise the external body— both transformed and untransformed—
taking them as an object by way of their commonality of nature through forms such as the livid, one dwells contemplating the body in the external body.
Based on that, whatever feelings, mind, and mental phenomena have arisen should also be understood accordingly.
In this manner, many such formulations should be understood through the distinctions of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena.
However, these few synonyms have been elucidated.
In that regard, as an antidote to the four perversions, the Blessed One established the four foundations of mindfulness.
In that regard, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure;
for it was in this way that the Blessed One, in the cultivation of the application of mindfulness to the body, taught the four charnel-ground contemplations associated with the foul (*aśubha*).
For one who frequently practices and attends to this,
the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure is abandoned;
therein, [the perception] "there is pleasure in what is pleasant" [is likewise abandoned].
The application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) is established as the antidote to error.
Dwelling in the contemplation of feelings,
one understands according to reality that "whatever is felt here, all that is suffering," and thus [overcomes] the error regarding suffering and pleasure, namely, the notion that "this is pleasure."
It is a perversion;
that is abandoned.
The perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent is abandoned.
The application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is established as the antidote.

By means of the various distinctions of the mind— such as being with passion and so forth— and by perceiving the manifoldness and many diverse modes of the mind throughout the passing of various nights and days, moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), and hours (*muhūrta*), that perversion which consists in regarding the impermanent as permanent is abandoned.
In this regard, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established as the antidote to the misconception that there is a self in what is not-self.

For those in whom afflictions such as the view of a self exist, and in whom wholesome factors such as the view of non-self do not exist, there arises a perception of a self within the aggregates; this occurs for them alone, and not for others, by way of [grasping at] specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*).
And for one who observes phenomena according to their general characteristics and sees them as they truly are,
that perversion which consists in regarding what is not-self as self is abandoned.
Another formulation:
for the world generally proceeds in this manner.
Not understanding, as they truly are, that within the aggregates there is only the aggregates and only phenomena, one remains dependent upon the body.
And since that which is the basis [of experience] is afflicted and purified by dharma and adharma through the arising of pleasure and pain,
the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is established there in order to remove delusion regarding the entity that is the basis of the self.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) was established for the purpose of removing delusion regarding the objects experienced by that very self;
and precisely within that which is the mind (*citta*),
the mental faculty (*manas*).
Regarding consciousness, for those who are deluded by the grasping at a self,
the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is established in order to remove that delusion regarding the reality of a self.
Another formulation:
where one performs an action,
and for what purpose one performs it.
And he who performs an action,
for whose sake he performs it,
and he by whom the action is performed.
And whatever he performs by means of that—
having condensed all of it into a single unity— the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are established.
Among these, he performs [the practice] with respect to the body.
For the purpose of feeling,
by means of the mind and wholesome or unwholesome factors;
this is another formulation.
Wherein one is defiled and purified; from what, who, and by what means one is defiled.
Because that by which one is purified, that which is purified, and that by which one is defiled and purified—
summarizing these as a unity— the four foundations of mindfulness are established.
Among them, one is defiled with respect to the body.
And it is purified.
The mind is defiled by feelings through dharmas;
and it is purified.

Regarding that, what is the meaning of "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*)? It is said: that upon which one establishes mindfulness, and that by means of which one establishes mindfulness.

That is called the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). That upon which one establishes mindfulness is the objective application of mindfulness (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*); that by means of which one establishes mindfulness is the instrumental application of mindfulness.
In that context, the wisdom and mindfulness that comprise concentration constitute the *smṛtyupasthāna* of intrinsic nature;
the other mental states and mental factors associated with them constitute the *smṛtyupasthāna* of association.
Moreover, a path dominated by body and sensation has arisen, which is wholesome, both with outflows and without outflows.
That is the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, it consists of that which is derived from hearing (*śrutamaya*), that which is derived from reflection (*cintāmaya*), and that which is derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
Among these, [the first] is that which is derived from hearing and reflection.
That which consists of cultivation may be either with outflows or without outflows.

Having thus cultivated familiarity with the four foundations of mindfulness, he eliminates even the coarsest form of perversion and becomes one who possesses direct knowledge of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
Immediately thereafter, for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome phenomena, he applies himself.
For the abandoning of arisen [unwholesome states],
for the arising of unarisen wholesome states,
and for the stabilization of those that have arisen; thus, in detail as before, he exerts his mind.
He exerts himself.
In that regard, what are the evil, unwholesome dharmas? They are the defiled bodily action and vocal action belonging to the desire realm.
Mental action,
which is comprised within the misconduct of body, speech, and mind,
by which those afflictions that give rise to it are produced, even though they are not currently present.
Those that have not yet become manifest are "arisen" insofar as they have been produced;
those that are present and have become manifest are "arisen.
In this context, wholesome factors (*kuśalā dharmāḥ*) are those factors which serve as their antidotes—that is, the antidotes to misconduct.
Those which are antidotes to the hindrances (*nivaraṇa*) or antidotes to the fetters (*saṃyojana*) should likewise be understood as unarisen when they have not yet arisen;
and regarding those evil, unwholesome states (*pāpakā akuśalā dharmāḥ*) that have already arisen, when one generates a longing for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He makes a resolve, generating the desire: "In every way and in all respects, I shall not produce [unwholesome states]";
or, regarding those already arisen and present, he thinks: "I shall not tolerate them in any way whatsoever, but shall abandon them."
I shall dispel [this] when there is a desire that arises and an aspiration is formed for evil, unwholesome states to arise beforehand, even though they have not yet arisen.
He does not wish to tolerate them;
this is the desire for the abandonment of arisen [unwholesome states].

Furthermore, those evil and unwholesome states arise and exist either with past objects as their objective support, or with future objects as their objective support, or with present sense-objects as their objective support.
Those which have as their object the aforementioned domain,
those which have as their object a directly perceived domain, and those which have as their object the states of the past and future—
these are the ones that have as their object the aforementioned domain.
Those [mental states] which have present objects as their objective support have perceptible objects as their objective support;
therein, for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unwholesome dharmas that have imperceptible objects as their objective support,
and for the sake of the abandonment of those that have already arisen.
He exerts himself;
furthermore, for those [factors] that have various objects within the sphere of direct perception,
he initiates vigor for the non-arising of those not yet arisen and for the abandonment of those already arisen.

For it is through their very firm application of energy that these [defilements] either do not arise or are abandoned; furthermore, it is for the sake of the non-arising of weak and middling afflictive states that have not yet arisen.
He exerts himself for the abandonment of those [defilements] that have arisen; he strives for the non-arising of those intense obsessions that have not yet arisen,
and he initiates vigor for the abandonment of those that have already arisen.
If he courses in a past object,
he courses in such a way that no affliction arises in him on account of that object.
If, however, it should arise again due to a lapse of mindfulness, he does not tolerate it;
he abandons it and eliminates it.

Just as it is with a past object of focus, so it should be understood for a future one as well. Thus, he is said to "strive for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, and for the abandoning of those already arisen. And if he practices with a present object of focus,
He conducts himself in such a way that no affliction arises through that object;
however, if it should arise again due to a lapse of mindfulness, [he applies the appropriate remedy].
He does not tolerate what has arisen;
he abandons it and dispels it.
He brings them to an end;
thus, for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, and for the sake of the abandonment of those already arisen, he exerts vigor— this is what is called "exerting vigor."
There are evil, unwholesome states which do not arise through the power (or force) of intention,
nor by the power of the sense objects.
There are those who [are born] by the power of volition and by the power of the object; among them,
those are born by the power of volition.
For example, while one is dwelling [in meditation],
those [mental states] that arise having the past and future as their objects [occur];
therein, under the influence of affliction (saṃkleśa)...
Nor do they arise solely through the power of the object;
for example, while one is moving about, they arise with a present object as their focal point. In that case, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) necessarily occurs.

In that regard, he exerts himself for the non-arising of those [defilements] that arise through the power of conceptual construction which have not yet arisen, and for the abandonment of those which have already arisen.

In that regard, he exerts himself for the non-arising of those [thoughts] that have not yet arisen and for the abandonment of those that have already arisen— those which arise through the power of sense objects and the power of conceptualization.
In that regard, for those [unwholesome states] that arise through the power of the sense objects and the power of conceptualization,
he exerts vigor for the non-arising of those not yet arisen and for the abandonment of those already arisen.
Therein, for wholesome states not yet arisen...
"He generates desire for the sake of production" means that for those wholesome dharmas which have not yet been attained and are not present,
he produces mindfulness for their attainment and for their manifestation.
He directs his mind;
a keen desire to acquire and a desire to bring [the object] into manifestation arise within him.
This is for the arising of unarisen wholesome states,
and for the stability, non-confusion, and increase of arisen wholesome states.
"He generates desire for the fulfillment of cultivation" refers to wholesome states that have arisen— those which have been acquired and those which are present.
In this context, it speaks with regard to the non-separation from what has been acquired and the non-decline of what has been acquired.
Regarding "stability," he says "for the sake of non-forgetfulness" with reference to the state of being unhindered through their manifestation.
And regarding the completion and final consummation of those very same acquired and manifested wholesome factors (*kuśaladharma*) through the sequence of their cultivation, he says: [the rest].
"For the fulfillment of cultivation"—
in that regard, he generates longing and directs his mind toward it as a vow.
And there arises in him an intense desire for stability, a desire for non-forgetfulness, and a desire for the fulfillment of cultivation;
this is called [the application of mindfulness].
There is the desire for the stability, non-confusion, and the fulfillment of cultivation of wholesome states that have already arisen;
therein, one exerts oneself means that one initiates vigor so that those [states] already attained may become manifest.
He exerts himself therein for the attainment of those not yet attained,
and for the stability of those already arisen.
For the sake of non-forgetfulness,
he exerts vigor;
for the sake of fulfilling cultivation.
Moreover, he exerts himself for the arising of weak and middling wholesome states that have not yet arisen,
and for the stability, non-confusion, and maintenance of those that have already arisen.
He exerts vigor for the arising of superior wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and for the cultivation and fulfillment of those already arisen; therein,
he applies the mind with firm resolve.
When that mind is applied to one-pointedness in the cultivation of calm abiding—
for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states,
and so on in detail, up to the arising of unarisen wholesome states once they have arisen— then...
And for those [wholesome states] that have arisen, he exerts vigor until their cultivation is perfected;
therein he uplifts the mind when that mind is applied to one-pointedness in the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
For the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states;
and so on in detail, up to the maintenance of arisen wholesome states.
For the sake of non-forgetfulness and for the fulfillment of cultivation,
that [mind] which has been thus withdrawn within tends toward lethargy;
and suspecting such lethargy, he observes it in this way.
Then, by means of one or another uplifting sign that inspires clarity, he takes hold of it;
he gladdens and thus uplifts the mind.
How does he apply himself?
When he perceives that the mind has become excited or is suspected of being excited at the time of exertion,
he then again withdraws it inwardly.
One applies oneself to calm abiding (*śamatha*); these are the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
There is the desire, exertion, arousal of energy, and mental application for the non-arising of unarisen states belonging to the dark side, and for the abandoning of those that have arisen.
These two exertions are the right abandonments for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;
they should be understood in detail as two types of right abandonment.

Namely, regarding the dark side, one is the abandonment through restraint, which—as described in detail—is the generation of desire for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.

The second is the abandonment of abandonments (*prahāṇaprahāṇa*), which is described in detail as "generating the desire for the non-arising of those things that have not yet arisen"; for indeed, what has already arisen must be restrained, as must evil objects.
That which has not yet arisen is abandoned by way of its non-occurrence; thus, it is to be abandoned by way of its non-manifestation.
The abandonment of what has already been abandoned is called "abandonment of abandonment" (*prahāṇaprahāṇa*).
In that regard, cultivation as abandonment is one [of the four right efforts], which he describes in detail as:
"for the arising of unarisen wholesome states," up to "he exerts the mind" and "he strives."
For in this way, wholesome phenomena, when practiced and cultivated,
are attained even if they were previously unattained.
Those [wholesome factors] already acquired are brought into manifestation;
therein, guarding is one form of abandonment,
as it is said:
For the stabilization of wholesome states that have arisen,
and so forth in detail, until he exerts his mind and applies effort.

For instance, when wholesome qualities have been acquired and brought into manifestation, that which consists in the avoidance of negligence and the cultivation of heedfulness serves for the stability of those wholesome qualities.
For the sake of non-forgetfulness and for the fulfillment of cultivation;
in this way, unarisen wholesome states are preserved. This, first of all, is the detailed analysis of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Furthermore, what is the summary of the meaning?
It is said:
For the sake of abandoning what belongs to the dark side and for the sake of attaining the object belonging to the bright side,
one must first be possessed of longing;
and likewise, for the sake of abandoning the secondary afflictions (paryavasthāna).
The perfection of intention and the perfection of application are thus elucidated;
therein, of this...
The perfection of intention consists in the generation of aspiration;
furthermore, the perfection of application consists in the wealth of exertion, the undertaking of vigor, the restraint of the mind, and non-negligence.
And this much is to be done by the yogin:
that for the sake of abandoning the thing to be abandoned and for the sake of attaining the thing to be attained, one must first of all give rise to a longing.
In order to abandon the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and to abandon the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), one should exert vigor and,
from time to time, cultivate the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), exertion (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
They are to be cultivated;
and those wholesome factors which serve as antidotes for the abandonment of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the abandonment of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are to be fully gathered.
All of this is elucidated by means of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); this is the summary of the meaning.
In that regard, there are four concentrations,
namely: concentration through desire,
concentration through energy, [concentration through mind, and concentration through investigation].
The concentration of mind and the concentration of investigation.
In that regard, the concentration which is obtained by making desire (*chanda*) the dominant factor is "concentration through desire" (*chandasamādhi*). [Likewise,
those obtained by making] vigor (*vīrya*) and mind (*citta*) [the dominant factors are "concentration through vigor" and "concentration through mind"].

Making investigation the dominant factor, this concentration is attained; it is called the *mīmāṃsā-samādhi* (concentration of investigation). When, for the time being, one generates mere desire alone...
And having generated desire, he [considers] those evil, unwholesome states by way of their intrinsic nature, their cause, and their disadvantage.
And by way of the counteragent,
he applies his attention correctly and sets forth one-pointed mindfulness.
In this way, one correctly applies one's attention to wholesome phenomena by way of their intrinsic nature and their cause, as well as by way of the unwholesome and the renunciation [of them].
He establishes one-pointed mindfulness;
he touches upon that one-pointedness characterized by frequent practice,
through the application of distancing the manifestation of the settled state.
Yet he does not give rise to even a latent tendency toward them;
this too is called the predominance of desire regarding evil and unwholesome states.
Whether it be past, or future or present objects that are conducive to evil and unwholesome states, and conducive to the manifestation of weak, medium, or intense afflictions, he (she)—
Exerting himself and arousing vigor for the sake of the non-arising of what has not yet arisen, or for the abandonment of what has already arisen.
Therein, as he dwells upon that object— examining that very object by way of its intrinsic nature, its cause, and its antidote;
as he reflects correctly and establishes one-pointed mindfulness— there arises for him, through frequent dwelling in this state, one-pointedness of mind.
However, by means of the yoga of distancing oneself from the state of being fully possessed [by those afflictions], one also eradicates their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This concentration (*samādhi*) has diligence (*vīrya*) as its dominant influence over evil and unwholesome factors (*dharma*).
Furthermore, when the mind is sunken, one uplifts it;
when the mind has been uplifted, one composes it;
and from time to time, one maintains equanimity toward it.
Because of the connection with evil and unwholesome states that correspond to evil and unwholesome phenomena, [one is led away] from the wholesome.
[He understands] wholesome phenomena and phenomena conducive to the wholesome and unwholesome in terms of their intrinsic nature, their causes, and their disadvantages.
From the perspective of its benefits,
from the perspective of its counteragent,
and from the perspective of its transcendence.
For one who correctly applies oneself to meditative concentration,
who establishes mindfulness with one-pointedness,
and who dwells frequently therein, there arise states of one-pointedness of mind, in detail up to this [point].
Concentration is dominated by the mind;
therein, there are factors that are conducive to evil and unwholesome states.
For one who attends to them inappropriately, those very things become conducive to unwholesome states; for one who attends to them appropriately, they become conducive to wholesome states.
When those states of obsession have been thus distanced, and when the qualities beginning with concentration— which are the antidotes to those states—
