have not yet arisen, those evil and unwholesome factors carry away one's wholesome qualities.

It occurs to him: "Do I not experience these evil, unwholesome states because they exist and are present, or rather because they do not exist and are not present? [He considers: "They do not exist and are not present."
I investigate this;
having made that investigation (mīmāṃsā) mental attention predominant, he investigates whether [the afflictions] have been abandoned or not yet abandoned.
He contemplates them correctly;
by dwelling frequently in that state, he touches one-pointedness of mind, through which he becomes free from conceit,
[arising] merely from the presence of the outbursts of passion.
The mind is liberated,
yet not entirely and completely from all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
and I have attained those wholesome factors, headed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which are the antidotes to them.
He understands as it truly is that [the mind] has been cultivated, but not as an antidote to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
this is called his "investigative concentration" (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*).
Having made that fourfold concentration his dominant influence, once the outbursts [of the defilements] have been distanced,
he acts for the total and complete eradication of the latent tendencies of all evil, unwholesome states, and for the sake of their wholesome antidotes.
One generates desire for the full realization of the dharmas;
"exerts oneself," and so forth, meaning one applies oneself through the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
For one who applies themselves in this way and has become thus, there arise the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
Those which function for the sake of uprooting the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and for the fulfillment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such as: desire (*chanda*),
thinking, "At some point I shall fulfill meditative concentration."
I shall abandon the latent tendencies;
there will be exertion regarding evil and unwholesome states, up to the cultivation of their antidotes,
for one who dwells with unremitting application and with unremitting yoga in faith.
It is faith and deep conviction regarding further realization;
therein lies serenity.

That which is preceded by faith and heedfulness, namely joy and rapture, and for one whose mind is gladdened, the gradual subsiding of the heaviness belonging to the side of evil and unwholesome states.
In that regard, mindfulness is that which is ninefold and which encompasses the ninefold abiding of the mind belonging to the side of calm (śamatha). As for desire and clear comprehension,
they are the wisdom belonging to the side of insight (vipaśyanā).
In that context, volition is the mental formation;

it is the mental formation of one who is investigating whether [defilements] have been abandoned or not abandoned, which, being conducive to calm abiding and insight, gives rise to bodily and vocal action.
In that regard, for one who dwells amidst past, future, and present bases for evil and unwholesome states, there is mental affliction and mental engagement [with them].

By these two causes— one being volition regarding objects that are out of sight, and the other being equanimity regarding objects that are out of sight— one discerns and knows the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
These are the eight formative forces of abandonment;
and these eight constitute the application of the formative forces of abandonment for the purpose of uprooting the latent tendencies.
In that regard,
zeal is that very same exertion which is vigor.
That which is faith is purity;
and that which is pliancy, that which is mindfulness, that which is clear comprehension,
that which is volition, and that which is equanimity.
Based on this:

all of this taken together— both those former concentrations of desire (*chandasamādhi*) and these formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) when the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been abandoned— [constitute this].
When concentration is fully developed, these are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) endowed with the formative forces of abandonment consisting of the concentration of desire,
as well as those of energy, mind, and investigation.
The basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is said to be endowed with the formative forces of concentration and abandonment (*samādhiprahāṇasaṃskāra*).
For what reason is it called a "basis of psychic power"?
He replied:
For example: he who possesses feet is capable of advancing, retreating, and exerting effort.
In the same way, for one in whom these qualities exist and this concentration exists,
it is complete.
When his mind is thus purified, cleansed, and free from blemish,
Free from secondary afflictions, become upright, workable, stable,
and attained to imperturbability.
One becomes capable of advancing and retreating for the sake of attaining and realizing supramundane dharmas.
For this is the supreme supernatural power,
the supreme prosperity; namely, that they are called supramundane phenomena.
The bases of psychic power.
Thus established in concentration,
relying upon that concentration,
he applies himself to the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom.
In that regard, for one who is practicing yoga,
there is the firm conviction, clarity, and state of faith toward the realization of others— the Teacher and his disciples.
It is called the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) in the sense of attainment (samāpatti).
But where does its sovereignty (adhipatya) lie? He says:
It exercises sovereignty over the arising of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, which are headed by the arising of supramundane dharmas;
it also exercises sovereignty over those very qualities such as energy for the arising of supramundane dharmas, and so on, up to sovereignty over their actual practice.
Up to the point where, through wisdom, there is sovereignty for the arising of supramundane dharmas; by virtue of that, these five beginning with faith are called faculties (*indriyas*).
Furthermore, for one who perceives a successive attainment of distinction from what preceded it, there arises—
following that [perception]— a firm conviction and clarity regarding the attainment of subsequent supramundane dharmas.
It is the state of having faith. Because it cannot be crushed, it is called the power of faith (*śraddhābala*).
By what, then, can it not be overcome?
That faith is indestructible and cannot be led astray by a god or anyone else.
Whether by Māra,
or by Brahmā,
or by anyone else in the world.
Because it is not overcome by either the dharma or by the obsession of the afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*), it is called "unassailable.
Those qualities beginning with vigor (*vīrya*) that have that [unassailability] as their head and that which precedes them are called "powers" (*bala*).
By means of those powers, being powerful, one applies oneself after having conquered the entire army of Māra.
For the sake of the destruction of the outflows;
therefore, they are called powers.
In that regard, whatever...
The faculty of faith and that which is the power of faith are to be seen within the four kinds of verified clarity;
for what reason?
That verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) which belongs to one who has entered the path of rightness (samyaktvanyāma) is caused by that,
conditioned by that, and has that as its source.
Therefore, by virtue of the relationship between cause and fruit, it is considered to be the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala) of that [path].
In that regard, it was said by the Blessed One: "It is to be seen," but not as having that as its body or that as its characteristic.
In this context, the faculty of energy (vīryendriya) is to be seen within the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa).
For what reason?

Which are those? They are the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), which are the preparatory right abandonments for the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaprahātavyakleśa*).
The right abandonments intended here are those, for they lead to the ultimate abandonment of evil, unwholesome states.
In that regard, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is to be seen in the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Thus, these four applications of mindfulness lead to the abandonment of both general and specific distortions (*viparyāsa*).
In that regard, the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) [is to be seen] in the four... [applications of mindfulness].
It should be understood in relation to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Those meditative absorptions which are preparatory for the state of non-retrogression—
in those, the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) should be understood as pertaining to the four noble truths.
That true knowledge which leads to the realization of the four noble truths and to the attainment of the fruits of asceticism—
these are the faculties.
In this way, the powers (balas) are to be understood.
Through the sequence of practicing, cultivating, and repeatedly performing these faculties (indriyas) and those powers, one generates the roots of merit conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya),
which are weak, middling, and superior.
Namely: the stages of heat (*ūṣmagata*), the stages of summits (*mūrdhagata*),
the summits themselves (*mūrdhan*), the patiences (*kṣānti*) that accord with the truths, and the worldly [supreme dharmas] (*laukikāgradharma*).
Regarding the stage of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
it is as follows: suppose a certain man, desiring to produce fire by means of fire,
and seeking fire, places the upper fire-drill upon the lower fire-drill and exerts himself.
He exerts himself, strives,
and likewise endeavors.
As he exerts himself and strives,
first of all, heat is produced in the lower kindling wood.
That very heat,
increasing further, rises upward;
increasing by a greater measure, it continues to grow.
One causes a fire without flames to fall; immediately upon its falling, a flame arises,
just as by means of that flame which has been produced and generated.
Once it has arisen,
one produces a mass of fire;
just as the exertion of friction is, so should the cultivation of the five faculties be regarded.
Just as the lower fire-drill first becomes warm, so should the stages of heat (ūṣmagata) be understood;
they are the precursors.

They serve as signs for the arising of the outflow-free (anāsrava) dharmas, which are like fire and burn away the afflictions. Just as that very heat rises upward, so too should the "summits" (mūrdhan) be understood.
Just as the appearance of smoke [indicates fire], so should the patiences that accord with the truths be regarded.
Just as the falling of a flameless fire is to be seen, so should the mundane supreme dharmas (laukikā agradharmāḥ) be viewed;
just as the subsequent arising of a flame is to be seen, so should the supramundane untainted dharmas (lokottarā anāsravā dharmāḥ) be viewed.
Those which arise immediately after the five faculties included within the mundane supreme dharmas—what, then, are they? He says: the seven factors of enlightenment.
That which is the realization of things as they truly are belongs to the person who has entered the path of certainty (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
These are its constituent factors.
For that is the realization of things as they truly are;
it is comprised of seven factors:
three belonging to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*), three belonging to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and one belonging to both sides.
Therefore, they are called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). In that regard, there is both the Dharma-Vinaya and diligence (*vīrya*).
And that which is joy—these three belong to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
In that regard, that which is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), that which is concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—these three belong to the side of tranquility (*śamatha*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) belongs to neither side.
It is called "all-pervading.
At that time, because he has for the first time attained the factors of enlightenment, he becomes a learner (*śaikṣa*) from that moment onward.
His afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned,
while those to be abandoned by cultivation remain.
For their abandonment, he cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path consisting of three aggregates.
In that regard, right view, right intention,
and right effort—
this is the aggregate of wisdom.
In that regard, right action and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*); therein,
there is also right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*).
And as for this right concentration, which is the aggregate of concentration—
for what reason is it called the Noble Eightfold Path?
He said:
This is the path, this is the practice, of the noble disciple in training who has seen the goal; it is comprised of eight factors.
It is without remainder;
it is for the sake of abandoning all afflictions and for the realization of liberation, and thus it is called the Noble Eightfold Path.
In that regard, there is the awakening to reality at the time of the factors of enlightenment.
Having attained it,
and having attained it, he establishes that very [attainment] through wisdom.
Just as for one who has understood what is free [from error],
those two taken together as a unity are called right view;
having made that right view the dominant influence.
When one forms a resolve for renunciation, a resolve free from ill-will, and a resolve for non-violence, this is called right resolve (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
And if, for the time being, the mind applies itself to these thoughts (*vitarka*).
He reflects upon such a reflection.
If, however, his mind wanders toward talk,
he makes right view his dominant influence and, by means of that—
He speaks a discourse on the Dharma arising from wholesome intentions;
this constitutes his right speech.
If he becomes a seeker after robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
or if he engages in the pursuit of them,
that is his forward movement.
He dwells with clear comprehension when moving forward and moving backward, and when looking ahead and looking aside; likewise when bending and stretching his limbs.
In the wearing of the saṃghāṭī robe, the outer robe, and the bowl;
in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting;
or again, when one has gone to the monastery or has gone out in search of robes and other requisites.
Whether standing or sitting,
up until the dispelling of drowsiness and fatigue, he dwells with clear comprehension;
this is called his right action.
He seeks those robes and all requisites for medicine in accordance with the Dharma; as long as he is free from wrong livelihood and devoid of unrighteousness, that constitutes his right livelihood.
Furthermore, those right actions and right livelihoods which are comprised within abstinence have already been acquired by him,
together with the factors of enlightenment, through the prior attainment of mental attention.
Furthermore, why are the precepts called "lovely" (*kānta*)?

For what reason? Because for a long time this has been desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the noble ones, the virtuous, and those who have attained the right path. [Thinking: "Might I perhaps [be free] from that misconduct of speech and misconduct of body..."
By refraining from wrong livelihood,
may I attain restraint,
which has been his desire for a long night.

That which is lovely, dear, and pleasing to the mind is obtained by him at that time; therefore, it is called "lovely and pleasing" (*āpakānta*). For thus, in those lovely and pleasing ethical precepts (*śīla*) he has obtained,
He does not speak false speech with full awareness;
he does not intentionally deprive a living being of life.
He does not take what is not given;
he does not engage in sexual misconduct regarding sensual pleasures.
Nor does one seek robes and so forth through unrighteous means;
thus, taking those agreeable moralities as the primary focus, one proceeds as far as necessary at the time of cultivating the path.
Furthermore, whatever constitutes bodily action and whatever constitutes livelihood, these too are called right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
For one who is engaged in cultivation by relying upon right view, right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood,
whatever desire [there may be]...
Energy, exertion, departure, valor, strength, and undertaking.
The thorough grasping of the mind and its continuity is called right effort and tranquility.
That mindfulness which, having the four foundations of mindfulness as its dominant influence, is comprised of non-perversion, possesses nine aspects, and encompasses the nine modes of mental abiding—
this is called right mindfulness and right concentration.
All of this, taken together, constitutes the Noble Eightfold Path as established both in what is to be done while moving about and in what is to be done while dwelling.
Among these, right speech, right action, and right livelihood pertain to what is to be done while moving about.
Furthermore, that which is to be accomplished in the monastery is twofold:
serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā). Among these, right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) is [the basis for] serenity.
Right intention and right effort constitute insight (*vipaśyanā*); therein,
right mindfulness and right concentration constitute tranquility (*śamatha*).
Relying thus upon these completely pure right speech, right action, and right livelihood, one cultivates serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
From time to time, one realizes the abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) without exception—the supreme fruit of arhatship—and attains it.
And [this state] is long-lasting.
The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) abandons the afflictions through repeated practice over a period of time.

The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which consists in the vision of things dependent solely upon knowledge, abandons the afflictions by the mere arising of that knowledge. For this reason, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are established as belonging to the path of cultivation.

Thus, this very practice and cultivation of these thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening in this sequential order is called the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-bhāvanā*).
In that regard, what is the fruit of cultivation? It is said:
the four fruits of asceticism.
The fruit of stream-entry,
the fruit of once-returning,
the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit of arhatship.
In that regard, what is asceticism?
What is the fruit? He said:
The path is the cause, and the abandonment of afflictions is the fruit.
Furthermore, the path that arises later is the fruit of the path that arose earlier; this is the intermediate [distinction].
Or again, as for that which is distinguished: for what reason are four established therein?
He said:
It is by way of being the antidote for the abandonment of the four types of afflictions.

That is to say, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) is established through the abandonment of those afflictions that lack a real objective basis (*nirvastuka*) and which serve as the cause for rebirth in the miserable realms, as well as through the arising of their antidote;
however, it is also established through the abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
By the Blessed One, with respect to three categories: the category of householders,
and the category of those for whom the Dharma and Vinaya are poorly proclaimed.
Because it acts as the cause for the increase [of the other fetters] so that the three fetters may give rise to the Path:
therein, on the side of householders, there is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
It is called the "view of a self-identity that causes terror from the very beginning" because, by means of it, one does not apply oneself to this [Path] from the outset.
In a poorly taught Dharma and Vinaya, there is the clinging to rules and observances;
even though one has set out [on the path], it leads to a false practice,
by which the Noble Path does not arise.
In the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, he has moved beyond doubt and is not practicing wrongly;
yet, due to his own lack of cultivation, he does not yet possess the vision of things as they truly are.
Regarding the object of knowledge, doubts and indecisiveness act as obstacles to the arising of the path.
For this reason, the establishment of the fruit of stream-entry is made.
For this stream-enterer, at most seven more existences remain;
and that is the continuity of his births.
When one abandons the afflictions that bind one to the cycle of birth—
those comprised within existence as a god and those comprised within existence as a human—
by the abandonment of which one brings about at most one further divine existence and one human existence;
At that time, the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) is established.
However, when one brings about rebirth only in the divine realm,
having abandoned the afflictions pertaining to birth in this world, then the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is established.
The fruit of arhatship, which is the supreme fruit, is established through the abandonment of those afflictions that lead to rebirth in all states of existence.
Furthermore, the fruit of once-returning is established through the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion.

Because of its subtlety, it was established by the Blessed One that the fruit of non-returning results from the abandonment of the five lower fetters; and the fruit of arhatship results from the complete exhaustion and abandonment of all defilements. This is called the fruit of cultivation.

In that regard, those persons who are characterized by conduct dominated by passion, hatred, delusion, pride, or discursive thought must first purify their conduct with respect to an object of focus intended for the purification of conduct.
Thereafter, they attain stability of mind.
For them, that object of focus is strictly determined; they must necessarily apply themselves to that specific object.
However, for one whose temperament is balanced (*samabhāgacarita*), it is whichever object they find most pleasant and agreeable.
In that case, he should apply himself solely for the sake of mental stability,
and not for the sake of purifying his conduct.
Just as it is with one whose conduct is characterized by equal proportions of the defilements, so too should one who has little passion be understood.
However, this is their distinction: one whose temperament is dominated by passion and so forth becomes an attainer only after a long time when practicing;
one of balanced temperament does not take too long; but one with little dust [of defilement] quickly and very swiftly attains stability of mind.
The characteristics of persons whose conduct is dominated by passion have been explained there previously.
What are the characteristics of a person whose conduct is balanced and of one who has little passion?
He replied:
All those characteristics belonging to individuals whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth are found in a person of balanced temperament;
however, those [traits] such as passion are not excessive.
They are not predominant;
likewise, for those whose conduct is characterized by passion and so forth, when conditions are present, these [defilements] reach a state of equilibrium and thus do not manifest.
In that regard, the characteristics of a person with little passion (*mandarajaska*) are as follows:
he is unobstructed, endowed with the equipment of primordial purity,
abounding in serene faith, intelligent, meritorious, and possessed of virtuous qualities.
In that regard, there are three obscurations:
the obscuration of karma, the obscuration of afflictions, and the obscuration of maturation.
The obstruction of maturation;
therein, the obstruction of karma consists of the five actions of immediate retribution.
And whatever other actions there may be—
whether intentional,
grave, or having already ripened as their result.
For the arising of the path,
it acts as a persistent obstacle;
therein lies the obscuration of afflictions.
It is the state of intense affliction and the state of prolonged affliction,
which cannot be purified in this present life by means of purifying one's conduct or purifying the object of focus.
In that regard, the obscuration of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*) is that in which the Noble Path does not arise or lacks clarity within the sphere of rebirth;
or where it brings about maturation in a place where the Noble Path would otherwise arise.

Having been reborn there, one becomes mute and dumb, communicating only by means of hand gestures, and is incapable of understanding the meaning of dharmas that have been well-expounded or poorly expounded.
In that regard, this is the initial purity. (Śbh_Sh 336)
And there is perfectly pure ethical discipline and upright view. In that regard, perfectly pure ethical discipline is to be understood by way of ten reasons.
In that regard, the state of being satisfied with one's view arises from association with faith.

For it is the view associated with faith— associated with resolute conviction— that, through its lack of guile, its well-considered understanding of the meaning of the Dharma, and its being an emergence through application free from desire and doubt, is held by the Noble Ones.

Through their resolute conviction in this Dharma and Vinaya which cannot be diverted, they experience impermanence and the impermanent bases of rebirth, as well as the profound teaching of the Buddhas and the Buddha’s disciples.
He resolves upon the indeterminate points;
he does not tremble, nor does he fall into terror.
And that view which is free from deceit and guile, by which one becomes upright,
of an upright nature,
and practices according to the instruction received.
And he reveals himself as he truly is,
beginning with the impermanence and suffering of phenomena.
The meaning of emptiness and selflessness becomes well-pondered,
well-weighed, and well-examined;
for this reason, he becomes free from doubt.
Free from doubt,
having entered upon the two-fold path, one proceeds toward distinction;
such is this fourfold view as it has been set forth.
It is called "straightness of view. In that regard, the detailed accumulation of the provisions has already been explained at length;
here it is presented in brief.
Furthermore, it is of four kinds:
the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of gnosis.
The former and that pertaining to the present life.
In that regard, the accumulation of merit is that by which even now favorable requisites appear,
things that are auspicious, and one obtains virtuous friends.
And for one who is thus engaged, there is no obstacle;
therein lies the equipment of knowledge,
by which one becomes wise.
He is capable of understanding the meaning of teachings that are well-spoken and ill-spoken;
he becomes a possessor [of this capacity].
Of the teaching of the Dharma that is in accordance with the truth,
of the teaching of its meaning, and of the instruction and admonition.
In that regard, it is due to the former [cause], by which one now obtains matured faculties,
owing to the accumulation of previous roots of merit.
In that regard, the benefit pertaining to the present life is as follows: a wholesome desire for the Dharma,
as well as the restraint of ethical discipline for one whose faculties have matured.
"Restraint of the sense faculties," and so forth, as detailed previously.
In that regard, there is an abundance of serene confidence;
he does not harbor doubt concerning the Teacher.
He does not doubt;
he gains serene confidence and becomes resolute.
Just as toward the Teacher, so too toward the Dharma.
"In training," and so forth, as detailed previously. In that context, *medhā* is that by which one quickly grasps the Dharma;
it does not allow the Dharma and its meaning to be forgotten over time.
One swiftly penetrates both the Dharma and the meaning.
In that regard, there is the state of having performed meritorious deeds.
By means of which one becomes handsome,
beautiful to behold,
pleasing, long-lived, and one whose words are authoritative.
He becomes renowned and famous; he possesses great merit and is a recipient of robes and other requisites.
He is honored and revered by kings and others;
in this context, "endowed with virtues" should be understood as possessing qualities such as having few desires and so forth.
As it is said in the *Śramaṇālaṃkāra*: "He is endowed with these very qualities by his very nature.
Thus, these and similar characteristics of a person of little passion (mandarajaska) are to be understood.
In that regard, there are six designations for persons (*pudgala*):
namely, the ascetic (*śramaṇa*) and the brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*).
A celibate student, a monk, an ascetic, and one who has gone forth.
In this regard, there are four types of śramaṇas:
the victor over the path and the teacher of the path.
There are those who live by the path and those who corrupt the path;
therein, he who is the Sugata is the Victor of the Path.
He who speaks according to the Dharma is the teacher of the path;
therein, he who practices it is one who lives by the path.
He who has practiced wrongly is a defiler of the path;
whereas the Sugata is said to be one who has attained the complete destruction of attachment, aversion, and delusion without remainder.
One who speaks the Dharma is one who teaches the Dharma for the sake of subduing attachment, aversion, and delusion.
One who has entered upon the good path is one who has practiced well for the sake of subduing attachment, aversion, and delusion.
One who has entered [the path] improperly; one who is immoral, of evil nature,
and practicing wrongly.

Moreover, those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called "victors on the path" because they have triumphed over the afflictions (kleśa) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation. In this regard, the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas are those who have set out for enlightenment in the future,
as are the Śrāvakas who uphold the Sūtras.
Those who uphold the Vinaya and those who uphold the Mātṛkā—
those who maintain the conventional Dharma and Vinaya.
They set in motion the eye of the Dharma;
these are called the guides of the path.
Among them, those virtuous ordinary persons who have set out for their own benefit are the Śrāvakas (guides of the path).
They are remorseful and desirous of training;
they are applied to the attainment of what has not been attained, the realization of what has not been realized, and the direct manifestation of what has not been directly manifested;
and they are capable and competent.
Up until the direct realization of that which has not yet been realized—
these are called those who live by the path;
even their "warmth" serves for the arising of this noble faculty of wisdom.
They are not dead; they are said to be "living.
For this reason, they are called "those who live by the path.
In that regard, there is a person who is immoral, of evil character, and so forth, up to one who is unchaste yet claims to be a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
This is called a corrupter of the path; by him the path is corrupted from its very root and from the beginning,
whereby he becomes incapable and powerless,
and unfit as a vessel for the arising of the path.
While the teaching of the path exists and while realization exists,
he is therefore called a "corrupter of the path. It was with this in mind that the Blessed One spoke.
In this regard, who is a śramaṇa?
Here, up to the fourth [fruit],
the doctrines of others are empty.
By śramaṇas and brahmins alike:
wherever the Noble Eightfold Path is known, there is the first śramaṇa, and so on up to the fourth.
In that regard, there are three kinds of brahmins:
namely, the brahmin by birth,
and the brahmin by designation.
And there is the brahmin by practice. Among these, the brahmin by birth is one who is born into a [brahmin] family.
Born from a womb, produced by a mother;
arisen from a mother and from a father.
In that regard, there is what is known in the world as a "brahmin by designation" (saṃjñā-brāhmaṇa); it is a designation, a common appellation.
Designation is conventional usage; a brahmin is one by way of practice; he who is... absolutely...
He becomes one who has accomplished his purpose;
by him, evil and unwholesome states have been expelled.
As it has been said: "There is nothing further to be done for a brahmin."
"A Brahmin is considered one who has accomplished his purpose.
In that regard, there are three types of religious students (*brahmacārin*):
namely, the one who undertakes renunciation (*viratisamādāyī*).
One who abandons that in the interval,
one who abandons that completely,
and therein, one who undertakes the vow of abstinence.
One who has desisted from the dharma of celibacy,
having undertaken the training,
yet abandons it in the interim— namely, the ordinary person who is free from passion for sensual desires by means of the mundane path.
In that regard, one who has completely abandoned those [defilements] is,
for example, a non-returner; or again,
from the state of arhatship, an arhat.
In this regard, there are five types of monks (*bhikṣu*).
One is a monk because he begs (*bhikṣati*); another is a monk by formal declaration (*pratijñā-bhikṣu*).
A monk by designation;
a monk because his afflictions have been destroyed;
a monk who has received full ordination through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.
In that regard, there are three types of ascetics (*yati*):
an ascetic by virtue of restraint from immorality;
one who abstains from unwholesome actions of speech and body.
The ascetic is one who restrains the sense objects,
whose gateway of the senses is guarded,
and whose mindfulness is protected.
Possessing steadfast mindfulness—
as described in detail previously—
he exerts himself in the restraint of the afflictions.

He whose afflictions to be abandoned by vision have been eliminated, and who, as each thought arises, abandons discursive thoughts associated with malice— namely, covetousness, malice, wrong view, false view, anger, resentment, concealment, and spite— which are states leading to the miserable destinies,
to hell, and to rebirth in evil realms.
He does not tolerate, abandons, and purifies whatever factors that make one a non-ascetic arise as they occur.
He brings it to an end;
this twofold restraint of the afflictions consists of restraint regarding the outbursts [of passion] and restraint regarding the underlying tendencies.
And there is restraint of both.
In that regard, there are two types of renunciants:
those for whom the Dharma and Vinaya are well-expounded,
and those for whom the Dharma and Vinaya are poorly expounded.
Therein, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya,
there are the bhikṣu, the bhikṣuṇī, and the śikṣamāṇā.
A novice monk (śrāmaṇera) or a novice nun (śrāmaṇerī);
moreover, because he has caused his own evil and unwholesome states to go forth [and be abandoned], he is called "one who has gone forth" (pravrajita) in the ultimate sense.
In that regard, there is the poorly proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; namely, [the teachings of] the non-Buddhist wanderers (parivrājaka).
Or a Nirgrantha,
or a wandering mendicant suffering from jaundice,
or anyone else of a similar kind.
Therefore, I am a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa,
and a brahmacārī.
The monk is a practitioner;
[having gone forth...
the distinction of time is that the path has been cultivated for a long duration.
Nor has he cultivated the path for a long time.
Thus, how do these four distinctions become the causes?
Or rather, [he is one who] knows the right occasion, knows the means; that is to say, he is skillful.

In the case of the category of constancy (*sātatyapakṣa*), practice is called "constant" (*sātatika*) and "thoroughly attentive" (*nipaka*). This is due to the distinction of having cultivated and repeatedly cultivated [the path] over a long period of time through the threefold division.

The classification of attained individuals according to the distinction between the time of yoga and its application is as follows: first, there is the individual whose faculties are not yet matured; such a person, even if they know the means, are constant in practice, and have completed their preliminary training, does not become a successful achiever of the meditative state that is wholesome.
In that regard, one whose faculties are matured becomes a knower of the [path];
one whose faculties are matured becomes a knower of skillful means, yet does not become one who attains higher knowledge quickly.
In that regard, one whose faculties are matured and who knows the skillful means may not yet be constant in practice.
He has not yet cultivated familiarity;
he has not yet accomplished his own purpose,
nor has he fulfilled what was to be done.
And whoever has mature faculties, knows the skillful means, is constant, and has practiced cultivation— such a person is one who succeeds and quickly attains higher knowledge.
And having accomplished his own task, he becomes one who has fulfilled what was to be done.
In this regard, a yogin engaged in yoga should understand the four Māras and the many activities of Māra.
And having fully understood them, they should be avoided.
In that regard, there are four Māras, namely:
the Māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra),...
The Māra of afflictions, the Māra of death, and the Māra who is a son of the gods.
The five aggregates of clinging are the *skandhamāra*;
they are the afflictions belonging to the three realms for those various sentient beings.
From each respective class of beings,
that which is death, the passing away,
and the act of dying is the "death-māra."

Furthermore, for one who is engaged in the unwholesome side in order to transcend the aggregates, the afflictions, and death, there may be a son of the gods born in the desire realm who has attained certainty and brings about an obstacle by creating a distraction.
This is called the Māra of the Son of Heaven (devaputramāra).
In this regard, there is where one dies,
that which is death, and that by which one is led toward death.
He causes one to stray by means of an obstructive thing;
with reference to this, the four Māras are established.
Therein, one dies when the five aggregates of clinging have arisen and are increasing.
It generates afflictions for the future; once born, one dies.
Death is the passing away and the state of dissolution for sentient beings, the cessation of the life-faculty, and the very nature of the completion of one's time.
And the Devaputramāra brings about an obstacle for one who is striving to transcend death,
by means of which one is simply unable to transcend the nature of mortality.
Or, with the passage of time, he transcends it;
therein, the ordinary person who has become free from passion through the mundane path falls under the power of Māra.
Whether remaining here or reborn there,
he is not under control;
furthermore, he is one who has not yet abandoned passion.
In that regard, one who is already free from passion is like one who has fallen into [another's] hands and can be dealt with as desired;
or again, one who is free from passion may yet be bound by the fetters of Māra.
Because he is not yet liberated from the snares of Māra, he will return again to maintain this realm.
In that regard, these are the deeds of Māra:
when a desire for the Dharma connected with renunciation has arisen in anyone,
[Māra exerts influence] through the predominance of sensual craving.
One should understand that when these [defilements] arise after having been cultivated, they constitute the work of Māra,
even for one who dwells with the doors of the sense-faculties guarded.

If one’s mind sinks into the grasping of signs and the grasping of secondary characteristics regarding pleasant forms, as well as the associated tastes and tangibles, it should be known that this is the work of Māra. Likewise, for one who dwells knowing the proper measure in food, if the mind sinks through attachment and desire into longing for exquisite flavors, [it should be known that this is the work of Māra].
In this way, when there is an inequality in food, for one who dwells devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night,
[there arises] a lack of interest in the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of reclining.
If the mind inclines toward the pleasure of reclining,
one should understand that this is the work of Māra;
likewise, for one who dwells practicing clear comprehension while remaining in the posture.
When walking or returning, upon seeing a woman of beautiful appearance who is attractive— a child— his mind plunges into it through improper grasping of signs;
or, having seen the various wonders of the world, his mind plunges into them, [thinking] "there is much to be gained."
The mind plunges into having many duties,
such as, for example, delighting in association with householders and renunciants.
When the mind inclines toward a shared resolve with evil friends and toward approval of [wrong] views,
it should be understood that this is the work of Māra.
Likewise, [faith] in the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha.
In suffering,
its origin, its cessation, and the path.
When doubts and perplexities arise regarding this world or the world beyond,
one should recognize that this is the work of Māra.
Whether one has gone to the forest, or...
Whether he has gone to the foot of a tree or to an empty dwelling, he sees something great, terrifying and formidable, causing alarm and making the hair stand on end.
Whether in the guise of a brahmin,
or in the guise of a human, or in the guise of a non-human;
Someone, having approached, improperly severs [him] from the side of virtue and incites him toward the side of darkness.
It should be understood that this is the work of Māra when the mind inclines toward gain and honor,
toward stinginess, and toward great desire.
In dissatisfaction, anger, enmity,
hypocrisy, flattery, and so forth;
If the mind inclines toward those qualities that are the opposites of the ornaments of a śramaṇa,
one should know that this is the work of Māra.
Thus, these and other similar works of Māra are to be understood as belonging to the four Māras, as appropriate.
In that regard, even for one who is correctly engaged, the undertaking may become fruitless due to four causes; namely:
through the non-acquisition of the faculties and through instruction that is not concordant.
And due to the weakness of meditative concentration,
if the faculties have not yet fully developed,
even though the instruction is conformable [to the truth].
And if one possesses only meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
yet the faculties (*indriya*) have not been fully developed, then his undertaking becomes fruitless in this way.
The instruction is not concordant,
yet the concentration is powerful;
thus, the undertaking is fruitless.
If the faculties have fully developed,
yet the instruction is contrary [to them] and concentration is weak, then the undertaking is indeed fruitless.
If the faculties have fully developed and the instruction is concordant,
yet concentration is weak, then such an undertaking is fruitless.
If the faculties have been fully developed,
the instruction is concordant,
and concentration is indeed powerful, then [it is so]. (Śbh_Sh 348)
An undertaking becomes fruitful through these three causes; it becomes fruitless through [the opposite of] these same three causes.
It is fruitful through these very three causes. Summary verse:
The persons, their establishment, and also by way of the object;
the instruction, the training, and likewise that which is concordant with the training;
the failure in yoga, yoga itself, and wise mental attention.
That which is to be practiced, cultivation, the fruit, and the enumeration of persons.
And Māra, along with his demonic deeds, would find his undertaking fruitless.
The second stage of yoga within the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
(Śbh_Sh 349) (Śbh_Sh 350) (Śbh_Sh 351)
III. The third stage of yoga:
when the classification of persons and the classification of objects have been established in this manner,

O knower of yoga, as long as one is a beginner, a person who desires their own welfare, a practitioner who desires to attain their own goal, and is established in the fruit of cultivation, they should [approach] either a master or a teacher.
Whether it be a preceptor,
a man,
or one who occupies the position of a teacher.
One should approach having established mindfulness upon four points:
with the intention of [attaining] supernormal knowledges, and not with a mind seeking to find fault.
With reverence, not with an attitude of equal pride;
seeking what is wholesome.
Not for the sake of self-exaltation,
thinking, "I shall join myself and others with roots of merit," nor for the sake of gain and honor; and having thus approached, having made an opportunity at the proper time, [one should speak].
Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder,
having placed his right knee upon the ground,
and having sat down on a lower seat,
One should request the yoga with reverence,
saying: "I am in need of this yoga."
"Out of compassion, please instruct me in yoga.
Thus requested once more, that yogi who knows yoga [should instruct] that beginner,
that novice who desires to apply himself to the mental cultivation of yoga.
He should be encouraged with very gentle words,
gladdened,
and the benefits of abandonment should be described to him.
Excellent, excellent,
Durmukha,
you who—
When people have fallen into negligence,
being inclined toward sense objects and attached to them, he desires to apply himself to heedfulness.
Having entered the stream of the miserable states (*apāya*), he desires to emerge from the stream of the miserable states;
having entered the stream where passion, hatred, and delusion are the bonds, he desires to cast off those bonds; [having entered] the difficult path of the great forest-fire of *saṃsāra*...
Desirous of crossing over; desirous of attaining an abundance of roots of virtue when one has encountered a great famine of roots of virtue caused by the afflictions;
[desirous of escaping] when pursued by the great terror of the thieves that are the afflictions.
Desirous of attaining the security of nirvāṇa;
being afflicted by the great disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he supremely desires to attain nirvāṇa; [he crosses] the four floods (*oghā*).
When the stream is obstructed, one who desires to cross over the flood;
when one has entered a counterfeit of great vidyā, one who desires to attain the light of great gnosis— except, O Venerable One, if you apply yourself in this manner.
He will consume the alms of the kingdom while still possessed of delusion;
yet you shall be one who carries out the Teacher’s word,
a meditator who has not cast aside contemplation.
Endowed with insight,
he frequents empty dwellings and is devoted to the yoga of his own body;
he is not censured by the wise.
He has set out for the common welfare of his fellow practitioners,
for the welfare of others,
and for the welfare of the many.
Out of compassion for the world,
for the sake, welfare,
and happiness of gods and humans— with such gentle paths of speech as these.
Having inspired him with joy and having shown the benefits of abandonment,
he should be questioned regarding the four points that serve as bases for inquiry.
Has any venerable one gone for refuge exclusively to the Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha?
If you do not perceive any teacher or any person worthy of offerings outside of this mind,
then— since your holy life has been purified from the very beginning for the sake of cultivation— is your moral discipline perfectly pure?
Is your view straight? Have you heard and mastered the Dharma concerning the summary and detailed exposition of the Noble Truths, whether it be little or much? Is your mind inclined toward Nirvana?
And having gone forth with the intention of attaining nirvāṇa,
if he acknowledges "yes" when questioned,
he must thereafter be examined in four points by means of four criteria.
He is to be examined by way of his aspiration;
he is to be examined by way of his lineage, his faculties, and his conduct through conversation.
He should be sought by means of his physical movements and by means of the state of his mental transformations.
In that regard, how is he to be investigated through questioning according to his aspiration?
He should be asked thus: "In what, O Venerable One, have you made your vow? [The answer is:
"In the Śrāvaka-yāna."
In the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas and in the Mahāyāna,
wherever he has made his vow,
there he will likewise predict his own [attainment].
In this way, one should investigate [the disciple] by means of questioning and by means of their aspiration.
How should lineage, faculties, and conduct be investigated through questioning?
He should be questioned in this way: "Venerable one, what is your lineage, or your faculties, or your temperament?"
What is my lineage?
What are my faculties like— whether they are dull, middling, or sharp?
Are they sharp? Is he one whose temperament is dominated by passion, or is he one whose temperament is dominated by hatred?
Thus, for the time being, it is said that he is "one whose conduct consists of applied and sustained thought" (*vitarka-vicāra-carita*).
If he is wise,
[the teacher] should examine his lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*) according to their sequence.
And his conduct has been observed and characterized;
that very [conduct]...
Or he provides an explanation; yet, if he is still engaged [in that practice],
he has not, through this sequence, yet made it into a mental sign.
Furthermore, his conduct is observed;
when questioned, he does not provide an answer.
Subsequently, through conversation with him, three things must be investigated.

In his presence, a discourse connected with the Śrāvaka vehicle should be delivered using various modes of exposition and elegant paths of speech. While that discourse is being delivered, if he belongs to the Śrāvaka lineage, he will be exceedingly delighted by that talk.
He becomes thrilled, filled with joy,
and filled with mental well-being;
yet he does not become serene, nor does he attain resolute conviction.

Furthermore, when a discourse connected with the Mahāyāna is being spoken, one who possesses the Mahāyāna lineage becomes exceedingly joyful and elated; indeed, he becomes serene and gains resolute conviction.
But the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are not like that;
if, moreover, he is of dull faculties, he becomes exceedingly joyful.
For the purpose of observing, grasping, and penetrating both the Dharma and its meaning.
He is not of middling faculties, but rather of sharp faculties;
he quickly discerns and grasps the Dharma.
He penetrates even when profound discourse is being delivered.
Furthermore, if he is one whose temperament is dominated by passion (*rāga-carita*),
he becomes exceedingly serene and finds delight when discourse conducive to serenity is being delivered.
She enters that very meditative absorption,
and she attains the shedding of tears and a state of affectionate continuity.
He demonstrates a state of gentle mind and a state of melting mind;
this is the case if he is one whose temperament is dominated by hatred.
When a discourse on penetration connected with nirvāṇa is being delivered, he becomes terrified and falls into a state of dread regarding that which is free from worldly gain;
as it was stated for one of dull faculties, so it should be understood here as well,
provided that he is one who follows after the Dharma.
He understands the meaning and desires to hear it,
yet he does not lend his ear,
nor does he establish his mind of wisdom accordingly.
Even when directed toward it, he does not grant his compliance in that way;
moreover, if it is accompanied by discursive thought (*vicāra*), even though he is attentive,
his mind becomes distracted.
He grasps what is wrongly grasped;
he does not grasp firmly,
nor with stability, and he causes what has been grasped to be lost.
Furthermore,
how does the questioning by means of discourse come about?
It is through discourse in this manner.
One should investigate the lineage, the faculties, and the conduct.
How is this done by means of behavior?
It is by means of those signs previously mentioned.
These are called the "conducts" of those belonging to the lineage of the śrāvakas and of persons whose temperament is dominated by passion;
and by means of that conduct, one should investigate, as appropriate, their lineage, their faculties, and their temperament.
In that regard, how are the lineages (*gotra*), faculties (*indriya*), and conducts (*carita*) to be investigated by means of the knowledge of the mental states of others (*cetaḥparyāyajñāna*)?
It is as follows: that practitioner, being skilled in yoga, becomes an obtainer of the knowledge of the mental states of others;
by means of that knowledge of others' minds, he [investigates] the lineage and the faculty.
And he understands conduct as it truly is.
Having investigated these four points by means of these four reasons, he disciplines [the disciple] in five areas, namely:
in the protection and accumulation of the equipment for meditative concentration;
In seclusion,
in one-pointedness of mind,
and in the purification of hindrances.
And regarding the cultivation of mental attention (*manaskāra-bhāvanā*):

therein, the protection and accumulation of the equipment for concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra*) consists in being endowed with such restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) that one dwells in heedfulness (*apramāda*) toward a person who has been instructed by the Buddhas and authorized by the Buddhas.

Through the practice of the precepts of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), one does not let diligence slacken. In this way, because he has not departed from the restraint of ethical discipline, he does not fall away from the path of training;
furthermore, he realizes the path of training that was previously unrealized.
Just as it is with the restraint of ethical discipline, so it is with the restraint of the sense faculties, moderation in eating,
and the application to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.
Dwelling with clear comprehension,
and so on up to the "ornament of a śramaṇa"—
whatever specific classification of the Dharma, sustained by its requisite accumulations, one comes to possess.
He protects that [attainment], and furthermore,
for the sake of fulfilling the analytical distinctions and for the sake of practicing more extensively than what has been taught, he dwells having generated the desire [for it].
One who has thus become free from sloth and has initiated vigor is said to be protecting and accumulating the equipment for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In this way, he becomes detached from those factors conducive to decline.
And by cultivating those factors conducive to the remainder, one becomes a dweller in seclusion.
What is seclusion?
That which is the perfection of place and the perfection of posture;
therein, the perfection of place is as follows:
either a forest, or the foot of a tree.
Or an empty dwelling— therein, a mountain cleft,
or a mountain cave,
or a heap of straw is called an "empty dwelling."
In that regard, the forest hermitage is called "the foot of a tree";
therein [are] the open air and the cemetery.
A remote lodging is said to be the forest;
these, taken together, should be understood as the [appropriate] place.
That is to say: remote lodgings such as forests, the foot of trees, empty dwellings, mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces, cemeteries, and wilderness tracts.
Furthermore, the excellence of the location is fivefold:
here, from the very beginning, the location is beautiful,
pleasing to behold, inspiring, and endowed with groves.
Endowed with groves,
endowed with lotus ponds,
and beautiful.
It was delightful,
without uneven elevations or depressions, and free from stumps and thorny thickets.
It should not be full of many stones, pebbles, or potsherds; rather,
it is where his mind becomes serene upon seeing it,
for the sake of dwelling, for exertion, and for application.
With a joyful mind and a delighted mind,
he applies himself to abandonment; this is the first perfection of the basis.
Furthermore,
this [place] is not crowded during the day;
at night it has little noise and few sounds, and there is little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and crawling reptiles— this is the second perfection of the location.
Furthermore, it is free from the terrors and fears of lions, tigers, leopards, thieves, enemy armies, humans, and non-humans; there,
one dwells in comfort with a mind full of trust and free from suspicion.
This is the third perfection of the place (*sthāna-sampat*).
Furthermore, those conducive requisites for life, such as robes and so forth,
are obtained there with little difficulty.
That by which one does not suffer from lack of alms-food, and where there is no need for preparation— this is the fourth perfection of the place. Furthermore,
it is without leaves.
He is embraced by spiritual friends;
such wise fellow-practitioners reside there who do not leave his unclarified points unresolved.
Having thoroughly penetrated the profound words of meaning through wisdom,
they clearly elucidate them for the sake of purifying knowledge and vision;
this is the fifth perfection of the place.
In that regard, what is excellence in deportment? One passes the day by means of walking meditation,
and likewise remains seated through the first watch of the night.
During the middle watch, he lies down on his right side.
And during the final watch of the night, he rises very quickly;
he passes the time either by walking or sitting. When that bed and seat have been properly prepared, [he sits upon it].
Likewise, on a couch or a chair or a grass mat authorized by the Buddha,
Or he sits upon a spread mat, having assumed the cross-legged posture. For what reason? Because, perceiving five reasons, tranquility arises through the body being drawn together.
"This posture is conducive to the arising of pliancy. Thus, he is able to pass the time by walking or by sitting;
moreover, his body does not experience fatigue through this posture.
Likewise, this mode of conduct (*īryāpatha*) is uncommon among other non-Buddhist sectarians and proponents of rival doctrines.

Furthermore, when others see him seated in this mode of conduct, they become exceedingly devoted; moreover, this mode of conduct has been practiced and authorized by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha.
Observing these five causes, he sits down,
having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect.
In that regard, what is bodily composure?
It is the state of the body being clear, uplifted, and poised,
with a mind that is not dejected, free from hypocrisy, and upright.
Therein, by means of an upright and well-sustained body, sloth and torpor do not remain as they take possession of the mind.
By means of a guileless mind, outward distraction does not remain as it takes possession [of the mind].
[By means of] pratimukhī...
Having established mindfulness,
what therein is "face-to-face" mindfulness?
That mindfulness which one establishes, associated with appropriate mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), is called "face-to-face."
Because it stands at the head of all dark factors and because it is contrary to them;
furthermore, mindfulness that has the signs of concentration as its object and the manifestations as its object is called "confronting" (*pratimukhī*).
Because it is preeminent among all objects of focus belonging to the stages of meditative concentration, this is called the perfection of deportment (*īryāpathasaṃpat*).
What is withdrawal (*vyapakarṣa*)?
He said:
There are two kinds of withdrawal: withdrawal of the body and withdrawal of the mind.
In that regard, physical seclusion is the state of not dwelling together with householders or those who have gone forth.
In that regard, mental withdrawal (*cittavyapakarṣa*) consists in avoiding afflicted and neutral mental attention,

and instead cultivating mental attention belonging to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmika*), or mental attention consisting of the preparatory application for the equipment of concentration (*samādhi-sambhāra-prāyogika*). This is called mental withdrawal when it is wholesome and associated with the goal.
In that regard, the perfection of the place consists of this perfection of deportment,
as well as this physical seclusion and mental seclusion.
Summarizing that unity, it is called "seclusion. In that regard, what is one-pointedness?
He says:

Furthermore, that continuum of mind which repeatedly takes as its object a similar state of mindfulness, and which is endowed with a continuous flow and faultless delight, is called concentration (*samādhi*);
it is also the one-pointedness of a wholesome mind.
What, then, does one repeatedly recollect?
He said:
those dharmas which have been grasped and heard.

Having received instruction and admonition from his teachers, he takes that as his primary focus; having brought the sign of the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*) before him, he maintains a continuous flow of mindfulness directed toward that object and fixes it there.
In that regard, what is the homogeneous object?
It is any object belonging to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmika*), which is of many kinds and of various diverse types.
That object upon which the mind is most thoroughly concentrated is called a "homogeneous object" (*sabhāga-ālambana*). To whom does this belong?
It is "concordant" (*sabhāga*).
He said:
because this is a counterpart to the object that has been exhausted, it is therefore called "concordant."
Furthermore, when mindfulness proceeds in a manner that is inexhaustible, without gaps, and uninterrupted—
continually and with reverence toward that object— this is what constitutes "being endowed with continuity."

Furthermore, for one who delights in that very same object of focus, there is an undefiled dwelling, a state in which the path flows effortlessly, and mindfulness; this is being endowed with blameless delight.
Therefore, it is said: "The mental continuum is repeatedly endowed with blameless delight through a continuous flow of similar objects of focus associated with subsequent recollection."
Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): it is indeed this one-pointedness belonging to both the side of calm (*śamatha*) and the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Among these, that which exists within the ninefold mental abiding belongs to the side of calm.
Furthermore, that which pertains to the fourfold basis of wisdom belongs to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
In this regard, what is the ninefold abiding of the mind?
Here, a monk causes the mind to abide internally.
He establishes,
settles, brings near, and tames.
He calms it,
he thoroughly pacifies it,
and he makes it one-pointed.
He composes [the mind].
How does he settle it? Having withdrawn [the mind] from all external objects, he binds it internally for the sake of non-distraction.
This establishment is for the sake of removing that very distraction which was first applied.
How does one thoroughly establish it?
That mind which was first applied is weak, gross, unsettled, and not well-established.
Upon that very same object, by means of the yoga of intensification and the yoga of serenity, making it subtle with firm restraint and condensing it, he establishes it.
How does he settle it?
He settles it if he settles the mind itself.
Due to the loss of mindfulness, the mind is distracted outwardly;
he then withdraws it back again in that very same way and thus establishes it.
How does one tame it?
By means of those signs by which his mind is distracted—
namely, the signs of moving objects and tangible things, and the signs of passion, hatred, delusion, woman, and man.
In that regard, he has previously grasped the perception of the disadvantage;
making that his dominant influence, he does not allow his mind to flow toward those signs.
In this way, he subdues it.
How does one pacify?
By means of those discursive thoughts, such as the thought of sensual desire,
and by means of those secondary afflictions.
The mind becomes agitated by the hindrance of sensual desire and the others;
in that regard, he has already previously grasped the perception of its disadvantages.
Making that [state] the dominant factor for that mind, he does not allow it any further movement toward those thoughts and secondary afflictions; in this way, he pacifies it.
How does one pacify?
Through the loss of mindfulness, when both of those manifest, one does not tolerate the discursive thoughts and secondary afflictions that arise again and again.
He abandons;
in this way he pacifies. How does he unify?
With application of effort,
he establishes a continuous, gapless, and uninterrupted flow of concentration and thus makes it one-pointed.
How does one attain composure? Through the sequence of repeated practice, the sequence of cultivation, and the sequence of frequent application, it proceeds effortlessly and proceeds spontaneously.
One attains the path by which there is no further volitional effort.
Without effort, a continuous flow of his mind’s concentration proceeds without distraction; in this way, he attains meditative absorption.
In that regard, the ninefold stability of the mind is accomplished by means of six kinds of powers,
namely: by the power of hearing and reflection,
and by the power of mindfulness.
By the power of vigor and by the power of familiarity.
In that regard, first, by the power of hearing and reflection:

Taking as the dominant influence that which has been heard and that which has been reflected upon, one establishes the mind from the very beginning upon the object of focus, and remains fixed right there.
By means of continuous application, he establishes [the mind];
there, following after the mind that has been bound, he settles it and stabilizes it through the power of mindfulness.
Then, by the power of clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), he tames and pacifies [the mind] by not allowing it to flow toward signs, discursive thoughts, or secondary afflictions,
through the power of vigor (*vīrya*).
He does not tolerate the manifestation of both of these;
he makes [the mind] one-pointed and,
through the power of cultivation, brings it to meditative concentration.
In that regard, among the nine modes of mental abiding, four types of mental attention (*manaskāra*) are to be understood:
forceful application, interrupted application, and uninterrupted application.
And it is effortless in its operation.
For one who is placing [the mind] and thoroughly placing it therein, there is mental attention that operates with effort.
of one who stabilizes, establishes, and tames [the mind],
For one who is pacifying and thoroughly pacifying, there is mental attention that operates with interruptions.

For one who is making [the mind] one-pointed, there is the mental application that suppresses and eliminates [distractions]; for one who is concentrating [the mind], there is [the mental application of] stabilization.
Mental attention becomes one that flows without effort.
Thus, these mental attentions pertain to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*) within the stability of the mind.
Furthermore, one who has thus attained internal tranquidity of mind applies himself to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
For him, these very four modes of mental attention belong to the side of insight.
There are four kinds of insight. What are they?
The bhikṣu investigates phenomena, thoroughly investigates them, and reflects upon them.
He engages in thorough investigation;
that is to say, by relying on internal mental tranquility.
And how does he investigate?
Either the object for purifying conduct,
or the object for skillfulness, or the object for purifying afflictions.
He investigates by way of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and discerns thoroughly by way of the manner of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
With a conceptual mental attention accompanied by wisdom,
while indeed taking it as a sign, he reflects thoroughly,
investigates, and enters into higher deliberation.
This very insight (vipaśyanā) should be understood as having three doors and taking the sixfold classification of objects as its focal point.
What are the three doors?
Vipaśyanā that follows after mere signs;
vipaśyanā that follows after investigation, and that which has already investigated.
It is that which follows upon investigation;
therein, it follows upon mere signs by means of which— *Śrāvakabhūmi*, Śikṣāsamuccaya-hṛdaya, p. 368.
Having heard and grasped the Dharma,
he attends to it with a mental attention belonging to the stage of non-concentration;
he does not reflect upon it.
He does not weigh it; he does not examine it;
this much constitutes merely following after signs.
But when one further reflects, deliberates,
weighs, and examines,
then it becomes characterized by investigative pursuit.
Furthermore, when one has determined and examined [the object], and then reflects upon it exactly as it was established,
at that time this insight (*vipaśyanā*) characterized by three doors becomes one that follows reflection.
What are the six objects consisting of the distinctions of things?
While searching,
he searches for six things:
the meaning, the entity, and so forth.
The characteristic, the position, and the time.
And while seeking the reasoning, by investigating these very [points], he examines them.
How does he seek the meaning?
He investigates the meaning in this way: "This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement.
How does he investigate the entity?
There are two kinds of entities: internal and external.
In this way, one investigates the entity.
How does one investigate characteristics?
There are two kinds:
the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) and the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
In this way, he investigates the characteristics.
How does he investigate the categories?
The side is twofold: the dark side and the bright side. One should regard the dark side in terms of its faults and its disadvantages.
Furthermore, one investigates the bright fortnight in terms of its qualities and benefits.
How does one investigate the time?
There are three times.
Past, future, and present.
Thus it was in the past; thus it will be in the future.
In the future time.
In this way, he investigates time as follows: "This is so even now, in the present time.
How does he investigate the reasoning?
There are four principles of reasoning:
the principle of dependence,
the principle of cause and effect, [the principle of valid proof, and the principle of natural law].
The reasoning of logical proof through evidence and the reasoning of the nature of phenomena.
Therein, by means of the reasoning of dependence, one [understands] the conventional from the perspective of the conventional, the ultimate from the perspective of the ultimate,
and the cause from the perspective of the cause.
He investigates.
By means of the reasoning of causal efficiency (*kāryakāraṇayukti*), he investigates the activity of phenomena: "This is a phenomenon..."
"This is the activity;
this is the activity of this [thing]"— thus,
by means of the reasoning that establishes through proof, one investigates the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
There are authoritative scripture, inference, and direct perception.
Regarding this, is there a self? Is it perceived through direct perception that it exists, or that it does not exist? Or is it not so perceived?
Is it employed by means of inference or not?

In that regard, through the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*), one resolves upon the suchness of phenomena— their established nature, their inconceivable nature, and their abiding nature— and does not conceptualize them.
He does not conceptualize in this way, but investigates the reasoning;
these are the objects of focus consisting of the distinctions among the six things.
In brief, insight has three aspects;
by means of these, all insight is subsumed.
Furthermore, for what reason are the six divisions established? It is said:
with reference to three kinds of realization, the meaning of what was spoken [is explained].
[These are] the thorough understanding of the object, the thorough understanding of the limit of the object,
and the thorough understanding of reality as it is.
Among these, through the search for the meaning, there is the thorough understanding of the meaning of what was spoken.
Through the search for things and the search for specific characteristics, there is the realization of the ultimate limit of the search for things;
therein, through the search for general characteristics, [there is the realization of the ultimate limit of the search for characteristics].
Through the investigation of the positions and the investigation of the timing and reasoning, there is an awakening to reality as it is;
and this much is to be known by the practitioner of yoga.
Namely: the meaning of what has been spoken,
the extent of existence (yāvadbhāvikatā) of the object to be known,
and its mode of existence (yathāvadbhāvikatā).
In that regard, the yogi engaged in the foul [meditation] investigates six objects. It is said:

Having taken as his dominant influence the Dharma concerning the foul that has been heard and mastered, he becomes one who experiences the meaning through a mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmika*), [perceiving]:
"By means of the foul, this is foul; this is its likeness;
this is repulsive; this is a bad odor; this is a raw stench."
Through these and similar modes, there arises for him an experiential realization of the meaning of that very dharma concerning the foul (*aśubha*) which he has previously heard.
In this way, he investigates the meaning by way of its foulness.
How does he investigate the object (*vastu*)?
Thus, experiencing the meaning in this way, he perceives that impurity established in two states, both internally and externally.
How does he search for its specific characteristic? First, regarding the internal, he resolves upon the impurity pertaining to the interior of the body as the "impurity of the repulsive."
In this body there are head-hairs and body-hairs, and so on in detail, up to the brain and the urine.
Furthermore, one resolves upon that manifold impurity within the body as being comprised of two elements:
the earth element and [the water element].
And by means of the water element: therein, starting from the head-hairs and body-hairs,
up to the liver and excrement, one resolves upon the earth element.
Based on the sensation of tears, up to urine, one resolves upon the water element;
or alternatively, one resolves upon external impurity as it exists externally, through such aspects as the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth.
In that regard, one resolves upon the livid corpse.
Whatever dead corpse has been seen by him himself,
or heard of before him, or imagined, whether it be that of a woman, or—
Whether it be of a person, or a friend,
or an enemy.
Or toward one who is indifferent;
or whether [the object] is inferior, middling, or sublime.
Whether of one who is young, or middle-aged, or old.

Therein, having grasped the sign, one resolves upon a corpse dead for one day, with blood protruding and having reached the state of pus, as being "discolored" (*vinīlaka*). One resolves upon a corpse dead for two days, having reached the state of pus.
One resolves that it is "not yet infested with worms and not yet putrefied.
One resolves that it is "dead for seven days, infested with worms, bloated, and emitting a foul odor," and "swollen.
One resolves that it is "being eaten by crows, kuralas, vultures, dogs, and jackals," and "torn apart."

Or again, one resolves upon a corpse that has been devoured by wild animals, from which the skin, flesh, and blood have disappeared, and which is bound together only by sinews, appearing as a bloody mass; likewise,
when the limbs and members are scattered and disarticulated in every direction, whether with flesh remaining or devoid of flesh.
When only a small amount of flesh remains,
one resolves upon it as "the scattered" (vikṣiptaka).
Or else, the hand bones in one place, the foot bones in another, the knee bones, the thigh bones, the arm bones, and the forearm bones in yet another.
Having observed the backbone,
the jaw-bone, the row of teeth in the middle,
and the skull, one should apply focused resolve toward the other bones.
Furthermore, when he brings to mind a connected skeleton that is unscattered and not yet decayed,
he grasps only the general sign (nimitta),
but does not grasp the specific details (vyañjana) of its various limbs and members.
In this way, one resolves upon the skeleton;
when, however, one perceives the secondary characteristics, then one resolves upon the skeleton of bones.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of skeletons: the skeleton of the body and the skeleton of the individual limbs.
Therein, the skeleton of the body begins from the pelvic basin.
As far as the spinal column,
where the skull is established,
the vertebrae are interconnected, and the bones of the arms are likewise joined.
In that regard, there is the skeleton of the body.
Therein, the skeleton of the body begins from the pelvic basin and extends up to the spinal column where the skull is situated.
The arm bones are connected by the joints of the individual members,
as are the thigh and shank bones;
therein lies the skeletal framework of the body.
That is called a "skeleton" (*śaṃkalikā*). Furthermore, that which consists of individual skeletal parts is called a "bone skeleton" (*asthi-śaṃkalikā*).
Moreover, there are two ways of grasping the sign (*nimitta-grāha*) of a skeleton: one made by a painter, or one made from stone, wood, or clay.
He attends to the mental image of either a real skeleton or an unreal skeleton.
At that time, one resolves upon the skeleton itself, not the chain of bones;
but when one again brings to mind the sign of the complete skeleton,
then one resolves upon the chain of bones itself.
[He contemplates] the skeleton.
When he again brings to mind the sign of the actual skeleton, then he resolves upon the skeleton.
Indeed, this threefold transformation of external appearance, which belongs to derived matter (upādāyarūpa),
is transformation by its own inherent nature (svarasavipariṇāma).
It is produced by another and belongs to both categories; therein,
it begins from the livid corpse up to the bloated corpse.
The transformation of natural decay (*svarasavipariṇāma*).
In this regard, from the "gnawed" stage up to the "scattered" stage, it is a transformation produced by external agents (*parakṛta*).
In that context, [there is] the "skeleton" (*asthika*)...
Or a skeleton— this is the transformation common to both sides.
One who understands this as it truly is thus investigates the specific characteristic of external impurity according to its aspects.
How does one investigate the general characteristic of foulness?
