It is by way of how the internal and external body is untransformed by the appearance and fear of foulness, up to the point where the external body is foul externally.
When the appearance of color has undergone transformation due to internal impurity, one resolves upon its similarity in nature and equality in nature with [one's own] appearance of color, thinking:
"This beautiful appearance of mine is also subject to such a nature.
Furthermore, whatever sentient beings are endowed with this beautiful appearance of color, their [appearance] is also subject to such a nature—just like this external [appearance].
In this way, he investigates the general characteristic.
How does he investigate the category?
It occurs to him as follows:

When he says: "By means of this [perception of] impurity, not understanding that impurity as it truly is—whether internally or externally—I give rise to passion for a pure appearance; this is indeed a perversion comprised within the dark side.
It is a phenomenon of escape [from which one has not escaped], accompanied by suffering, accompanied by affliction, accompanied by calamity, and accompanied by feverish distress."
On account of this,
there arise in the future birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; yet,
regarding this beautiful appearance and complexion, [there is no such thing].
The contemplation of things as they truly are, which conforms to the nature of impure phenomena, belongs to the side of purity;
this phenomenon is without suffering and without affliction.
To whatever extent, from this cause, afflictions cease;
therein,
this dark side must not be tolerated.
That which is to be abandoned must be purified;
furthermore, that which belongs to the white side (the wholesome), if unarisen, must be brought into being,
and once arisen, its stability, increase, and expansion must be effected.
In this way, he investigates the side.
How does he investigate the time?
It occurs to him as follows:
That internal appearance of impurity is based upon the present time; furthermore, this external appearance of impurity is also based upon the present time alone,
whereas that which is based upon the past time—
It was beautiful. Thus, having taken the past time as a basis, it was beautiful just as it is for me now; and having taken the present time as a basis, it is likewise.
In this sequence, starting from the present time, this unattractiveness has come to be; thus,
although this appearance of mine is unattractive with respect to the present time,
one might think that it will not be unattractive in the future time.
This is not possible;
just as this [body] is external, so it is with respect to the present time.
For indeed, in the past, future, and present times, this body of mine was, will be, and is of such a nature.
Being thus constituted and not transcending this very nature of phenomena (dharmatā), he investigates time in this manner.
How does he investigate reasoning?
It occurs to him:
"There is no such thing as a self or a sentient being, whether internal or external."
Whatever is perceived externally, whether it be beautiful or ugly, is moreover merely form, merely a mass of sores, wherein this notion, designation, conceptualization, and conventional usage occurs—
namely, "beautiful" or "ugly. Furthermore—
When these— vitality, warmth, and consciousness— abandon the body,
it then lies cast away, insentient like a piece of wood.
Of this very person who has died and passed away, these successive stages of transformation are perceived, namely:
the livid state, and so on, up to the skeleton; "this body of mine, too, was pierced by former karma and afflictions."
Born from the impurities of mother and father, and nourished by boiled rice and gruel;
for such is the cause.
By what cause this temporary, beautiful appearance of color is perceived,
whereas the internal body is always, at all times, both internally and externally, impure— thus it is from the perspective of the causes of both conventional and ultimate truth.
He investigates the principle of dependence;
it occurs to him: "This is the nature of foulness;
when practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in this way, it leads to the abandonment of sensual desire."
And sensual desire must be abandoned;
thus he investigates by means of the principle of causal efficiency.
It occurs to him: "For it has been said by the Blessed One:"
"The cultivation, development, and frequent practice of the foul leads to the abandonment of sensual desire"—this, first of all, is my authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
Furthermore, my own direct knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*) proceeds within me:
"In whatever way I cultivate the foulness..."
I attend to it in such a way that the obsession of sensual desire which has not yet arisen does not arise,
and that which has already arisen passes away.
There is also this conformable method:
how is it that now, for one who is attending to a factor that is an adverse element,
a defilement arises by taking that very adverse element as its object?
Thus he investigates by means of the reasoning that establishes through proof.
It occurs to him:
"This very nature of phenomena is indeed an established reality; it is an inconceivable nature of phenomena."
Since the cultivation of the foul is the antidote for the abandonment of sensual desire,
it should be contemplated, but not conceptualized.
It is to be resolved upon.
In this way, one investigates foulness through the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*).
This, first of all, is the insight (*vipaśyanā*) of one engaged in the practice of foulness, which has three gateways and takes as its object the distinctions of the six things.
How does one engaged in loving-kindness (*maitrī*) investigate the six objects while practicing insight (*vipaśyanā*)?

Having made the Dharma governed by loving-kindness the dominant influence, for one who has entered into the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for welfare and happiness, loving-kindness is characterized by the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) to bring about happiness toward all beings; it is for the purpose of fully experiencing this meaning that one investigates.
Having thus experienced the meaning, he further investigates: "This is the side of friends, this is the side of enemies, and this is the side of neutrals.
He resolves that all these sides are external objects because they belong to the mental continuums of others.
Or, he regards the side of friends as internal and the sides of enemies and neutrals as external; in this way, he seeks loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward these objects.
Furthermore, he discerns:
"May these three groups, who are neither suffering nor happy and who desire happiness, become happy."
In this context, a friend is characterized by assistance;
an enemy is characterized by harm;
and the neutral party is characterized by being distinct from both of those.
Furthermore, regarding those classes of beings who are neither suffering nor happy and who desire happiness, three kinds of desire for happiness are observed:
some desire the happiness of sensual pleasure; some desire that which belongs to the realm of form and is accompanied by rapture; and some desire that which is free from rapture.
In that regard, for those who are afflicted by sensual pleasure,
that which is characterized by the opposite of both [sensual pleasure and its lack] is the enemy;
therefore, let those who enjoy sensual pleasure do so blamelessly.
In this way, it should be understood through both bliss accompanied by joy and bliss devoid of joy.
Thus he investigates loving-kindness according to its specific characteristics;
furthermore, he analyzes it.
That which is the side of friends, that which is the side of enemies, and that which is the side of neutrals.
"But I must practice equanimity of mind"—
this is even-mindedness.
And for what reason?
In regard to those who belong to the side of friends, it is not difficult for me to provide them with happiness; and so too it is for those who belong to the side of neutral persons.
Even among those,
it is not very difficult for me [to practice] toward this side of enemies.
(Therein lies this side of enemies:
therein it is exceedingly difficult;
therein, first of all, I must provide the means for their happiness.
How much more so, then,
toward those on the side of friends or those on the side of neutrals?
For what reason?
In this, there is no one at all who reviles or is reviled,
nor anyone who provokes anger or is provoked to anger.
He mocks, or is mocked;
he strikes, or is struck.
Elsewhere, these syllables merely resound;

this is nothing more than sound, merely a bean-sized trifle. And likewise, this body of mine has arisen as something material, gross, composed of the four great elements, wherein, while I abide, such sensations as these impinge upon me—namely, the contact of sounds.
This body of mine is subject to contact with hands, clods of earth, sticks, or weapons;
it is impermanent. Even those contacts which are harmful are themselves impermanent. Furthermore:

All sentient beings indeed possess the nature of birth, aging, sickness, and death; they are suffering by their very nature. Therefore, it would be unbecoming of me if, toward these beings who are already suffering by nature, I were to further inflict only more suffering upon them rather than providing happiness—that would be like an enemy.
One should perform for a friend that which these beings perform for themselves by themselves.
Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One:
"I do not perceive anyone who is so easily found."
Through the passage of a long time, one has been mother, or father,
or brother,
or sister.
Whether it be a teacher, a preceptor,
or a guru,
"Or he may be in the position of a teacher.
Thus, by this method as well, it is simply the side of the enemy that is "my side of the enemy";
and herein, there is no real establishment of anything whatsoever.
The nature of a friend is not fixed; even a friend may become an enemy after some time, and even an enemy may become a friend.
Even an enemy becomes a friend;
therefore, there is no impartiality of mind toward all sentient beings.
One should cultivate the view of equality,
as well as an equal intention for their welfare and an equal resolute intention for their happiness.
"The bringing about of happiness" and "resolute conviction regarding the bringing about of happiness"—
in this way, one investigates loving-kindness by means of its general characteristic.
He further investigates:
"That malice toward beings who have committed evil which I felt—that death is their natural law," and so on in detail as before;
or again, this present absence of malice...
"This is the Dharma in battle," and so forth in detail as before; or again, this present absence of ill-will is likewise [the result] of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
He investigates the dark, white, and bright fortnights;
he further discerns that those beings who, based on the past time, desired happiness have already passed away.
Furthermore, what happiness shall we bestow upon them? Moreover, as for those sentient beings who exist in the present, by means of the present time,
may they be happy at all times, extending even unto the future path.
Thus he investigates the time for loving-kindness;
he further discerns it as follows:
There is no such thing as a self or a sentient being who might desire happiness,
nor is there anyone to whom happiness is bestowed.

Moreover, he investigates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) through the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), thinking: "This is merely the aggregates (*skandha-mātra*); this is merely conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-mātra*); herein lies this designation (*saṃjñā*), this communication (*saṃjñapti*), and this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, those formations have karma and afflictions as their cause.

He investigates loving-kindness through the reasoning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*), thinking: "Indeed, this is the established nature of phenomena (*prasiddha-dharmatā*), this is the inconceivable nature of phenomena (*acintya-dharmatā*), that the cultivation of loving-kindness leads to the abandonment of ill-will (*vyāpāda*)."
In this regard, how does one engaged in insight cultivation, taking conditionality and dependent origination as their object, investigate the meaning?

Having formed a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the teachings (*dharma*) that have those [conditions] as their dominant influence, they investigate: "With the arising of this or that phenomenon (*dharma*), this or that phenomenon arises."
Through the cessation of this or that phenomenon, those respective phenomena cease;
herein there is no underlying entity whatsoever, no Lord, no agent, and no creator.

One who experiences the meaning in this way— namely, that [the Tathāgata] is the creator of phenomena, neither their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) nor another person (*puruṣāntara*), and the one who sets phenomena in motion— seeks the meaning.
Again and again, he discerns the twelve factors of existence;
he gains conviction regarding both the internal and the external.
In this way, one searches for the object;
furthermore, one investigates it:
that which is ignorance (avidyā).
"Non-knowledge regarding the past," and so forth, in detail, as in the *Pratītyasamutpādavibhaṅga*, he thus investigates its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore...
He discerns thus:

"All these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are dependently originated; because they come into being after not having been, and because they pass away after having been, they are impermanent in their prior and subsequent states, and are subject to the nature of birth, aging, sickness, and death."
They are suffering because of the lack of autonomy; they are empty and non-self because no internal person is to be found.
And he investigates their general characteristic; furthermore, he discerns it as follows:
it is the thorough delusion regarding these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, as they truly are.
Death is this phenomenon belonging to the dark side;
non-delusion,
on the other hand, belongs to the bright side— thus it is explained in detail.
He thoroughly investigates this side;
he further discerns:
"Karma exists; its maturation exists."
But no agent is perceived—
one who might be either a doer or an experiencer— other than as a conventional designation for phenomena;
[this occurs] precisely within those very conditions of ignorance.

Regarding the formative forces up to aging and death conditioned by birth, there is a designation, a conceptual construction, and a conventional usage such as "an agent," "an experiencer," "one with such a name," "of such a birth," or "of such a lineage."
Thus was his food, thus did he experience pleasure and pain, and thus was his lifespan long and his duration of stay extended.
"Thus is the limit of life. Furthermore, this fruit is twofold; likewise, the cause is twofold: the fruit of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) and [the fruit of experience].
And there is the fruit of the enjoyment of objects.
Furthermore, there is the projecting cause and the actualizing cause.
Among these, the fruit of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is that which consists of the six sense bases born of maturation (*vipākaja*); the fruit of the enjoyment of objects is that which—
Feeling arises from the six types of contact and is governed by desirable and undesirable karma.

In this regard, the projecting cause consists of the meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations (*saṃskāra*) preceded by delusion or non-delusion with respect to the two kinds of fruit,
as well as that which is grasped by those formations.
It is the seed for the manifestation of the sprout of consciousness in a future existence;

it is the seed of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) pertaining to rebirth, the seed of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and the seeds of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), which serve to produce— within the future—
the consciousness, name-and-form, six sense bases, contact, and feeling that are designated as "birth."
The prior grasping of the seed in its proper sequence is this projecting cause.
Furthermore, when one experiences feeling born from contact with ignorance, through craving directed toward that object, one generates craving for rebirth;
one grasps at clinging, which belongs to the side of craving and the side of delusion.
By whose power and by whose presence that karma becomes capable of yielding its maturation—this is the cause of actualization (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*).

Having made these two kinds of causes the predominant factor (*adhipati*), there occurs the origination (*samudaya*) of this entire mass of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*), which consists of three kinds of suffering.
In this way, he investigates the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
This conditionality is dependent origination.
When practiced and cultivated, it leads to the abandonment of delusion.
This is both authoritative scripture and a method that is personally realized as well as inferential.
"This is also the established nature of phenomena for you"—
in this way, he investigates the reasoning of cause and effect, the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of the nature of phenomena.
In that regard, how does one who is engaged in insight (vipaśyanā) having the analysis of the elements as its object investigate the meaning?
[One investigates] the meaning of lineage (gotra), the meaning of element (dhātu), and the meaning of designation (saṃjñā).
The meaning of the cause;
the meaning of the intrinsic nature—thus perceiving the meaning, he investigates the meaning.
[He does not [investigate] the six elements, earth and so forth.]
Resolving upon both the internal and external objects, he investigates them:
earth has the characteristic of solidity;
up to wind, which has the characteristic of motion; and consciousness, which has the characteristic of discernment.
He investigates its specific characteristic thus: "The space element has the characteristic of being hollow, is formless, and is characterized by non-manifestation.
All these elements are exactly equal in their impermanence.

Thus he investigates the general characteristic as far as "selflessness. In this way, he investigates the side [of phenomena]: that for one who perceives a whole and does not know the diversity of the elements, there is pride and conceit regarding this body composed of diverse elements—this is the nature of death—and that which belongs to the dark side; whereas by the opposite, it belongs to the bright side. Thus he investigates the side.
In the past, future, and present time periods, the descent of the embryo into the mother’s womb occurs in dependence upon the six elements;
thus one investigates the time.
For example, it is like [the arising of fire] in dependence upon grass.
Just as wood or space, when enclosed, comes to be designated as a "house," even though it is not a house [in itself], so too, by depending upon the six elements,
and depending upon bone and sinew, and skin and flesh...
When blood is enclosed within space, there arises the designation, the conceptual construction, and the conventional usage:
"body," "body.
Furthermore, one investigates the reasoning based on dependence, [realizing] that past karma and afflictions, as well as their own seeds, are the causes of these.
The analysis of the elements, when practiced and cultivated,
leads to the abandonment of lethargy.

This is also the authoritative scripture; this method is both based on personal realization and inference. Thus, one investigates the reasoning of cause and effect, the reasoning of logical proof, and the reasoning of the nature of phenomena—namely, the well-known nature of phenomena and the inconceivable nature of phenomena.
How does one seek the meaning for the purpose of application to the collection of objects for mindfulness of breathing?
One seeks it thus: "Mindfulness of breathing is the non-forgetfulness and the non-discursiveness of the mind when it is bound to the object of inhalation and exhalation. Thus one seeks it.
One searches for the object in this way: "Inhalation and exhalation are perceived internally; because they are dependent upon the body, they are included within the external sense-sphere.
There are two types of inhalation: that which is the air entering [the body], and...
That which is inhalation and that which goes out is exhalation;
these are long inhalations and exhalations.
"These are short; I experience these with my entire body.
Thus he investigates their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
When inhalation has ceased, exhalation arises.
When inhalation (or exhalation) has ceased, there is inhalation;
and [there is] that which is connected to the increase of inhalation and exhalation.

The body consists of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and is accompanied by consciousness; thus, inhalation and exhalation are impermanent and constitute a great flux (*mahāśravaṇa*). In this way, he investigates their general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). For one whose mindfulness is not established regarding inhalation and exhalation, there arises a mental agitation produced by discursive thought (*vitarka*), which is of the nature of death.
"This dharma belongs to the dark side;
by the opposite, it belongs to the bright side"—
in this way, he searches for the sides in detail.

He investigates time in this way: "In the past, future, and present times, the body is dependent upon inhalation and exhalation, and inhalation and exhalation are dependent upon the body and the mind;
there is no one else whatsoever who inhales or exhales, nor do these inhalations and exhalations belong to anyone other than this [body and mind]."
Rather, regarding conditioned phenomena that have arisen from causes and are dependently originated,
he investigates the principle of dependence in this way: "This is a designation, a conceptual construct, and a conventional usage."
Mindfulness of breathing, when practiced and cultivated, leads to the cutting off of discursive thoughts;
this is both the authoritative scripture and a method that follows from personal realization.
He investigates the principle of cause and effect, the principle of logical proof, and the principle of the nature of phenomena, thinking, "The nature of phenomena is established and inconceivable.
Having thus investigated the six objects by means of the focal object that purifies conduct,
he repeatedly calms the mind within.

Again and again, he investigates this very same object as it was previously sought after, by means of the modes of insight (*vipaśyanā*). For him, based upon calm abiding (*śamatha*), insight becomes purified.
Relying upon insight, calm abiding attains vastness (extensiveness),
as does insight regarding skillful objects and the purification of afflictions.
I shall explain the sixfold nature of the task later in its proper place.
In that regard, there is a ninefold application comprised of the wholesome,
which is the opposite of that [unwholesome] state.
Furthermore, the ninefold [practice] comprised within the dark side (kṛṣṇapakṣa) should be understood by the yogin as follows:
application that is not conformable,
and application that has been practiced excessively.
Unmistaken application,
unremitting application,
and timely application.
The application of observation,
the application of non-contentment,
and the application of non-neglect.

And there is right application. By means of these nine types [of factors] comprised within the white side, the mind is very quickly concentrated and proceeds toward the excellence of meditative absorption.
To whatever extent there is ground for him to travel and reach, he arrives there very quickly and without delay; yet,
due to the nine types of application comprised within the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), his mind is not concentrated with great speed,
nor does it proceed toward a distinction in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, regarding however much ground he has yet to traverse and reach,
he is slow in proceeding there;
what, then, is "appropriate application"?
If he is one whose temperament is dominated by passion, he fixes his mind on the foul; if his temperament is dominated by hatred, on loving-kindness;
and so on, up to one whose temperament is dominated by discursive thought, who fixes it on mindfulness of breathing.
Furthermore, one whose conduct is characterized by equal proportions and who possesses little passion applies himself to whichever object he finds pleasant to ascend;
this is "appropriate application."
What is the state of practiced application (*abhyasta-prayogatā*)?
It is that by which practice has been performed, even if it be only slight; one does not remain entirely and in every respect a mere beginner.
For thus, even when a beginner is engaged with a suitable object of focus, hindrances and the coarseness of body and mind do not repeatedly manifest,
by which [he is not hindered].
The mind becomes concentrated;
this is the state of practiced application.
In that regard, what is the state of non-lax application?
He practices with constancy and he practices with reverence;
yet, if he should emerge from that state again, [he does so].

Whether for the sake of meditative concentration, for the sake of alms-food, for the sake of honoring and attending to a teacher, for the purpose of attending to the sick, for the performance of respectful service,
or for any other such purpose— for whatever reason one acts, with a mind inclined toward that, directed toward that, and focused upon that.
And he performs it all; and having performed it very swiftly, having brought it to completion,
He applies himself once again;
having restrained himself for the sake of solitary retreat, if he should come together with an assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, kṣatriyas, or brāhmaṇas,
he does not spend much time in their company.
He speaks in moderation; he does not initiate a continuous stream of discourse,
nor does he withdraw elsewhere.
And furthermore, he exerts such vigor as this:
"May I attain today itself that which is to be attained.
For what reason?
There are many conditions for my death: either my wind-humor (vāta) might become disturbed,
or my bile-humor (pitta), or my phlegm-humor (śleṣman).
Or my food might be indigestible,
whereby choleraic cramps would remain in my body; or a snake might bite me.
Whether it be a scorpion or a centipede,
or even from a human— fearing these things, he does not remain in those places at all times, and he dwells with vigilance; furthermore, he dwells thus with vigilance.
"Alas, would that I might live for seven days, or six, five, four, three, two, or one day; for a watch, or half a watch, or even a muhūrta, or half a muhūrta!
Oh, would that I might live just long enough to consume this single morsel of food!"
"As long as I am breathing in,
may I breathe out;
and for as long as I live, may I apply myself with yoga and mental attention to the teaching of the Teacher."
"If by this much I have performed my many duties— that is, within the teaching of the Teacher"— this is "unrelaxed application.
In that regard, what is "non-erroneous application"?
From time to time, he cultivates the sign of tranquility, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity;
and he understands tranquility as well as the sign of tranquility.
The time for calm abiding; and insight, the sign of insight, the time for insight;
as well as exertion and the sign of exertion.
The time for exertion,
equanimity, the sign of equanimity, and the time for equanimity.
In this context, calm abiding (*śamatha*) is the ninefold mental abiding.
And that mind there becomes signless, non-conceptual, calm, and thoroughly pacified.
It is established in tranquility and is exclusive;
therefore, it is called "tranquility."
In that regard, the sign of calm abiding (*śamatha-nimitta*) is twofold: the sign of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*) and the sign of the cause (*nidāna-nimitta*).
The sign of the object is a mental image (*pratibimba*) that is similar in nature to the thing to be known (*jñeya-vastu*).
The objective support by which that mind is calmed—
so that when the mind has been cultivated by calm abiding (*śamatha*), there may subsequently be the complete purification of calm abiding—
is the application of insight (*vipaśyanā*); this is the causal basis (*nidāna*), not the sign (*nimitta*).
What is the time for calm abiding (*śamatha*)? It is said: when the mind is agitated or when one suspects it will become so, that is the time for the cultivation of calm abiding.
Likewise, when the mind has been cultivated through insight (*vipaśyanā*) but is impaired by distractions regarding what must be done, it is the time for the cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*).
In that regard, insight is fourfold in aspect, threefold in gate, and consists of the investigation of objects distinguished by six categories.

In that regard, the sign of insight (*vipaśyanā-nimitta*) is twofold: the sign of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*) and the sign of the cause (*nidāna-nimitta*). Therein, the sign of the object as the sign of insight is the reflected image (*pratibimba*) belonging to the side of calm (*śamatha*), which is concordant with the object of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu-sabhāga*); it is the object by means of which one investigates with wisdom (*prajñā*). Therein, the sign of the cause is the application of the mind to the image of calm (*śamatha-bimba*) for the sake of further purification of insight once the mind has been cultivated by insight.

In that regard, the time for insight (*vipaśyanā*) is when the mind has been thoroughly cultivated by tranquility (*śamatha*); from the very beginning, it is the time for the cultivation of insight in order to realize the objects of knowledge as they truly are.
In this context, what is exertion (*pragraha*)?
It is [the application of the mind] by means of taking up any one of the various inspiring objects of focus (*ālambana*).
It consists of gladdening the mind, demonstrating, and instigating.

In that regard, the sign of exertion (*pragrahanimitta*) is that by means of which one exerts the mind through a pleasing object and sign; it is the time for exertion when there is the application of vigor and what is conducive thereto. When the mind is sunken or when one suspects it is becoming sunken, it is the time for the cultivation of exertion.
In this context, what is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
It is the evenness of mind belonging to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), which, when the mind is undefiled with respect to its object,
flows naturally and smoothly.
The pliancy of a pliant mind,
which is the effortless functioning consisting in the application of the mind;
therein, the sign of equanimity [is as follows].

The object by which one maintains equanimity toward the mind, and the state of not counteracting the intensity of energy toward that very same object— this is the time for equanimity, when both the sides of calm abiding and insight are balanced.
When the mind is free from agitation, it is the time for the cultivation of equanimity;
this is application according to the proper time.
In that regard, what is equanimity characterized by (or marked by) application? It is those very signs which have been well-grasped and well-observed,
because of their being well-grasped.
When he so desires,

he emerges from that state, relinquishing the reflected image of the meditative object by means of mental attention directed toward the extraordinary focal objects belonging to the stage of meditative equipoise.
This is the application of discernment.
In that regard, what is the application of non-contentment?
One is not content with wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.
And being non-contentious,
desiring a more excellent state through his laughter, he dwells for the most part in a state that is superior,
not with a mere trifling [attainment].
One falls into despondency midway,
even when there is only a small portion remaining of what must be further accomplished.
This is the application of non-contentment. In that regard, what is the application of non-abandonment? It is not breaking the undertaking of the precepts of training.
He does not cause [the precepts] to be broken;
nor, upon seeing a woman of beautiful complexion and alluring appearance, does he seize upon her general marks or her secondary characteristics;
and he is moderate in eating.
One who is devoted to wakefulness, having few concerns, few duties, and few distractions,
is one who remembers what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago, and is one who causes others to remember;
such qualities as these are called "unflagging application."
These factors are conducive to one-pointedness of mind;
they are not remote, nor do they lead to mental distraction or outward dispersion.
It is not for the sake of internal mental unworkability;
this is called "unswerving application.
In that regard, what is "correct application"?

Right application is said to consist in the cultivation of the object through repeated resolute conviction. And this occurs when one is engaged in the meditation on the foul and attends to the foul with its various aspects by means of insight that follows after mere signs.

Therefore, the mental attention directed toward that object should be cultivated repeatedly and brought into presence again and again. Furthermore, cultivation is fivefold, beginning with the inward withdrawal of the mind.
Through non-recollection and non-mental attention; through mental attention directed toward something other than that; and through mental attention directed toward the remedy.

And it is through the mental attention to the signless realm. In that regard, by means of the ninefold abiding of the mind preceded by insight (*vipaśyanā*), there is the internal withdrawal of the mind from the outset through the complete elimination of all signs.
For one who binds [the mind] to prevent distraction, by means of non-recollection and non-mental-attention;

and for one who, from an object belonging to the stage of meditative equipoise, attends to another object belonging to the same stage of meditative equipoise, by means of mental-attention directed toward that other [object] and away from anything else;
and by means of the aspect of impurity as the antidote to the aspect of beauty.
To the extent that one attends to mindfulness of breathing as the antidote to discursive thought (*vitarka*),
and attends to the element of space as the antidote to form (*rūpa*), through the mental application of the antidote;
and by not attending to any signs (*nimitta*) and by attending to the signless realm (*ānimittadhātu*), through the mental application of the signless realm.
Moreover,
while the characteristic of cultivation has been established as pervading that objective support, in this context it is intended by way of the internal condensation of signs,
and through non-recollection and non-mental-attention.
In that regard,
from the very beginning, the beginner— the one who is a neophyte— should not direct the mind toward anything whatsoever.
One should bind [the mind] to an object of focus, whether it be the foul, or that [specific part],
or this [part].
It is not for anything other than to prevent distraction:
"Is my mind signless, non-conceptual, and peaceful?"
"One delights in the inner self, which is tranquil, immovable, unshakable, free from longing, devoid of activity, and without further pursuit.
Thus applied, one practices non-recollection and non-attention toward every external object as it arises.
This is his cultivation of the object through non-recollection and non-mental attention. While applying himself to that, he grasps it;
he practices with conceptualization upon an object that is signless, such as the foul and so forth.
And how, moreover, does he practice?
By means of insight (vipaśyanā) that follows mere signs and proceeds through investigation and examination;
yet, he does not apply himself to insight exclusively.
Turning back again from the sign of insight (vipaśyanā), he attends to that very same object by way of calm abiding (śamatha). At that time, that object becomes liberated for him.
It has not been grasped;
because calm abiding (śamatha) proceeds with that as its object,
it is therefore not liberated.
Because one does not take it as a sign and does not conceptualize it, therefore it is not grasped; thus, internally, it is summarized in this way.
He eliminates the focal object.

In that regard, for one who has grasped the sign of insight (*vipaśyanā*), there is again the focal object consisting of the sign of the knowable thing; if he resolves upon that focal object as being uniform, [he attains one-pointedness].
Furthermore, one should not cultivate it repeatedly;
his resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) would not become progressively more purified.
It proceeds in a purified state,
until it reaches the direct perception of the objects of knowledge.
Furthermore,
because he resolves again and again and cultivates [the object] again and again,
his resolve becomes increasingly superior.
It proceeds as more purified, as most purified,
until it reaches the direct perception of the objects of knowledge.

It is, for example, like a painter or a painter’s apprentice who, being engaged in painting for the first time, takes a model from his teacher preceded by instruction; having seen it again and again, he makes a likeness,
and having made it again and again, he analyzes it.
He destroys it and creates it again; in whatever manner he repeatedly breaks it, in that same manner he creates it.
In that very way, his subsequent form appears increasingly pure and increasingly radiant.
Thus, being correctly applied, after some time he attains equality with the teacher,
or even a state superior to him.
If, however,
one were to repeatedly produce that very same form upon it again and again without interruption,
the blind person would never attain the purification of that form; in the same way, this principle should be understood here as well.
In that regard, one cultivates the meditative elimination for as long as one resolves upon the object;
however, it is not necessarily the case that one continues the cultivation for as long as one performs the meditative elimination.
To that extent one resolves;
one resolves upon the limited,
and one brings the limited alone to manifestation.
In this way, up to the measure of the "greatly developed" (*mahadgata*); furthermore, having cultivated the "limited" (*parītta*), one should further cultivate it.
Sometimes one resolves upon what is limited; sometimes upon what is vast;
and the same applies to the measure of what is vast.
It should be understood as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that regard, the sign (*nimitta*), reflection (*pratibimba*), or appearance (*pratibhāsa*) of material phenomena (*rūpī dharma*)—
Then, that which is gross, resembling a magical creation, or, in the case of formless phenomena, preceded by names and conventions, appearing according to the dominant influence of experience—
this is called "correct application."

This very ninefold application, which conforms to calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), should be understood as belonging to the white side (*śuklapakṣya*). Likewise, by way of its reverse, there is a ninefold discordance. Thus, through the distinction between the black and white sides, this becomes an eighteenfold application; this is called one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).
In that regard, what is the purification of obstructions? It is said:
by means of four causes, a yogi who is thus correctly engaged purifies his own mind of obstructions.
By means of the full understanding of intrinsic nature, the full understanding of the cause and the disadvantage, and the cultivation of the remedy.
In that regard, what is the intrinsic nature of the obscurations?
It is said: there are four obscurations.
Exhaustion, hindrance, discursive thought,
and self-exaltation.

In that context, "distress" refers to the afflicted longing, dissatisfaction, yearning, dejection, and agitation experienced by one engaged in renunciation and seclusion. In that context, "hindrance" refers to the five hindrances, beginning with sensual desire.
In that context, *vitarka* refers to the discursive thoughts of sensual desire and so forth—
namely, afflicted discursive thoughts.
Among those, "self-exaltation" (*ātmasampragraha*) is when [one clings] even to the slightest [fault].
By means of mere excellence,
and by means of mere knowledge, vision, and touch,
one fully sustains oneself.
"I am one who has attained gain, whereas others have not"—
this should be understood in detail as before; this is the nature of the obscuration.
In that regard, "distress" refers to as many as six causes;
namely, the predominance of past karma,
or the weakness of the physical basis due to the affliction of disease.
Excessive application,
half-application,
and initial application.
Abundance of afflictions and lack of practice in solitude are the bases for the hindrances; likewise,
discursive thoughts and self-exaltation are the bases for the hindrances.

In regard to states conducive to the absence of applied thought and states conducive to self-exaltation, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) practiced extensively is the cause of the hindrances, applied thought, and self-exaltation.
When one does not attend to foulness but instead attends to attractiveness, this is what is meant here by "improper."
Having thus brought to mind loving-kindness,
having abandoned the perception of signs, having brought to mind the perception of light, and having brought to mind the signless tranquility,

Discursive thoughts concerning relatives, the country, and the gods; memories of former playings, laughter, delight, and amusements— these, without having brought to mind this conditionality and dependent origination, or the notion of "I" regarding the three times, [are abandoned].
Or, when one attends to the notion "this is mine," which is improperly formed, this is here [an instance of] improper mental application (*ayoniśas*). In that regard, what is the disadvantage?
While these four kinds of obscurations exist and are present, one does not attain what has not yet been attained, nor does one fall away from what has already been attained;
one falters in the application of yoga and dwells in a state of affliction.
He dwells in suffering and instructs himself in this regard; he receives instruction from others,
and after the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in the states of woe.
This is the disadvantage here. What is the remedy for it? In that regard, the remedy for distress is, in brief, the recollections (*anusmṛti*).
The antidote is that, by means of the mental attention of recollection, one gladdens the mind and thereby dispels arisen dejection while preventing unarisen dejection from arising.
In that regard, there is the physical weakness, the lack of application, and the initial application.
In that regard, the equality of vigor is its cultivation;
it is the application of effort by one who has entered [the path].
In that regard, there is the desire to hear.
The remedy is thorough inquiry;
for whatever abundance of afflictions there may be, the application of objects such as the foul and so forth is employed accordingly.
The antidote:
for that which is non-habituation, such analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) is the antidote. Previously, by me...
I have not practiced seclusion,
which is why now, as I am engaged in seclusion, weariness arises in me;
if I do not practice it now, [that weariness will continue].
"In the future, such a rebirth will occur;

having reflected thus, I must abandon discontent and cultivate delight. In this way, the cultivation of appropriate attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*)—as the opposite of inappropriate attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*)—should be understood as the antidote to the hindrances (*nivaraṇa*) and other such undesirable states.
In that regard, having fully understood its intrinsic nature by way of obscuration and by way of affliction, there is,
for the time being, an abundance of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Indeed, this insight (vipaśyanā) should be understood from the perspective of the dark side as something that must be abandoned.
Furthermore, because of the avoidance of its cause, there is the avoidance of this [fault];
thus, one investigates the cause.
And because of the non-avoidance of that which is to be avoided, what is the disadvantage? Thus, one investigates the disadvantage (*ādīnava*).

Furthermore, as to how there comes to be the non-arising [of defilements] in the future for one who has abandoned them, he therefore cultivates the antidote; in this way, his mind becomes purified from the obscurations.
In that regard, to the extent that there is an abundance of instruction conducive to insight (*vipaśyanā*), to that same extent there is an abundance of insight;
and to the extent that there is an abundance of insight, it should be understood that there is no other [limit] than its being infinite.
Namely, by means of these very three gateways, through the method of entering into each of the six objects with infinite aspects;
and in whatever way the insight of one who is correctly engaged attains its expansion, growth, and vastness.
It proceeds by making the power of purification through practice its predominant influence;
and so, and so.
It should be understood that there is also a broad increase and expansion of the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*) which generates physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
for as his body and mind become increasingly pliant, [so does that side].
In this way, through one-pointedness of mind upon its object— that is, as he increases the basis—
just as one-pointedness of mind increases, so too do the body and the mind become pliant.
Thus, these two factors are mutually fulfilled and mutually bound, namely: one-pointedness of mind and the arising of direct knowledge.
In that regard, to what extent is the meditation on the foul (aśubhā) attained?
To what extent is mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) said to be attained? [The answer is:

from this point on, as this practitioner proceeds—whether walking or dwelling—by means of the sequence of cultivation, the sequence of development, and the sequence of frequent practice regarding the application of the foul (*aśubha*), [mindfulness of breathing is attained].
Even when the object is present before one and even through the examination of its signs, by its very nature and without volitional effort, there is a much greater manifestation of foulness.
This is because, due to the thorough cultivation of foulness, the mind does not enter into nor become settled upon those phenomena that are the basis for sensual desire.
One does not resolve [upon it];
equanimity remains;
this should be understood as weariness and aversion.
"The yogi has attained it; the foul has been attained by me. By this much, the fruit of cultivation—the foul—has been acquired."
By the opposite, they should be understood as not yet attained.
Just as it is with the meditation on the foul, so it is with loving-kindness and with dependent origination through specific conditionality.
The analysis of the elements and mindfulness of breathing should also be understood;
in this regard, however, there is this distinction: benevolence of mind appears more extensively.
There is no sign of resistance;
the mind does not incline toward phenomena that are occasions for malice, and so forth. Impermanence is more predominant.

Suffering and selflessness appear; there is no appearance accompanied by views of permanence, pleasure, or a self, nor any sign of delusion regarding those phenomena conducive to the obsession of ignorance.
"The mind does not leap forward," and so forth;
there appears a perception of the differentiation of body and mind, consisting of a greater degree of manifoldness of elements (*nānādhātukatā*) and a unity of elements (*ekadhātukatā*).
But there is not even the perception of a mind, for the mind does not incline toward those phenomena that are conducive to the obsession of pride; such is the detailed explanation.
There is a much greater perception of internal tranquility.

It is the perception of tranquility; it appears as such, and not as the perception of conceptual proliferation, for the mind does not incline toward those phenomena conducive to the obsession of discursive thought— so it is said in detail.
Therein, calm abiding and insight are fixed; both become friends and proceed in equal union,
whereby it is called the path that proceeds with the two joined together.
He said:
"It is one who has attained the ninth mode among the nine modes of mental abiding, namely, the state of being composed."
And relying upon that perfected concentration, he applies himself to the insight into phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*) regarding higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
At that time, as he is thus discerning phenomena, [the following occurs].
The path itself becomes one that flows by its own natural momentum, proceeding without effort;
through the absence of volitional construction, insight becomes completely pure and thoroughly cleansed.
The practice of the application of calm abiding proceeds, having been conceived and undertaken.
Just as they abide in calm abiding (*śamatha*), it is said that for them both calm abiding and insight (*vipaśyanā*) have become friends and proceed in equal union;
thus, there arises the path that carries the yoke of calm abiding and insight joined together.
The intermediate summary verse.
The search for the grasping of signs follows the gateway of analytical observation;
it is, however, joined with meanings, characteristics, aspects, times, and reasonings.
Suitability, as well as practice, slackening, and the reverse; contentment characterized by time, lack of failure, and application.
Right application itself is considered to have nine bases, which are twofold:
by way of intrinsic nature and by way of cause, as well as by way of seeing the disadvantage.
And indeed, purity is manifested through the removal of obscurations.
In that regard, what is the cultivation of mental attention (*manaskāra*)?

One who is a beginner, a novice at this very first task, when the pervasive characteristic has been thus established, avoids false application with respect to one-pointedness and the purification of hindrances.
And he trains in right application.
From the very beginning, thinking "I shall attain one-pointedness of mind and delight in abandonment," he applies himself by means of four mental attentions (*manaskāra*).
Which four? By means of the mental attention that warms the mind, and...
By means of mental attention that causes the mind to flow, generates pliancy, and purifies knowledge and vision.
In that regard, what is the mental attention that torments the mind? It is said:
it is by means of this mental attention that...
That which causes the mind to be stirred by means of things that provoke spiritual urgency is the mental attention that torments the mind.
In that regard, what is the mental attention that moistens the mind?
It is that by which one gladdens the mind through a mental attention that inspires serene confidence.
Mental attention that moistens the mind.
In that regard, what is mental attention that generates pliancy?
It is said:
By means of this mental attention, having from time to time caused the mind to feel spiritual urgency regarding things that inspire urgency,
and having from time to time gladdened the mind regarding things that inspire gladness, he causes the mind to settle within itself in tranquility,
in the signless state.

In this state of non-conceptuality, one establishes one-pointed mindfulness and brings it forth; by this cause and by this condition, as an antidote to the coarseness of body and mind, there arises physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) and mental pliancy (*citta-praśrabdhi*), which bring refreshment to the body and mind.
This is called the attention that generates pliancy.
In that regard, what is the mental attention that purifies knowledge and vision?
It is that mental attention by which, from time to time, he pacifies internal doubt with his mind;
through it, he repeatedly and constantly applies himself to the yoga of the insight into phenomena (*dharmavipaśyanā*) regarding higher wisdom.
That is to say, by relying on that very same internal tranquility of mind (*cetaḥśamatha*).
This is called the mental attention that purifies knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśanaviśodhana-manaskāra*).
What is it? From time to time, he causes the mind to be stirred with a sense of urgency regarding those things that provoke spiritual agitation; in this way, his mind becomes heated.
It is being scorched, agitated, and deeply distressed regarding those phenomena that serve as the basis for the outflows (*āsrava*).
What are all the situations that cause such agitation? [They are as follows:]
He said: "There are four; namely, the ruin of oneself,"
Furthermore, the misfortune of others—
when it is present, encountered, and manifested before one— becomes a ground for spiritual agitation through the application of wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
In that regard, there is the excellence of oneself.
And as for the prosperity of others:

when a moment has passed, ceased, departed, and changed, through the consequence of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo manasikāra*), it becomes a basis for spiritual agitation (*samvejanīya-sthāna*).
From time to time, he gladdens his mind with things that inspire joy.
As he gladdens it in this way, his mind becomes supple and moistened.
It is fluid and clear, and it is serene.
In that regard, what are the phenomena conducive to joy?
He said:
There are three kinds [of bases for confidence]: the four bases of confidence, the jewels, and...
Purity of the training precepts;
and the absence of mental contraction in one who has developed the conviction that they will attain spiritual distinction within themselves.
Thus pursuing these jewels, he gladdens his mind, thinking: "It is a gain for me, a great gain, that my Teacher is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
it is a gain for me, a great gain, that..."

I have gone forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; it is a great gain for me, a gain well-attained, that my fellow practitioners of the holy life are virtuous, endowed with qualities, and gentle.
Possessing virtuous qualities,
my death will be auspicious; my passing will be auspicious.
The future state is auspicious.
Thus, recollecting these four things, he gladdens his mind.
How does he recollect the purity of the training rules and the purity of ethical conduct?
He gladdens his mind, thinking:
"I have gained great gain, for I am in the presence of the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, and in his well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
And in that well-practiced community of disciples,
I have attained commonality of virtue and commonality of training with these fellow practitioners of the holy life.
He possesses bodily, vocal, and mental actions characterized by loving-kindness; he has attained conformity with right view; and he shares his enjoyments in common.
Thus, by recollecting the purity of the training rules and the purity of ethical discipline,
he gladdens his mind.
Namely, by means of joy preceded by the absence of regret.
In that regard, how does one, based on the confidence regarding one's own realization, think: "I am indeed capable; I possess such completely pure ethical discipline and am a fit vessel"?
Together with these fellow practitioners of the holy life, he has attained commonality in virtue,
attained commonality in view, and attained commonality with those who are virtuous (or those who have gone rightly).
"I am indeed capable, being such as I am, and practicing in this manner, in the company of virtuous persons."

In this very life, for the attainment of what has not yet been attained, for the realization of what has not yet been realized, and for the direct manifestation of what has not yet been directly manifested.

Thus he generates joy; in this way, by means of the basis of confidence in his own attainment, he gladdens his mind. Furthermore, as he recollects the specific attainment made by previously dwelling with initiated vigor, and having placed his faith in a further specific attainment, he gladdens his mind—this is another [way].

Heating his mind with regard to phenomena that inspire spiritual urgency, he turns his mind away from the outflows and from those phenomena conducive to the outflows; he makes it free from defects and establishes it in a state of direct confrontation.

While gladdening himself with respect to those phenomena that are conducive to joy, he causes his affectionate mind to turn toward, adhere to, and delight in those phenomena born of renunciation and seclusion; thus he joins it.
In this way, his mind—[is joined].
By means of these two factors,
one turns away from the entire dark side and turns toward the entire bright side.
It proceeds by means of both agitation and joy; for, having turned the mind away from the dark side in this way,
and having turned it toward the white side through mental attention that causes the mind to feel heat, [it proceeds].
From time to time, he applies himself inwardly with a moistening mental attention;
that is to say, from time to time, he investigates and scrutinizes the phenomena with a mental attention that produces pliancy through mental serenity.
He reflects and applies thorough investigation for the purpose of purifying knowledge and vision.
Not by means of mental attention;
thus, from time to time, his mind is embraced by calm abiding and insight,
and is assisted by the causes for all aspects and all qualities.
With the passing of those various nights and days,
moments, instants, and hours,
he proceeds toward excellence.
It is just as when gold or silver is repeatedly heated from time to time by a skilled smith or a smith’s apprentice;
it becomes free from impurities and dross, yet does not become overly liquefied.

In each case, it has been brought face-to-face with the work of ornamentation through its application of softness and adaptability; then, a skilled smith or a smith’s apprentice, by means of corresponding technical knowledge and the materials for the craft, [works upon] that which is desired—
When that mind of the yogin has been turned away from the impurities of covetousness and so forth by means of the transformation of the ornament, and has become agitated,
and has been gladdened by being turned away from afflicted dejection.
Wherever the yogi applies this—
whether to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*) or the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*)— it becomes well-adapted, well-attached, complete, and unshakable in each instance.
And he proceeds toward the accomplishment of his intended purpose.
In that regard, how is the beginner, one who is a neophyte in this practice, applied to the cultivation of mental attention (manaskāra),
so that by being thus applied and practicing accordingly, he attains realization?

First of all, the knower of yoga, when instructing a beginner engaged in yoga practice, instructs them in this way from the very beginning: [to cultivate] delight in abandonment and one-pointedness of mind.
Come, gentle-faced one,
relying upon the three causes that apprehend signs— namely, what is seen, or what is heard, or...
Or, based on the predominance of inferential reflection,
grasp five signs within your conceptualization: that which is to be stirred with spiritual urgency, and so forth.
[These are] the sign of serenity, the sign of disadvantage, the sign of light, and the sign of the investigation of objects.

If that beginner engaged in yoga is one whose temperament is dominated by passion (*rāga-carita*) and is to be trained by means of the foul (*aśubha*), how is he instructed in the apprehension of the five signs?
He is instructed as follows:
Come,
friend; whichever village or town you dwell in dependence upon,
if it be in another village...
Or you hear of someone in a village, whether a man or a woman, who is afflicted,
suffering, or severely ill.
Whether it be a dead person who has passed away, whether a man or a woman; moreover, of that man or...

Or, by a woman, any one of her friends, ministers, kinsmen, or blood relatives; or by an enemy army; or there may be a calamity regarding food for the body of people belonging to that village, caused by fire, or caused by the removal of water.
Whether caused by the ruin of poorly executed undertakings, or caused by the collapse of ill-applied enterprises,
or caused by the acquisition of unpleasant heirs.
Whether it be caused by a family wick or by total destruction—
if you do not hear it,
yet you see it directly before your eyes.
Neither in another village or town, nor even in that very same village or town.
You are not merely touched by others, but by yourself as well—
by bodily sensations that are painful, intense, and so forth, as described in detail previously.
Having seen and heard all this, arouse a sense of spiritual urgency in your mind:
"Alas, this saṃsāra is suffering! It is a hardship to obtain a physical existence in which such forms [of suffering] for oneself occur."
And the misfortunes of others are perceived; namely,
misfortune regarding health and also misfortune regarding birth.
The loss of enjoyments, as well as illness and the nature of illness;
death, and the nature of death.

Moreover, some undergo both a failure of ethical discipline and a failure of view; on account of these, sentient beings dwell in suffering in the present life and go to an evil destination in the future life.
And those prosperities which lead to a pleasant dwelling in the present life and to rebirth in a happy destination in the future— those too are impermanent.
Their impermanence is also discerned:
if misfortune has become manifest,
at that time prosperity has turned away.
Even when misfortune has not yet manifested, prosperity is difficult to obtain and is subject to destruction;
having thus stirred the mind [to revulsion],
it is well [to proceed].
And apply yourself thoroughly and with proper attention:
this state is not to be relied upon, it is not to be trusted— that while wandering in saṃsāra, [I might fall under the power of Māra].
For one who has not attained final nirvana and whose mind is not yet liberated, these misfortunes and prosperities would neither come into manifestation nor turn away from manifestation for me.
"Or rather, suffering does not arise for me on this account— suffering that is intense, harsh, bitter, disagreeable,
and unbearable; therefore, making all these goals my primary concern, I must delight in abandonment and remain vigilant."
"Thinking, 'If I dwell frequently in this way, perhaps there will be the non-occurrence of this misfortune,' apply yourself with wise attention (*yoniśas*).
Having thus grasped the sign that inspires spiritual urgency (*saṃvejanīya-nimitta*), you should again grasp the sign that inspires serene confidence (*prasadanīya-nimitta*)."
Furthermore, grasp it in this way:
examine your own moral conduct; are your precepts pure or impure? Whosoever...
Whether through loss of mindfulness,
lack of respect, abundance of afflictions, or lack of proficiency, there may be some transgression of the training.
Or, having transgressed the training, have I, through making amends according to the Dharma and with a resolute intention, generated the mind of non-repetition?
Is it so?

"What ought to be done has been done, and what ought not to be done has not been done; in brief, has it been accomplished? Am I endowed with the right intention and endowed with the right application?"
That is to say,
regarding the precepts;
thus, by one who reflects in this manner.
If that aggregate of ethical discipline is completely pure,
you need not entertain the thought,
"Might remorse arise in me? for this is simply the nature of things.
When, for one whose ethical discipline is thus purified, non-regret arises,
then one who is free from regret need not form a further volition, thinking, "May joy arise within me."
Moreover, this is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that joy arises for one who is free from remorse.
First, by means of this single basis for joy, one should generate joy preceded by the two kinds of freedom from remorse;
having generated it, one should gladden the mind by means of the subsequent basis for rapture.
If, however, you proceed from the former to the latter, even upon attaining a slight distinction, joy should be generated: "I am capable; I am competent."
Thus, with his ethical discipline completely purified and well-established in the trainings of the Blessed One,
he strives for the attainment of what has been attained in this very life and for the realization of what has not yet been realized.
For the sake of realizing that which has not yet been realized,
gladden your mind with this basis as well.
If, moreover, he should obtain a further successive attainment of the distinction of others' minds,
then, taking that as his dominant influence, he [should apply it] toward the perfect attainment of distinction by others— namely, in the case of the Tathāgata or among the disciples of the Tathāgata.
And having developed a firm conviction regarding the attainment of further superior qualities for oneself, one gladdens the mind;
that joy of the mind through these aspects is what is called "the state of being joyful-minded" now,
as opposed to the previous state of being glad.
In this way, he causes [the disciple] to grasp the sign that inspires serene confidence; having caused him to grasp it, he further instructs him:
"Come, O gentle-faced one!"
With a mind tormented by signs that cause spiritual urgency,
and with a mind moistened by a mind that inspires serene confidence, you will dwell frequently in the world, having abandoned covetousness and dejection.
And upon whatever object of focus you shall apply yourself.
Whether on the side of tranquility or the side of insight, the mind will remain settled upon this or that object of focus.
You will attain a state well-established within, as well as physical and mental pliancy and one-pointedness of mind;
thus, turning away from the dark side and facing toward the bright side, namely, through the flow of spiritual urgency.
Furthermore, grasp all the signs of its disadvantage (*ādīnava*), namely: from signs (*nimitta*), from adverse factors (*vipakṣa*), and from secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
In this context, the signs are the ten, beginning with the sign of form;
the discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) are the eight, beginning with the thought of sensual desire.
The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are five, beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*);
furthermore, you should grasp the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) in them as follows.
Thus, these signs are the causes of mental activity;
thus, these discursive thoughts are the causes of agitation for the mind;
thus, these secondary afflictions are the causes of non-quiescence for the mind.
That activity of the mind which is produced by signs,
that which is produced by discursive thought once agitation has been released,
and that which is produced by secondary afflictions— this is the mind’s dwelling in suffering.
Therefore, these signs, discursive thoughts, and secondary afflictions are painful, ignoble, conducive to harm, and causes of mental distraction and agitation.
Having grasped such signs of disadvantage, one achieves non-distraction of the mind in one-pointedness and mental stability. (as above)

Grasp the sign through six aspects, namely: by means of the perception of signs; or by means of the perception of non-activity regarding the signless; and by means of the perception of non-conceptuality.
And in the non-conceptual state, by means of the perception of lack of longing and lack of agitation, and by means of the perception of tranquility,
through tranquility itself.
By means of the perception of impurity, characterized by freedom from feverish distress and tranquility;
having thus grasped the sign, furthermore, grasp another sign, namely, the sign of light, such as from a lamp.
Or, having grasped a sign from a mass of fire, or from the solar disk, or from the lunar disk.
Having approached a cemetery or similar place,
take up the sign from a livid corpse, or even from a skeleton.
Whether it be [the image] of corpses or skeletons,
you should apprehend the sign not from an actual cemetery, but rather from one painted on a canvas or constructed from wood as a mock-cemetery.
Having taken it up, go to a place for lying down or sitting; having gone there, whether you have entered a forest or gone to the foot of a tree,
Whether he has gone to an empty dwelling,
or to a couch, or to a seat;
Or sit upon a grass mat;
having washed your feet, assume the cross-legged posture.
Having set the body erect and established mindfulness directed toward the front,
Having sat down, first of all, fix your mindfulness upon one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind; and therein cultivate the six perceptions:

the perception of non-conceptuality, the perception of pacification, the perception of non-activity, the perception of lack of longing and lack of agitation, and the perception of freedom from feverish distress, cessation, and impurity.
And in that regard, let your attention be established upon the thorough knowledge of distraction and non-distraction;

by means of that attention consisting in the thorough knowledge of distraction and non-distraction, you should thoroughly understand distraction with respect to signs, discursive thoughts, and secondary afflictions in their various forms, and you should understand non-distraction with respect to one-pointedness of mind accompanied by the cultivation of the six perceptions.

And therein, with respect to distraction and non-distraction, be so attentive that your entire mental continuity and stream of consciousness— bound to one-pointedness and bound to internal tranquility of mind— are established in a continuous sequence from beginning to end.
It should proceed signless, non-conceptual, and tranquil. However, if—

due to forgetfulness or a lapse of mindfulness— when the mind has attained calm abiding (śamatha), signs, discursive thoughts, and secondary afflictions should appear because of the fault of past habituation, [one must apply the appropriate antidote].
They manifest pleasure and take it as an object;
toward each of these as they arise, one should practice mindfulness and non-attention.
That is to say, having made that which was previously seen the dominant influence, by means of such recollection and mental attention toward that object,
it will be cultivated until it becomes confident and established in a state free from appearances.
And this, O gentle sir, is as follows:
The object of focus is subtle;
you have thoroughly penetrated that which is difficult to penetrate.
"One must maintain intense zeal and exertion.
It was with reference to this objective that the Blessed One said:
"Monks, regarding 'the beauty of the land, the beauty of the land,' a great crowd of people would gather."
Then a man of immature nature might come,
and someone would say to him: "O man, this is yours."
Suppose there were a vessel full of oil, level to the brim and not to be spilled, and while it was being carried, a great crowd of people were to gather in its path;
that same woman, the most beautiful in the land,
would likewise be in their midst.
"You must attend this great assembly.
Furthermore, this executioner with drawn sword is following closely behind you.
If you let even a single drop fall from this bowl of oil onto the ground, then this executioner with drawn sword will strike off your head, cutting it from its very roots."

"What do you think, monks? Would that man, without paying attention to the bowl of oil, without paying attention to the bowl of oil, and without paying attention to the executioner with his sword raised, pay attention to the Beauty of the Land [Janapadakalyāṇī] in the midst of a great crowd of people? "No, Venerable Sir."
For what reason? Because that man had seen the executioner with sword raised following closely behind him, he would think:
"If I were to let even a single drop fall from this oil-bowl onto the ground..."
Therefore, this executioner with his sword raised will strike off my head, cutting it from its very roots;
unless, indeed, that man were to disregard the Beauty of the Land or the great assembly.

In the same way, monks, those who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness with reverence, honoring them and attending to them with their whole mind—they are these very ones. Just as one would carry that very bowl of oil correctly while attending to it with all one's mind, even so, monks, are those who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness with reverence, honoring them and attending to them with their whole mind. They are these very ones.
Regarding the term "disciples" (*śrāvaka*):
therein, "the beauty of the land" (*janapadakalyāṇī*) is a designation for those factors conducive to the outbursts of secondary afflictions such as desire for the body;
"supremely excellent dancing, singing, and instrumental music" is a designation for those factors conducive to the agitation of discursive thought and conceptual proliferation.
"Great assembly" (*mahāsamāja*) is a designation for the ten signs, beginning with the sign of form (*rūpanimitta*).
"A person who partakes of what is not of the foolish" (*abālabhāgīyaḥ puruṣaḥ*) refers to one who does not share in the qualities of the ignorant.
"Oil vessel" is a designation for the practitioner of yoga;
it is a designation for the mind that is bound to calm abiding (*śamatha*).

In the sense of providing pliancy and moisture to body and mind, "the executioner with sword raised" is a designation for the previously grasped fault regarding signs, discursive thoughts, and secondary afflictions;

"he dwells with reverence and does not let even a single drop fall upon the ground" is a designation for the path of calm abiding (*śamatha*) which is embraced by the focused attention that thoroughly understands distraction and non-distraction.
By means of which, through the power of vigor, he causes this entire mental continuum and stream of consciousness to proceed uninterruptedly and sequentially— signless, non-conceptual, and tranquil—
and yet he does not give rise to even a single thought.
Either having a sign as its object, or having discursive thought and secondary afflictions as its object.
The yogin instructs that very beginner who is thus engaged in calm abiding:

"O gentle-faced one, as long as the mind of one thus engaged in the path of calm abiding remains embraced by such skillful means, accompanied by mindfulness and clear comprehension, and is full of delight..."
For that long, you should cultivate only the path of calm abiding (*śamatha*).

However, if—due to the loss caused by a lack of practice—you do not find delight, then, employing the proper means, you should emerge from that non-conceptual object and fix your mindfulness upon a conceptual object.

Specifically, bring to mind that very sign of the foul (*aśubhanimitta*) which you previously grasped; first of all, apply insight (*vipaśyanā*) that follows the mere sign, namely, the livid-blue corpse (*vinīlaka*), or...
Or one that is festering, up to a skeleton.
And having applied yourself in that way, from the very beginning,
resolve upon one livid corpse,
up to a single chain of bones, until you have become proficient in this practice.
And that luminous resolve proceeds;
at that time, there are two objects, then two,
then three.
Four,
five, ten.
Twenty,
thirty, forty,
fifty, a hundred of the livid, a thousand of the livid.
Until all the cardinal and intermediate directions— visualize them as being continuous from the east in terms of their measure and form,
such that there would be no space for even the tip of a staff to be inserted.

Just as it is with the livid corpses, so it is with everything up to the skeletons; relying on all such attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), enter into attention to reality (*bhūta-manasikāra*).
And enter it in this way:
"All these livid corpses, up to the skeletons, that have been resolved upon by me, are immeasurable from my beginningless past."
In various states of existence, births, deaths, and rebirths,
regarding one who has died and passed away, there are those stages beginning with the appearance of livid discoloration, up to the formation of a skeleton.
If someone were to collect all those [particles] whose prior limit is not known as they are being withdrawn, and even when collected they did not perish;
Nor would they become putrid;
there is no spot on earth where there would be room for them,
even for those who belong to a single eon.
Suppose there were someone who could collect all those skeletons until they formed a heap as vast as a mountain with broad slopes,
reaching as far as the limit of the eastern direction.
"Starting from this very point, until the furthest limit,
you must apply yourself thus: 'I shall not fail to bring an end to suffering.'"
Relying on mental attention, you will enter into authentic mental attention.
These stages, from the livid corpse up to the skeleton, are not to be observed all at once by one engaged in insight meditation;
rather, having resolved upon a single livid corpse, the mind should be calmed again, and that very livid corpse should be the object of resolution for as long as it takes.
As long as that [mind] is not enveloped by distress regarding that object of focus— being delightful and luminous—
one does not yet face the time of death.

At that time, one should pacify the mind internally; just as with the livid corpse, so it should be understood, by this same method, up to a single skeleton and even up to immeasurable [skeletons]. Having thus pacified the mind internally, [one should proceed].

Then, one should liberate oneself from all of them, starting from the very last: immeasurable livid corpses, up to immeasurable skeletons; by means of internal concentration of the mind, one contemplates these and establishes them in a state free from appearance, yet one does not abandon those mental signs.
He does not conceptualize even those things that involve conceptualization;
rather, he establishes the mind—having that very [object] as its focal point—as signless, non-conceptual, and tranquil.
Furthermore, he is instructed:
"O gentle-faced one, that sign of light which you previously grasped, attend to that also during the practice belonging to the side of calm abiding."
Also, during the application belonging to the side of insight (vipaśyanā),
with a mind accompanied by light and accompanied by radiance, [one practices].
Cultivate calm abiding and special insight with luminosity that is free from darkness.
And as you thus cultivate the perception of light within the path of calm abiding and special insight,
if from the very beginning the higher liberation regarding the object of focus becomes indistinct, there will be a correct appearance.
By that cause and by that condition,
