there will be a distinction from what merely resembles cultivation.
And there is the state of having abundant manifestation;
furthermore, if from the very beginning it becomes clearly manifest,
it will have abundant manifestation.

It will proceed to a greater degree of clarity and a more abundant manifestation. You, therefore, by means of this well-grasped sign of spiritual urgency and the sign conducive to serene confidence, [should apply yourself].
By means of the sign of calm abiding, the sign of insight,
and the sign of the world.
Having well grasped [the teaching], from time to time reflecting on the mind internally, and from time to time investigating phenomena,
enter into the foundations of mindfulness by means of insight that follows mere signs;
that is to say, by making the practice of the foul (aśubha) itself the primary focus.

Furthermore, while investigating in this way, having grasped the signs of the thirty-six substances within the body, from the hair to the excrement, one should resolve that all these internal substances are impure and thereby pacify the internal mind.
"This will be your internal bodily contemplation of the body, namely, beginning with your own internal body; furthermore,
you should again resolve upon the external sign of impurity that has been grasped— whether it be a livid corpse, or even up to a skeleton."
Whether by means of limited resolve, exalted resolve, or immeasurable resolve, having resolved again and again, pacify the mind within;
this will be for you.

Regarding external observation of the body by means of the body— that is, beginning with the external body belonging to another— you, moreover, [should observe] yourself within your own internal body with a mind cultivated in the perception of foulness, and the external body of another with a mind cultivated in the perception of foulness, both internally and externally.
Resolve upon one who is dying,
or again, one being carried out to the cemetery or already carried out,
or one cast away in the cemetery.
Or resolve upon it as discarded, or in the state of a livid corpse, or in the state of a festering corpse, up to the state of a skeleton.
This shall be for you the essence of the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external body.

Furthermore, through the predominant influence of hearing and reflection, by means of grasping the signs of conceptualization, resolve upon the four formless aggregates in three parts: those belonging to the side of tranquility, and those belonging to the side of distraction.

And regarding the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*): when one withdraws the mind within, there arise the four formless aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with feeling— having as their objective non-distraction— which possess the aspects of being signless, non-conceptual, and peaceful, and the aspects of being effortless, free from longing, unagitated, free from feverish distress, and characterized by the perception of the bliss of tranquility.
Resolve with conviction that [these phenomena] proceed moment by moment as something ever-changing, being ever-new and devoid of antiquity;
this will be for you regarding internal and external feelings and the mind.
The existence of the contemplation of phenomena among all phenomena,
which previously involved the grasping of sense objects.

Those [skandhas] which have fallen into the level of non-concentration, having descended upon objects as their focal points, are exhausted; and those four formless skandhas—feeling and so forth—which now arise when there is distraction of the mind due to the loss of mindfulness, being dominated by the focal points of signs, discursive thoughts, and secondary afflictions: [he contemplates] their nature of leading to states of woe, their temporariness, and their fleeting presence.
Do not fail to abandon their state of peril, instability, and lack of reliability;
this shall be for you.
Having again grasped the sign of insight (vipaśyanā-nimitta), he remains established in attention (manaskāra) and conceptualization (saṃkalpa) that possess signs;
[thereby] those [states] which arise internally, having as their dominant condition objects of focus (ālambana) that are accompanied by conceptualization and signs.
Resolve, as before, upon the four formless aggregates beginning with sensation— namely, their moment-by-moment newness, their lack of antiquity, and their mutual distinctness.
This will be for you regarding external sensation and mind.
[The existence] of the contemplation of phenomena within phenomena.
For in this way, by making the practice of the foul your primary focus, you will have entered the four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness:
Furthermore, in practice,

you should apply yourself from time to time to calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā). Thus, with mindfulness established in this way, regarding whichever village or— among the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna)— you may enter, you should remain there.
Whether you dwell depending upon a village or a town, you [should do so] with a mind that is constantly directed toward that very village or town.
With your mind inclined toward that, with that as your primary focus, and relinquishing the objective support and the signs of the objective support, enter for alms.

The practice of avoiding the company of a fierce elephant, a fierce horse, a fierce ox, and a fierce osprey; and the avoidance of snakes, pits, stumps, thorns, ponds, precipices, streams, excrement, potsherds, and filth as regards one's conduct, bed, and seat.
Your self becomes unprotected;
and regarding those objective signs toward which your faculties ought to be directed, your faculties remain unrestrained through a lack of effort;
or again, regarding those signs toward which your faculties ought not to be directed.
Mindfulness is established in each of those instances,
namely, for the sake of ensuring that the afflictions do not arise.
Thus, with your body well-guarded, your sense faculties well-restrained, and mindfulness well-established, you—
With a mind directed toward that [goal], partake of almsfood with moderation;
and be one who shares in measured portions together with householders and renunciants who are disciplined.
He speaks at the proper time, he speaks what is true, he speaks with straightforwardness,
and he speaks with tranquility.
Furthermore, you must completely avoid all unrighteous discourse.
Even when delivering righteous discourse, you must not engage in contentious speech.
Why is that?
When a person who dwells devoted to the pursuit of the intensity of contentious discourse has his mind fixed upon that abundance of talk, then, because of that abundance, there is restlessness;
when there is restlessness, there is a lack of tranquility;
and for one whose mind lacks tranquility, the mind remains far from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

"You who practice in this manner, do not proceed so very hurriedly without having relinquished my object of focus; rather, today, by means of the very sign as it was grasped for calm abiding and insight, apply yourself to yoga through either attenuation or final termination. (Thus he said to him.)
And by means of the practice of fire-churning, through constant and respectful application, be one who acts continuously;
furthermore, direct your mind in this way:
"If all the life-spans of all the humans in Jambudvīpa throughout the entire duration of their existence were combined together, it would now belong to me alone."

Thus, for as long as my life lasts, through the application of the practice of the immeasurable and by means of constant and respectful application, I shall be one who acts continuously. Furthermore, you should direct your mind in this way: "As long as I live in Jambudvīpa, may I not neglect the yoga of mental attention toward calm abiding and insight."
That is to say, having understood the great fruitfulness and the great benefits of this very application of yoga, he applies himself to it from the very beginning,
even when his life is short and his existence has reached its end, being counted as no more than a hundred years.
For in this way, acting continuously and acting with thoroughness as you have been instructed,
you will not be an obstacle to that goal for the sake of which you have undertaken this abandonment;
rather, you will first examine it.

He will attain a mild physical pliancy and one-pointedness of mind, and from that, he will subsequently achieve a vast success, both mundane and supramundane. Thus, this beginner, a novice in his first practice,
being exhorted by a teacher skilled in yoga while engaged in the meditation on the foul, correctly...
Being thus exhorted, one who practices accordingly becomes one who has practiced correctly,
just as one who is to be guided by the meditation on the foul practices it.

In the same way, those who are to be trained through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, up to mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), should be understood according to their respective applications; however, there is this distinction therein. I shall clarify that [distinction] regarding the other gateways of entry later.
In that regard, for a beginner engaged in the cultivation of loving-kindness:

Having grasped the signs from those on the side of friends and from the side of neutral persons, one who has gone to a suitable lodging and seat should, with a mental attention characterized by a resolute intention toward happiness belonging to the stage of meditative concentration, first resolve upon one friend, one enemy, and one neutral person.
And toward those three groups, one should apply oneself with a mental attention that has entered into the resolute intention for their welfare and happiness equally:
"May these beings, who possess bodies of happiness, become happy— namely, by means of blameless sensual happiness and by means of blameless happiness accompanied by joy."
by means of faultless bliss free from rapture;
thereafter, two friends, three [friends],...
Four,
five, ten.
O Viṃśa, as before, they resolve that the twenty, the thirty, and so on, up to all the cardinal and intermediate directions, are filled with friends and enemies.

Where there is no interval—meaning not even a gap as small as the thickness of a staff-tip between [the friend and the others]—just as it is with the faction of friends, so too should it be understood regarding the factions of enemies and neutral parties.
And he does not abandon the practice of loving-kindness;
rather, while cultivating loving-kindness, he enters into the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
How, then, does one enter? One enters by means of resolute conviction (*adhimucyamāna*).
Just as I am regarded by others as a friend, regarded as an enemy, and regarded as neutral;
and just as I too desire happiness and am averse to suffering.
This is his internal contemplation on the body within the body;
these beings, too, are either friends or enemies to others.
And those who are neutral—
just as they, like me, desire happiness and are averse to suffering— this is the reality of his external contemplation of the body:
"Just as I am, so too are these sentient beings."

Just as happiness is to be sought for myself, so too, by way of the equality of self and the likeness of self, should happiness be brought about by me for these sentient beings. This constitutes his contemplation of the body in the internal and external body. And these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
By taking the aggregates as a combined object, the application of mindfulness becomes one with a combined object (*saṃbhinnālambana*).
Having grasped the sign of form— the signs of color, shape, and representation— from the categories of friends, enemies, and neutral parties, the yogi...
He resolves upon it; therefore, this is established as precisely the application of mindfulness to the body.
Relying on that attention consisting of resolute conviction, he...
He enters into correct mental attention (*bhūta-manaskāra*), and by resolving in this way, he enters:
"I have resolved that these beings are immeasurable,
with a resolute intention directed toward their welfare and happiness."
Therefore, those beings who, since beginningless time, have passed away as my friends, enemies, or neutral parties; those who, having been my friends,
became enemies, and having been enemies, became friends or neutral parties— in this manner, all beings are exactly equal.
In this regard, there is no state of friendship, enmity, or neutrality that is fully established; rather, by this very method, one should practice the bringing about of equal benefit and happiness.
Just as starting from the past limit (*pūrvānta*), so too starting from the future limit (*aparānta*):
while saṃsāra and the cycle of existence persist, those sentient beings whom I have compassionately regarded with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) since the past limit—
whether they be those who have passed away or indeed those whom I now compassionately regard, namely, with a mind free from turbidity (*niṣkaluṣa*).
On account of that state of being unharmed:
"O, those beings are indeed happy;
they have been, will be, [or were] truly so."
Furthermore, may those who have not yet come into being be happy in the future time.
For one who is thus established in such mental attention and dwells in loving-kindness (*maitrī*), whatever overflow of merit and overflow of virtue there may be—
that is the mass of merit belonging to one who dwells in the loving-kindness of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*).
It does not approach even a hundredth part,
nor a thousandth part;
it does not bear comparison in number, nor as a fraction.
It does not even admit of calculation or comparison;
the rest is as before.

In this regard, the beginner in the dependent origination of specific conditionality does not, by means of the predominance of hearing and reflection, grasp at the signs of the imagined nature— namely, the ignorance and delusion of other sentient beings,
by which they perceive what is directly evident as impermanent to be permanent, what is directly evident as impure to be pure, and suffering to be happiness.

These beings are inverted with respect to selflessness as being a self; due to the cause of inversion, they are attached to the self-existence in the present life through sensations, and in the future life.
They thirst;

and being thirsty, they perform actions rooted in birth, whereby in the future, through the causes of karma and afflictions, they bring about nothing but pure suffering. Having grasped this sign in such a way, one becomes inwardly convinced:
"This entire mass of suffering has arisen in exactly this manner."
And those personal existences which are infinite and boundless, whose very beginning cannot be discerned starting from the past limit—
they too are of such a nature;
for all the past, future, and present personal existences of these sentient beings are likewise produced, being comprised entirely within the aggregate of suffering.
They do not arise in the future.
Indeed, this mental attention to dependent origination as conditionality is itself a mental attention to all that exists; it is not merely a matter of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*).

If, moreover, he does not attend to his own present aggregates as dependently originated, then he dwells contemplating phenomena in the internal body, and so on, up to phenomena in phenomena. And when he again attends to the present aggregates of others as dependently originated, [he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena].
Then he dwells contemplating phenomena in the body internally and externally, and so on up to phenomena;
when he attends to his own and others' past and future aggregates as dependently originated,
then he dwells contemplating phenomena in the body internally and externally, and so on up to phenomena.

The remainder is as before. Therein, the beginner engaged in the practice of the classification of elements, having grasped the sign of external earth-hardness— namely, from such things as the earth, mountains, grass, forests, pebbles, gravel, gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, stones, and coral— resolves upon internal hardness.
Having grasped the sign externally from the water element—
from such things as rivers, springs, ponds, wells, and so forth—
Likewise, from a great mass of fire; or from the earth heated by the rays of the sun; or from all things possessed by spirits;
or from grasses scorched by a great fire; or from external wind-masses, from the winds of the east, south, west, and north, up to the entire circle of winds (*vāyumaṇḍala*).
Those regions which, being permeated by the movement of wind, are porous,
hollow, and spacious;
From that space-element, he grasps the sign and resolves upon the internal water-element,
fire-element, wind-element, and space-element,
by means of that which is conceptually constructed under the influence of hearing and reflection.
In this way, one grasps the sign of the consciousness element:
provided that the internal sense-base of the eye is unimpaired and a visible form has come into range.
And the attention arising from that is not present,
nor does the visual consciousness arising from that manifest;
it manifests through the opposite conditions.
In this same way, up to the mental consciousness with respect to mental phenomena, it should be understood.
Having thus grasped the signs of all these consciousnesses, one resolves that their seed, element, lineage, and nature reside within this body composed of the four great elements.
These four great elements are, from the very beginning, present in the limbs and members.
Even without an actual object, one resolves upon it;
thereafter,
one resolves upon the further subdivisions of its increasingly subtle parts.
In this way, up to the point where he enters through the openings, by means of the equality of satisfaction;
and in this way, up to the point where he gradually resolves upon it atom by atom.
He resolves upon each individual limb and member as being composed of a collection of atoms.
How much more so, then, for one who is devoted to the analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*) regarding the entire body?
This is the limit of the analysis of objects concerning the material elements; as for the space element, it is even greater.

Furthermore, the application of attention toward the thorough knowledge of distraction and non-distraction during that practice—the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*)—is what constitutes his clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) and equanimity of mindfulness (*smṛtisamatā*).

Furthermore, when the sign of spiritual urgency and the sign conducive to serene confidence have been well grasped— this being for the sake of subduing covetousness and dejection— for him who dwells thus ardent, [and so on] up to (d).
In the second stage, covetousness and dejection have already been eliminated at the very time of commencing correct practice;
a subtle mental pliancy, which is difficult to perceive,
arises therein for one who is cultivating calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Or, in the case of insight (vipaśyanā), it is the state of the mind being healthy,
the state of the body being healthy,
and the serviceability of the mind and body.
This is the pliancy of body and mind here.

That very same subtle one-pointedness of mind and pliancy of body and mind, having become more excellent and coarse, brings about a one-pointedness of mind and pliancy of body that is easily discernible;
namely, by means of the application of the complete exhaustion of causes.
Before long, a coarse pliancy of mind and body and one-pointedness of mind will arise for him, clearly characterized.
To the extent that its precursor arises as a prior appearance of non-reverence,
yet this is not characterized by affliction,
immediately following its arising, there occurs that which acts as an obstacle to the joy of abandonment.
The mental depravity (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the faction of those afflictions is abandoned,
and by means of its antidote, there arises mental flexibility (*cittakarmaṇyatā*).
Mental pliancy arises.
With its arising, the great elements—specifically the winds—that are conducive to the arising of physical pliancy enter into the body.
Due to their entry, whatever bodily rigidity there was departs.

And by means of the physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) that belongs to the side of abandoning the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and serves as their antidote, the entire body is filled, as if with a delight in abandonment.
There might be [an experience of] meditative absorption (*dhyāna*);
then, at its initial onset, there is rigidity of mind (*citta-dauṣṭhulya*).
At that time, the mind appears as being accompanied by joy, mental attention, and gladness, and as having a delightful object; subsequently,
there arises that initial surge of pliancy which first descends upon it.
It becomes gradually and increasingly relaxed;
a pliancy follows him like a shadow and pervades the body, as does that which was previously restlessness (auddhatya).
That too is abandoned from the mind;
it is that which functions as calm abiding (*śamatha*) when the mind, having a tranquil aspect, possesses an object of focus.
Thereafter, this beginner yogin becomes one who possesses mental attention (*samanaskāra*) and is reckoned as "one with mental attention. For what reason?

In accordance with the pursuit of the object of form, the mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration is first attained in a limited degree; therefore, it is called "possessing mental attention. For this beginner who possesses such mental attention, these are the signs that appear.
By this, a limited mind belonging to the form realm has been attained;
there is limited pliancy of body, pliancy of mind, and one-pointedness of mind,
such that he becomes capable and competent.
The object for the purification of afflictions is present during his application, and his mental continuum proceeds with smoothness.
When his conduct has been purified by being embraced by calm abiding (śamatha),
even if he engages with an object that provokes passion,
he does not give rise to an intense outburst of lustful attachment.
And by means of a mere slight degree,
a mere small degree, by relying on the counteragent, and by a mere effort, one is unable to purify it thoroughly;
as it is with that which is provocative of passion, so it is with that which is provocative of hatred.
It should be understood that this applies to that which is conducive to delusion, conducive to pride, and conducive to discursive thought.
Furthermore, as he sits and directs his mind toward solitary retreat, his mind becomes very quickly tranquilized.
The body and the physical dysfunctions do not excessively afflict him,
nor does the manifestation of the hindrances occur excessively.
Furthermore, perceptions and mental attentions associated with excessive longing and accompanied by the exhaustion of passion do not arise,
even when one has emerged [from meditative absorption] and is acting with an emerged mind;
there is pliancy.

One should understand that such signs and marks as these— namely, that some degree of measure has been attained in the mind, the body, and the mental continuum— are the purified indicators of one who possesses mental attention and is a beginner.
The summary verse of the section:
Approaching, gladdening, questioning, and seeking;
assignment, protection, and accumulation; seclusion, and oneness of being.
In this [stage], there is the cultivation of mental attention that is preeminent due to the purification of hindrances.
The third stage of yoga within the *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi* is completed.
(Śbh_Sh 435) (Śbh_Sh 436) (Śbh_Sh 437)
IV. The Fourth Stage of Yoga. In this regard, for the yogin who has attained mental attention and has thus entered into the joy of limited abandonment, there are two subsequent courses.
They are not different.
Which two?
Namely, the mundane and the supramundane.
In this regard, this beginner practitioner of yoga,
possessing mental attention,
thinks: "I shall proceed by way of the mundane course."
Or by means of the supramundane [path]:
he repeatedly cultivates that very same mental attention;
and in whatever way he repeatedly cultivates it, [so it becomes].
In that same way, that pliancy and one-pointedness of mind undergo expansion,
growth, and increase as those various nights and days pass by;
and when his mental attention has become steady and firm in its vision.
Exhausted, the resolve toward the object of focus proceeds;
and signs pertaining to the side of calm abiding and special insight have been grasped.

Then, desiring to proceed by either the mundane path or the supramundane path, he begins the application therein. In that regard, how many types of persons are there who, in this very life, [proceed] by the mundane path alone?
They inquire by means of the mundane path, not the supramundane one.
He said:
There are four types, namely: one who is entirely outside [the teaching];

one here who, though practicing the Dharma, is dull-witted; one who previously practiced tranquility (śamatha) but whose roots of virtue are still immature; and likewise, one who has not yet matured his roots of virtue.
A bodhisattva who desires to attain awakening in the future,
but not in the present life—
these four types of persons practice the worldly path in the present life.
They do not exist.
Furthermore, that progression by means of the mundane path is of two kinds:
[that] of ordinary persons who possess all fetters, and...
And for those whose fetters are incomplete, and for those in training (śaikṣas).
Furthermore, what is that?
It is for one who perceives the coarseness of sensual desires.

When one perceives the first dhyāna as having its afflictions terminated through both meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*), one attains detachment from that desire realm; in this same manner, it should be understood up to the point of detachment from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
The same applies to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).
By relying on the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), there is the accomplishment of the five [other] consciousnesses along with the sixth.
In that regard, a practitioner (*yogī*) engaged in the pursuit of detachment from sensual desires attains detachment from sensual desires by means of seven mental orientations (*manaskāra*).
What, then, are those seven mental attentions? He said: the attention consisting of the discernment of characteristics, and so forth.
The stage of resolute belief,
the stage of seclusion,
and the stage that gathers joy.
The mental application of investigation,
which culminates in the final stage of practice.
and the fruit of the culmination of application.
Among these, what is the mental attention of discerning characteristics?
It is said:

By means of which mental attention one experiences the coarse characteristic of the sense-desires and the peaceful characteristic of the first dhyāna— how, moreover, does one experience the coarse characteristic?
He said:
"While searching for the six objects of sensual desires, [one considers] their purpose (*artha*), their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),..."
[He investigates] the general characteristic,
the position, the time, and the reasoning.
Therein, he first investigates the coarse meaning.
Thus, these sensual pleasures are accompanied by disadvantages, many calamities, and many misfortunes.
"Having many calamities" refers to the great many disadvantages found in these sensual pleasures, up to and including their having many calamities.
This is the coarse meaning. In that regard, one searches for the object [as follows]:
"There exists within me, with respect to sensual pleasures, a desire for sensual pleasures."
Therein, one investigates their specific characteristics:
"These are desires for afflictions;
these are desires for objects."
Furthermore, these are conducive to pleasure, conducive to suffering, and conducive to neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Those things conducive to pleasure are the basis for sensual desire;
they are the basis for the perversions of perception and mind.
Those things conducive to suffering, moreover, are the basis for hatred and the basis for anger and enmity.
Those things conducive to neither-pain-nor-pleasure are the bases for hypocrisy, spite, deceit, guile, lack of shame, and lack of dread; they are also the bases for the perversion of views.
Thus, these sensual pleasures are accompanied by corrupted feelings.
Having thus eliminated the afflictions, he investigates the specific characteristic of sensual pleasures.
In that regard, how does he investigate the general characteristic?
All these sensual pleasures are equally and continuously bound to and pursued by the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, and so on, up to the suffering of the frustration of one's desires.

Even those who enjoy sensual pleasures and dwell in great abundance of desires are not exempt from the nature of birth and so forth; that abundance of theirs is merely temporary. In this way, one investigates the general characteristic.
How does one investigate the category?
These sensual desires fall within the dark category;
they are comparable to a skeleton.
They are like lumps of flesh, like grass torches,
like pits of glowing coals,
and like venomous serpents.
They are like dreams,
like borrowed ornaments,
and like the fruit of grass.
Even while seeking sensual pleasures, sentient beings experience the suffering caused by that very seeking.
That which is caused by protection,
that which is caused by the loss of affection, that which is caused by lack of satiety, that which is caused by lack of autonomy, and that which is caused by misconduct. (Śbh_Sh 441)
And they experience suffering;
all this should be understood in the same way as previously described,
as it is for one who indulges in sensual pleasures.
Five disadvantages have been stated by the Blessed One: sensual pleasures provide little enjoyment, but involve much suffering and many disadvantages.
Indeed, for one who indulges in sensual pleasures, there is no such thing as satiety or sufficiency;
for this reason, sensual pleasures have been censured by the Buddhas, by the disciples of the Buddhas, and by the virtuous who have attained the right path.
By the noble ones:
indeed, for one who indulges in sensual desires, the fetters increase;
and I declare that there is no evil or unwholesome deed whatsoever that such a person would not commit.
Thus, these sensual pleasures cause lack of contentment, are common [to all], are causes for unrighteousness and uneven conduct,
and increase craving for sensual desires.
They are to be avoided by the virtuous;
they quickly lead one toward the sensory realms and are masters over conditions.
They are grounds for negligence, empty, impermanent, and hollow.
They have the nature of falsehood and deception, are like an illusion, and are mere chatter for the foolish.
And those sensual pleasures belonging to the present life, those belonging to future lives,
and those that are divine;
And as for those pertaining to human beings, this is the domain concerning Māra;
this is Māra’s bait, wherein these various kinds of evil, unwholesome mental states arise.
Namely: covetousness, ill-will, or agitation.

Furthermore, those things which are obstacles for a noble disciple who is not training— namely, that these sensual pleasures mostly fall on the side of darkness— he investigates them in this way through many methods.
In the past, future, and present times, these sensual pleasures are impermanent at all times and unstable at all times;
thus, they are fraught with many calamities.
"They have many calamities and many disadvantages"— in this way he investigates time.
How does he investigate reasoning?
With great agitation,
with great seeking, and with great exertion, sensual pleasures are acquired through various and diverse crafts and occupations.
They are brought forth and accumulated;
furthermore, even when well-accumulated, they...
Even when they have been well-prepared,
as long as these external objects of attachment exist— namely, mother, father, son, wife, female slaves, male slaves, laborers, servants, friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relatives.

Furthermore, for this internal, material, gross body— composed of the four great elements and accumulated through boiled rice and gruel— it serves only to counteract the suffering that arises again and again, by means of constant massaging, bathing, rubbing, breaking, cutting, scattering, and destroying, which are themselves subject to destruction.
Food is for the sake of counteracting the suffering of hunger;
clothing is for the sake of warding off the sufferings of cold and heat,
and for the sake of covering one's shame and modesty.
And clothing;
and bedding and seating for the sake of counteracting the suffering of sleep and fatigue;
and for the sake of counteracting the suffering of walking and standing.
And for the sake of counteracting the suffering of disease,
there is "medicine for the sick"; thus, these sensual pleasures are merely remedies for suffering and should not be enjoyed by one who is lustful.
Just as this authoritative scripture is like medicine for the sake of pacifying a disease,
so too are these sensual pleasures coarse in such and such ways;
and I have personal knowledge and vision of this as well.
This rule would also apply to that which is inferential.
Furthermore, this is the nature of desires: it is a beginningless established dharma-nature, an inconceivable dharma-nature.
She should not be thought about;
she should not be conceptualized—
in this way, one investigates through reasoning.

Having thus realized the coarse characteristic of sensual desires by means of six points, he realizes the peaceful characteristic in the first dhyāna. He realizes this coarse characteristic by reflecting that "in the first dhyāna, there is none of this coarseness whatsoever that exists in the desire realm. And in the first dhyāna, there is the peaceful characteristic; this is called the mental application of realizing characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
Indeed, this mental attention should be understood as being interspersed with hearing and reflection.
Having thus fully understood sensual desires, he [proceeds] to the thorough investigation of the first dhyāna, the first dhyāna, exactly as it is.
Having transcended both hearing and reflection by means of the coarse and peaceful characteristics, one becomes resolved through the mode of cultivation alone;
one cultivates calm abiding and insight precisely with that as their objective support.
And while cultivating, in whatever way one repeatedly resolves upon that coarseness and peace, [one proceeds].
Thus it is established:
there is attention consisting of resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika-manaskāra*).
Through the sequence of its cultivation, the sequence of its development, and the sequence of its frequent practice, for the first time, the affliction (*kleśa*)...
The path arises for the sake of abandonment;
and when the path has arisen for the abandonment of the afflictions, that mental attention directed toward the Blessed One is called "pertaining to seclusion."

At the very outset, through the abandonment of the afflictions and other factors to be abandoned belonging to the desire realm, and through the removal of the corresponding dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*), he thereafter comes to delight in abandonment.
Delighting in seclusion,

he perceives the benefits of abandonment therein and, touched by the limited joy and happiness of solitude, from time to time gladdens his mind with a mental attention that inspires serene confidence.
One arouses a sense of spiritual urgency through a thought that inspires urgency,
precisely for the sake of abandoning sloth, torpor, and restlessness; this is called [the application of mindfulness].
This is the attention that gathers delight.

For one who thus delights in abandonment, delights in cultivation, and is correctly applied— whoever they may be— while moving about or dwelling, the outbursts of afflictions and karma associated with sensual desire, which obstruct the application toward the side of the wholesome, do not manifest.
It occurs to him:
"Do I experience a desire for sensual pleasures that actually exists, or one that does not exist? I wish to investigate this thoroughly."

He brings to mind one or another pleasing and auspicious sign. Because the underlying tendency toward it has not been entirely abandoned, as he brings that sign to mind, his mind becomes inclined toward indulgence and tends toward indulgence.
It is the absence of revulsion or lack of opposition toward service, characterized by a state free from expectation or offense.
It occurs to him:
"My mind is not rightly dispassionate and liberated with respect to sensual pleasures;
my mind is constrained by conditioned formations, held fast like water."
Since this [state] is constrained by the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
what if I were to dwell with even greater measure in delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation, for the sake of the complete and total abandonment of that latent tendency?
This is called the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*).
He dwells with an even greater degree of delight in abandoning.
He delights in cultivation,
is endowed with tranquility and insight,
and investigates repeatedly.

And for one who cultivates its antidote and periodically investigates whether [the defilements] have been abandoned or not yet abandoned, the mind becomes dissociated from all the afflictions belonging to the desire realm;
however, this occurs through a temporary application and does not constitute the permanent uprooting of the seeds.
And at that time, having reached the culmination of the preparatory path of the preparatory dhyāna,
there arises a mental attention that is the antidote to all afflictions; this is called the mental attention culminating in application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manaskāra*).
And with that mental attention as its condition and cause, one enters the first dhyāna;
the mental attention that accompanies the fundamental first dhyāna is called the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).

Therein, abiding in the attention of seclusion (*prāvivekya-manaskāra*) and in the attention that gathers joy (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*), he refreshes the body with the joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*).
Occasionally, due to some slight manifestation [of distraction], there may be a lack of joy during the time of the attention that culminates the application (*prāyoganiṣṭhā-manaskāra*).

At times, through the manifestation of an even more expansive state of meditative absorption, when he abides in the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*), there is nothing for him to be reminded of from anywhere; rather, his entire body and so forth are suffused with the joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*). In that state, he...

At that time, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, he dwells having attained the first dhyāna, which possesses five factors— accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), born of seclusion, and characterized by joy and bliss.
Established in the fruit of the cultivation of the antidote to the realm of desire, he is said to have attained detachment from desire (*kāmavairāgyatā*).
Therein, by means of the attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāraḥ*),
one correctly understands that which is to be abandoned;
and for the sake of abandoning what is to be abandoned and attaining what is to be attained, one directs the mind with resolve.
With the attention consisting of resolute belief (*ādhimokṣika-manaskāra*), one undertakes the correct application for the sake of abandonment and attainment.
With the attention of seclusion (*prāvivekya-manaskāra*), one abandons excessive [worldly] delight.
With the attention that gathers joy (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manaskāra*), one abandons that category of afflictions.
By means of the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*), one establishes the mind in the state of being free from conceit regarding what has been attained.
By means of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭha*), one abandons the mild category of afflictions (*kleśa*).

By means of the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*), one experiences the fruit of cultivation regarding these categories of afflictions that have been cultivated and well-cultivated.

Furthermore, both the attention that experiences the characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) and that which consists of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*) are called conformable attention (*ānulomiko manaskāra*), and they are accompanied by the antidote to revulsion (*dūṣaṇāpratipakṣasahagata*).
That which is the attention of seclusion and that which is the attention culminating in application—
this is the counteractive attention pertaining to the antidote for abandonment.
In that regard, the attention that gathers delight is both counteractive and inspiring;
therein, the attention of investigation is the attention of discernment.
Thus it is said.
This being so, among the six modes of attention, four modes of attention should be understood as being free from obstacles, namely:
the conformable [attention].
The antidotal,
the inspiring,
and the analytical.
Just as the attainment of the first dhyāna is by means of seven mental orientations (*manaskāra*), so too are the attainments of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; likewise,
the attainments of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are each by means of seven.

By means of mental attentions (*manaskāra*). Therein, that by which one perceives the coarse characteristic in discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) and the peaceful characteristic in the second dhyāna, which is without discursive thought, is the mental attention that perceives characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
For the sake of attaining the second dhyāna,
one who has entered that meditative absorption and has attained the first dhyāna perceives coarseness within the applied thoughts (*vitarka*).

That coarse mental discourse which, even on a level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), bears the weight of a forceful object and is gross toward the object due to its being the very first to descend upon it, is *vitarka*.
That subtler mental discourse which follows and tracks that [initial thought], like a movement that wanders distractedly toward the object, is *vicāra*.
Furthermore, these two—*vitarka* and *vicāra*—are...
Furthermore, the mental factors arise as they arise in the mind:
they are co-existent, associated,
and function with a single object.
In this way, these arise internally,
as well as those comprised within the external sense-bases;
and all of them are indeed past.
Those of the future and present,
arisen from causes,
and dependently originated.
First, the bodily [afflictions] are like sprouts;
they appear for only a short time, cause agitation of the mind, and persist in an agitated manner.

Starting from the higher stage, because it is followed by an abiding in suffering, it belongs to the dark side; yet this stage, which follows the benefit of the joy and bliss of seclusion from desire, is by its very nature such that for one established therein, there is certainly and at all times [the state] accompanied by vitarka.
With discursive thought, the movement of the mind proceeds;
through such modes as "it is not calm" or "it is not tranquil," one experiences the coarse characteristic within discursive thoughts.

In every respect, this coarse characteristic does not exist in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied thought (*avitarka*); therefore, the second dhyāna is "peaceful" because of the departure of this coarseness.

As for the remaining mental attentions (*manaskāra*) for the attainment of the second dhyāna, they are as follows: (Śbh_Sh 449) [The remainder of the mental attentions for the attainment of the second dhyāna are: ... [as previously described] ... [until] ... the attainment of the second dhyāna.
Yoga is to be understood as previously described.

In this manner, for each successive stage up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, seven types of mental engagement (manaskāra) are to be understood according to their respective applications.

Furthermore, the characteristic of coarseness (audārikalakṣaṇa) in all the lower stages, extending down to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), should be understood briefly as being of two kinds.
It is more painful to dwell in the lower realms and to dwell in a state that is not peaceful.
And [the state of] having a shorter lifespan—
this is the twofold coarse characteristic;
one investigates it appropriately by means of six objects.

Whichever stage one desires to become detached from, and whichever higher stage is appropriate, up to the mental application that is the fruit of the culmination of practice (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala-manaskāra*), therein [one contemplates] "secluded from sensual pleasures.
Sensual pleasures are of two kinds: the sensual pleasure of afflictions (*kleśakāma*) and the sensual pleasure of objects (*vastukāma*).
(Śbh_Sh 450) Discursive thought concerning sensual desire is also twofold:
separation through dissociation and separation through the object. Thus it is said: "separated from evil, unwholesome states."
The secondary afflictions are unwholesome states caused by desire, namely: misconduct of body,
misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
The taking up of sticks and the taking up of weapons, as well as quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, deceit, fraud, guile, and false speech, come into being.

Through the abandonment of these, one is secluded from evil, unwholesome states; and because one does not see fault in the absence of applied and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*), one possesses the wholesome applied and sustained thoughts belonging to that level which serve as the antidote to sensual desire.

The mental attention that culminates in the stage of application (*prayoganiṣṭha-manaskāra*) is accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*). It arises immediately after the seclusion from sensual desires (*kāmaviveka*),
and has that as its cause.
That [happiness] has that as its cause;
therefore, he says it is "born of seclusion" for one who has attained the desired and longed-for object,
or because of seeing the defects in pleasure.

And through the departure of all functional rigidity (*dausthulya*), by means of vast pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the serviceability (*karmanya*) of mind and body, one who counts [the stages] in succession attains joy and bliss.

First, having arisen from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), through the correct contemplation of the object and the binding of one-pointed mindfulness, one enters the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) as the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala*).
Furthermore, it is subsequently perfected through the frequent cultivation and completion of meditation.
One who obtains [it] at will,
one who obtains it without difficulty, and one who obtains it without hardship.
Being thus a recipient [of these states], he passes the night through meditative attainment;
likewise, during the day, as long as he desires, he dwells for seven days and nights by means of that [attainment].
Having withdrawn his mind from those states accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), he turns it away.
One binds [the mind] to the signs of concentration that are without applied thought or sustained thought.
Having detached the mind from an object that functions with distraction, the mind proceeds—calm and serene—as a single nature upon an object that functions without distraction;
thus one establishes it.

Therefore it is said: through the subsiding of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), through internal clarity (*adhyātma-saṃprasādana*), and through the cultivation of that very same concentration free from applied and sustained thought, one transcends the state of concentration characterized by applied and sustained thought— which is marked by interruptions and gaps— and attains a state that is uninterrupted and continuous.

Therefore it is said: "Due to the unification of the mind, through the complete abandonment of applied and sustained thought in every respect, there arises immediately after that preparatory mental application (prayoganiṣṭha-manaskāra), which is itself concentration, a state that is without applied or sustained thought; having that as its cause, this [second dhyāna] arises.
Therefore it is said: "Born of concentration," because of the attainment of desired and blameless objects, or because of seeing the defects in joy.

As he counts in succession, joy and bliss arise because of the departure of all coarseness belonging to the side of discursive thought, investigation, and the afflictions of the first dhyāna, and because of the presence of the pliancy, mental and physical serviceability, and bliss that are their antidotes; having thus seen the fault in the signs of joy, everything is to be understood as previously described up to the second [dhyāna].

Therefore it is said: "from detachment from joy. And at that time, as he applies his mind to the third dhyāna, which is devoid of joy, two kinds of defects that cause agitation of the mind have been overcome by him.
In the second dhyāna there are applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), and now there is joy (prīti);
therefore, he says that one dwells in equanimity (upekṣaka).
For these two factors cause agitation of the mind and act as obstacles to uninterrupted equanimity. In that regard, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) exist in the first dhyāna.
Because of which uninterrupted equanimity does not proceed;
in the second dhyāna there is joy,
because of which here too uninterrupted equanimity does not proceed.
Therefore, this meditator does not possess [these] in the first and second dhyānas; for that reason, it is said that he dwells with equanimity in the third dhyāna.
Being equanimous and with mindfulness thus established,
he dwells in such a way that those perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by joy do not recur.

If, however, because the third dhyāna has not been cultivated, occasionally and at some time, perceptions and mental engagements associated with joy should arise in his mind due to a lapse of mindfulness,
he very quickly penetrates them with wisdom.
He understands correctly; and as each [unwholesome thought] arises, he does not tolerate it,
but abandons it and dispels it.
He eliminates [them] and maintains equanimity toward the mind;
therefore, it is said that he is "mindful and clearly comprehending."

At that time, for him who dwells thus in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, through the sequence of cultivation and the sequence of frequent practice, that which is accompanied by rapture—
which produces mental agitation—
is abandoned; it becomes free from rapture.
A feeling of peace and profound tranquility arises in the mind; at that time, by means of the form-body, there arises an opposition to joy.
With the mind and body, one experiences pleasure and the pleasure of pliancy;
such pleasure does not exist below the third dhyāna, nor is there uninterrupted equanimity. Although equanimity is found above the third dhyāna, it is not of that same nature.
But it is not pleasure (*sukha*),
because below that level there is an absence of both pleasure and equanimity (*upekṣā*), and above it there is an absence of pleasure.
This is that sphere (*āyatana*), namely the third dhyāna, which the Noble Ones (*ārya*) describe.

With reference to the person who dwells having attained [this state], the Noble Ones—the elders and the elder disciples—declare: "Possessing mindfulness, dwelling in happiness, he enters and abides in the third dhyāna.
This is because [the former case] is of a different nature from that.
Because the antidote, which is pleasure, has not been declared as the antidote for abandoning [the first dhyāna],
that very abandonment of pleasure effected by its antidote is what is declared.
But what, then, is this antidote?
Namely, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
Through the cultivation and repeated practice of these, he moves away from the third dhyāna, wherein he abandons that bliss belonging to the level of the third dhyāna.
Therefore it is said:
"And through the abandoning of pleasure, and because of the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection,
at that time— namely, at the moment of attaining the fourth dhyāna— that meditator reaches the transcendence of pleasure and pain."
Therefore, that which was previously abandoned, and that which is now being abandoned;
Summarizing that, he spoke thus:
"From the abandoning of pleasure and from the abandoning of pain,"
Furthermore, because joy (*saumanasya*) and grief (*daurmanasya*) have already ceased previously— namely,

at the time of attaining the fourth dhyāna through the abandoning of pleasure (*sukha*), at the time of attaining the second dhyāna through the abandoning of pain (*duḥkha*), and at the time of attaining the third dhyāna through the cessation of joy— it is so.
At the time of attaining the first dhyāna,
because of the abandonment of both pleasure and pain, there is for him only a feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhā*).
It does not become distinguished.
Therefore it is said:
at that time, from the first dhyāna onwards, all defects belonging to the lower stages have been abandoned; thus it is neither painful nor pleasant.
Namely: applied thought and sustained thought, joy, inhalation and exhalation;
and the equanimity that arises there from their abandonment.
And that mindfulness becomes completely pure and cleansed,
by which his mind, having entered the fourth dhyāna, remains imperturbable.
It is the sphere of all movements.
Therefore, it is said:
"purified by equanimity and mindfulness."
In this context, "the fourth" is to be understood as previously explained.
In the places such as the dimensions and so forth, as they are.

In that regard, one who has resolved upon space transcends the perception of color—associated with blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth—by means of its lack of substantiality, its lack of pleasure, and its lack of dispassion.
Therefore, it is said:
"of the perceptions of form" (rūpasaṃjñānām).
Because of its transcendence and because it leads to the state of non-appearance, that perception of obstruction— which is of many kinds, of various sorts, and caused by the accumulation of colors—
becomes absent. Therefore, he says:

Due to the subsiding of perceptions of resistance, or rather, because of the cause for the departure of those [perceptions], those accumulative perceptions— which have operated toward those remaining and distinguished aggregates, such as the perceptions of food, drink, clothing, ornaments, houses, gardens, forests, armies, mountains, and so forth—
no longer operate for him even with regard to them in any way whatsoever.
Therefore it is said:
"Because of non-attention to perceptions of diversity.
Having thus cultivated the perceptions of form, resistance, and diversity, he becomes resolved upon space through its infinite aspect.
Therefore it is said:

having transcended the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of infinite space, from the mental application that constitutes the culmination of the practice, one enters the fundamental attainment, which is the fruit of the culmination of the higher practice.
Therefore it is said:
"Having attained and dwelt in the sphere of infinite space,
he does not yet enter the fundamental absorption."

For one who has attained meditative absorption with space as the object, there are that very [space] and the other aggregates belonging to its own level; furthermore, in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*), there are also the aggregates belonging to the lower levels.
At the appropriate time, by means of consciousness, one resolves that space is infinite.
That very same consciousness, which resolves upon infinite space through its manifold aspects,
one who desires to attain the sphere of infinite consciousness must turn away from the perception of the sphere of infinite space.
That very consciousness is resolved upon as having infinite aspects;
together with its preparatory stage, one transcends the fundamental sphere of infinite space.
Therefore, it is said:
Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space,

thinking "consciousness is infinite," he transcends the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of infinite consciousness up to the mental applications culminating in the practice (prayoganiṣṭhā-manasikāra), and thereby enters the fruit of the fundamental practice culminating in the goal (maulaprayoganiṣṭhāphala).
Therefore, it is said:
"Having attained and dwelt in the sphere of infinite consciousness," he,

having moved beyond the sphere of infinite consciousness and searching for an object of perception further than consciousness, does not find anything whatsoever associated with it, whether possessing form or formless.

Not finding that object of focus, he transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), including both its preparatory and fundamental stages, and resolves upon no other object whatsoever.

He becomes one who is resolved solely upon the perception of nothingness (*akiñcana-saṃjñā*). Through the cultivation of that resolution regarding that perception, he transcends the preparatory stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-sāmantaka*) up to the culmination of the application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā*).
Through mental attention, one enters the fundamental attainment that is the fruit of the culmination of application.
Therefore, it is said:
"Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] 'there is nothing at all,' one attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness."
"He dwells" means that he is conscious, namely, having emerged from the sphere of nothingness.
Perceiving the perception of nothingness as coarse and perceiving it as a disadvantage, he turns away from the perception of the sphere of nothingness.

Because previously, at the time of attaining the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, he had transcended the perception of "nothing," he now transcends that very perception of "nothing."
Therefore it is said: "one is percipient," namely, either through the perception of something,
or through the perception of nothing,
or through the perception of nothingness.
Furthermore, this perception of his has not ceased in every respect,
as it does in the case of the state of non-perception or the attainment of cessation.
That subtle perception does not function toward any other objective sign;
it is neither perception nor non-perception.

Thus, one who is resolved upon that sphere (āyatana), having transcended the base of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) along with its preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*), [attains] the preliminary stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

From the mental attention that culminates in the application (*prayoganiṣṭhā-manasikāra*), one enters the fundamental attainment which is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhā-phala*).
Therefore, it is said:
"Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), one dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)."
In that regard, at the time of entering meditative absorption (dhyāna-samāpatti), the sign of the body's manifestation is like descending into the subterranean realm (rasātala);
at the time of entering the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti), it is like falling from the sky.
In that regard, correct application consists in maintaining equanimity at the proper time for calm abiding (*śamatha*).
In this context, there are two mindless attainments (*acittika-samāpatti*): the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

In that regard, it is only an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who enters the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñāsamāpatti*) by means of a mental attention (*manaskāra*) directed away from perception; however, only a noble one (*ārya*) enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
In these two attainments, entry into the meditative state occurs through two types of mental attention.

For example, [there is] the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) by means of a mental attention (*manaskāra*) that is turned away from perception; and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by means of a mental attention that has transcended both perception and non-perception and in which the objective referent (*ālambana*) has been completely stilled.
In that regard, perception is a disease, perception is a tumor,
and perception is a thorn.
"This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the state of non-perception.
Having grasped the mental attention that turns away from perception, he follows after each successive arising of non-perception through mindfulness and non-mental engagement.
Through the cultivation of that [attainment], there occurs a state of consciousness during the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
Furthermore, for one who has entered meditative absorption with mental attention (*manaskāra*), the mind no longer functions.
Thus, by means of mental attention preceded by the perception of deliverance (*niḥsaraṇasaṃjñā*), one becomes free from passion for the "Wholesome Realm" (*śubhakṛtsna*).
The cessation of the mind and mental factors for one who is free from passion for the Bṛhatphala heaven is called the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
And furthermore, its acquisition occurs in this way.

In that regard, an noble one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and desires to dwell in a state even more peaceful than that does not withdraw the mind from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
That mind, once withdrawn, no longer finds its object;
failing to find it, it ceases.

"It does not proceed" means that for a trainee (śaikṣa) or an arhat who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana), the cessation of the mind and mental factors through a mental attention preceded by the perception of dwelling— this is called the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Furthermore, this is how its acquisition occurs.
In that regard, by relying upon meditative absorption (dhyāna), there is the accomplishment of the five superknowledges (abhijñā).
And how does this come about? It is as follows: the meditator becomes an attainer [of these states].
Regarding purified dhyāna:
relying upon that purified dhyāna, whatever dharma conducive to the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) has been heard and mastered by him,
He has mastered it— namely,
concerning the domain of supernormal powers (*ṛddhiviṣaya*),

or former abodes, the divine ear, death and rebirth, and the knowledge of others' minds— while attending to that very object with a mental engagement belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmika*), he becomes one who experiences the meaning.
And he experiences the Dharma.
For him who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dharma, in such and such a way...
For one who forms mental volitions through the sequence of frequent practice,
there comes that time, that occasion, when his meditations bear fruit.
The five supernormal knowledges arise.
Moreover,
he (experiences that object) in such a manner.
Experiencing the Dharma, one cultivates twelve perceptions for the sake of accomplishing all superknowledges (*abhijñā*); namely,
the perception of lightness and the perception of softness.
the perception of the space-element;

the perception of the unification of body and mind; the perception of resolute conviction; the perception of recollecting the sequence of previously experienced conduct; the perception of the convergence and resonance of various kinds of sounds; and the perception of the signs of pure forms.

The perception of the transformation of form caused by the afflictions, the perception of resolve, the perception of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the perception of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Among these, regarding the perception of lightness, one resolves upon oneself as being light, just like a tuft of cotton.
Or like a ball of cotton;
resolving upon it as being within a circle of wind, he impels it there by means of that very attention consisting of resolute intention (*adhimokṣika-manaskāra*),
just as one moves from a couch to a stool, and from a stool to a couch.
In this way, from the bed to the grass mat upon the bed,
he perceives them as soft;
he resolves that his body is soft.
For example, like silk, wool, or linen;
this [perception] nourishes the perception of softness and the perception of lightness.
The favoring [perception] is that by which, when being favored, the perception of lightness proceeds toward a state of vast increase (or expansion).
Therein, the perception of the space-element is that perception by which one resolves upon the lightness and softness of oneself.
If one should desire to go somewhere, [one does so].
In that regard, one resolves upon that intermediate space which is obstructive, material, and intended for movement as being empty space;
this is through resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*).
By means of mental attention (*manaskāra*). In that context, there is the perception of the conjunction of mind and body, by which one applies the mind to the body or the body to the mind.
By which his body becomes lighter,
softer,
and more pliable.
It is more luminous;
it follows the mind, is bound to the mind, and exists depending upon the mind.
In this context, there is the ideation of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-saṃjñā*), by which ideation [one perceives] the distant as near.
One resolves upon what is near as being far,
and the subtle as being coarse.
The gross and the subtle, earth and water, water and earth— in this way, each great element should be applied to the others.
He resolves upon that which has been thus emanated in detail,
whether it be an emanation of form or an emanation of sound.
By means of these five perfected perceptions of meditative cultivation, he experiences various kinds of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*): having been one, he manifests himself as many;
that is to say, by means of the perception of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*) and the perception of emanation (*nairmāṇika*).
While manifesting himself as many therein, he again becomes one.
That is to say, by means of the perception of resolute conviction regarding the disappearance of emanations, he goes with a body that meets no resistance through walls or enclosures.
Wherever he goes,
he performs the act of emerging from and sinking into the earth.
Just as one walks upon water as if on solid ground;
just as one traverses the sky cross-legged as if on the earth.
Just as a winged bird,
or these very sun and moon— so powerful and majestic— he touches and strokes them with his hand.
He exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.

He performs all this by means of a perception that encompasses the conjunction of the light, soft, and subtle space-element with the mind and body, and by means of a perception of resolute conviction;
this should be understood according to the appropriate application.
In that regard, there are two ways in which one exercises mastery over the Brahma-world: by means of the body and by means of going.
One exercises mastery through these.
Whether by way of resolve (*adhimukti*),
there is in beings the desire to move downward from the Brahma-world, as well as [the desire for] certain types of derived form (*upādāyarūpa*).

In that regard, there is the perception (*saṃjñā*) consisting of the recollection of the sequence of previously experienced conduct, by means of which his memory proceeds, beginning from his state as a youth.
It is not obstructed;
wherever the Noble One has gone or stands, [there it follows].
Whether sitting or lying down, he reviews in detail, in their most extensive and coarse form, all the modes of conduct previously experienced, following them in succession without skipping any.
By means of what does he recollect and recognize?

Through the sequence of its cultivation, as a fruit of that cultivation, he recollects his various former abodes in detail, with their specific locations, extending back as far as cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
In that regard, the designation "resonance" refers to the convergence of sounds of various kinds;
[whether] in a village, or a town, or a guild, etc.
Whether in a group, or in an assembly,
or in a long and spacious house,
Or in a private room,
amidst a great multitude of people seated and assembled together, that which is variegated and diverse—
A sound issues forth;
that which is called a clamorous noise,
or the roar of a great flowing river.

In that regard, having grasped the sign, there is a cultivation of perception by which, through mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative equipoise, one restrains the application [of the mind] toward noble and ignoble sounds, divine and human, and those that are distant or near.
Through the sequence of its repeated cultivation, he attains the divine ear as the fruit of meditation; by means of this,
he hears both divine and human sounds,
whether they are far away or near.
Therein, the perception of the sign of the form of illumination is as follows: having grasped the sign of light as before, one attends to that very sign;
this is the perception of the sign of the form of illumination.
Through the sequence of cultivating that [meditation], he obtains the fruit of cultivation, which is the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*).
By means of that purified divine eye, in detail, up until the dissolution of the body, he perceives those who are reborn among the gods in the heavenly world after death.
In that regard, there is the perception of the transformation of form caused by afflictions (*kleśa*).

By means of this, one observes and discerns the state of the form of those beings who are impassioned, hostile, or deluded, whose minds are enveloped by the afflictions and secondary afflictions— such as anger, resentment, malice, burning regret, lack of shame, and lack of dread— and who are thus engaged in them.
In this way, for one who is not attached to form, there occurs the state of form and the transformation of form; namely,
such things as the state of having agitated faculties.
A smiling countenance: such is the physical state and physical transformation of one who is hostile.
For example: discoloration of the face, a faltering voice, and the knitting of the brows— such are the outbursts of agitation that occur in one who is deluded.
It is a distortion of form;
for example, muteness, the inability to comprehend the meaning [of what is said],
or speech that is either ordinary or extraordinary.
By these and similar modes, whatever state of form or transformation of form occurs for one who is possessed of the outbursts of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*).
Then, having grasped the sign, he attends to it; that is to say,
through the sequence of repeated practice, the fruit of cultivation— the knowledge of the mental states of others—
arises, by which one knows, as they truly are, with one's own mind, the thoughts and reflections of other beings and other persons.

In this regard, the cultivation of the designations of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) should be understood as previously described,
namely, as in the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitā bhūmi*).
It is by means of this cultivation that one brings forth noble supernormal power (*āryarddhi*).
[It is] that which transforms the basis, that which is emanated, and that which is produced through resolute conviction;

namely, the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*), namely: the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisamvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisamvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisamvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisamvid*).
In this regard, there is this distinction between noble (*āryā*) and non-noble (*anāryā*) supernormal power (*ṛddhi*):
by means of noble supernormal power, whatever object one transforms, [it becomes exactly that].
Whatever sign he creates,
it becomes exactly so and not otherwise.
By means of all that, the task can be accomplished;
however, it is not by an ignoble [means], nor does it simply remain as it is,
but rather it appears merely as a demonstration by a magician.

Thus, through the frequent cultivation associated with these twelve perceptions, one should understand that there occurs, as appropriate, the actualization of the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and the noble qualities (*āryaguṇa*) which are not shared by ordinary worldlings (*apṛthagjana*), each according to its proper application. In that regard, by means of the first dhyāna cultivated to a weak, middling, or superior degree, as appropriate, [one is reborn] among the Brahmakāyika gods.
One is reborn into the fellowship of the Brahmā-purohita gods and the Mahābrahmā gods;
when the second dhyāna is cultivated to a weak, medium, or intense degree, one is accordingly reborn into the fellowship of the Parīttābha and Ābhāsvara gods.

When the third dhyāna has been cultivated in its weak, medium, and intense degrees, one accordingly attains rebirth in the commonality of the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, and the Śubhakṛtsna deities.
When the fourth dhyāna has been cultivated to a weak, medium, or superior degree, one is reborn accordingly into the fellowship of the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, or Bṛhatphala deities.
If, moreover, that non-returner cultivates the fourth *anāsrava* dhyāna interspersed with the *sāsrava*,
then in that [state]...
When cultivated to a mild, medium, intense, more intense, or most intense degree, one accordingly attains rebirth among the five classes of gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*),
such as the Avṛha.
In the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Sudarśanas, and the Akaniṣṭhas;

and when the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception have been cultivated in weak, medium, and intense degrees, one is reborn into the commonality of those gods who have reached the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
And since the formless deities have no distinction made by different locations, there exists for them only a distinction made by their mode of dwelling;
when the attainment of non-perception has been cultivated, one is reborn into the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of the non-percipient beings among the gods.
In that regard, what are the signs of one who is free from passion? It is said:
his bodily actions become steady and his faculties are immovable.
Furthermore, his posture is not quickly exhausted;
he passes a long time even in a single posture without becoming weary,
nor does he long for another posture.
He is one who speaks softly and speaks with tranquility;
he does not delight in socializing.
He does not delight in social company,
and his speech proceeds with steadfastness.
Having seen forms with the eye, one experiences the forms,
but does not experience passion for the forms;
likewise, one experiences sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
But he does not experience attachment toward tangible objects;
he becomes confident,
possessing profound intelligence, and is embraced by a vast tranquility of mind and body.
One who is free from covetousness is unshakeable;
being patient, evil thoughts such as sensual desires do not disturb his mind.
Such qualities as these should be understood as the marks of one who is free from passion. This, for now, is the analysis of proceeding by the mundane path.

Now, when one desires to proceed by means of the supramundane path, seven mental orientations (*manaskāra*) arise for him in successive order, beginning with the four noble truths and culminating in the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*), up until the attainment of arhatship. These begin with the mental orientation consisting of the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*) and so forth.
In this regard, the practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) has mastered the four noble truths along with their summaries and detailed analyses through the exertion of a recluse (*śramaṇa*).
Either one who has well-cultivated mental attention, or one who has attained the fundamental dhyānas and formless attainments,
experiences the characteristic of the truth of suffering through four aspects.
Namely, by way of the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, and the aspect of non-self.
The truth of origination is [to be understood] by way of four aspects, namely: as cause, as origination, and as production.
And by way of its conditions:
one experiences the characteristic of the truth of cessation through four aspects,
namely, as cessation, and so forth.
As peaceful,
as sublime,
and as an escape.
One experiences the characteristic of the truth of the path through four aspects, namely: as the path, as the method, as the practice, and...
And as leading to liberation;
this constitutes for him the attention consisting in the discernment of characteristics.
In that regard, examining the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) through ten aspects, one enters into four aspects.
By which ten? They are as follows:
[It is] present by way of the aspect of transformation, the aspect of non-destruction,
and the aspect of separation.
by way of the aspect of phenomena, by way of the aspect of the nature of reality; by way of the aspect of the fetters and bonds,
and by way of the aspect of the undesirable.
in the aspect of lack of security, in the aspect of non-benefit,
and in the aspect of non-attainment;

And by way of the aspect of lack of autonomy. Furthermore, one examines these ten aspects through the reasoning that establishes proof. In this regard, first, concerning scripture: as it was said by the Blessed One, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
Furthermore, those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), in brief, consist of the world of sentient beings (sattvaloka) and the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).
