And it was said by the Blessed One with reference to the world of sentient beings: "I see,
O monks," [he said].

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— in detail, up to how they pass away at the breaking up of the body and are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods. By this method, by this very method, the Blessed One, the Visionary One who perceives directly, has explained the impermanence of the world of sentient beings.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "It happens,
monks,"
That time comes when, after the passing of a long period, there occurs the successive appearance of seven suns in the world—
just as described in the *Sūtra on the Seven Suns*—
until indeed this great earth and Sumeru, the king of mountains, [are consumed].
And as far as the Brahma-world, when the receptacle world has been burnt and consumed, not even soot is perceived;
not even a residue of ash is perceived.
By this method, the Blessed One [described] the receptacle world.

Having thus explained the impermanence of the [conditioned] state, this yogi, relying upon the authoritative scripture (āptāgama), attains a certainty regarding the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) through the predominance of faith.
Having thus attained such certainty, through the predominance of faith, he repeatedly realizes for himself— both directly and indirectly— that state which is not dependent on another.
And he investigates impermanence;
furthermore, how does he investigate it?
He said:
"One establishes two kinds of entities.
He said:
Internal and external.
Therein, the internal object is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
the external object is [the rest]. Having thus attained certainty, through the predominance of faith, he should repeatedly examine it so as to achieve non-obscurity and independence from others.
And he investigates impermanence.
He said:
It establishes two kinds of entities:
internal and external.
Therein, the internal entity is that which consists of the six sense bases; the external entity is...
It is of sixteen kinds, as follows:
the category of earth, such as villages, towns, houses, shops, and so forth;
the category of groves, such as grasses, medicinal herbs, and forest trees.
The category of mountains, such as various mountain formations,
springs, and lakes.
The objects consisting of ponds, rivers, and springs;

the object of fields; the objects of treasuries, stores, clothing, ornaments, dancing, singing, instrumental music, perfumes, garlands, ointments, vessels, and household utensils; and the objects of service by women and men—these constitute the sixteen objects.
Having thus established internal and external objects,
he first investigates the impermanence of change regarding internal objects through a mental attention dominated by direct perception, by way of the aspect of transformation.
In that regard, there is a fifteenfold transformation of internal entities and eight causes of transformation. Among these,
what is the fifteenfold transformation?
Of an internal object, namely: that produced by its state, produced by its color, and produced by its shape.
That which is caused by prosperity and adversity;
that which is caused by the completeness or deficiency of limbs; and that which is caused by exhaustion.
caused by the assault of others,
caused by cold and heat,
and caused by postures.
[Self-made],
produced by affliction, [produced by agriculture], produced by death,
The transformation produced by the livid state and so forth is a transformation consisting of the complete non-appearance and total exhaustion [of the object].
In that regard, there are eight causes of transformation.
Which ones?
He said:
namely, long duration of time;
enjoyment through external assault,
the change of seasons,
and fire conflagration;
Namely: moisture from water,
drying by wind,
and contact with other conditions.
In this context, "aging through time" refers to those material entities which, even when placed in their own location, are observed to become decrepit after a lapse of time;
it is a state of decay, a transformation of form.

In that regard, "assault by another" refers to when another person brings about various deformations through various forms, various weapons, and various specific types of assault. In that regard, "consumption" refers to when the owners, while enjoying various forms, bring about deformations by falling under the power of enjoyment— that is, by making it the dominant factor.
In that context, "transformation of the seasons" refers, for example, to the fact that in winter, grasses, medicinal herbs, and forest trees become pale and withered;
whereas in summer and the rainy season, they again become fully lush.
And its greenness;
likewise, the abundance of fruit and the abundance of flowers.
There is the prosperity and the misfortune of those very same things.
In that regard, what is called "being consumed by fire" is as follows: just as when a fire is released, it proceeds along, burning villages, towns, districts, and royal capitals.

In that regard, what is called "water-damage" is as follows: nevertheless, that great mass of water arises and passes by, burning down villages, towns, royal capitals, and kingdoms; in that regard, what is called "water-damage" is as follows: nevertheless, that great mass of water arises and passes by, flooding villages, towns, royal capitals, and kingdoms.
In that regard, "drying by wind" means that even so, moist regions of earth,
moist objects, and types of crops are dried up very quickly by a great mass of wind.

The emergence of other conditions refers, for example, to the emergence of a contact conducive to pleasant feeling in one who is experiencing a pleasant feeling in dependence upon a contact conducive to pleasant feeling;
likewise, [the emergence of a contact conducive to painful feeling] in one who is experiencing a painful feeling.

The arising of a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant occurs for one experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, or it is the arising of a contact to be experienced as unpleasant or to be experienced as painful.
Likewise, for one who is impassioned, there is the arising of the signs of aversion, through the arising of which the obsession of passion departs.
And the outburst of aversion arises;
in this way, for one who is hateful or deluded,
the emergence of discordant factors that serve as the cause for the arising of afflictions should be understood.
For example, when visual consciousness has become manifest, there is the emergence of the object of sound; likewise for odors, tastes, and tangibles;
and there is the emergence of the signs of mental objects (*dharma-nimitta*), by which other dissimilar objects arise.
Thus, these are the eight causes of transformation;
whatever transformation occurs,
whether of material things or of immaterial things.
All these phenomena [are comprised] by these eight; there is nothing beyond this, nor anything more than this.
In that regard, how does one investigate the transformation of internal entities based on their states?
Here, one observes the state of oneself or others, from the stage of infancy up to the stage of old age;
one perceives that the latter state is dissimilar to the former.
Having seen the continuity of conditioned phenomena as distinct and subject to transformation, this thought occurs to him:

"Alas, these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) of mine are impermanent; nevertheless, this very alteration from earlier to later is perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa). In that regard, how [could there be permanence] for those things made of gold?"
He investigates the impermanence of transformation;
here, he [investigates] for himself or for others.
That former state of excellent complexion.
[He perceives] excellence of complexion, excellence of skin-color;
and subsequently, bad complexion, poor skin, roughness, and a rough color.
He sees it;
having seen it, he turns back again, and at another time he sees that very same state of golden color and the state of the skin’s pure complexion. It occurs to him: "Alas, these are impermanent!"
In these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
such a transformation of color is perceived directly before one's eyes.
In that regard, how does he investigate the impermanence consisting in transformation produced by shape?
Just as color has been described, so too should shape be understood in terms of its thinness or stoutness, as well as its excellence or deficiency—
such as, for example, excellence of kinship or excellence of wealth.
Or, it is the perfection of ethical discipline and right view;
its opposite is failure.
How, then, does one investigate the impermanence resulting from the transformation of the major and minor limbs?
In this case, by means of this [meditation], whatever former state of golden hue or beautiful complexion belonged to oneself or to others—
A pure complexion of the skin is seen; or there is success in [rebirth], success in wealth, or success in morality and view. By the opposite of this, there is failure.
In that regard, how does one investigate the impermanence of the transformation of the limbs and minor members?
Here, by means of this [contemplation], one investigates either for oneself or for another.
Previously,
it was seen to be complete,
yet at a later time, one sees it to be incomplete due to the king or other causes.
Whether from a thief,
or from a human,
or from a non-human being.
And having seen this, it occurs to him again:
"Alas, these formations of mine are impermanent," as before.
Thus, one perceives the exhaustion and fatigue of both oneself and others while running or leaping.
Or when jumping, or when running, or when performing various verbal actions rapidly;
at a later time, he perceives the absence of fatigue and exhaustion.
It occurs to him, as before: "Alas, these conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
In this way, he investigates the impermanence of transformation produced by such exertion.
In this way, one observes a physical alteration in oneself or others resulting from an external assault,
such as being struck by creepers or by whips.
Or by means of canes or leather thongs;
likewise, through various contacts with gadflies, mosquitoes, and reptiles;
or again at another time, he does not see that disfigurement.
And having seen this, it occurs to him: "Alas, my conditioned phenomena are impermanent," as before; in this way, he investigates the impermanence of transformation caused by external assault.
Likewise, when the time for [practicing] ethical discipline has arrived, one perceives oneself or another as having an unrefined body.
He sees [the body] with its limbs contracted,
overcome by the obsession of cold and seized by a longing for warmth; or again, when the hot season has arrived, he sees the body lacking clarity.

He sees [the person] with his body huddled together, overcome by the obsession of cold, with limbs drenched in perspiration and a body tormented by heat; sighing and overcome by thirst, he longs for the touch of cold. Having seen him, and then turning back again, he sees him once more during the cold season in the very same manner as previously described.
Having seen this, it occurs to him again: "Alas, these conditioned phenomena of mine are impermanent! Thus, as before, he investigates the impermanence of transformation caused by cold.
Furthermore, he sees either himself or another, by means of one or another of the modes of deportment— walking, standing, sitting, or lying down— either internally or with respect to others;
moreover, he sees them at another time being thus sustained by that very same [mode of deportment].
And having seen this, it occurs to him as before: "Alas, these conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
In this way, he investigates the impermanence of transformation produced by the modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*).
How does he investigate the impermanence of transformation produced by contact? Touched by a contact to be experienced as pleasant,
and experiencing the pleasant feeling arisen in dependence upon that contact to be experienced as pleasant.
He discerns for himself the state of pleasant feeling;
as he does with the state of pleasant feeling, so too with the states of painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.

His prior investigation was as follows: having seen that these feelings are ever-new, not old, subject to decay, temporary, momentary, and subject to change, upon seeing this, it occurred to him: "Alas, these conditioned phenomena are impermanent. This was his former [investigation].

In that regard, how does one investigate the impermanence of transformation caused by afflictions? One fully understands a mind that has arisen as being possessed of lust, or as being free from lust; likewise, one understands it as being possessed of hatred or free from hatred.

He thoroughly understands a mind that is deluded, or one free from delusion, or one defiled by any one of the various secondary afflictions as "defiled"; and he thoroughly understands a mind that is not defiled as "not defiled. For him, [the following occurs]...

Having observed, through their successive occurrence, that the continuum of consciousness is transformed, undergoing change, or not yet changed by these primary and secondary afflictions, it occurs to him: "Alas, these conditioned phenomena are impermanent!
For thus is their transformation produced by defilement perceived directly.
In that regard, how does he investigate the impermanence of transformation caused by disease?
Here, having at one time observed both himself and others, [he reflects as follows].
They become free from disease, happy,
and strong.
Then, at a later time, he sees himself or another person afflicted with illness.
One who is suffering, severely ill,
and afflicted by bodily feelings that are painful and intense— [as described] in detail as before.
In that regard, how does one investigate the impermanence of transformation caused by afflictions?
Here, having at one time seen himself and others to be free from disease, [he later sees them otherwise].
Happy and strong;
later on, at another time, he sees himself, or—
Or else, he is afflicted with illness and suffering.
He was severely ill,
afflicted by physical pains;
yet at another time, he saw him free from disease.
And seeing him happy and strong, it occurs to him again: "Alas, these things are impermanent!"
"These are my formations," as before.
In that regard, how does he investigate the impermanence of transformation caused by death? Here, he observes this life as it is being sustained, as it persists, and as it remains.
While he was thus maintaining himself, at a later time he sees that [person] has died and passed away;
and having seen the body devoid of consciousness, it occurs to him once more as described in detail previously.
In that regard, how does he investigate the impermanence of transformation produced by the livid state and so forth?
At a later time,
he sees that same skeleton remaining in its state as a chain of bones.

He sees that very same corpse at one time in the state of discoloration (*vinīlaka*); at another time in the state of putrefaction (*vipūyaka*); and so on in detail until he sees it in the state of a skeleton (*asthi-śaṅkalikā*). Having seen this, the thought occurs to him: "Alas, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of mine are impermanent," and so on in detail as before.
In that regard, how does he investigate the impermanence of transformation caused by non-exhaustion?
At another time, he [examines] that...
He sees it remaining as a skeleton;
it becomes entirely destroyed, shattered, and disintegrated.
In every respect, they do not come within the range of his vision;

yet, having seen them, it occurs to him: "Alas, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of mine are impermanent! For indeed, through their successive sequence, such a transformation is perceived by direct perception itself."
Transformation.
Thus, first, by means of mental attention dominated by direct perception, one investigates the impermanence of transformation of an internal object through fifteen aspects. Having investigated it,
He investigates the impermanence resulting from the transformation of the sixteen kinds of external objects.

Those regions of earth that he previously saw when they were not yet constructed, he later sees as having been constructed— whether as dwellings, marketplaces, rest-houses for merit, temples, or monasteries— and he sees them both when they have been constructed and when they have not, seeing them as new, well-built, and well-smeared with plaster.
Then, at a later time, he sees them aged,
decrepit, with their limbs broken and mangled, and worn out.
Indeed, seeing those fallen from their positions, burnt by fire, or carried away by water,
it occurs to him again: "Alas, these things are impermanent!"
These are my formations;
nevertheless,
through their sequence of preceding and succeeding moments, there is this very kind of perceptible transformation.
Transformation is perceived;
thus he investigates the impermanence of transformation in the earth.
Likewise, he observes that the grasses, herbs, and forest trees, as well as the groves and gardens, possess flourishing leaves, flowers, and fruits.
He takes away those [green things] which are pleasing and delightful;
at another time, he sees them withered.

He sees trees devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruits, or burnt by fire; likewise, he sees mountains that were once abundant with rocks, but which at other times have their stones stripped away and their peaks fallen.
Their peaks have collapsed; they are uneven with rises and hollows, scorched by fire,
and drenched by water.
Likewise, he sees at one time springs, lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, wells, and so forth, abounding with water, and at another time, their waters completely exhausted.
Or else, all the hollows have completely dried up and become barren.
Likewise, he sees at one time various occupations succeeding, and at another time failing—
namely, agricultural occupations, maritime occupations, occupations involving correct trade, and various types of artisanal crafts.
He observes at one time the accumulation and at another time the depletion of various and manifold stores of wealth and granaries,
as well as food and drink, which are sometimes not yet prepared.

At one time he sees it in its natural state, at another time in a state of being conditioned; at one time it is seen as drenched with a flow of saliva, and at another time even in the state of excrement and urine.
Likewise, he sees various vehicles at one time well-adorned, well-decorated, and new, and at another time devoid of ornaments, stripped of finery, and dilapidated.
Likewise, he observes at one time the newness of garments and at another their antiquity;
at one time their decay and at another their purity, and at another their soiling.
Similarly, he observes at one time the unworked state of ornaments, at another their being worked, at another their excellence, and at another their being broken, shattered, or worn out.
Likewise, he perceives that dances, songs, and instrumental performances—which have arisen through various present applications—possess the nature of the destruction of existence (*bhava*).
Likewise, he perceives that perfumes, garlands, and ointments possess a fresh fragrance and lack of withering;
yet at another time, he perceives them as no longer very fragrant, foul-smelling, withered, and dried up.
Likewise, he perceives the lack of essentiality and the state of being broken in vessels and utensils, whether they are unconditioned or conditioned.
Likewise, he perceives the arising and passing away of light and its reflections.
Likewise, he perceives the arising and passing away of the conduct of men and women.
And having seen their instability, it occurs to him again: "Alas, my conditioned phenomena are impermanent, for such is the case with these external conditioned phenomena."
The direct perception of the six objects of appropriation and the ten attendants of the body, as well as their transformation.
This very thing is perceived as being of such a limited measure;
this same abbreviated formula is to be understood everywhere.

By means of these eight previously mentioned causes of transformation, he investigates the impermanence of this internal and external entity— according to its respective application— through a mental attention dominated by direct perception, in the form of such transformation. In this way, that impermanence of transformation becomes directly seen and experienced by him.
And in that state, he becomes independent of others and not led by another;
recollecting exactly as it was, he investigates and becomes certain.
Therefore, it is called "mental attention governed by direct perception.
Having thus investigated the impermanence of transformation through this mental attention governed by direct perception, he...
Regarding those material conditioned phenomena which exist and are present, yet whose dissolution— occurring in the very moment of their arising and breaking—
is not perceived; therein,
relying on mental attention governed by direct perception, one performs an inference, and furthermore, one performs an inference in this manner:
For these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which arise, break, and dissolve in every moment, this subsequent transformation from a prior state is logical;
it is not so for those that remain exactly as they were.
Thus, conditioned phenomena are momentary; when various conditions are present, they arise in such and such a manner.
Once arisen, they perish by their own inherent nature (*svarasa*) without depending on a cause of destruction; however,
those which are causes of transformation serve as conditions for the arising of something else.
They serve as the causes for the arising of a transformation,
but not for its destruction. For what reason?
Because it is observed that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), having perished along with that very cause of destruction, proceed in a dissimilar manner; however,
it is not the case that there is a total cessation of activity in every respect.
Furthermore, regarding those formations whose non-occurrence is perceived in every respect—

just as when water is being boiled, it undergoes total exhaustion at the end, and when the receptacle-worlds have been consumed by fire, not even soot or ash is perceived. And likewise, [there is no residue].
Even what remains is no longer perceived, because even those [remaining parts] are exhausted through successive transformations until, in the end, there is a total absence of everything.
Yet this is not brought about by fire alone;
therefore, these eight causes of transformation as described are merely conditions, whereas destruction occurs by its own inherent nature (*svarasa*).

Having thus gained certainty regarding the momentary arising, breaking, and dissolving of conditioned phenomena through this inferential mental attention, he further applies inference to the occurrence of unconditioned phenomena in the perceptible world beyond.
And furthermore, he performs an inference in this way:
there are sentient beings who are even without color.
Those of poor complexion are found,
as well as those of high birth and those of low birth.
even those born into poor families, even those of little renown,
[may] have long lives.
Some have speech that is worthy of being accepted, while others have speech that is not worthy of being accepted;
some also possess sharp faculties.
This diversity of sentient beings is logical only when there is a diversity of karma;
it is not so when there is none.
By whatever forms of beings, whatever form of wholesome or unwholesome karma was previously performed, created, painted, and accumulated, by that cause, [they experience the result].
By that condition, this diversity of their personal existences was brought about.
Furthermore, it is not logical that this [world] has the creation of a Lord (īśvara) as its cause.
If it were caused by the creation of a Lord, it would either have the Lord alone as its condition, or the Lord would create it by means of some other material cause (upādāna).
If it had the Lord alone as its condition, then there would be simultaneity between the Lord and these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).

If the Lord exists first and the formative forces (saṃskāras) exist later, then the formative forces would not have the Lord as their condition. Furthermore, if the Lord’s volition (praṇidhāna) were the cause of creation, [then...]
Nor is it the Lord alone;
therefore, that desire must be either with a cause or without a cause.

If it were caused, it would be caused by Īśvara alone; therefore, due to that previous fault, it is not tenable as being identical [to the case of non-causation]. Alternatively, if it were caused by something else, then desire and effort [would be its causes].

"Since volition (*praṇidhāna*) has no other cause than the Lord (*īśvara*), likewise all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) must have only phenomena as their cause; what is the use of this vain conceptualization of a Lord?"— through such inferential mental attention (*ānumānika-manaskāra*) of this kind, he gains certainty regarding the activity of conditioned phenomena in the next world.

Thus, through the predominance of these three types of mental attention— namely, that which has faith as its predominant factor, that which has direct perception as its predominant factor, and that which has inference as its predominant factor— he investigates impermanence. In this regard, there is the fivefold impermanence previously mentioned, which is accompanied by cultivation in five aspects.
In that regard, [impermanence] is described through the aspect of transformation and the aspect of destruction.
What is impermanence in the aspect of dissociation and the aspect of non-existence?
He said:
It should be understood with reference to both the internal and the external.

In that regard, with reference to the internal, it is as follows: for instance, someone previously was the master of others, not a slave, not a servant, and not a laborer performing tasks for another.
At a later time, having abandoned his status as a master and his state of non-slavery, he enters into the state of slavery for others;
he is separated from the status of a master.
In this way, existing and present enjoyments remain unaltered.
They are stolen from the king—
either by thieves, or by those who are unfriendly.
Impermanence should be understood through these heirs.

In that regard, impermanence in the sense of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatākāra*) refers to both the impermanence of transformation and the impermanence of destruction of that very same [conditioned thing].

Even regarding the present time, he penetrates the true nature (*dharmatā*) of that which has not yet come together and of that which will exist in the future when [the path] has passed— namely, that "these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have such a character in the future as well"—
and thus [he understands] their manifest form within these [present phenomena].
From this very [contemplation], one perceives the impermanence of transformation,
the impermanence of destruction,
and the impermanence of dissociation as being present and fully manifested.

Thus, through these five aspects, by means of frequent mental attention applied as appropriate to the fivefold impermanence of internal and external conditioned phenomena, and through the mastery of cultivation that establishes proof, he attains [this realization]; immediately thereafter, he enters into the aspect of suffering.
It occurs to him as follows:
It is appropriate that these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which are impermanent, possess the nature of impermanence by virtue of their being subject to birth;
for these very conditioned phenomena are indeed subject to birth, and birth is suffering. When...
Thus, birth itself is old age, sickness, and death;
it is association with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant.
And the frustration of one's desires is to be understood;
in this way, first of all, one enters into the aspect of suffering by way of its undesirable form.

Regarding those aggregates which are to be experienced as pleasant, being with outflows and with clinging, he enters into them by way of the aspect of suffering through the mode of the fetters and bonds.
For indeed,
that basis for the fetter of craving is its mode;
and the fetter of craving is the bond for birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
And it is the basis for the bondage of passion, hatred, and delusion.
Therein, by way of the absence of security (*ayogakṣema*), one enters into the aspect of suffering regarding the aggregates that are the basis for neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

For indeed, those aggregates which are the basis for neither-pain-nor-pleasure are accompanied by grasping, associated with dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*), followed by seeds, and are not liberated from the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
And because of the suffering inherent in change,
they are impermanent and subject to cessation. In this way, the practitioner [contemplates] conditioned phenomena that are conducive to pleasure.
And he penetrates the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) within pleasant feeling;

that is to say, by way of the mode of fetters and bonds, he penetrates the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) within painful feeling and within those conditioned forces (*saṃskāra*) that are the basis for painful feeling. And he penetrates [the suffering] within those conditioned forces that are the basis for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, by way of the mode of the undesirable.
And regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he has entered into the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), namely, by way of its lack of security (*ayogakṣema*);
thus it occurs to him:

Taking as his dominant influence the aspect of fetters and bonds, the aspect of the undesirable, and the aspect of lack of security, he reflects that whatever is felt within the three types of sensation is here [in this context] suffering; thus, by means of mental attention preceded by the aspect of impermanence, he enters into the aspect of suffering.
It occurs to him: "There is merely the sense-faculties..."
He perceives only the object.
That which is born from that is mere experience;
it is mind-only, with the self destroyed—
mere name.
It is mere perception, mere conventional designation;
there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
This being so, it is merely the aggregates; within these aggregates, there is no permanent [self].
Permanent,
eternal, and inherent:
some self or sentient being.
or whoever might be born, or decline, or die;
or there,
he would experience the ripening of the fruits of those actions performed there;
for thus, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty.
"Devoid of self"—thus, by way of the aspect of non-apprehension, he enters into the aspect of emptiness.
It occurs to him:
"Furthermore, these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), by their own characteristic and by the characteristic of impermanence,"
Those things which are endowed with the characteristic of suffering are also not independent because they are dependently originated;

and those which are not independent are non-self. Thus, by means of the aspect of non-independence, one enters into the aspect of non-self. In this way, the yogi, through the four aspects thus grasped in ten ways, comes to experience the characteristic of the truth of suffering.
Therein, the aspect of impermanence is subsumed by five aspects, namely:
the aspect of transformation, the aspect of dissociation, and so forth.
By way of the aspect of presence and by way of the aspect of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
The aspect of suffering is comprised of three aspects.
The aspect of fetters and bonds is subsumed under three aspects: the aspect of the undesirable, the aspect of lack of security, and the aspect of non-attainment.
The aspect of emptiness is subsumed by one aspect, namely, the aspect of non-apprehension.
The aspect of selflessness is subsumed by one aspect, namely, the aspect of lack of autonomy.
Having thus entered into the four aspects by means of these ten modes and having experienced the characteristic of suffering, he considers:
"What is the cause of this suffering?"
What is its origin, its source, and its condition?
By means of these four aspects—"by the abandonment of which there would be the abandonment of this suffering"—one experiences the characteristic of the truth of origination:
as "cause" (*hetu*), because craving is the source of suffering;
as "origination" (*samudaya*), because it projects and brings about [rebirth]; and as "bringing forth" (*samudānaya*), because it leads to [the continuation of] origination.
It is [suffering] by way of manifestation because it is characterized by suffering; by way of origination because it is the source of suffering;
furthermore, by way of sequence because it grasps the seed of future suffering;
and by way of condition because it brings about the arising of suffering.
Another formulation:
because existence (bhava) caused by grasping (upādāna) comes into being, and because birth (jāti) arises preceded by existence,
[one understands] the conditionality of birth.
And birth is the cause for the manifestation of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and so forth;
it is [the truth of suffering] from the perspective of its cause and its origin.
From the perspective of their arising and from the perspective of their conditions;
this should be understood according to what is appropriate.
Another formulation:

that latent tendency of the afflictions which is the basis and the cause for the production of renewed existence, as well as for the outbursts arising therefrom, should be understood according to the case.
This is another formulation.
That underlying tendency of the afflictions which is the basis, such as the underlying tendency of craving and so forth,
is the cause for the production of renewed existence in the future; and it is, as appropriate, the origin (*samudaya*) and the source (*prabhava*) of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) born thereof.
And as for the condition:
it is from the accumulation of the craving for rebirth that [suffering] arises.
Furthermore, that craving for rebirth is accompanied by delight and passion.
It becomes the source; furthermore, that craving—which is accompanied by delight and lust—is abundant.

It serves as the condition for that craving which finds delight here and there. Thus, by resorting to this craving, which exists as both latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and as the three types of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), there occurs the production and manifestation of renewed existence in the future.
Therefore, it is said: "by way of cause (hetutaḥ), by way of origin (samudayataḥ), and by way of production (prabhavataḥ)."
And by way of conditionality.
Thus, through these four aspects, this yogi experiences the characteristic of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

Having experienced the characteristic of the truth of origination, he contemplates the cessation of this truth of origination—the cessation consisting in its complete subsidence—as the aspect of cessation (*nirodha*).
[The aspiration for the truth of suffering is] from the desire for its complete cessation;

[the aspiration for the truth of origination is] from its being foremost, excellent, and internal to that [cessation]; [the aspiration for the truth of cessation is] from its being sublime; [and the aspiration for the truth of the path is] from its being permanent and its being the definitive escape.
Thus, in these four ways, he experiences the characteristic of the truth of cessation;
having experienced it, for the purpose of investigating the knowable,
for the purpose of investigating reality, and for the purpose of proceeding by way of the four sufferings.

As the path, from the perspective of being the path, from the perspective of being the right method, and from the perspective of being the practice, in the sense of being the single way leading to Nirvana.
And he contemplates it as leading to liberation.
Thus, through these four aspects, he experiences the characteristic of the path;
this is called his internal, personal experience of the characteristics regarding the four noble truths.
This is said to be his mental attention toward the four noble truths.

Having thus examined and investigated the individual aggregates by way of their conditions— both those that are perceptible and those that are imperceptible and belong to a different realm— he [proceeds].
One refutes the aggregates by means of inference, thinking:
"These phenomena are also thus; they too fall within this same principle.
Whatever is conditioned, in every case and in every respect—it is thus that the mental attention which experiences it accordingly functions.
Having examined and investigated by means of inference, one refutes the imperceptible aggregates belonging to dissimilar realms through logical deduction:
"Those [aggregates] are also of such a nature; they too fall under this same principle. Thus, whatever is conditioned, in every case and in every respect, is of that very same nature.

And its cessation is peaceful; it is the path that leads to liberation for the sake of abandoning it. When there is knowledge of the truths regarding those internal aggregates which have been described as the adverse side, [that is the realization].

Furthermore, that inferential knowledge regarding things that are imperceptible and belonging to a different realm serves as the seed for the arising of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
This attention characterized by the discernment of marks (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*) should be understood as being interspersed with hearing and reflection.
When this yogin has thus attained certainty regarding these four noble truths through the sixteen aspects, beginning with the sequence of correct investigation (*samyag-vyavacāraṇā*),
by means of the reasoning that establishes [the truth] through logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*), [then...]

That is to say, having transcended the mental attention consisting of hearing and reflection regarding the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), he becomes resolutely intent upon that which proceeds by way of penetration, exclusively through the mode of cultivation;
this constitutes his mental attention consisting of resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika-manaskāra*).
Having truth as his object and being entirely concentrated,
through the subsequent application of that [concentration], he attains boundless knowledge with respect to two truths: the truth of suffering and the truth of origination.
By means of which one resolves upon the impermanent as "impermanent," [realizing] the boundlessness of impermanence.

Thus, there is the boundlessness of suffering, the boundlessness of the emptiness of the aggregates, the boundlessness of affliction, the boundlessness of going to the miserable realms, and the boundlessness of prosperity.
...the limitlessness of falling away; he [sees] the limitlessness of disease, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
In that regard, "limitless" means that there is no end to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
In saṃsāra, there is no end or limit to these phenomena; as long as there is saṃsāra...
These phenomena are subject to arising;
with the complete cessation of saṃsāra, there is the cessation of these.

There is no other cessation; thus, through the aspect of wishlessness and the aspect of non-reliance toward all states of existence, destinies, deaths, and rebirths, [one perceives them] as being contrary [to liberation].
By way of the aspect of non-reliance and by way of the aspect of opposition,
one who is resolving through the heading of contrariety cultivates the mental application of resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika-manaskāra*).
Thus, from all states of existence and rebirths...
having caused the mind to be agitated;
having terrified; having caused to be terrified.
With resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), he directs his aspiration toward *nirvāṇa* in one way or another;
yet for a long time, that mind of his has been delighted by various forms, and delighted by sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
It is accumulated and built up— accumulated and built up by forms,
sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Even with such a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), they strive for nirvāṇa,
yet they do not enter into it, nor do they find serene confidence (*prasīdati*) in it.
It does not abide;
it is not liberated;
it does not turn back.
It is mental, because it does not characterize the realm of peace;
by means of causing distress, it repeatedly agitates and terrifies that mind.
Having become weary and terrified of the truth of suffering and the truth of its origin, he repeatedly directs his resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) toward *nirvāṇa*.
Nevertheless, he does not penetrate it.
Why is that? Because such a coarse conceit (*asmimāna*) acts as an obstacle to clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Having entered into mental engagement, he proceeds with intervals and gaps, thinking:
"I am one who has been conditioned; I am one who will transmigrate."
"I am one who shall attain parinirvāṇa; I am one who cultivates wholesome dharmas for the sake of parinirvāṇa;
I am one [who contemplates] suffering as suffering."
I see arising as arising, cessation as cessation;
I see the path as the path.
"I am empty as emptiness, wishless as wishlessness,

and signless as signlessness; I perceive these phenomena as mine because of that cause and that condition, yet my mind does not enter into a resolute intention toward nirvana, even by way of a superior intention."
Having very quickly penetrated with wisdom that conceit, which acts as an obstacle, [as being] "an obstacle," he [proceeds].
Having abandoned mental attention once it has proceeded spontaneously,
and having turned away from external objects of knowledge, [he enters] that which has entered into non-mental-attention.
Accompanied by mental attention,
he begins the analytical investigation of the truths.
He sees each thought as it arises being ceased and broken by the immediately succeeding thought,
through the process of continuous succession.
In this way, he takes that thought as an object and masters it with his mind.
Just as that conceit of "I am" (asmimāna), which has entered into his mental attention and acts as a bond of opposition,
finds no opportunity for the production of renewed existence.

When the yogi is thus engaged, he perceives, in their sequential order, the mutuality, the ever-newness, the state of perishing, the temporariness, and the fleeting presence of that mental continuum; this constitutes its impermanence.
Furthermore, when he perceives that very mental continuum as being comprised within the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), this constitutes its suffering (*duḥkhatā*) therein.

That mind which does not apprehend any phenomenon—this is here the emptiness [of that mind]; and in that regard, seeing that very mental continuum as dependently originated and lacking independence, this is its selflessness.
In this way, one has first entered into the truth of suffering.
It occurs to him: "This mental continuum of mine as well is caused by craving."
They have craving as their origin, craving as their source, and craving as their condition.
The cessation of this mental continuum is also peaceful;
the path leading to its cessation is also conducive to liberation.
In this way, by means of the application of examination to unexamined mental attention, one does not yet enter into those Noble Truths through subtle wisdom.
Through the sequence of such cultivation and through the sequence of meditative development, there arises for him a knowledge in which the object of cognition and the cognizer are equal;
by means of this, his manifest pride of "I-am-ness," which acts as an obstacle to the delight in Nirvana due to its coarseness,
is abandoned.
As he contemplates and applies his mind to nirvāṇa, it enters into it;
his mind does not turn back.
Based on the removal of weariness,
one takes up delight through resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).
For one who has become thus, the knowledge in which the object and the subject are equal and identical, accompanied by weak receptivity (*mṛdukṣānti*), is called "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*).
That which is embraced by medium patience is called "delusion";
that which is comprised by superior patience is called "medium conformable patience."

Having thus abandoned that conceit of "I am" which acts as an obstacle, and having embraced a delight in *nirvāṇa* through his resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), he abandons that volitional activity (*abhisaṃskāra*)— which is the progressive refinement of the mind— and deposits his non-conceptual mind in the state of non-volitional activity (*anabhisaṃskāratā*).
At that time, his mind appears as if it has ceased.
And that [object] does not become ceased; it appears as if without an object,
yet it does not actually have an object.
To him, that mind appears as if it were stilled and departed;
yet it has not departed,
nor does it [depart] again in that [state].
At that time, although that mind is overcome by the sleep of the honey-bee, it appears as if ceased;
yet it has not actually ceased.
This state serves for those who are dull and deluded to develop the conceit of realization, thinking, "This mind is indeed for the sake of realization."
"If such a state of mind as this arises, it will not be long before one enters the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-nyāma*)."
That final, non-conceptual mind of his, immediately after which he directs his internal attention toward the sentient beings previously contemplated,
constitutes the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikā agradharmāḥ*).
Beyond that, only a supramundane mind arises for him.
They are not mundane;
this is the limit of mundane conditioned phenomena, and this is their boundary, which is why they are called the "supreme mundane dharmas."
Immediately after those [moments], he enters into the truths that were previously examined;
as soon as there is focused attention (*ābhoga*), they follow their previous sequence.
Regarding the truths that have been examined—in both those that are directly perceived and those that are beyond perception—he proceeds precisely in successive order toward non-conceptualization.
Definitive knowledge, which is direct perceptual knowledge, arises.

With its arising, that which belongs to the category of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision—which range over the three realms and are established as a basis for functional rigidity—is abandoned.
Through its abandonment, if one has already previously become free from passion for sensual desires, [one attains the fruit of stream-entry].
Simultaneously with the realization of the fruit,
at that moment he is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
Those very same signs should be understood for him as those previously described for one free from passion; however, this is the distinction:
he is of miraculous birth (*aupapāduka*).
There he attains final nirvāṇa;
he does not return again to this world.
Furthermore, if he becomes even more detached from passion, [he proceeds further].
Through simultaneous realization of the path, one becomes a once-returner.
However, if one is still not free from passion, then through the further subsiding of that same corruption, one becomes a stream-enterer.
Knowledge comes into union with the object of knowledge through direct perception;
therefore, it is said to be "by way of clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).
For example, when a kṣatriya encounters a kṣatriya face-to-face, it is said that he has subsequently attained realization; the same should be understood for brahmins and others.

These are his signs: he has attained four knowledges while investigating the mental engagements regarding the conduct and abodes of sentient beings— namely, the knowledge of mere phenomena, the knowledge of non-annihilation, the knowledge of non-eternality,
and the knowledge that conditioned phenomena produced through dependent origination are like an illusion— even as he practices within this sphere.
Even an extremely intense outburst of afflictions,
though it may arise from a lapse of mindfulness,
very quickly passes away for him through mere application of attention.
Likewise, he does not go to states of woe,
nor does he transgress the training that has been undertaken.
Nor does he deprive a living being born in the animal realm of life;
nor, having renounced the training, does he turn back toward its abandonment.
He becomes incapable of committing the five actions of immediate retribution;
he does not regard pleasure and pain as being self-made,
nor as being made by another.
It is neither self-made nor made by another;
it is not produced without cause by either self-action or action by another.
He does not seek any other teacher outside of this.
He is not worthy of offerings;
he does not look for the well-being of others, nor does he examine their happiness, among other ascetics and brahmins.
They are not otherwise: they have seen the Dharma,
attained the Dharma,
and fully penetrated the Dharma.
Having crossed over doubt and transcended uncertainty,
he is independent of others and not led by another; he has attained self-confidence regarding the phenomena within the Teacher’s dispensation.
He does not believe that purity comes from curiosity or auspicious rites,
nor does he bring about an eighth existence;
he is endowed with the four kinds of verified faith.

For him, as long as he has not yet realized the truths, there is the attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-manaskāra*) following the worldly supreme dharmas; once the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have been abandoned, there is the attention of seclusion (*prāvivekya-manaskāra*), and that which leads to abandonment.

Thereafter, for one who cultivates and practices the path as it has been attained, through the abandonment of the superior and middling afflictions belonging to the desire realm, one becomes a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*).
All the characteristics of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) should be understood to apply to this person as well.

And this is the distinction: regarding objects that are the basis for lower afflictions, even when they are conducive to intense outbursts of defilement, he produces a bound state of afflictive obsession and quickly removes it;
having come to this world but once, he makes an end of suffering—he is a non-returner (anāgāmī).

The marks of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) are as previously described. In that regard, the entire path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is characterized by repeatedly examining, through the mental application of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-manaskāra*), whether [the defilements] have been abandoned or not abandoned, as manifested by the path as it has been attained. In this context, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of cultivation?
What is that action? What is its classification?
It is the repeated practice of these wholesome, conditioned phenomena by means of a mental attention belonging to the level of meditative concentration, whether mundane or supramundane.
Familiarization (*paricaya*), constant and respectful practice,
and the state of the mental continuum being permeated by that [object]— this application (*upanaya*) is called the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In this regard, the activity of cultivation is eightfold.
Cultivating certain dharmas, he attains them;
through cultivation, he practices certain dharmas;
he purifies certain dharmas, dispels certain dharmas, and fully understands certain dharmas.
He abandons some factors, he abandons other factors,
he realizes some factors, and he distances himself from other factors.
In that regard, first, those wholesome and distinguished factors which have not yet been attained, he attains them.
Some [factors] have been acquired through the cultivation of the Dharma and are present;
he cultivates them.
In that regard, those [factors] which have been acquired but have not yet become manifest will be brought into manifestation in the future through the cultivation of factors of a similar nature.
They arise there as more completely purified and more thoroughly cleansed, insofar as they are free from those defilements arising from the loss of mindfulness.
They practice those phenomena;
by the power of cultivating wholesome qualities, he endures them and abandons them.
He dispels them;
he eliminates them; or, regarding those dharmas yet to arise that are to be abandoned, he thoroughly understands them as a disease, and he reviles them.
As a thorn, as a boil, as a calamity,
and as impermanent.
One thoroughly understands it as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
He causes [the afflictions] to be corrupted;
through the repeated practice of their thorough knowledge, the path of immediate succession arises for the sake of abandoning the afflictions.
That by which one abandons [the afflictions],
and having abandoned them, further realizes liberation;
and in whatever manner one ascends to the higher stages.
In this way, the factors of abandonment belonging to the lower stages become increasingly distant until the final goal is reached;
this should be understood as the eightfold task to be cultivated.
In that regard, within cultivation, an elevenfold classification of types should be understood, as follows: the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha-bhāvanā*),...
The cultivation of insight (vipaśyanā-bhāvanā), [as before, therein] the cultivation of the mundane path (laukika-mārga-bhāvanā),
and the cultivation of the supramundane path (lokottara-mārga-bhāvanā).
The cultivation of the weak, medium, and intense [levels]; the cultivation of the path of preparation; and the cultivation of the paths of uninterrupted transition, liberation, and excellence.
In that regard, the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) consists of the nine modes of mental abiding as previously described;
the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) is exactly as before.
Therein, the cultivation of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) consists in viewing the lower stages as coarse and viewing the higher stages as peaceful.
Up until the attainment of detachment from the sphere of nothingness,
there is the cultivation of the supramundane path therein, consisting of attending to suffering as suffering, up to attending to the path as the path.
That which consists in proceeding by means of the untainted path—beginning with right view and so forth—until the attainment of detachment from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
therein, the cultivation of the weak path is that by which one abandons gross, non-excessive afflictions;
therein, the cultivation of the middling path is that by which one abandons middling afflictions.
In that context, the cultivation of the superior path is that by which one abandons the mild category of afflictions;
all [afflictions] are to be abandoned last.
Therein, the cultivation of the path of preparation is that by which one initiates the application for the abandonment of afflictions.
In that regard, the cultivation of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is that by which one abandons [the afflictions].
Therein, the cultivation of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is that by which, immediately after the afflictions have been abandoned, one realizes liberation.
Therein, the cultivation of the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) is that by which... [one cultivates] those [qualities].
From that point upward, as long as one has not begun the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the afflictions of another level,
or has reached the final consummation (*niṣṭhāgata*) and does not begin it—
this should be understood as the elevenfold distinction of the types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

For one thus engaged in cultivation, examining from time to time whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not yet abandoned, and from time to time causing the mind to feel spiritual urgency regarding those things that inspire urgency;

By gladdening himself from time to time in matters that inspire joy, he develops the attention that gathers delight (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manaskāra*). Through the sequence of practicing, cultivating, and repeatedly performing this attention that gathers delight, for the sake of abandoning the afflictions that are to be abandoned by cultivation without remainder, there arises the final,
adamantine-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) of one still in training (*śaikṣa*).
With its arising, all afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation are abandoned.
For what reason is it called "diamond-like" (*vajropama*)? It is as follows: (Śbh_Sh 507)
Vajra is the most essential and the most solid of all other jewels, such as gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, and coral; it scratches them all,
yet it cannot be scratched by those other jewels.
In this very way, this samādhi is the foremost of all the samādhis of those in training;
it is the most excellent, the essence of all, and it overcomes all afflictions,
yet it is never overcome by the afflictions that arise again.
Therefore, it is called "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).
Immediately following that diamond-like concentration, because the seeds of depravity belonging to the side of all afflictions are utterly eradicated, the mind is resolved toward absolute [purity],
and one attains the purification of the lineage (*gotra*).
Knowledge arises for the sake of destroying all corruption and the darkness of the afflictions;
and because of the destruction of the cause, knowledge of non-arising arises so that suffering will not manifest in the future in any way whatsoever.
At that time, he becomes an Arhat.

His taints were exhausted; he had accomplished what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and his mind was well-liberated through right knowledge.
He is endowed with the ten qualities of one beyond training:
with right view, right intention, and so forth, up to right liberation and right knowledge of one beyond training;
and he becomes a master over his own mind.
Regarding both the dwelling and the mental attention,
at whatever time he desires—
whether by means of a noble dwelling, or otherwise.
He dwells by means of that or that— whether it be the divine or the brahmic.
Whatever wholesome and meaningful phenomenon he desires to attend to in his mind—
whether mundane or supramundane—
he attends to that very thing.
In that regard, the noble dwellings are the dwelling in emptiness,
the dwelling in signlessness, the dwelling in wishlessness, and the dwelling in the attainment of cessation;
the divine dwellings are the dwellings in the meditative concentrations and the formless attainments.
The divine abodes (*brāhma-vihāra*) consist of the abidings in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

They become utterly stainless, utterly pure, and reach the ultimate consummation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). You have emerged as it were, having been lifted up... [text missing] ...thus you are one who has abandoned five factors and is endowed with six factors.
The agent... (Śbh_Sh:
509) ...in this [case].
The basis of the qualities of the field;
driven away, he returns... enters... [and] departs.
With a mind thus liberated, with wisdom well-freed, solitary, and having transcended [all bonds], he is called a person.
Furthermore, he becomes endowed with these qualities;
and upon seeing the other shore, he is truly glad at heart.
He becomes well-minded, equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
likewise with sounds through the ear,
and odors through the nose.
Having cognized tastes with the tongue, tangibles with the body, and mental phenomena with the mind.
...or [the feeling] above that;
he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. At that time, he experiences the complete destruction of passion without remainder.
Through the exhaustion of passion, hatred, and delusion, he does not perform that which is their abandonment;

rather, he becomes one of even mind, like an axe or sandalwood, honored and revered by the gods including Indra and the Pitṛs, and established in the realm where no further path remains— he is called one who has crossed over, reached the further shore, and bears his final body.

Due to the spontaneous cessation of the five aggregates— which have been impelled by past karma and afflictions— or due to their non-reappropriation, he enters the realm of nirvana without remainder and becomes completely extinguished (*parinirvṛta*).
Just as they have not transmigrated,
nor do they go elsewhere— whatever suffering there was has ceased, it has been stilled, it has become cooled, and existence has come to an end. Peaceful, peaceful is this state.
That is to say: the departure from all acquisitions, the exhaustion of all perceptions, dispassion, cessation, and Nirvana; these should be understood as its characteristics of this kind.
A monk who has exhausted the outflows [should be recognized] by five points... [he] disciplines [himself].
Thinking thus, he was unable to attain it; therefore, O gentle one, he practiced the religious life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and abstained from the practice of sexual intercourse.
Being fully aware (*saṃprajānan*), [he remained].
He is incapable of speaking falsehoods; he is capable of enjoying sensual pleasures with little agitation.

Likewise, he is capable of realizing that pleasure and pain are self-made, as previously described, up to: "one who acts by oneself," and [the view] that intense suffering arises without cause, which was produced by those who have not cultivated themselves.

When one encounters meat that causes terror, or any other thing that is frightening and terrifying, and one falls into a state of extreme dread— this is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which is the mental attention culminating in application (*prayoga-niṣṭha-manaskāra*). Furthermore,
the mental attention comprised within the supreme fruit of arhatship is the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoga-niṣṭhā-phala-manaskāra*).
Through these seven modes of mental attention, by means of the supramundane path, one reaches the ultimate limit; this is called "attainment" (prāpti).

This is the summary of all the Perfectly Awakened Ones, together with their disciples—those things which serve as the basis for instruction and those which serve as the basis for realization; namely, the collections of all names, phrases, and phonemes, the poetic compositions, the treatises, and the *mātṛkā*.
// Summary Verse //
There is the stage of discerning characteristics, likewise that of resolute conviction,
that which grasps the joy of seclusion, and that of investigation.
Furthermore, there is the final [stage] consisting of the culmination of application, its subsequent activity, and its fruit;
and there is also mental attention (*manaskāra*).
The classification of the meditative absorptions (dhyānas) and the formless attainments (ārūpyas).
The meditative attainments, the superknowledges, and rebirth; the characteristic marks, the investigation of the truths, and likewise penetration.
The analysis of meditative cultivation and its final culmination constitute the last [section].
The Fourth Yoga Station in the Śrāvakabhūmi.
The Śrāvakabhūmi is completed.
